News.title: Brigitte Macron’s daughter, 42, finds love with student 20 years younger in echo of mum’s marriage to French president
News.content:
BRIGITTE Macron’s daughter has fallen in love with a student 20 years younger than her – in a bizarre echo of her mum’s relationship with Emmanuel.

Tiphaine Auzière, 42, appeared head over heels for her new boyfriend, Antoine Lecomte, 22, in a social media picture of their Amsterdam holiday.



Their 20-year age gap bears a striking similarity to the one between Brigitte, 73, and the 48-year-old French president Emmanuel Macron.

Tiphaine and Lecomte reportedly met this summer at Le Touquet, a glamorous seaside town on France’s north-western coast.



The business student was working there as a kitesurfing instructor and eventually started teaching Tiphaine how to use an e-foil, a type of electric surfboard.

A close friend of the French president’s stepdaughter told Gala: “It was immediately obvious between them.

“They have a lot in common: a love of Le Touquet and thrills, but also travel and entrepreneurship.”

Her new relationship comes after she broke up with Cyril Hanouna, a polarising TV host in France, in May 2026.



Reports also indicate that Tiphaine has introduced Lecomte to her two children, Élise, 12, and Aurèle, 10.

President Macron was a 15-year-old student when he first met Brigitte.

She was a married mum-of-three and teacher at the private school he attended, La Providence, in Amiens.



Macron’s parents took him out of the school when their affair came to light.

His mum, Francoise Nogues-Macron, previously said: “We just couldn’t believe it.

“What is clear is that when Emmanuel met Brigitte, we couldn’t just say, ‘That’s great’.”

She added: “What mattered to me was not the fact he was having a relationship with Brigitte but that he was alive and there weren’t any problems.”

The president’s dad Jean-Michel said he “almost fell off his chair” after hearing the news.



Tiphaine is one of Emmanuel’s three stepchildren from his marriage to Brigitte.

The French president has no biological children of his own.

Tiphaine was just nine when the affair between Emmanuel and Brigitte began.

She said in 2018: “They were quite smitten and it was quite obvious between them and very difficult.”

Brigitte’s daughter added that she and her siblings, Sébastien and Laurence, “suffered as little as possible” their parents split up in 2006.



Macron married Brigitte when he was 29 and she was 54.

Brigitte is reportedly ecstatic about her daughter’s new relationship,

A source told Gala: “She reacted just like any mother would. All that matters to her is her daughter’s happiness, so she’s very happy to see her thriving.

“She’ll be delighted to meet Antoine.”

It comes after Tiphaine separated from her ex-partner Antoine Choteau in early 2025, after being together for 15 years.

News.title: Three million more kids are eligible for free school meals from TODAY as new rules come into force
News.content:
OVER three million children are now eligible to receive free school meals.

From September, 1,400 new free breakfast clubs are introduced in schools across England.

Around three million families receiving Universal Credit are now eligible to receive free school meals from today.



The breakfast club iniative aims to help children start the school day with a healthy meal, while simultaneously providing free before-school childcare.



Education Secretary Lucy Powell has said the latest update will “ease the back-to-school squeeze” for families.

“For parents the start of term can be one of the most expensive times of the year,” she said.

“From school uniforms and lunches to childcare and all the other costs that come with a new term, the bills can quickly add up.”

Powell explained that the intiative will allow families to “finally start to feel the benefit of our support back in their pockets”.

The education secretary said: “We’re helping ease the back-to-school squeeze with thousands of savings that give parents the breathing space they need”.

“That breathing space means families can focus on what matters most: helping their children learn, grow and thrive, while I focus on delivering an education system that gives every child a clear route to success,” she said.

Meanwhole, CEO of the charity Sutton Trust Nick Harrison described the update as “a significant step towards taking hunger out of the classroom”.



“Children can’t learn effectively when hungry, so these efforts will help tackle the effects of child poverty, as well as improving education outcomes for disadvantaged young people,” he said.

“Giving free school meals to all families who are eligible for Universal Credit is also easier for parents to understand, so has the potential to increase take up rates.”

While he clarified the expansion is “not ‘job done’ on ending child poverty” he said the initiative is “a genuine improvement in the cost of living for many families around the UK”.

It comes as a number of other new school rules are brought into force, including limits on branded school uniforms, updated attendance regulation, and a mobile phone ban.

News.title: Dad, 55, found dead after being electrocuted while working at five-star hotel is pictured as pals pay tribute
News.content:
'TRUE GENTLEMAN' Dad, 55, found dead after being electrocuted while working at five-star hotel is pictured as pals pay tribute

TRIBUTES have been paid to a dad and “true gentleman” who was tragically found dead after being electrocuted while working at a luxury seaside hotel.

Emergency services were scrambled to the five-star Harbour Hotel in Southampton, Hampshire, on Thursday after Jason Gledhill, 55, was injured while working.



Police were snapped carrying bags of evidence from the scene including a pair of Adidas trainers, a set of keys, a wallet, and a drill before a body was removed and placed in a private ambulance.

An inquest has now heard that Jason had been working alone in a maintenance room in the luxury hotel when he appeared to suffer an electrocution.



The 55-year-old, from Denton, Manchester, was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.

His tragic death has led to an outpouring of tributes from Denton St Lawrence Cricket Club – where he was described as a “true all-round club-man.”

A spokesperson said: “It is with great sadness that we share the news that one of our much-loved and highly respected members Jason Gledhill, sadly passed away on Thursday 13th August.

“Jason was a true all-round club man and someone who always had time for everyone. He gave so much of himself to our club over the years and played an important part in so many areas.



“More importantly, he was a friend to so many and a familiar, welcoming face who will be remembered with enormous affection.

“His passing is a huge loss to the club and all those who had the pleasure of knowing him. He will be greatly missed.

“Rest in peace, Jason. You will always be remembered as a true gentleman and will be greatly missed by everyone at the club.”

The club offered its condolences to Jason’s wife Paula, daughter Georgina and his wider family and friends.

Phone lines at the waterfront hotel were temporarily unavailable as a result of the incident, with guests advised to use an alternative entrance.



Cops cordoned off the hotel entrance and placed signs warning of “danger” outside.

At the time of the incident, three fire engines, two ambulances, an air ambulance, a police van and electrical engineering van were all at the scene.

A van from Scottish and Southern Electricity Networks (SSEN) also arrived at the scene and engineers appeared to investigate an outdoor utility room.

News.title: I feared my shop had a ghost after seeing items mysteriously moving… but checked CCTV & couldn’t believe the real cause
News.content:
A GIFT shop owner feared she had a ghost after items mysteriously started moving and smashing – before CCTV unmasked the real culprit.

Rachel Eaton, who runs Curiosity in Swanage, Dorset, was left puzzled after footage appeared to show a Buddha statue moving on its own.



But CCTV finally revealed the bandit was a young hedgehog staging an extraordinary late-night assault course.

The naughty hoglet was caught on camera clambering up a large wooden beam before tumbling into a hanging basket and dangling before eventually dropping to the ground.



Rachel said she feared something “a little bit freaky” was going on after she checked her cameras and found a statue appear to smash on its own accord.

But the following evening, the camera caught the hedgehog scaling a wooden beam in her shop before falling into the basket.



Rachel believes the animal had become trapped in the shop’s yard, which is locked overnight.

She said staff found the whole thing “hilarious” and had been “cooing” over their unexpected little customer.



The shop owner added: “We are generally wildlife-free.

“Though we did have a squirrel once, which got into a store room at the back of the shop.”

The hedgehog was safely collected by staff and rescued by a wildlife charity.



Jim Dunne, who has run Dorset Hedgehog Rescue for 13 years, said he had never seen such an “adventurous hedgehog” before.

He said the animals have “poor eyesight” and rely on their sense of smell and hearing to get around, meaning they tend to “blunder into things”.

Jim added: “If they can get themselves into trouble they will.”

The rescue centre cared for the young female before releasing her safely back into the wild.

News.title: Immigration fury & benefits bill… Andy Burnham’s daunting in-tray as he prepares to make first Commons speech as PM
News.content:
BURNING ISSUES Immigration fury & benefits bill… Andy Burnham’s daunting in-tray as he prepares to make first Commons speech as PM

ANDY Burnham will enter Parliament for the first time as Prime Minister today as he begins to set out his plans.

He was only sworn into Parliament at the end of June after winning the Makerfield by-election last week.



After a summer policy blitz he is facing a daunting in-tray of problems facing the country.

Here are the six biggest challenges he faces:



Immigration

Controlling immigration is one of the top priorities among voters – both legal net migration and the small boats crisis.

Mr Burnham so far appears to be backing Shabana Mahmood’s reforms to cut the numbers and clamp down on Channel crossings.



He said immigration must fall further and agreed with the “broad thrust” of the home secretary’s plans.

Ms Mahmood has reformed Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) which means migrants will have to wait ten years instead of five to claim benefits.

Almost 17,000 migrants have crossed the Channel so far, down 43 per cent on the same time last year.

Prisons

The early release scheme was the first crisis Mr Burnham faced as PM.



In one of his first acts he barred rapists, serious child sex and grooming offenders from being released early.

But he hit the buffers when it emerged PC’s Harpers killers Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers could be released early.

There were mounting calls for the PM to backtrack and block those convicted of manslaughter from early release.

Mr Burnham has since expanded the list of people ineligible for early release and had consistently said he wanted to go further.

Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being released in tranches from October to ease overcrowding in jails.



There is a growing demand to prevent hardened criminals from being released early and build more prisons across the country.

Justice Minister Alex Norris told LBC the early release scheme could continue in some form for the next decade.

Defence

Allies of Mr Burnham believe this will be the most difficult department to fund, while Sir Keir’s flagship Defence Investment Plan (DIP) appears to be on ice after his resignation.

Mr Burnham has backed plans by ministers to increase defence spending, but signalled he would be relaxed in borrowing more money to fund the armed forces.

After John Healey’s resignation he said he would reduce the welfare bill to spend more money on defence.



But the next Chancellor has sparked a hypocrisy row after backpedalling on a military cash boost he previously demanded.

He notoriously quit as Defence Secretary earlier this year after then-PM Sir Keir Starmer failed to put a timeline on when armed forces spending would hit 3 per cent of GDP.

It remains unclear what taxes Mr Burnham would raise or what welfare cuts he would be willing to make to pay for this uplift.

Welfare

Attempting to slash the welfare bill shattered Sir Keir Starmer’s authority with Labour backbenchers, after his own party torpedoed efforts to cut benefits by a mere £6billion.

At the time Mr Burnham joined the rebellion claiming the government had made “the wrong choice”, helping him win over friends on the Left of the party.



But since then Mr Burnham has backtracked after admitting the welfare needed to be cut in a different way.

Britain’s welfare bill is expected to soar to £400billion by the end of the decade and is increasingly unaffordable.

Labour grandee Alan Milburn is preparing his final report on youth unemployment as almost one million under-25s remain out of work and education.

Welfare minister Stephen Timms has also been looking at Britain’s ballooning disability benefits bill.

But both reports are set to be released after the Budget and are unlikely to be tackled this year.



Even trimming parts of it will be incredibly unpopular with many of his own MPsand supporters who helped him return to Parliament.

Economy

Mr Burnham inherits an economy plagued by sluggish growth, high taxes and enormous debt.

He will set out his first Budget next month with difficult decisions on tax and spending yet to be made.

Labour’s fiscal headroom has fallen from £22billion to £15billion in just one year.

External factors such as the war in Iran has made the cost of oil more expensive and started to have an impact on prices for consumers.



As Manchester mayor he advocated for stronger public ownership of transport and water and more spending which will cost billions of pounds.

But he has vowed to stay within Rachel Reeves’ borrowing rules to avoid racking up debt, and so will have little money to play with.

Brexit

Resetting UK-EU relations was central to part of Sir Keir’s mission as prime minister.

However, his government had strict red lines which ruled out bringing back free movement and rejoining the customs union.

Mr Burnham in the past has said he would like to see the UK rejoin the European Union in the future.



During the Makerfield by-election campaign he promised not to re-run the Brexit campaign and backtracked on his vision to rejoin the bloc.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But last week it was reported Mr Burnham could be open to cutting university fees for EU students for more trade access.

News.title: Man killed after being crushed to death by bin lorry after stealing backpack and hiding from cops inside dumpster
News.content:
DEADLY CRUSH Man killed after being crushed to death by bin lorry after stealing backpack and hiding from cops inside dumpster

A MAN was crushed to death after climbing inside a garbage container to hide from police.

The freak incident happened in the early hours of Monday morning in the port city of Cartagena, Spain.



The unnamed victim was on the run after allegedly stealing a backpack, and had hidden inside an anchored bin.

He was lying low when a lorry arrived to pick up the trash at around 1am.



Without the truck driver initially noticing the man inside, the rubbish was unloaded onto the vehicle, and the truck then proceeded to crush all the waste.

As soon as their colleagues spotted that someone was hiding inside, they stopped, but it was already too late.



Emergency services could do nothing to save him and he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Firefighters had to remove his body from the inside of the truck before it was taken away.

The truck driver received medical attention after suffering a panic attack.

A spokesperson for the National Police in Murcia confirmed the dead man was allegedly being hunted by police after stealing a backpack.



“He was seen stealing a rucksack belonging to a homeless man and police lost him as they tried to intercept him,” they said.

“That was because he had hidden inside the rubbish container.”

A source added: “Unluckily for him he hid where he did just before the bin lorry arrived and as it always does, it activated the compaction system to empty the contents in the back of the vehicle.”

No details have been released about the age or nationality of the victim.

While extremely rare, such incidents have happened before.



In October last year, Sajmir Beca, 30, suffered catastrophic injuries and died a week later in hospital after being tipped from a bin into a lorry.

The incident happened in Northampton, and again, bin collectors did not spot that there was a person inside.

News.title: Brit, 47, found ‘tortured to death’ in Caribbean holiday home – as UK cops launch probe into horror
News.content:
DEATH RIDDLE Brit, 47, found ‘tortured to death’ in Caribbean holiday home – as UK cops launch probe into horror

POLICE in the UK are investigating after a Brit was allegedly found tortured to death in the Caribbean, an inquest heard.

Andrew Donald Frederick, 47, was discovered in Grenada on January 4, 2026.

His body was brought back to the UK after investigations by the Grenada authorities which ruled it “an accidental death”.

The verdict came despite a pathologist, approved by the Royal Grenada police force (RGPF), finding that Andrew had been tortured.





Senior coroner Lydia Brown today confirmed the Met Police are now investigating his death.

She told West London Coroner’s Court: “There was a private family post-mortem from Professor Daisley which stated that the death was homicide.”

His case of death in the UK is currently “unascertained” and it is understood that there is ongoing “diplomacy” with the authorities in Grenada, it was said.

Ms Brown suspended the inquest pending the outcome of the police probe.



Andrew’s family, who attended the hearing, previously called for an urgent review into his death.

They referred the case to the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, who were provided with the post-mortem from Grenada that found Andrew was tortured.

But the FCDO reportedly refused to refer the case to its murder and manslaughter team.

The family said at the time: “We have been unable to grieve properly for Andrew because grief requires a degree of resolution or at least the belief that those with the power to act are acting.



“Instead, nearly five months have been spent driving a campaign for justice while carrying the weight of what was done to him.

“This includes examining horrific pictures and the knowledge that the organisations that exist precisely to help families in these circumstances have, at every turn, forced us to fight for the most basic engagement.

“This is not what grief should look like. It is what institutional failure looks like.”

The FCDO previously confirmed it was supporting Andrew’s family and was in contact with the “local authorities”.

News.title: Travellers bulldoze field with ‘20 lorries’ in ANOTHER Bank Holiday ‘land grab’ – after police stand-off 40 miles away
News.content:
LAND WAR Travellers bulldoze field with ‘20 lorries’ in ANOTHER Bank Holiday ‘land grab’ – after police stand-off 40 miles away

TRAVELLERS have bulldozed a field in an attempted Bank Holiday weekend land grab after a police stand-off unfolded just forty miles away.

As council offices closed for the long weekend on Friday, travellers set to work building an encampment on privately owned land in Rochford, Essex.



Locals said the work ruined their Bank Holiday with some 20 lorries arriving and construction work carrying on all weekend.

The local authority has said it issued a stop notice on Saturday but it was ignored and construction at the traveller site continued anyway.



Council officers have since visited the site to assess the building, collect evidence and serve a stop notice with police present when the notice was handed over.

According to Rochford District Council the notice was the quickest way to stop building because the landlord had granted permission to the travellers.



Further action will be considered under planning law, while council officers said the site would continue to be monitored.

One resident said: “If they had planning permission, it wouldn’t be a problem, but they have zero planning permission. Everyone else has to abide by the planning rules.



“They have been working there all night on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. It’s heartbreaking for everyone who lives in the area.”

Another added: “It’s worrying. Since Friday it’s been horrendous. On Saturday there must have been around twenty lorries from various companies.

“It’s been a horrendous weekend. We heard them working on it all night. Our concern is about them doing this illegally. You shouldn’t carry on if there is a stop order.

“They just came along and did what they want.”

Leader of Rochford District Council Adi Malviya said: “The Council are aware of unauthorised development on privately owned land at Lower Road/Greensward Lane.



“This is a planning enforcement issue, which means the same procedures cannot be used as they would be for an unauthorised incursion on council land.”

It follows another Bank Holiday land grab just forty miles away that saw workers begin to put in fences and lay hardcore and pipes on a wetland and nature reserve in Sawbridgeworth, Hertfordshire.

Up to 100 locals watched over the wildlife area — less than a mile from Sir Rod Stewart’s £4.65million mansion — after diggers turned up at the weekend.

The travellers had recently bought three fields in the area and ignored a temporary stop notice from East Hertfordshire District Council on Saturday.

They also refused access to Environment Agency officials concerned by the effect of pipework on the nearby River Stort.



Residents monitored the site through Sunday night as the council sought an injunction — and when the workers returned police were called.

Locals said officers threatened the travellers with arrest if work continued — thanks to a sweeping High Court injunction that banned further development and caravans or mobile homes being occupied.

One Hertfordshire resident said: “It was a festival atmosphere overnight.

“We were warned not to interfere when the travellers came back, just to let them start working but tell the police as soon as the injunction was broken.

“They came and turfed them out quickly and they say they will now keep guard.”

News.title: Laundry rooms to be turned into cells to tackle prison overcrowding
News.content:
The government is to create more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

An investment of Â£110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the Ministry of Justice said.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris is also due to give more details in the Commons later on changes to the early release scheme, which aims to free up space in prisons as they near maximum capacity.

He told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" for them and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Norris told BBC Breakfast victims were being sent letters to tell them about criminals being released early and they would have be offered support from victims' liaison officers.

He insisted offenders would face restrictions on release, including tagging and bans on attending football games.

Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman said victims wanted to know how these early releases would affect them, especially those who had faced domestic abuse or stalking.

Norris, who is also Lord Chancellor, said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

But Chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."

Norris said the government had delivered more than 3,200 prison places in two years.

Investment on prison spaces was announced as part of last year's spending review, which covers plans up to 2030. This included a Â£7bn capital investment to create 14,000 prison places by 2031. The Â£110m for more prison cells is not new money.

News.title: New storm names for 2026-2027 released by Met Office
News.content:
Storm names are selected jointly by the Met Office, Met Ãireann and KNMI, with the final list aiming to reflect communities across the UK, Ireland and the Netherlands.

In 2025 the three meteorology agencies invited nominations for names from the public.

More than 40,000 were submitted - we saw names such as Amy, Isla and Marty selected for the 2025/2026 storm season.

This year's list continues to draw on those suggestions, reflecting not only popular choices, but also some of the personal stories behind them.

For example Austen was suggested in honour of Austen Nagle, the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service.

Chloe was selected by the Met Office after being nominated more than 130 times, including once by the mother of a five-year-old who is described by her mum as "fascinated by the weather" but can also "create a storm by herself" when she is tired.

And Ivy was nominated in honour of a nine-month-old Labrador puppy affectionately known as "the absolute destructor".

Any remnant of a tropical storm or hurricane that crosses the Atlantic will keep its original name, for example ex-Hurricane Erin, which brought a large swell to South West England in August 2025 and was named 'Storm Erin'.

To ensure consistency with the US National Hurricane Centre naming conventions, names that begin with the letters Q, U, X, Y and Z are not used.

News.title: Man in court charged with murder after fire deaths
News.content:
A 23-year-old man has appeared in court charged with murdering a woman and her seven-year-old niece who died in a house fire.

Natalie McDonald, 34, died in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August, along with Valentina Foster.

Jaden Wright appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court charged with two counts of murder as well as multiple grievous bodily harm offences.

Wright, of no fixed address, was remanded in custody during the hearing that lasted less than two minutes, and is next due to appear at Teesside Crown Court on Thursday.

He is also accused of two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two charges of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent.

These charges relate to the six people in the house at the time of the blaze.

No pleas were entered during the hearing on Tuesday morning.

News.title: Israeli fire kills three in Gaza City during reported raid, medics say
News.content:
At least two Palestinian children and a woman have been killed by Israeli fire in western Gaza City, Palestinian medics say.

Unconfirmed local reports say that an Israel-backed Palestinian militia carried out a raid and that the Israeli military carried out shelling and air strikes after it was discovered.

A third child was killed in a separate incident in central Gaza.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said that a senior Hamas official had been arrested, but it is not clear whether the announcement is related to the incident in Gaza City.

Videos from Gaza City captured chaotic scenes, with the sound of gunfire and the aftermath of air strikes.

Initial Palestinian reports said that a special Israeli unit infiltrated a crowded area using a van and motorcycles.

It is not clear whether those involved were Israeli forces or members of an Israel-backed Palestinian militia.

A local source told the BBC that a senior Hamas security official was believed to have been targeted.

The Israeli military reportedly carried out drone strikes to try to secure the special unit after its presence was uncovered.

The military has only confirmed striking several targets in Gaza "in order to remove threats to the security forces", adding that there were no injuries to its troops.

News.title: US army secretary resigns after months of tension
News.content:
US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation after about 18 months in the role.

His departure was confirmed by CBS, the BBC's US media partner, which reported it came after months of conflict between him and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The youngest-ever army secretary has often been referred to as President Donald Trump's "drone guy".

Driscoll, 41, has been "highly effective" in advancing Trump's agenda "to Make America Strong Again" and provided "outstanding leadership" during military operations, the White House said in a statement given to CBS.

The BBC has contacted the White House, Pentagon and Army for comment.

Driscoll is the latest in a string of recent high-profile military leaders to depart, including Navy Secretary John Phelan who abruptly quit in April.

Other notable departures include Army Chief of Staff Randy George, Army Gen David Hodne and Maj Gen William Green.

Since entering the Pentagon, Hegseth has fired more than a dozen senior military officers, including the chief of naval operations and the Air Force's vice-chief of staff.

The details of the behind-the-scenes friction between Driscoll and Hegseth are unclear but CBS notes that the army secretary is good friends with George, who was reportedly asked by Hegseth to resign.

The post of army secretary is the top civilian leader of the US Army, directing active duty troops, along with the National Guard and reserve soldiers.

Driscoll previously served in the Army and was an officer in 2007 before leading a cavalry platoon and deploying to Iraq for several months in 2009.

As army secretary, Driscoll became known as Trump's "drone guy" due to his embrace of emerging battlefield technologies.

He took on a leading role last year in talks aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, taking on foreign trips and meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

He's also a close ally and friend of Vice-President JD Vance, whom he met at Yale Law School.

During his tenure as head of the US Army, he was a key figure in Trump's deployment of the National Guard to US cities.

He also took over the role of acting director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

News.title: It's taken me a long time to process Olympic experience - Raygun
News.content:
Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.

Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.

Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut.

"I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.

She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team.

"I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.

Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.

Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself.

"Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.

What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.

There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack".

"It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.

Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been.

"It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said.

"You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."

That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health.

"I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.

In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency.

"It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport.

"It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."

News.title: Feeling nostalgic for summer? How to beat the back-to-work blues
News.content:
It can be tempting to launch straight into tackling the hardest task first.

But careers coach Sarah Robinson says it's better to "ease back in" by starting with small, manageable tasks and "quick wins".

"It's about trying to build momentum, because I think sometimes it can just feel overwhelming when you've got a massive inbox," she says.

Counsellor Susan Carr agrees. She says it isn't possible in every industry but where viable "be a bit kinder with your expectations of what you need to do on that first day back in the office."

That could mean spending the day going through emails rather than a full day of back-to-back meetings.

Tara Humphrey, a primary care leadership consultant, advocates keeping her out-of-office on for her first day back.

"It's about hiding, if you can, just to give yourself that bit of headspace."

She also says re-entry into work life can be made easier by a clearly-written out-of-office message, encouraging people to follow up when she is back in the office - that eases the stress of whether you have missed something important while on holiday.

There is an alternative. She recalls a colleague who would simply delete all the emails he had been sent during his holiday.

"He said, 'if people want me, they'll come back to me'."

News.title: Djokovic's tearful loss leaves future uncertain
News.content:
Be warned: Novak Djokovic has made a fool of those who have doubted him before.

Some questioned if the Serb would challenge for the sport's top honours again after he dropped out of the world's top 20 amid a two-year major title drought in 2018.

Djokovic proceeded to win four of the following five Grand Slams, doubling his tally of majors with 12 across the next six years.

But three years have now passed since he landed his men's record 24th major title at the US Open.

And, as the 39-year-old fought back tears mid-match on Sunday night, this latest loss in New York felt different.

Staring at a first opening-round Grand Slam exit since 2006, one of sport's all-time greats simply had nothing left, beaten 7-6 (7-5) 5-7 4-6 6-2 6-1 by Argentina's Navone.

For so long now Djokovic has not only defied time, but appeared to be improving with it.

That was evident at this year's Wimbledon, where he outlasted Felix Auger-Aliassime, 14 years his junior, in a five-set thriller that became the longest quarter-final in the tournament's history.

Even in his late 30s, Djokovic has been the one challenging Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, the new dominant forces in the men's game.

At the Australian Open in January, he ended Sinner's bid for a third-straight title in a sensational five-set comeback victory. He then led Alcaraz by a set in the final, before fading to a four-set defeat.

After early exits in Paris and New York, there is an inevitable sense that Melbourne was his best chance to secure an outright record 25th major triumph and cap a career unparalleled in every statistical measure.

Djokovic was despondent after the match, saying he "despised every moment I spent on the court for that".

"When it comes to the match itself, and the overall feeling of how I felt with my body and playing, it was really not enjoyable," Djokovic said.

"But, from the perspective of the crowd and support, it was incredible.

"I'm very sorry that I didn't perform as well as I should have, could have, or wanted - for them."

News.title: Hundreds remember Heaton Park synagogue attack victims at memorial event
News.content:
The Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis and Communities Secretary Angela Rayner were among about 800 people who attended a memorial event for the victims and survivors of last year's Heaton Park synagogue attack.

Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed, and three others injured, as they tried to defend their place of worship from attacker Jihad al-Shamie on 2 October 2025.

Relatives of the bereaved and some of the survivors were among the speakers at Monday's service of remembrance at the synagogue in Manchester.

Prior to the event, Rabbi Daniel Walker said the Jewish community feels less safe now than it did immediately after the attack.

He said rising antisemitism, combined with a lack of action to "deal with core problems", had left many members of Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation â and British Jews more widely â feeling increasingly vulnerable.

Two seats remained empty for the service, bearing the names of Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby.

News.title: Flu vaccine rollout begins as NHS regroups from 'busiest summer'
News.content:
Last winter's flu season was unexpected, beginning more than a month earlier than usual, external with the Super-K strain.

Super flu is not a medical term, and it does not mean the virus has become harder to treat, just that people are yet to build up immunity against it.

Flu vaccines are updated annually to ensure they are a good match for the type of flu circulating. Influenza viruses constantly mutate and experts have to predict these changes ahead of time.

This year's vaccine has had a few tweaks, including one to better match subclade K.

It is not clear when flu will hit this year, and whether it will be a bad season. But experts often look to southern hemisphere countries, like Australia and New Zealand, to gain a better understanding of how the UK could be affected.

Their flu season peaks in July or August. Australia has had fewer cases than last year, external, but New Zealand has seen high numbers, external.

Dr Amanda Doyle from NHS England said it was best to be cautious.

"Last year's flu season came early and was made worse by a new variant, which had a major impact for patients and put enormous pressure on urgent and emergency care services across the country," she said.

"With the NHS experiencing its busiest summer on record, staff have started preparing for this winter earlier than ever â and with services already under significant pressure, it is vital that everyone offered the vaccine comes forward."

News.title: Boy, 16, appears in court charged with murder
News.content:
A teenage boy has appeared in court charged with the murder of a man in Dungannon, County Tyrone, and the attempted murder of two other people in the same incident.

The body of the dead man, who was 61, was found alongside his injured eight-year-old daughter at a house on Lisnahull Road on Saturday morning.

The man's 48-year-old wife sustained non-life threatening injuries during the attack.

The 16-year-old defendant, who cannot be named because of his age, was also charged with making threats to kill. He appeared in court in Omagh on Tuesday morning and was remanded in custody.

The teenager spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address.

BBC News NI understands the man who died was from Guinea-Bissau, but had lived in Northern Ireland for more than two decades.

During the hearing, the defence solicitor said there were "clear concerns" about the defendant's mental health.

Faloon said the defendant had been examined by a mental health nurse over the weekend but not at psychiatric level.

The judge made an order to conduct a mental health assessment of the defendant.

He is due to appear on 15 September at Dungannon Youth Court.

News.title: Swinney to cut number of health boards in efficiency drive
News.content:
Plans to cut the number of health boards could result in just two bodies running local NHS services on mainland Scotland.

Details of proposed changes to the current 14-board model are to be set out by First Minister John Swinney in his programme for government at Holyrood later.

It is expected to major on public service reform aimed at saving money and improving efficiency by cutting layers of management.

Opposition parties have said they want to see further action on the NHS and cost of living.

Swinney said it was time to "embrace change", with reforms to sit at the heart of his programme for government.

He has already appointed a new cabinet minister to lead on public service reform.

The SNP leader is also expected to set out a range of policies aimed at growing the economy, eradicating child poverty, transitioning to net zero and addressing "the epidemic of violence against women and girls".

News.title: Man dies near Notting Hill Carnival after entering canal
News.content:
A man died near Notting Hill Carnival in London on Monday afternoon, the Metropolitan Police have confirmed.

Police officers had attempted to stop the man, believed to be in his 20s, as he approached the event. He fled on foot with officers in pursuit, and entered the water in the vicinity of Meanwhile Gardens a short time later, the force said.

Taken to hospital by ambulance the man was pronounced dead a short time later.

Cdr Claire Smart said: "This is a tragic incident and our thoughts are with the loved ones of the man who has lost his life."

The Met Police said officers had attempted to stop the man at about 15:19 BST near Harrow Road.

The man entered the water in the vicinity of Meanwhile Gardens, off Kensal Road.

Officers and members of the public went in after him and pulled him from the water, police said, and officers immediately started CPR.

Paramedics were called and continued treatment at the canal side before taking the man to a central London hospital. He was pronounced dead at 16:43.

The Met Police said on Monday night that urgent enquiries were ongoing to locate and inform his next of kin.

Smart, gold commander for the Notting Hill Festival, said: "Any death following contact with the police is passed to the Independent Office for Police Conduct so the circumstances can be fully investigated.

"I would encourage everyone to avoid speculation while this work takes place."

She added: "I acknowledge the efforts of the officers and members of the public who entered the canal to rescue this man. I know they will be devastated that his life couldn't ultimately be saved."

The Met Police said the two days of the festival had passed "largely without incident".

There were two assaults with knives - one stabbing and one slashing. Neither resulted in life-threatening injuries.

On Monday evening, police said there had been 315 arrests that day, bringing the total number of arrests to 560.

News.title: Holy Cross school dispute was 'hatred at its worst'
News.content:
The priest who helped shield schoolgirls during the 2001 Holy Cross dispute has said the "hurt" of that ordeal could happen again.

Speaking on the 25th anniversary of Holy Cross, Fr Aidan Troy said that possibility is what keeps him "devoted to dialogue, to conversation, to searching for justice and to caring about people".

Fr Aidan said the sectarian dispute was "hatred at its worst".

It happened in north Belfast when loyalist protesters tried to block the route taken by Holy Cross school pupils and their parents, who were from a Catholic background, on their walk to class.

Following the initial violence, the police and Army put up crash barriers to keep a corridor route open for the Holy Cross pupils.

The images of terrified schoolgirls having to run the gauntlet between lines of armoured police officers in order to get to their primary school were beamed around the world.

Protestants claimed that Catholics were attacking their homes and said the school protest was their way of highlighting their concerns.

Stones, bottles, fireworks and even a blast bomb were thrown during weeks of unrest.

Fr Aidan, who was parish priest in Ardoyne at the time, told BBC News NI that "none of us want to see hatred".

News.title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Andrew Bailey warns G20
News.content:
The governor of the Bank of England has warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could cause a global economic downturn and pose a significant cyber security risk to financial systems.

Andrew Bailey said any collapse of growth in the AI sector could lead to a "future market correction" that spreads worldwide.

In an open letter to finance ministers in the US on Monday, he said companies around the world should prepare for security breaches "involving simultaneous disruption across multiple firms".

Earlier this month, a group of 100 firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, urged countries and groups to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.

Bailey told the G20 finance ministers that a combination of highly priced stock markets, increased borrowing by investors, and the growing concentration of money into a small number of major technology companies could amplify any future market correction.

"The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more, but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration, in particular the increasing cross-investment between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and hyper scalers, in a way that could amplify a future market correction," he said.

Bailey has called on those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis".

Bailey, who was writing in his capacity as chairman of the Financial Stability Board international watchdog (FSB), expressed concern about the "volatility" prompted by the effect of energy supply shocks caused by the US-Iran war.

His warning comes as the UK government is seeking to grow the country's "sovereign AI" capacity, developing homegrown AI technology to ensure the UK is not dependent on services from abroad.

Ministers want to see companies compete for the funding to help tackle challenges like cutting waiting lists in the NHS and bolstering cybersecurity and defence.

But there is growing concern that AI companies are increasingly developing models that can easily override the safeguarding systems of banks and financial centres.

News.title: Nursery fined after baby boy burned by bleach
News.content:
Defence advocate Barry Smith KC said the first priority of a nursery was the safety and wellbeing of the children there.

He added: "It is of the utmost regret from all involved - from the director and all staff - that this accident occurred and injury was caused to a young child."

In a statement released via law firm Digby Brown, the family said: "We've had to wait five years for Little Dreams Nursery to admit what happened to our son was their fault but we don't feel the severity of his injuries have been acknowledged.

"We trusted them to take care of him and for such an injury to happen to a 10-month-old baby is indefensible.

"In the months and years that followed, we had to watch our boy deal with the consequences of something that was never his fault. No parent should have to experience that, but we are thankful what happened hasn't had a more serious or longer-lasting impact."

The statement concluded: "Today we close the most horrific chapter of our lives and we want to thank everyone who has supported us during this time and now request our privacy as we move forward."

Little Dreams said the safety, wellbeing and care of every child entrusted to them was of the "highest priority".

"We deeply regret that this incident was able to occur and are profoundly sorry for the distress and impact it has had on the child and their family," the nursery said.

Tadej Pogacar has undergone successful surgery on a collarbone fracture sustained in a nasty crash at the Vuelta a Espana, his team has confirmed.

The six-time grand tour winner had been leading the Vuelta by nearly four minutes from his closest challenger, Enric Mas, when he crashed on an innocuous, flat stretch of road on stage eight.

He sustained deep cuts to his left shoulder and the left side of his face and after initially attempting to remount his bike conceded that he could not continue, with his withdrawal marking the first time he has abandoned a race since Liege-Bastogne-Liege in 2023 and his first-ever abandon at a grand tour.

His UAE Team Emirates-XRG outfit later confirmed he had suffered a concussion, multiple abrasions, a displaced left clavicle fracture and a stable C7 cervical fracture. He was taken to hospital in Valencia before being transported to Barcelona, with surgery on the collarbone fracture initially delayed as a precaution due to his concussion.

UAE’s medical director Dr Adrian Rotunno said on social media on Monday that the surgery had been successfully completed.

He wrote: “This afternoon, Tadej underwent successful surgery on his left clavicle after receiving the all-clear to proceed with the operation. The procedure went well and he will remain in hospital for post-operative monitoring for a few days.

“When ready, Tadej will travel home to begin his recovery and rehabilitation under the supervision of the team’s medical staff. We will continue to monitor his progress closely throughout the recovery process.”

The team have not confirmed the cause of the crash, although footage appeared to show the Slovenian hitting a rock on the road and being unable to stop his fall after swerving. He was immediately attended to by medical staff before stepping into a waiting ambulance.

The injuries he sustained makes a defence of his world title - and chance of winning a third straight rainbow jersey - in Montreal at the end of this month highly unlikely, while he is also likely to miss out on a home European Championships, in which he is also the reigning champion, in Ljubljana in October.

Lisa Kudrow is happy to fulfill most Friends fans’ requests when they meet her — but she draws the line at one thing.

Kudrow, 63, starred as the ever-quirky Phoebe Buffay opposite Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Matt LeBlanc, David Schwimmer, and the late Matthew Perry on the beloved sitcom from 1994 to 2004.

There is one song on the show that Kudrow’s character was particularly known for, which appeared in the sixth episode of the second season, “The One with the Baby on the Bus.”

“Sometimes people will stop me and say, ‘Oh, sing Smelly Cat,’” Kudrow shared on a recent episode of NPR’s Fresh Air radio show. “I don’t want to do that. I really don’t want to do that.”

Musician Chrissie Hynde guest stars in the episode as Stephanie Schiffer, a singer hired to replace Phoebe as Central Perk’s in-house musician, to whom Phoebe eventually teaches “Smelly Cat” — a song about a stray cat.

open image in gallery Lisa Kudrow has admitted she refuses to sing ‘Smelly Cat’ for ‘Friends’ fans ( Getty )

The tune evolved into a running gag and became an integral component of Phoebe’s character.

Despite admitting she refuses to sing for fans, Kudrow made clear she has “zero complaints about Friends or anything to do with it,” even when fans ask her to say famous lines or call her Phoebe.

“Just the relationship with the other actors; we had fun,” Kudrow said of her co-stars. “That is so rare. And real honest respect, mutual respect.”

“It was a really good relationship that took some work, and we did the work,” she continued. “It was great.”

open image in gallery David Schwimmer, Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Matthew Perry and Lisa Kudrow starred in 'Friends' ( Getty )

In a recent interview, Kudrow revealed she attempted to go for the role of Rachel after being cast as Phoebe.

“I told my agents, ‘I can do Jewish American Princess and make that really funny.’ And so they said, ‘Uh-huh. All right. Well, we’ll tell them,’” she said.

At the time, Kudrow didn’t “clock that” Rachel was supposed to be the romantic lead opposite David Schwimmer’s Ross.

“They went, ‘No, no. It’s so hard for them to find Phoebe. They’re not messing with that.’ So that was the sweet way of saying, ‘Yeah, you are not the romantic interest.’” The role eventually went to Aniston.

Earlier this year, Kudrow told The Independent that “nobody cared” about her character.

“There was no vision for me, and no expectations about the kind of career I could have,” she commented. “There was just, like, ‘Boy is she lucky she got on that show.’”

It wasn’t until a few years later, when she made the Robert De Niro comedy Analyze This, about a mob boss in therapy, that “agents and business people started circling, wanting to put me in romantic comedies and things,” she said.

“I knew that wasn’t gonna work. I’m just not adorable!”

News.content:

The “Burnham bounce” has ended, just weeks after the new prime minister entered Downing Street, leading pollsters have said, as they warned there would be no point in Labour calling an early election.

Labour surged in the polls by around five to six points – finally leapfrogging Nigel Farage’s Reform UK after 18 months – after Andy Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer on 20 July.

But experts say any bounce triggered by the change of leadership appears to have already peaked, with Labour failing to make any gains since last week – and even falling behind Reform again in some cases.

It comes as Mr Burnham prepares to face MPs in the Commons on Tuesday for the first time since getting the keys to No 10. After a series of small giveaways during his summer tour, including removing VAT from fuel bills and capping bus ticket prices at £2, the PM will be under pressure to lay out wider policies to move on from his predecessor – especially with a difficult Budget in October.

According to The Guardian, the prime minister will use his speech to call for more public control over water, energy and transport in a bid to drive economic growth. The publication also quoted a No 10 source who said Mr Burnham was “optimistic about our country’s future”.

But top pollster Professor Sir John Curtice told The Independent: “I believe that the ‘Burnham bounce’ came to an end after two weeks.”

open image in gallery The ‘Burnham bounce’ appears to have come to an end ( Reuters )

He added: “There is no rational basis for Labour to call an election now.”

Sir John pointed out that, during polls throughout August, Labour had – at most – an average one point lead over Reform.

While some polls give Labour a lead of up to four points, and others a lead of up to three for Reform, Mr Burnham’s party is generally seeing scores in the mid-20s. They are around seven points ahead of Sir Keir’s low of 17 per cent, but still well below the party’s election share in 2024 of 32 per cent.

One poll published this weekend gave a much bleaker look, suggesting Labour are only up two points – to 23 per cent – compared to the end of July. Reform are unchanged on 23 per cent, according to the poll by Politico.

Polling expert Lord Robert Hayward agreed there is “a strong possibility that the Burnham bounce has peaked”.

He added that Labour’s boost may have been linked to Mr Farage and Green Party leader Zack Polanski taking a popularity hit due to scandals within their parties.

He told The Independent: “That bounce could have reasonably been caused, in part, by a decline in support for Green Party leader Zack Polanski and Farage – as much as Burnham not being Keir.”

Although the polls show a mixed picture, six different surveys, published in the week between 17 and 23 August, suggested Labour would still struggle to convincingly beat Reform UK in any national election.

Labour had no change in two and went backwards in three polls, by -1 or -2 per cent. They had a gain of just 1 per cent in the sixth.

The first poll of last week (from 24 August) by More in Common again showed Labour on no change, although they were four points ahead of Reform. A Find Out Now poll saw Labour drop one point to 22 per cent with Reform up two, to 25 per cent.

Meanwhile, a Survation poll on Friday gave Labour a three-point lead – up by one to 27 per cent, but helped by Reform slipping two points to 24 per cent. And over the weekend, an Opinium poll had both Labour and Reform unchanged, with a Labour lead of 27 per cent to Reform’s 25 per cent.

For the latest political headlines delivered straight to your inbox, 

A more positive poll for Labour by BMG on Friday suggested the Burnham bounce was continuing with Labour having a four-point lead over Reform. But Labour’s share of the vote had still dropped by one point.

Lord Hayward concluded: “There is not a strong basis from which to be planning to call an early election.”

He said Labour could still dramatically improve or worsen its standing, but that it would be down to policies and decision-making rather than Mr Burnham replacing Sir Keir as leader.

Labour MPs had been concerned that the new prime minister may try to secure a proper mandate by calling an election between October this year and May 2027, although Mr Burnham has previously insisted he would not call an early election.

Pressure for an early election comes from the restrictions of Labour’s 2024 manifesto which, among other things, precludes it from raising the major taxes.

Mr Burnham has already conceded on tax and borrowing policy, as well as sticking to Sir Keir’s Brexit red lines, that he feels bound by Labour’s 2024 election mandate and would need a fresh election to make significant changes.

Sir John said Labour had received a boost of around 6 per cent since Sir Keir announced his resignation, including a Starmer “unbounce” – worth around two points – and around four to five points since Mr Burnham took over.

But he described this as “normal” for when a party changes from an unpopular prime minister. It has parallels with Boris Johnson taking over from Theresa May, and Rishi Sunak from Liz Truss.

While Mr Burnham had a positive trip to Kyiv where he gave Ukraine the blueprint for Storm Shadow missiles, he has also been hit by the harsh realities of government.

Having declared that his would be a “cost of living government”, the prime minister this week saw the energy price cap go up by an inflation-busting 4 per cent, hitting domestic and business bills ahead of the winter.

open image in gallery Professor Sir John Curtice ( PA )

There are also continuing questions over where he will get the money to fund some of his giveaways. He will also come under pressure to explain what he will do to fund defence.

YouGov founder Peter Kellner, a Labour Party member, said: “Among established pollsters, all polls conducted in August have ranged between a four-point Labour lead and a three-point Reform lead.

“Given sampling error, they all suggest the popular vote is too close to call. But I do agree that if they stay anything like this, there will be no early election.

“I reckon that Labour needs a sustained double-digit lead, say for six to eight weeks, before it makes sense for Burnham to put a landslide majority at risk.”

Grantchester and Soldier Soldier star Robson Green has hit out at a new wave of actors entering the industry, saying that many expect to stumble upon success “without doing the work”.

The 61-year-old, originally from North Tyneside, rose to fame in ITV’s Soldier Soldier as Dave Tucker before topping the music charts with co-star Jerome Flynn after the pair covered Todd Duncan’s “Unchained Melody” in the drama. He went on to star in comedy drama Northern Lights, detective series Grantchester and ITV docuseries Tales from Northumberland with Robson Green.

The actor runs his own production companies, which aim to create opportunities for creatives in the north-east of England – but has claimed that he’s struggling to find actors and writers who are prepared to work hard for roles.

open image in gallery Robson Green in ITV’s ‘Grantchester’ with James Norton

“There’s been a lot of levelling up in the North East. But there are a lot of [actors and writers] who are just expecting things to happen without doing the work,” he told The Telegraph. “It’s not just the North East; there’s a generational sense of embittered belief. The attitude is very much, ‘Why not me?’”

He added that he finds that a number of actors come to set without knowing their lines. “I cannot believe actors come in [to film a scene], and they’ve got the script in front of them. I go, ‘Do you want this or not?’ But a lot of them think they can fast-track it without putting in the work.”

Green also bemoaned the lack of quality in TV roles he’s being offered at the moment, admitting that he’s being sent “a lot of crap scripts”. He continued: “And I mean crap stuff that is on the nose, like an A-level paper or something. There’s some good ones out there, but that influx of really good writing seems to be lacking.”

open image in gallery Green revealed that he asks actors who turn up not knowing their lines: ‘Do you want this or not?’ ( Getty Images )

He added that many writers “don’t have the care and attention and the nurturing they deserve”, with a lot of it being down to lack of investment in the arts. “I know there are people tearing their hair out at the quality of some of the theatre in the North East at the moment,” he said.

Throughout his career, Green has dedicated time to supporting projects in the North East of England. Earlier this year, Green partnered with the Kielder Observatory in Northumberland National Park to create a new stargazing experience near Hadrian’s Wall with a telescope named “Robson’s Reflector”. He’s also set to star in new BBC drama Northumbria Mysteries, which has been filmed in the local area.

“That’s a WIND REEL AND PRINT (WRAP) on The Northumbria Mysteries,” he wrote on Instagram last month. “One of the most Joyous filming experiences of my career. What a story what a team! Transmission TBC. A series for all the family set against the magical and jaw dropping backdrop of Northumberland. Watch this space.”

Richard Hammond has admitted he’s “a little uncomfortable” over his daughter’s driving career due to his past crash experience on Top Gear.

Hammond, 56, was left in a medically induced coma in 2006 after a grievous crash on the BBC show, and earlier this year, influencer Izzy, 25, was taking part in a Formula E influencer event in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, known as Evo sessions, when she lost control of her car and smashed into a concrete barrier.

While she suffered no injuries, ex-Grand Tour presenter Richard said he finds her Formula E racing career “a little uncomfortable because I know from personal experience that things can and do go wrong”.

open image in gallery Richard Hammond is ‘little uncomfortable’ about daughter’s driving career ( ITV )

He added to Metro: “I’m a father, like any other father. I don’t want to see my little girl hurt, but I don’t want to hold her back from opportunities that present themselves. She’s carving her own career, so I can sit back and watch her do that and only applaud.”

When Izzy first crashed, she said her first thought was “Oh my god, everyone’s watching, my dad’s watching – can someone just tell him I’m OK?”.

The accident came 20 years after Richard crashed a 288mph jet-powered dragster at Elvington airfield while attempting a land speed record while filming BBC’s Top Gear.

He landed upside down in a field and was left with serious head injuries, including a frontal lobe brain injury.

open image in gallery Richard Hammond’s influencer daughter, Izzy ( Getty )

In a 2024 interview with The Sunday Times, Hammond reflected on how he thinks his frontal lobe brain injury has already started to affect his memory at 54.

“It did have a knock-on effect. I’ve discussed it since with my family. I’m 54 and my memory’s getting shaky,” he said.

Last week, it was revealed that Top Gear will officially return to the BBC almost four years after host Freddie Flintoff was seriously injured in a high-speed crash while filming in Surrey.

Flintoff was driving a three-wheeled car at more than 100mph when the vehicle flipped and skidded down a track, leaving him with broken ribs and severe facial injuries that required extensive surgery.

Production of the 34th series of the motoring show was halted following the incident, and the BBC later announced that it would “rest” for the foreseeable future.

In 2023, Flintoff and the broadcaster reached a settlement over the crash, with the former host reportedly paid about £9m.

Hammond will next be seen cameoing on The Grand Tour, offering advice to new hosting trio Francis Bourgeois, Thomas Holland and James Engelsman. The new iteration of the Prime Video series launches on Friday (4 September).

Indian prime minister Narendra Modi implored Vladimir Putin during a meeting in Kyrgyzstan that Russia’s war in Ukraine needed to end for the sake of humanity.

Mr Modi called the Russian president “my ⁠friend” and hailed growing economic ties between their countries before pivoting to the years-long war in Ukraine.

Mr Putin looked tense, constantly tapping his feet, at the beginning of the meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek on Monday.

“Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, whilst every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace. We need to move from endless war to an end to the war, to a cessation of hostilities,” Mr Modi said.

“And we will need to move precisely in this direction.”

Mr Modi went on to call for a peaceful settlement of the conflict that began in early 2022. “India supports all peace ‌efforts in this regard, and we shall continue to do so in the future,” he said.

open image in gallery Vladimir Putin and Narendra Modi greet each other during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation ( AFP/Getty )

“Thank you very ​much, prime minister,” Mr Putin responded. “We are moving forward along this path.”

India is one of ​the ⁠biggest buyers of Russian oil, and that trade is helping Moscow replenish its budget despite sweeping Western sanctions.

Russia says that the only way to end the war is on Moscow’s terms, but Ukraine dismisses it as an unacceptable demand.

In a statement reported by the TASS news agency, the Kremlin said Mr Putin had briefed Mr Modi ‌on how the special military operation – Russia’s description for the Ukraine war – was progressing.

The same day, Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said he had a “detailed and constructive” call with US president Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and that they were working to finalise dates for a visit to Kyiv.

open image in gallery Narendra Modi and Vladimir Putin pose for a photo during their meeting on the sidelines of the SCO summit ( AP )

Mr Modi had previously called for peace in eastern Europe, but stopped short of criticising Russia over the war.

“India is not neutral,” he told the Russian leader during his December 2024 visit to India. “India has a position, and that position is for peace. We support every effort for peace, and we stand shoulder to shoulder with every initiative taken for peace.”

Mr Putin is expected to attend a summit of the Brics bloc in Delhi in September.

Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine continued to launch drone attacks at each other’s energy facilities and warehouses.

Russian forces struck ⁠military and energy infrastructure ⁠in ⁠Kyiv and ⁠Odesa overnight, and targeted surrounding areas, killing at least nine people, Ukrainian officials said on Tuesday. The attacks killed eight people and wounded five ​in ⁠Kyiv and caused fires around the capital, the city’s emergency service said on Telegram.

China has said Taiwan will face “consequences” for its presence at the annual Pacific leaders’ summit in Palau on Monday.

Palau is hosting this year’s gathering of Pacific nations and the archipelago is among the handful of countries to maintain diplomatic ties with Taiwan.

The US, EU, Britain, Canada, India, and Japan are also among the 21 dialogue partners of the forum.

The tensions between Beijing and Taipei were visible at the summit at which Asia-Pacific allies gathered to demonstrate regional unity.

Taiwan sent its foreign affairs minister, Lin Chia-lung, as the representative at the forum, where he was invited for meetings and side events held alongside the talks.

Mr Lin said his country was “honoured to serve as a partner in the Pacific, continuing to stand with everyone and work together to make the Pacific more prosperous and peaceful”.

China’s special envoy for Pacific Island affairs, Qian Bo, said his nation had serious concerns with Taiwan in attendance as the self-governed island is not a dialogue partner with the forum.

“There will always be consequences," Mr Qian said, without specifying the nature of the consequences. He denied the remarks were a threat and didn’t provide further details. Beijing has long sought Taipei’s exclusion from international summits through diplomatic pressure.

"This is objected ⁠to by all, so this should not have happened. We think it's very inappropriate to do so," the Chinese official told reporters ​on Monday after an opening ceremony in Palau.

The Chinese envoy said his nation had “serious concerns” about Taiwan being given space at the forum despite Beijing claiming its smaller neighbour as its own territory. China views Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out taking over the democratically-governed island with force, “if necessary”.

open image in gallery China's special envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo leaves the opening ceremony during the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in Koror ( Reuters )

He added that China has the “understanding and support” of most Pacific nations. “We have made our position very clear to the government of Palau and the secretariat,” he said.

The archipelago of over 500 islands has maintained diplomatic ties with Taiwan.

China’s reactions to Taiwan were also condemned by Pacific allies present at the forum.

Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese said "the Pacific Islands Forum determines what happens here, not any other country", when asked by reporters about the Chinese envoy's remarks.

"This is primarily a gathering of the Pacific family ... and I look forward to the engagement," Mr Albanese said on Tuesday, refusing to directly criticise China’s comments towards Australia’s Pacific neighbours.

New Zealand’s foreign minister Winston Peters said the group is not taking instructions from countries outside of it.

Host nation’s president Surangal Whipps Jr also indirectly addressed the reservations from China in his remarks during the forum’s opening ceremony.

"Our partners are welcome to sail with us, but they do not choose our destination."

open image in gallery Traditionally dressed artists perform during the opening ceremony of the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in Koror ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Lin said: “If we go to a party, we always follow the directions of the host.

“However, whenever China goes to a party, it makes itself as if it's the host and China ruins the whole atmosphere of the party.”

Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said Taiwan was "not qualified to participate in the activities of the forum at all".

"The Taiwan authorities sent Lin Chia-lung ​and other Taiwan independence separatists to make sneaky visits around in a vain attempt to attract eyeballs and attention, and the result can only ​be inviting disgrace upon themselves," he said at a regular news briefing in Beijing on Tuesday.

China has previously raised questions on Taiwan hosting diplomatic forums and officials from other democratic nations attending them. It has gradually whittled away the number of Pacific Island countries with ​formal ties to Taipei, with ​only three remaining – Palau, Tuvalu ⁠and the Marshall Islands.

The leaders of Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa, Solomon Islands and Kiribati did not attend the gathering of the 18-member group that counts Australia, New Zealand and Pacific island nations ​as members. Ministers are attending in their place.
