Thank you for your feedback.

Aside from Mbappé the most in-form striker in La Liga might be Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang. The 37-year-old scored for the third game in a row as Deportivo beat Valencia 3-1 at Riazor for their first top-flight victory since 2018. Aubameyang could not suppress a giggle at the mention of Adama Traoré in a post-match chat with the media – his former Barcelona teammate has just signed from West Ham: “I’ve told him: ‘We are waiting for you.’”

View image in fullscreen Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang finds the net again for Deportivo. Photograph: Jose Manuel Alvarez Rey/Getty Images

Despite competition from Deportivo’s Bright Ede, who crossed the ball into his own box for Valencia to score, defensive mishap of the weekend goes to Matías Dituro. The 39-year-old Elche goalkeeper tried to juggle the ball into his own penalty area to pick it up but was beaten to it by Levante’s Yassir Zabiri, who poked in the first of a hat-trick in Racing Santander’s first win in primera since 2012. “Matías is a very daring goalkeeper. We had spoken to Yassir: I thought he could win the ball off him – and look how it turned out,” said Racing’s prophetic head coach, José Alberto.

Sports.title: BBC ‘fully committed to women’s football’ despite cancelling flagship highlights show
Sports.content:
BBC Sport is insisting it remains “fully committed to women’s football and the WSL” despite discontinuing its flagship BBC One highlights programme The Women’s Football Show for the new Women’s Super League season.

It is understood the BBC will focus on digital platforms to showcase highlights instead, including showing them on its newly launched YouTube women’s football channel, instead of the weekly television show with a studio, presenter and pundits, which had aired previously on BBC One at 11.30pm on Sundays, after first going live on BBC iPlayer at 9pm.

The Guardian understands the BBC is also planning a new YouTube chat show about women’s football, presented by Alex Scott, which multiple sources have said is expected to be in the “style of the Overlap”, Gary Neville’s football show. BBC Sport did not wish to comment when contacted about that plan specifically. Further England internationals, past and present, are expected to be part of the regular panel.

The decision to move away from the more traditional, linear television highlights show and focus on digital platforms appears to follow a similar strategy that was demonstrated this summer during the men’s World Cup, during which the BBC opted not to air a nightly highlights show for much of the tournament and instead drew in millions of viewers to its match-by-match highlights packages that were published online and on iPlayer.

A BBC spokesperson told the Guardian: “BBC Sport remains fully committed to women’s football and the WSL. As we build towards the 2027 Fifa Women’s World Cup, audiences will be able to watch highlights from every WSL match across BBC platforms, including iPlayer, YouTube and the BBC Sport website and app.

“In addition, BBC Sport will broadcast 25 live WSL matches, alongside live Uefa Women’s Champions League coverage, ensuring fans can follow the biggest stories and moments from the women’s game on free-to-air platforms.”

The BBC and Sky Sports are about to enter the second season of a five-year domestic broadcast rights deal that runs until 2030, with every match shown live and the vast majority by Sky Sports.

Last year, the BBC lost the broadcast rights for the Women’s FA Cup to Channel 4 and TNT Sports, who will show the competition live in the UK and Republic of Ireland until 2028. Earlier this year the BBC also stopped airing Football Focus, the long-running magazine-style show, presented by Scott, which frequently showcased women’s football. But on Tuesday, BBC sources were adamant the broadcaster was not cutting back on its women’s football coverage nor its investment, but simply evolving the way it delivers highlights in line with changing audience habits.

Yet the Guardian understands the decision to axe the women’s football show has still disappointed several BBC Sport insiders and also came as something of a surprise. Multiple sources who had worked on the Women’s Football Show last season – which was produced by the independent production company Aurora Media, and not by BBC Sport staff – have told the Guardian they first learnt the show was being cancelled when the news was reported by the Cutback in August.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Nevertheless, WSL Football is understood to be comfortable with the assurances it has received from the BBC that it will be enhancing its coverage across its platforms. The new league season gets under way on Friday when the big-spending London City Lionesses host Manchester United.

The Women’s Football Show was co-funded between the BBC and the league. The production of the show is understood to have been funded by WSL Football – and previously, by the Football Association, when it oversaw the division prior to in 2024 – while the BBC covered the cost of the on-screen talent.

Multiple sources have told the Guardian that the BBC’s director of sport, Alex Kay-Jelski, made the strategic decision to discontinue the show, although other sources at the BBC have insisted this was not the case and that such calls are made collaboratively through consultation rather than by one person. The former editor-in-chief of the Athletic, Kay-Jelski has been in his role at BBC Sport since he succeeded Barbara Slater in April 2024.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 11: Manchester City
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 1st (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 1st

Prospects

Champions again at last, after a 10-year wait, Manchester City now face an even tougher task: defending their title. They appear to have a good chance of succeeding, especially after keeping their star striker, Khadija “Bunny” Shaw. The WSL’s top scorer and best player of 2025-26 performed a dramatic U-turn by signing a new four-year contract in May rather than leaving on a free transfer, and that may prove crucial in continuing City’s positive momentum.

Their squad looks to be of a similar strength to last season. The Brazil forward Kerolin left for Barcelona but Beth Mead arriving from Arsenal in essence replaces her. Similarly, the exit of left-back Leila Ouahabi will be compensated for by the acquisition of Niamh Charles from Chelsea. Perhaps the only minor question is whether there is sufficient depth to sustain a challenge in the Women’s Champions League as well as domestically, but the core of regulars looks as formidable as any club in Europe.

The team scored plenty last term and had great success down the flanks, with the right-back Kerstin Casparij providing the joint-most assists in the division. Defensively they look solid. The most intriguing challenge could be psychological, as they switch from hunters to hunted, becoming the team that everybody wants to beat. They start at home to one of the promoted sides, Birmingham City, and first meet a fellow title hopeful – Arsenal – at the start of October, when they will aim to lay down a marker in the title race.

Off-field picture

Owned by City Football Group and led off the pitch by the managing director, Charlotte O’Neill, and director of football, Therese Sjögren, City enter the season with a new women’s team building at the training centre. The £10m building offers everything from underwater treadmills to a barista-style coffee machine in the canteen, with every element tailored towards maximising performance for female athletes. Previously the women’s team sometimes had to share a gym with City’s boys’ academy.

The manager

Andrée Jeglertz’s first season could scarcely have gone better, as he oversaw a league and cup double. He arrived in Manchester after a relatively uninspiring spell in charge of Denmark women but his CV is full of extensive high-level experience, including a 2004 European title with the Swedish club Umeå. The 54-year-old is a calm presence on the touchline, unwavering in his belief that his team will “find a way to win”, and has avoided controversy in press conferences, which he handles assuredly.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Beth Mead joins the champions from rivals Arsenal. Photograph: Kate Green/WSL/WSL Football/Getty Images

Mead was the headline signing on a free transfer after nine years at Arsenal. City are hoping that the England forward – the Golden Boot winner and player of the tournament at the 2022 European Championship – is not past her best, at 31, and can flourish across a three-year contract. She is the all-time leading assist provider in the WSL. Mead also has 81 caps and will want to be part of any Lionesses squad at next summer’s World Cup.

Stat attack

If teams want to defend more effectively against the champions, they could start by focusing on free-kicks and corners. City scored at least twice as many set-piece goals as anyone else in 2025-26. As strong as they were elsewhere, this was their superpower.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Set for a breakthrough

The 18-year-old full-back Sacha Lewis signed her first professional contract with City in August, having been with the club since under-14 level. The younger sister of the club’s men’s first-team full-back Rico Lewis, she has been a regular for England Under-19s and has been named in the England Under-20 squad that will go to Poland for September’s Women’s Under-20 World Cup. She was the player of the season for Manchester City’s “Next Gen” team last term and, with City juggling European and domestic football, may get a chance in the first team.

What they say

“Our biggest challenge this year is to continue winning and, at the same, compete in other competitions and also want to win those. Winning in one year is one thing, but being able to win in the next year, that is even tougher. Of course we can do that [compete on multiple fronts] and we have good enough players to be able to play with one starting XI on Saturday and do a couple of changes on Wednesday and still win. That was our biggest challenge last year – we had too many good players that were not playing enough games, so this year we will have the possibility to explore the whole squad. Each player will be more important than they’ve ever been for the club” – Jeglertz speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live.

Where are they playing their home games?

The Joie Stadium is the women’s team’s usual home, across the road from the Etihad Stadium, where they will play two home league fixtures. Those will be against Arsenal on 4 October and against Manchester United on 14 February. The 7,000-capacity Joie Stadium, that hosted matches at Euro 2022, has been the women’s team’s home for more than a decade and they were unbeaten at home in the league last season. They haven’t lost a home WSL game at the Joie Stadiumsince a 4-3 thriller against Arsenal in February 2025.

Sports.title: Saka settles gruelling battle with Aston Villa to extend Arsenal’s winning start
Sports.content:
The smile on Declan Rice’s face with six minutes of normal time remaining said it all. He had just shut down Ian Maatsen as the Aston Villa full-back zoomed into the box. Arsenal, for whom Bukayo Saka scored the only goal, were authoritative and seemingly took great satisfaction in keeping Villa at arm’s length.

Unai Emery’s work‑in‑progress side struggled to test the champions, David Raya untroubled. The records will show Villa have lost their first two league matches of a season without scoring for the first time since 2002 but, despite successive defeats, this time there was no capitulation.

For Villa, this was a marked improvement on defeat at Brighton in their opener. After 31 minutes in their previous game, they trailed 4-0 and after 40 were down to 10 men.

Here they could take plenty of encouragement from a promising if not fruitless performance, the debutants Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson impressing, having taken the No 1 and No 11 shirts vacated by Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins respectively. Suzuki and Jackson were the only changes to Villa’s starting XI but they appeared far more cohesive. Suzuki’s eye for a pass was particularly noticeable, pinging 50-yard passes to George Hemmings, the 19-year-old who kept his place, and John McGinn within a few minutes of each other.

Emi Buendía smacked the crossbar after Boubacar Kamara overawed Christos Tzolis – Martin Ødegaard subsequently asked questions of the referee, Jarred Gillett – but Jackson otherwise created Villa’s best opening. The Senegal forward, who worked under Emery at Villarreal, pinched possession from Gabriel Magalhães a few yards into the Villa half and galloped into the other before sending a near-perfect cross in from the right. Hemmings burst into the six-yard box but was unable to convert. Villa are just the second team to fail to register a shot on target in their first two Premier League matches in a season since 2003-04, along with Swansea City in 2017-18.

This fixture last season ended in despair for Arsenal, their players splayed across the turf after Buendía’s 95th-minute winner with the last kick of the game. Arteta said that defeat still haunts him and reminded his players as much before this game. “That was still in my tummy and I spoke to my players about it, the image of the players on the floor, totally gutted,” the Arsenal manager said. “We used that [as inspiration].”

View image in fullscreen Zion Suzuki, Aston Villa’s new goalkeeper, applauds the home fans after the final whistle. Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty Images

In that game last season Eberechi Eze was at fault for Matty Cash’s opener and was subsequently hooked at half-time. Here it was a case of role‑reversal, Eze shining after coming on for the second half in place of Christos Tzolis, who was booked after a foul on Cash and muted.

“I think he learnt a lesson,” Arteta said of Eze, who was involved in Arsenal seizing the lead approaching the hour. Arsenal slowed things down and then punished Villa for switching off. Cristhian Mosquera pushed a pass to Eze, who was afforded space by Cash, Villa’s defender concerned about an unmarked Riccardo Calafiori. Eze promptly spied Calafiori’s underlapping run and the Italian steered the ball across the six-yard box where Saka beat Maatsen to the punch and scrambled the cross into the net.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

This is a new-look Villa, on and off the pitch. A handful of staff in hard hats were positioned in the closed North Stand moonlighting as ball boys; the corner of rubble between the remaining skeleton and the Trinity Road Stand remains akin to an excavation site. Ibrahim Mbaye, whose £47m move from Paris Saint‑Germain is to be announced on Tuesday, was in the directors’ box. Taylor Harwood-Bellis is also poised to sign in a £25m deal from Southampton. Six of Villa’s starting XI from their Europa League triumph may have departed but Emery has made no complaints and has relayed his no-excuses mantra to his squad. “We do not look backwards,” he said.

Villa’s frustrations were palpable. McGinn, in a hurry to get Villa level, was booked for wiping out Merino. Aaron Wan-Bissaka replaced Cash for his Villa debut and his first job was to stretch his legs to muffle an advancing Eze. Alejandro Garnacho entered in place of Ross Barkley. Arteta introduced Ezri Konsa for his debut, adding further steel.

Villa could not find a way through and Arsenal’s winning habit already appears ominous. “It is painful to lose,” Emery said. “But we can feel optimistic with how we competed.”

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s international retirement serves as a reminder: watch him while you still can
Sports.content:
It was among the defining moments of the 2026 World Cup: Lionel Messi standing arms akimbo, looking up towards Argentina’s fervent supporters after losing the final. Tears streamed down his face after his team’s embarrassing loss to Spain in what we now know was Messi’s final match wearing that famous Argentina kit.

It was not the first time he’d cried at the tournament. There had been tears of joy in Argentina’s opening match, when Messi rolled back the clock to his glory days with a trio of spectacular goals against Algeria. There had been more when his brace against Austria pushed Argentina through to the knockout round as group winners, and even more when his equalizer against Egypt threw la Albiceleste a much-needed lifeline. Later, the world found out that Messi had been struggling all the while with the health struggles of his father, Jorge, a fact that clearly weighed heavily on him as Argentina made a dramatic return to the final in a bid to defend their 2022 title.

There were tears in the weeks that followed the tournament as well, when Jorge passed away. It led Messi – among the most private, reserved megastars in the world, football or otherwise – to provide a rare moment of public vulnerability as he mourned the loss of his father on social media. But buried in that remembrance was something that caught many football fans off guard.

“All I did was play football,” Messi wrote, “and now I have serious doubts that I’ll do it for much longer.”

Messi announced his retirement from international football this week at age 39, a move that was somewhat expected given his age and the sheer emotional exhaustion that had clearly accompanied his final tournament. He finishes his Argentina career with the most men’s World Cup appearances of all time – 34 spread across six tournaments, the joint-most tournaments played alongside Cristiano Ronaldo and Guillermo Ochoa. He scored or assisted 185 times in his 207 caps, a record 35 of which came at a major tournament. And of course, he was the leading figure in that legendary run that saw Argentina win the 2021 Copa América, the 2022 World Cup, and then defend their Copa América title in 2024. Internationally, there was little left for him to accomplish.

Yet Monday’s announcement still came as a bit of a surprise to many, largely because Messi’s brilliance is still so readily apparent. Few, if any players, have assembled the run of major tournament performances that Messi just put together, regardless of age.

View image in fullscreen Messi won the 2022 World Cup with Argentina, his crowning international honor. Photograph: Friedemann Vogel/EPA

He remains the best player in Major League Soccer as well. Just this past weekend, the Argentinian scored four goals and provided an assist against Montreal, pushing him into the lead for the league’s golden boot.

He remains under a guaranteed contract at Miami through 2028, but Messi’s international exit has now cast understandable doubt on whether he will play that deal out. Messi essentially runs the show at Miami, a club that signs and discards players and coaches at his whim. Guaranteed contracts mean little to the club’s megastars. Just last year, Jordi Alba walked away from a three-year contract after just a few months, choosing retirement and making the MLS Cup final his last professional game. Messi is an idol at the club and would seemingly face little resistance if he chose to bring his career to a close at the end of this season.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi scored four goals for Inter Miami over the weekend. Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty Images

All of which is to say: If you’re in North America, or if you can make it there, go see Lionel Messi now, while you still have a chance.

Three years after his arrival, those of us who live and breathe soccer in Canada and the US have grown almost accustomed to Messi’s presence and all of the magic that accompanies it because it has become so routine. Miami’s traveling bazaar of Messi and aging European megastars was a genuine sensation at first but has since retreated into the shadows at times along with the rest of MLS. His four-goal effort against Montreal would have made international headlines in 2023 but now does little to move the needle. If anything, it’s to be expected. Even in Miami, where Messi was embraced readily, Messi’s presence no longer guarantees the hysteria it once did.

Yet Messi’s level, in MLS at least, has not declined. He remains a must-see player and Miami remain a must-watch team. MLS has a sometimes deserved reputation for being a “retirement league,” yet that same reputation provides fans in North America with an opportunity few of them would have otherwise: to witness global greatness in person, and for a relative bargain.

For other players – Thierry Henry, David Beckham and the like – those moments of greatness were sometimes sporadic in MLS. Messi, though, seems to provide those moments at each and every turn.

His star no longer shines as brightly as it did years ago at Barcelona or even months ago, in an Argentina shirt. Yet even the slightly dimmed, more fleeting light Messi produces in Miami is worth watching. His first, presumably permanent, exit from the global stage is a good reminder that soon enough it will be gone for ever.

Sports.title: Liverpool sign Barcola in £123m deal and expect Gakpo to stay after City offer £80m
Sports.content:
Bradley Barcola is aiming to win the Premier League after completing his move to Liverpool from Paris Saint‑Germain for an initial £106m, which could rise to £123m. The France international has signed a five-year deal.

Andoni Iraola has prioritised signing wingers this summer after replacing Arne Slot. Barcola follows the arrival of Victor Muñoz as the former Bournemouth head coach aims to rebuild the front line.

“It took a long time but I’m really happy today to be able to play for Liverpool and all I want is to be on the pitch and be able to play,” Barcola said. “I hope to achieve very big things. First of all, winning the Premier League – it’s one of my biggest dreams in my life. It is to do that and to stay in this team in the long term – that’s why I signed a long contract – and I hope I can do it.”

Barcola, who will be 24 on Wednesday, was a long-term target for Liverpool, who have tracked his progress over a number of seasons. Completing the transfer has been delayed while PSG waited to make signings to compensate for the exit of the former Lyon player, who attracted interested from other clubs but was adamant that he was willing to join only Liverpool.

Quick Guide How do I 

“When I knew about Liverpool’s interest in me, I didn’t ask questions and I knew it was a very big club for me,” Barcola said.

The Frenchman will probably be Liverpool’s final incoming. The club are expecting Cody Gakpo to stay after rejecting an £80m offer from Manchester City for the Dutchman over the weekend. Liverpool would regard selling a first-team player at this stage as problematic because it would allow little time to source a replacement.

Harvey Elliott is expected to join Valencia on loan for the season. The midfielder returned this summer from a similar spell at Aston Villa, where he failed to make an impression and although he was part of the pre-season plans, has failed to make the squad for the opening two Premier League fixtures.

Liverpool have targeted younger players in this window, evidenced by the signings of Barcola, the 21‑year‑old Jérémy Jacquet and the 23‑year‑old Muñoz in the hope of building a squad for the long term.

Sports.title: The secrets of Ollie Robinson's glorious summer: Bowling slower, more lacquer and the crucial role of Joe Root
Sports.content:
The secrets of Ollie Robinson's glorious summer: Bowling slower, more lacquer and the crucial role of Joe Root

Unlock more of the best of our cricket coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

There may never have been a better moment for Ollie Robinson to have made his return to Test cricket than the summer of 2026.

As he sat beside Joe Root at Sunday evening’s post-match press conference at Lord’s, it felt like a symbolic alliance, an official welcoming back into the England fold after more than two-and-a-half years in the wilderness.

Even his first Test back, against New Zealand at Lord’s in June, was followed by a mini-hiatus. First a knee injury ruled him out of the second Test at The Oval. Then, with Trent Bridge expected to be flat and temperatures punishing, old doubts resurfaced. Did Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes trust their man to pull through? They did not.

Only when Root resumed the captaincy on a full-time basis did the next phase of Robinson’s career properly begin. And to the seven for 77 he took against New Zealand, he has since added eight for 80 against Pakistan at Headingley, and a ridiculous eight for 35 off 27 mainly unplayable overs at Lord’s. He has been player of the match in all three, improving his career-best match figures each time.

With the third Test at Edgbaston still to come and England eyeing a whitewash, his summer’s work amounts to 23 wickets at 8.34 – the kind of numbers more normally associated with cricket from the 19th century, when batting techniques were rudimentary and pitches even more of a lottery than Lord’s has been of late.

Of the five Tests England have played this summer, they have won the three in which Robinson has appeared, and lost the two in which he has not. The evidence is beginning to suggest it is no coincidence.

There may never have been a better moment for Ollie Robinson to have made his return to Test cricket than the summer of 2026

Joe Root has backed Robinson and the rewards have come - he has been player of the match in all three Tests he has played this summer

So where has it all gone right? In essence, several factors have come together at the same time, allowing Robinson to make the best use of his height and accuracy, as well as the wobble-seam tactics that leave bowlers as unsure as batsmen which way the ball will deviate.

For a start, Robinson’s three Tests have all taken place in favourable conditions: two at Lord’s, where the sideways movement has been lavish and the bounce variable, and one at Headingley, which on a cloudy day remains the spiritual home of English swing and seam.

Then there’s the mediocrity of the Pakistan batting lineup, which is yet to reach 200 in four innings this summer, and has managed only two half-centuries. On and off the pitch, the tourists are a shambles.

Finally, this year’s batch of Dukes balls is proving especially helpful. Root suggested after his side’s 194-run win on Sunday that they now have a lacquer on the seam itself, and that its hardness has created dents in the pitch for the bowlers to exploit. By way of evidence, he said bats were being cracked in practice. Dukes deny they have done anything differently, but Root – who keeps getting out lbw – disagrees.

For tall, accurate seamers like 6ft 5in Robinson, hammering the ball into the surface time and again and waiting for the deviation has become cricket’s answer to the Chinese water torture. Of his 23 wickets this summer, 11 have been lbw and five bowled.

But it would be unfair to ascribe all his success to external factors. After all, in the three Tests Robinson has featured in this summer, his haul of 23 wickets at 192 has outstripped Josh Tongue’s 18 for 250, Gus Atkinson’s eight for 164 and Jofra Archer’s eight for 175. And, of the quartet, only Robinson now boasts a Test average below 20 – the first England bowler with at least 50 wickets to do so since Frank Tyson in the 1950s.

Most importantly, perhaps, he now feels comfortable in his own skin. The wisdom in the Bazball era, often made explicit by managing director Rob Key, was that he was no good to man nor beast while operating at 75mph, but among the best in the world at 82mph.

Yet Robinson is slower now than when he first played for England, five years ago. His average speed so far in this series is 78.12mph, the least rapid of the ten Test series in which he has played, and more than 4mph slower than his quickest: 82.74mph against South Africa in 2022.

For tall, accurate seamers like 6ft 5in Robinson, hammering the ball into the surface time and again and waiting for the deviation has become cricket’s answer to the Chinese water torture

His new-ball alliance with his Jofra Archer (left) has proved a mesmerising study in contrasts – Robinson threatening their pads, stumps and outside edges, Archer examining their reflexes

Even this summer, he has eased up as he has gone along: an average of 79.50mph against New Zealand, followed by 78.39 against Pakistan at Headingley and 77.82 at Lord’s – closer to what the management previously regarded as the unacceptable end of the spectrum. Thanks to the existence of his 90mph colleagues Archer, Tongue and Atkinson, it is a scenario about which both he and England are intensely relaxed.

‘Being able to be my own bowler and not trying to be too attacking has definitely helped,’ said Robinson after Lord’s. ‘With those guys at the other end, it does allow me just to sit in, be very consistent, be very patient, which is my super strength. I probably wouldn’t have picked up those wickets in this series without those other guys.’

In particular, his new-ball alliance with his Sussex colleague Archer has, for Pakistan, proved a mesmerising study in contrasts – Robinson threatening their pads, stumps and outside edges, Archer examining their reflexes and ticker. Equally, Robinson’s economy-rate this summer of 2.4, meaner than any of his team-mates, has meant that the absence of a frontline spinner able to keep opponents in check has not mattered.

Might England have fared better in the Ashes last winter had he been available? We’ll never know, though Robinson himself said he wasn’t match-ready. But he says he has worked harder than ever on his fitness, while Stokes and McCullum, who became so wound up by his attitude during the tour of India in early 2024 that they washed their hands of him, are no longer on the scene.

Not that Robinson intends to lapse into the complacency of old. ‘We’ve just got to be careful we don’t get too comfortable in this four-man attack,’ he said. He seems a more perceptive cricketer now, in more ways than one.

Sports.title: 'Fans have been walking away for years - the people asking questions of the WRU are not the problem': Welsh rugby's civil war deepens as critics' leader hits back at claims scrutiny has been 'toxic'
Sports.content:
Hayley Parsons OBE, a leading critic of the Welsh Rugby Union, has hit out at the governing body and claimed Wales’ national game has ‘deteriorated on all fronts’ under the current regime, refuting the views of WRU chief executive Abi Tierney that she has led ‘toxic’ attacks on its leadership.

The WRU have come under intense fire for their plan to cut one of Wales’ four men’s domestic teams by 2028 amid significant sporting and financial challenges.

Parsons, who was a director at Cardiff Rugby until last year and is one of the country's most successful businesspeople having founded GoCompare, has led the criticism, as part of a 'coalition of the willing' alongside former Wales internationals Jonathan Davies and Tom Shanklin.

In an exclusive interview with Daily Mail Sport last week, Tierney hit back at Parsons and Co, accusing them of ‘toxic tactics’ and insisting the consequences would be ‘cataclysmic’ for Welsh rugby if the proposal to move to three sides didn’t happen.

In July, the WRU confirmed that Cardiff – who are owned by the governing body – and the Newport-based Dragons were given first refusal on licences to continue, leaving one spot in West Wales for the Ospreys and Scarlets to fight for.

‘I have a lot of respect for several members of the board and my issue has never been about individuals,’ Parsons told Daily Mail Sport. ‘It’s about whether the collective leadership of the WRU is working and if you look at the facts, we’re now three years into the current regime and the landscape has deteriorated on all fronts.

Hayley Parsons (left), leader of the 'coalition of the willing' has hit back at claims from Abi Tierney (right) she is leading a 'toxic' campaign to remove the Welsh Rugby Union hierarchy

It has been a torrid few years for Welsh rugby on and off the pitch, with Parsons insisting 'the landscape has deteriorated on all fronts'

'Criticism and asking for accountability given the current situation are not personal attacks and to suggest those questioning the WRU are responsible for falling ticket sales, sponsorship difficulties or damage to the Welsh rugby brand is quite extraordinary.

‘Sadly, the supporters have been walking away for years and Welsh rugby’s problems were not created by the people now asking questions about them.’

Parsons and Shanklin have both called for the entire WRU board to resign on the basis they believe they are not fit to lead Welsh rugby. But such a scenario is far from simple under complex governance rules.

A vote of no confidence in the WRU would have to come from a minimum of 10 per cent of the WRU’s near 300 member clubs forcing an extraordinary general meeting (EGM). In April, that threshold was met but the clubs then asked for the EGM to be cancelled at the last minute after then WRU chair Richard Collier-Keywood confirmed he would be leaving.

That EGM took place anyway, with the WRU insisting it must do so. Parsons said the ‘coalition of the willing’ will speak to WRU member clubs to see if there is an appetite for a second EGM this year.

The WRU insist there is no other option than to cut a team, but their critics have said the way the situation has been handled has been poor, also citing a lack of evidence for the decision. The WRU have said their decision has not been made easily and has been based on rigorous research.

‘I have never taken a position on whether Wales should have three or four professional teams,’ said Parsons, whose previous criticism of both former WRU chief executive Steve Phillips and Collier-Keywood led to their departures. ‘I have yet to see any full evidence or business case required to make such an enormous decision. My concerns are around the governance, transparency and processes by which we have arrived here.

'The only voice that matters now is the clubs. I think the public argument has now gone far enough. The clubs are the shareholders of Welsh rugby and they must now decide whether they have confidence in the current board and executive leadership to take the game forward. Now is the time to act. We are in a small window of opportunity.

'Do we act now or live with the outcome until a further three years has passed? And where will we be then? Down to two regions and an even more inward-looking landscape?

The Ospreys and Scarlets are now battling against each other to survive, with only one spot remaining for a professional team in West Wales

'Over the coming weeks, we will be engaging privately and respectfully with clubs and asking them a very simple question – do you have confidence in the current leadership of the WRU to lead Welsh rugby for the next three years?

'If over 50 per cent of clubs tell us they do, I will accept that democratic verdict and walk away. However, if 50 per cent or more tell us they do not and are prepared to vote accordingly, then an EGM should follow.

‘I have nothing to gain from this campaign. I’m just using my own platform to speak out where others are afraid to. I desperately want to try and make things better.

‘This isn’t about personalities anymore. It’s about the future of Welsh rugby and creating a future that ultimately belongs to its clubs.’

Sports.title: Viktor Gyokeres feels the full force of Mikel Arteta's ruthless streak, Christos Tzolis gets a rude awakening - and the psychological battle facing Arsenal's opponents: THINGS WE LEARNED as the Gunners beat Aston Villa
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta’s ruthlessness is well-documented.

Just ask Aaron Ramsdale or, most recently, Gabriel Martinelli, the pair having been moved on after losing their starting spots.

The needs of the team supersede feelings or perceived fairness.

Viktor Gyokeres is feeling that wrath right now, having failed to come off the bench once again.

It’s a second consecutive match without appearing, only mustering a run out in the 74th minute of Arsenal’s Community Shield victory over Manchester City.

On paper, Gyokeres’ 21 goals across all competitions last season makes the absence of minutes an unusual case.

It is further emphasised after the display of Kai Havertz on Monday night against Aston Villa, an ineffective showing masked by the Gunners’ victory.

The German consistently reminded viewers just why the north London club have been linked with Alvarez, fans desperate for an attacking addition before the window closes.

It’s a second consecutive match without appearing for Viktor Gyokeres, only mustering a run out in the 74th minute of Arsenal ’s Community Shield victory over Manchester City

Havertz's performance in general lacked the composure of a leading Premier League team’s striker, marked by clunky play and an ineffectiveness around the goal frame

On 14 minutes, having been played through by Martin Odegaard, Havertz struck the ball well wide while in the area.

He ought to have done better — and it got worse. Substitute Bruno Guimaraes set the forward free in the second period, yet he could only strike straight at Zion Suzuki.

His performance in general lacked the composure of a leading Premier League team’s striker, marked by clunky play and an ineffectiveness around the goal frame.

All this emphasised Gyokeres’ failure to come off the bench, falling out of favour so badly to not have been turned to by Arteta.

The decision was a surprise and almost a nudge to the ownership ahead of deadline day.

It will not have done the Swede’s confidence any good, or helped him believe he has a place in the team.

The coming weeks are huge for Gyokeres. A failure to play anytime soon could well be the start of a slippery slope out of Arteta’s plans.

Welcome to the Premier League, Christos Tzolis

The plaudits rung loud after impressive displays against Man City in the Community Shield, and Coventry in the Premier League.

He couldn’t put a foot wrong, dancing around players and playing piercing deliveries forward.

Yet, against Villa, he just could not get going in a real crash down to Earth.

The Greek seemed flustered from Matty Cash’s physicality and failed to make an impact on the ball.

He started in a wide position, hugging the touchline, trying to drive inwards.

When he was in possession, Tzolis often gave the ball away or succumbed under the opposition backline’s pressure.

When he was in possession, Tzolis often gave the ball away or succumbed under the opposition backline’s pressure

It was a reversal from the carefree marches in the final third from just a week ago.

To top it off, he received a yellow card for a foul on Cash, before being hooked at half-time after going close to a second bookable offence just before the break.

The performance reflected how Tzolis has been brought in to compete for the left-wing spot, rather than as a certified starter.

He’s only 24, and internally Arsenal view him as a player with a high ceiling for the future.

Plus, the Premier League is arguably the most demanding league in world football.

It’s no coincidence that Arsenal are looking to further bolster their frontline in this window at left wing.

Tzolis is a promising player with a bright future ahead. Yet, putting the burden on him right now at Arsenal would be unwise.

Gunners hold the fort

Arteta’s obsession with a rock-solid defence came into focus once again.

In the 29 matches since the start of last season in which Arsenal scored first, the Gunners have won 26 games, had two draws and lost just once.

Adding to this, the signing of Ezri Konsa has strengthened Arsenal’s most formidable area — and it’s already forming their title defence.

The Gunners weren’t at their attacking best but, as has often been the case in the past year, a sole goal is enough because of their backline.

That is a psychological battle opponents will have to deal with, knowing that even if they don’t concede, scoring a goal will still be extremely hard to come by.

The foundations to further potential trophies are being laid.

Sports.title: Naomi Osaka makes dramatic US Open entrance with striking ensemble honoring NBA legend Allen Iverson
Sports.content:
Naomi Osaka makes dramatic US Open entrance with striking ensemble honoring NBA legend Allen Iverson

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Naomi Osaka honored 'The Answer,' NBA legend Allen Iverson, with her dramatic on-court ensemble at the US Open on Monday night in New York.

Before beating unseeded Russian Anastasia Zakharova 7-6 7-6 in the opening round, the trend-setting Osaka donned Iverson's famed arm sleeves and headband as she walked onto center court at Arthur Ashe Stadium in a wide-tulle floor-length skirt and a sleeveless hoodie.

Interestingly, her grey sweatshirt included burnout newspaper clippings of her career exploits sewn into the tattered fabric.

'It's my, I guess, my tribute to Iverson. I really like him a lot,' Osaka said after the win. 'I mean, Nike said basketball, so I said, 'OK, you want basketball, I´ll give you basketball.''

The look was part of Nike's effort to connect tennis with basketball for this year's US Open. Earlier on Monday, Aryna Sabalenka sported a mesh jersey for her first-round win over Camila Osorio.

But Osaka happens to be a big fan of Iverson, the legendary Philadelphia 76ers point guard, whom she credits for setting trends both on and off the hardwood.

Naomi Osaka honored 'The Answer,' NBA legend Allen Iverson, with her dramatic on-court ensemble at the US Open on Monday night in New York

Facing unseeded Russian Anastasia Zakharova in the opening round, the trend-setting Osaka donned Iverson's famed arm sleeves and headband

The 2001 NBA MVP, Iverson still has a cult following in basketball and fashion circles

'For me, he's a trailblazer,' Osaka said earlier in the week, while donning a t-shirt featuring an old issue of SLAM magazine with Iverson on the cover. 'I think he's also someone that I look up to a lot, because he's done a lot in fashion. Whether it's on purpose or not, he's shifted the way that NBA players dress. I also think the whole conversation around clothes in sports, and also just expressing yourself through style, I feel like he's someone that I look up to in that regard.'

Osaka said she has never met the basketball Hall of Famer, but said 'hopefully he'll see this,' suggesting a future meeting could be arranged.

Fortunately, Iverson caught wind of Osaka and now he's interesting in meeting. As the Georgetown product wrote on Instagram: 'Wow, what a honor!! BIG FAN can't wait to meet you.'

Designers Téla D'Amore and Ev Bravado were happy to use the 51-year-old point guard as inspiration.

'The look references Allen Iverson, more specifically, his gray sweats and the nonconformist cadence with which he moved through the world as an athlete,' they told Vogue. 'Naomi and Law sent two images our way of Iverson wearing a headband—head only—and from there, we had roughly 30 hours to figure out the rest.'

Osaka would exit the court several hours later after surviving a valiant comeback effort by the relentless Zakharova.

Fortunately for Osaka, her serve was strong, as she finished with 11 aces to just three double faults. Howsever, she also finished with 30 unforced errors on the evening.

Now the four-time Grand Slam winner moves on to play Kateřina Siniaková in the second round on Wednesday in Queens.

Osaka acknowledges the crowd in Flushing, Queens before her first-round match

Anastasia Zakharova, of Russia, returns the ball to Naomi Osaka during the first round

Naomi Osaka did not get an easy first-round draw against Russian Anastasia Zakharova

The 28-year-old made a fashionable start to her tournament before the action began, with a number of staged photoshoots inside the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center.

Locations included the media room, the player garden, and Arthur Ashe Stadium itself, with Osaka sporting a variety of different looks shared daily in the build-up to the start of the event's main draw.

Osaka even enlisted Zendaya's stylist Law Roach to assist with the creation of one of the outfits, posing up a storm in an archival Spring/Summer 2003 Dolce & Gabbana dress among the desks and monitors in the press workroom.

On-court however, her outfits have been even more creative.

The four-time Grand Slam champion kicked off this season's majors series at the Australian Open, where she sported an outfit some fans perceived as a 'jellyfish-inspired' look.

Osaka arrived at the Rod Laver Arena with a wide-brimmed hat with a white veil and parasol before warming up in a frilled jacket and dress that looked like tentacles.

In June at the French Open, Osaka was accused of not coming to Paris 'to play tennis' by her first-round opponent Laura Siegemund after arriving for her opening match in a flowing black skirt and corset made from her old Nike outfits before unveiling the shimmering gold dress, which the Japanese star said she thought looked like the Eiffel Tower at night.

The black corset and skirt was designed by couturier Kevin Garmanier, who works with upcycled materials. The pleated black skirt was made using the inner layers of one of her jackets while her old tennis skirts and dresses were also cut up and reused. The outfit was then covered in hundreds of hand-applied crystals.

'I came here to play tennis, not to put on a fashion show,' Siegemund had told TNT Sports. 'And if others want to put on a fashion show, then they should go ahead and do it. That's totally fine with me.'

Osaka made a fashionable run-up to the tournament with a series of photoshoots around the Billie Jean King National Tennis Centre

Join the discussion Does Naomi Osaka¿s bold fashion overshadow her tennis or inspire a new era of athlete expression?

Her second-round opponent Donna Vekic took a different view, calling for critics to 'relax'.

'Some people take tennis way too seriously,' she said. 'Relax, it's just an outfit. I think it's good that she's doing different things, expressing herself through fashion.

'Whether it's good or bad, that's a different thing, it's fashion.'

At Wimbledon, Osaka played with the tournament's strict all-white outfit by turning to Japanese designer Hana Yagi for a kimono-inspired look which referenced both Kill Bill star Lucy Liu, and kirigami, the Japanese art of paper-cutting.

Osaka sported the custom white outfit, covered with embroidered cranes and cherry blossom, both enduring symbols of Japanese culture, with bell-shaped sleeves, an obi belt, and a trailing tulle skirt.

Osaka finished the outfit with a kanzashi hair ornament, historically worn by geisha, and Mikimoto jewellery from the famous Japanese luxury pearl brand.

As Osaka progressed throughout the tournament, she subtly changed the styling of the outfit, opting to wear just the belt and trailing tiered skirt, or the jacket open instead of cinched at the waist.

The Australian Open saw Osaka wear an outfit some fans compared to a jellyfish with its billowing veil

In Paris, the 28-year-old was inspired by local landmark the Eiffel Tour for Roland-Garros

Her opponent in the first round Laura Siegemund was critical of her choice, but received compliments from elsewhere in the draw

At Wimbledon, Osaka was able to get creative with the tournament's strict dress code

After defeating Aryna Sabalenka to book her spot in the quarter-finals however, Osaka changed her tune somewhat, saying that she felt inspired to 'dial back' her focus on outfits, and instead switch it to tennis.

Discussing her photoshoots before the tournament, Osaka shared that she had been inspired by her own experiences spending time on-site late before the crowds pour in.

'I feel like I've just been running around the grounds earlier in the morning just before, like, the crowds come in, and I feel like I've also just been exploring places that I've never been to before,' Osaka shared. 'And I always feel a little, like, am I allowed to be in here? But we keep getting by.

'So I would say we just open doors and kind of like peek in. But also Seb (photographer Sebastian Arriagada) kind of led me into the media room. Yeah, thank you for letting me take photos in your workplace.

'Honestly, like, nothing I do, I do it to make a statement. I think it just ends up being that way,' she said of her eye-catching on-court looks.

'But I literally do the things that I love to do, and I feel like people relate to it, and I'm really glad and grateful for that, because I feel like the type of person I am, a lot of people can see themselves in me. I really, honestly, I love that about myself.'

Sports.title: Unai Emery becomes distracted by transfers and it undoubtedly affects Aston Villa's performances at the start of every season - but here's why they can be an effective counter-attacking side, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE
Sports.content:
The skeleton of the North Stand at Villa Park was an apt background to Unai Emery's grand rebuilding project at Aston Villa.

Villa hope their stadium will be in working order from next season but Emery does not have that much time to get his team firing on all cylinders again.

Put a line through the 4-0 opening day thrashing at Brighton. The Ollie Watkins saga overshadowed that match and Villa were almost beaten before they had started.

The good news for Villa is that we can see the framework of their new plan. The bad news? Zero points and zero goals from their opening two games and a trip to Hull, who have six points from six, on Saturday.

August blues

Across his spells at Arsenal and Aston Villa, Emery has lost nine of his 17 matches in the opening month of the season. For a manager who has had such success at Villa Park and who did a reasonable job in north London, that is an astonishing record.

Unai Emery's August record as a Premier League manager leaves a lot to be desired and he will cite the distraction of the summer transfer window

Emery believes the transfer window should close before the season starts and made the point again in his programme notes. If it did, it would be much better for Emery's state of mind. So meticulous in his coaching and preparation, Emery becomes distracted by transfers and it undoubtedly affects the performance of his team.

Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson made their Villa debuts against Arsenal and there could be more debutants at Hull. Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis should have their moves made official on Tuesday while Leon Goretzka could also feature.

At least the window closing should allow Emery to take a breath. But at some point, he will surely realise he cannot simply write off the first month of the season.

What is the plan?

Strange to say this about a team who have still to register a shot on target this season, but Villa have the makings of an effective counter-attacking side this term.

Suzuki has an excellent kicking range with either foot. The Japanese had shaky moments under the high ball and with one shot from distance on Monday but if Villa can iron out those kinks, they will have a highly effective attacking weapon.

One pinpoint delivery sent George Hemmings scurrying towards the byline and Suzuki was also able to find his full-backs with angled passes.

When he gains match sharpness and starts to understand his team-mates, Jackson will test defences. Given Arsenal's back line is clearly the best in the league, he should have more joy in forthcoming games.

When Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi start to fit into the team alongside Jackson, Villa will have pace. Now it is for Emery to work out how best to use it.

Zion Suzuki has excellent distrubtion range and that will enable Villa to counter-attack quickly

Fitness doubts

Villa's business is exciting on paper but dig a little deeper and there are some concerns. Manzambi was signed for nearly £60m – but with a knee problem. While it was not enough for Villa to pull out of the deal (and it is understood Newcastle were also happy to proceed) it is always a risk to sign injured players.

It does not seem as though we will see Manzambi this side of the international break, either. 'We must be careful with him, admitted Emery.

'He had an injury and we want his comeback to be clear and strong, with no risk. Progressively, he is working individually and is starting collectively with the group this week.'

It is a similar issue with Goretzka, who Emery hoped could be involved against Arsenal but was not fit enough to start. 'He needs more sessions on the training ground to get his fitness and the level we want. He is good and hopefully on Saturday after three days of training, he should be ready.'

It sounds as though including him would be a risk, though. In the Premier League, players at half-speed will quickly be exposed – even if they are Champions League winners.

Emery hoped summer signing Leon Goretzka would have been fit to face Arsenal from the start

Quiet deadline day

Tammy Abraham's decision to stay at Villa Park rather than accept a loan move to Ipswich may have irked Emery, as it stopped him adding another forward to support Jackson and Brian Madjo, who is currently injured.

With Villa's business largely done, the focus on Tuesday will be to find a club for Leon Bailey, who is surplus to requirements but is among the club's higher earners.

Bailey has already rejected the chance to move to Hull and if, like Abraham, he stays, it is hard to imagine him featuring much in the months ahead.

Sports.title: Wild US Open clip goes viral as female player is spotted obliterating her racket in furious outburst... while her opponent celebrates just yards away
Sports.content:
Wild US Open clip goes viral as female player is spotted obliterating her racket in furious outburst... while her opponent celebrates just yards away

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

French tennis star Lois Boisson has gone viral after furiously destroying her racket following her defeat to American star Emma Navarro in the first round of the US Open.

Boisson, 23, was sent crashing out of the competition after a 7-6, 6-7, 6-3 defeat to her US counterpart on Monday afternoon - and refused to hide her emotions after.

After the two players shook hands, Boisson immediately began taking her frustrations out on her own racket, smashing it into the ground numerous times.

Meanwhile, in the same frame, Navarro was waving to the crowd as they cheered on the American star after booking her place in the next round.

It appeared that Navarro was unaware of Boisson's fury following the result.

Their first round match had initially begun on Sunday before being postponed due to rain that hit the area, forcing outdoor action to be paused.

French tennis star Lois Boisson has gone viral after smashing her racket after her defeat

Boisson, 23, was sent crashing out of the competition after a 7-6, 6-7, 6-3 defeat to Navarro

'It was really tough stopping at the point of the match we were at,' Navarro said.

'I just felt like I had worked really hard to get to that point, and then all of a sudden, it's like we're gonna come out tomorrow and we both have a clean slate. It's it's really unique because you feel like you should feel like you're ahead, but you kind of don't.'

Navarro had been leading the contest prior to the match being postponed and managed to hold on despite a rejuvenated Boisson in her way.

'It was really tough. Kind of took me a little while to find my bearings,' Navarro said.

'I think it was after I got broken in the third when I was like, okay, now I'm klnow I'm where I want to be. I'm ready to play.'

The American star will now face the winner of Catherine McNally and Anouk Koevermans' match, which takes place later on Monday afternoon.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.
