To date, the institute has distributed 800 application forms and received roughly 300 completed registrations. Of those, about 156 high school graduates are currently enrolled in the tutorial enrichment program.

The enrichment program provides intensive, short-term academic support in Mathematics, English, Technical Reading and basic science to ensure students meet prerequisites for hands-on vocational instruction.

It also includes orientation sessions on workplace safety, student codes of conduct and expectations for practicum placements.

Staffing and facilities

Institute leaders say most staff positions have been filled, including department heads, instructors and administrative personnel. Temporary classrooms and workshop spaces have been fitted with basic tools and equipment to begin training, while plans continue for permanent facilities and expanded labs.

Officials described the temporary campus as a mix of renovated community buildings and newly constructed simple classrooms and workshops.

Dr. Gono expects phased upgrades as funding and partnerships come online, including construction of specialized labs for radiography and laboratory technology and a purpose-built automotive workshop.

Partnerships with Jackson Fiah Doe Hospital

Dr. Gono emphasized the importance of a partnership with Jackson Fiah Doe Hospital for the allied-health programs.

“We are depending on Jackson Fiah Doe Hospital as the referral hospital that people in Nimba and beyond rely on,” a representative said.

“Training allied-health students locally, with Jackson Fiah Doe Hospital (JFD) partnership for practical placements and mentoring, will benefit the community, the county and the country.”

Under the partnership, allied-health and laboratory students will complete supervised clinical attachments at Jackson Fiah Doe Hospital (JFD).

Hospital staff will provide mentoring, assessment of practical skills and input into curriculum relevance to ensure graduates meet local healthcare needs.

Regional workforce development

Speakers at the ceremony pointed to past collaborations, including training partnerships that supported geology and mining education at Nimba University as models for workforce development that aligns training with local industry demands.

“We know it’s difficult work, but it can be done,” institute leaders said.

“Students trained here will augment human-resource needs across sectors while improving lives in their families and communities.”

Local impact and next steps

Community leaders at the event welcomed the institute, saying it will create employment opportunities, reduce youth unemployment, and supply skilled technicians and health assistants to local businesses and health facilities.

Several small business owners and representatives from county government attended the ceremony and pledged support for student internships and apprentice placements.

The institute is now accepting final registrations ahead of its full-term opening. Officials say they will continue recruitment outreach in schools and neighboring counties and are seeking additional funding and equipment donations to accelerate construction of permanent training facilities.

World.title: Eswatini, Tanzania, Zimbabwe present at HH inauguration
World.content:
The Deputy Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Eswatini, Thulisile Dladla, the President of the United Republic of Tanzania and the President of the Republic of Zimbabwe have arrived in the country, ahead of the inauguration of Zambia’s President-elect Hakainde Hichilema.

All three leaders were received at the Kenneth Kaunda International Airport Presidential Pavilion by senior government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and envoys from their respective missions.

Eswatini and Zambia share a bond rooted in history, culture and the liberation struggle.

Zambia and Eswatini enjoy cordial relations anchored on trade, education, health and cultural exchange within SADC.

Both countries cooperate in agriculture, with exchange programmes in sugar, livestock and small-scale farming.

Eswatini has expertise in sugar production and agro-processing, while Zambia offers opportunities in maize, horticulture and agro-industrial development.

Zambia and Tanzania share one of the strongest partnerships in the region, dating back to the liberation struggle.

The Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority, TAZARA, links Dar es Salaam Port to Zambia and facilitates trade in copper, fuel, maize and manufactured goods. Both countries are working to modernise TAZARA to boost efficiency.

Tanzania is a major gateway for Zambian imports and exports through Dar es Salaam Port, trade includes copper, cement and agricultural products from Zambia, and fuel, building materials and consumer goods from Tanzania.

Zambia and Zimbabwe share historical, cultural and economic ties which includes Victoria Falls and the Zambezi River are symbols of the shared heritage and tourism potential between the two nations.

Trade between Harare and Lusaka continues to grow, with Zimbabwe exporting manufactured goods, steel, agriculture products and energy equipment, while Zambia exports copper, maize, cement and electricity.

Both countries are key partners in the North-South Corridor, which links the region to ports in South Africa and Mozambique.

The two governments cooperate closely in energy through the Kariba Dam and the Zambezi River Authority, in agriculture, mining, and tourism.

Thousands of Zambians and Zimbabweans live and work across the border, strengthening family and business ties.

World.title: M’membe Warns Zambia’s UN Peacekeeping Role At Risk
World.content:
Zambia risks losing its international standing as a respected contributor to United Nations peacekeeping and military observer missions, Socialist Party president Dr Fred M’membe has warned. In a statement, M’membe cautioned of far-reaching consequences arising from what he described as state-sponsored military actions carried out during the August 13 general election period.

M’membe pointed specifically to the death of former Lunte member of parliament and ex-minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, who died during a military raid on a residential property in Kabulonga. He described the incident as the most tragic and damning of a series of events he said undermined the constitutional boundary between the Zambia Army and party politics, arguing that when the military behaves like a political militia, the fundamental trust between the state and its citizens fractures.

The Socialist Party leader was dismayed by what he called the extensive deployment of elite units of the country’s army to directly interfere with the electoral process in favour of ruling party candidates and intimidate citizens into silence. He said the harrowing events of the August 13 elections suggested a deeply disturbing shift, arguing that under the command of Lieutenant General Geoffrey Zyeele, elite army units did not act as neutral guardians of peace but instead appeared as active instruments of intimidation.

M’membe specifically named Lieutenant General Zyeele, Brigadier General Moses Shapwaya and Major Lyempe Kapumpa, stating that the uniform they wear does not grant immunity from accountability and warning that their conduct will cost the nation. He cited Article 2 of the Zambian Constitution, which grants every person, including citizens, residents and state entities, a fundamental right and solemn duty to defend the Constitution and resist any attempt to overthrow or illegally abrogate it.

He further argued that commandos entering civilian polling spaces, threatening electoral staff and interfering with opposition representatives at Mulungushi International Conference Centre represented an unacceptable overreach of state power. According to M’membe, a democracy cannot function when voters and election officials look at their own army not with a sense of security but with fear, a dynamic he said was on full display during the election period.

M’membe stated that the primary duty of the Zambia Army is to defend the Republic, protect its sovereign borders and uphold the Constitution of the Republic of Zambia as established, and that the army was trained to respect and uphold national and international law. He said that for decades Zambia had proudly stood as a beacon of peaceful transitions and democratic resilience in Africa, but that this reputation was severely compromised during the 2026 election cycle.

While government publicists have scrambled to frame the military deployments during the election as routine measures to maintain order, M’membe said the reality on the ground felt like a coordinated suppression of dissent. He argued that no institution should expect to be free from scrutiny of those who gave it their loyalty and support, and those who did not, a pointed reference to the army’s constitutional obligation to serve all citizens regardless of political affiliation.

The warning comes at a particularly sensitive moment, with President Hichilema being sworn in for a second term today even as questions over the conduct of security forces during the election period remain unresolved. Zambia has historically maintained a strong international reputation as a contributor to UN peacekeeping and observer missions across the continent, a status M’membe argues is now genuinely at stake if the concerns he has raised are not addressed.

Whether M’membe’s allegations translate into any formal inquiry, whether domestic or through international channels, remains to be seen. For now, his statement adds another layer of scrutiny to an election period that has already produced a treason case against the losing presidential candidate, dozens of parliamentary petitions, and mounting public debate over the boundary between military conduct and political interference in Zambia’s democracy.

Do you believe the allegations raised by Dr M’membe warrant a formal, independent investigation into military conduct during the election?

World.title: Analysis: What the flood of petitions really tells us about ECZ
World.content:
Political analyst Dr Lawrence Mwelwa has urged the ruling United Party for National Development to abandon its widespread election petitions, warning that challenging opposition wins after declaring the presidential poll free and fair smacks of selective justice. He made the remarks in an interview just as the country marks President Hichilema’s second-term inauguration, with the volume of contested results now spanning provinces well beyond the handful of cases that made early headlines. This situation has significant implications for governance and democracy in Zambia.

Mwelwa argued that if UPND has consistently maintained the presidential election was free, fair and credible, consistency demands the party also respect the verdict of the electorate in parliamentary, mayoral and council elections where it lost. He noted the closure of the Constitutional Court Registry during the presidential petition window, taken over by soldiers, denied the opposition a chance to test the presidential result in court, a decision he said continues to shape public perception of the process and can affect the political landscape in Zambia.

Citing the biblical story of Prophet Nathan and King David, Mwelwa said leadership is measured by fairness and restraint, particularly where a party already enjoys an overwhelming electoral mandate. He warned that justice should never appear selective, especially from a government with little to fear from a strong opposition, adding that a confident administration protects political plurality as an investment in Zambia’s democratic future rather than treating it as a concession. The integrity of Zambia’s political system relies on such principles.

The petitions Mwelwa is referring to extend well beyond the seven cases already before the Lusaka High Court. In Mwandi, UPND’s Sibeso Sefulo lost to independent candidate Iris Kaingu by fewer than 500 votes and has petitioned the result, alleging Kaingu’s agents engaged in vote-buying and interfered with the electoral process. Sefulo has also accused the Electoral Commission of Zambia of failing to properly supervise how results were counted and announced, and is seeking either a full re-run of the election or a recount.

In Ndola Central, former minister Frank Tayali lost by just 819 votes to Resolute Party’s Emmanuel Mulenga and has filed his own petition contesting the result. On the Copperbelt, UPND’s Joseph Kazhila has challenged the outcome in Chingola Central, alleging NRPUP supporters were seen handing out food and money to voters, with one incident reportedly sparking a physical altercation at a polling station. In Kabushi, UPND’s Emeldah Mpumpuni has gone further, alleging that agents for NRPUP’s Tillas Sichinga concealed cash inside pens to distribute to voters undetected.

Further petitions have been lodged in Mwense, Nchanga, Nkana, Kalabo South, Bangweulu, Siavonga and Zambezi Central, while even Lusaka Mayor Simon Mwewa’s own election is now being challenged. Taken together with the Kabuswe, Masebo and other cases already before the courts, the total number of parliamentary and local government petitions filed since polling day now runs into the dozens, a scale of litigation that legal observers say will keep Zambia’s High Court registries occupied for months.

It is worth pausing on what this volume actually signals. A handful of petitions after any election is normal; disputed margins happen everywhere. But when the ruling party itself, the very party that spent weeks insisting the presidential contest was free, fair and beyond reproach, turns around and files petitions against results it lost at parliamentary, mayoral and council level, a fair-minded observer has to ask what changed between the presidential count and everything below it. Either the same electoral machinery was competent everywhere and UPND’s petitions are opportunistic, or something in how ECZ ran this election left enough doubt that even the winning party does not fully trust its own declared outcomes down the ballot.

That question becomes sharper when set against what did not happen. No presidential petition was permitted to be filed and tested in court, in part because the Constitutional Court Registry was closed and taken over by soldiers during the very window the law sets aside for that challenge. If the process was as clean as officials maintain, there was no institutional reason to fear a court testing it. A commission confident in its own numbers does not need the petition window shut by force; it lets the numbers speak in front of a judge. The optics of that closure, whatever the stated justification, invite exactly the scrutiny ECZ has since tried to avoid.

Cases like Mandevu and the Lusaka mayoral contest deserve particular attention in this light. These are races where control of a capital city’s local administration, and by extension patronage, contracts and grassroots political machinery, is at stake in a way that a single rural parliamentary seat is not. If there is anywhere an “underhand method,” as some describe it, would be worth deploying to tilt a result, it is precisely in high-value urban contests like these rather than in far-flung constituencies with little national leverage. That is speculation, not proof, and it should be treated as such. But it is not an unreasonable question for citizens to ask when the party that won comfortably at the top of the ballot is simultaneously contesting results it lost near the bottom.

None of this proves fraud. Zambia’s courts, not newspaper columns, are the proper venue to establish whether any of these petitions have merit, and due process must be allowed to run its course for every single one, Kabuswe’s, Sefulo’s, Tayali’s, and the rest. But an election that produces this scale of litigation, this many allegations of vote-buying and procedural failure, and a shuttered court registry during the one window meant for testing the presidential result itself, cannot honestly be described as Zambia’s smoothest electoral outing. If anything, it may be the most contested since the return of multiparty democracy.

The opposition also has a responsibility in Mwelwa’s assessment. He said it must reject violence, intolerance and reckless language while remaining steadfast in defending democracy and holding government accountable within the law, a balance he argued neither side has fully managed since the election. But healing, he stressed, cannot be achieved through speeches alone, and requires dialogue between political leaders, civil society, the Church and other stakeholders in spaces where difficult issues can be discussed without fear.

Should a party that declares an election free and fair be bound to accept every result on that ballot, even the ones it loses, and should ECZ be compelled to explain why the presidential result alone was shielded from the same courtroom scrutiny it now allows everywhere else?

This is an analysis piece. Views expressed are the author’s own.

World.title: Thirty Parliamentary Poll Petitions Filed In Court
World.content:
About 30 parliamentary election petitions have been filed before the Lusaka High Court, with losing candidates, including former ministers Paul Kabuswe and Sylvia Masebo, seeking nullification of results over alleged malpractice and non-compliance with the Electoral Process Act. The Electoral Commission of Zambia is cited as a respondent in all the petitions and is accused of failing to comply with various provisions of the Act, with petitioners claiming the breaches affected election outcomes in their respective constituencies.

Former Minister of Mines and Minerals Development Paul Kabuswe is challenging the election of Resolute Party candidate Nsofwa Kabwe Lupele in Chililabombwe. Kabuswe polled 8,986 votes against Lupele’s 10,920. He claims Lupele’s campaign was characterised by character assassination, alleging that public rallies were told he was a thief who had stolen and sold copper, and that Lupele accused him of giving mines to a named individual and of employing only relatives while he served as minister.

Kabuswe further alleges that his agents witnessed voters being offered between K50 and K100 at Ishuko Tavern polling station, and that people who had been ferried in his Nissan Hard Body to cast their votes were blocked at Fikolongo in Chitambi ward after rocks were placed across the road, preventing them from reaching the polling station.

In Chongwe East, former Minister of Health Sylvia Masebo is challenging independent candidate Anita Kamanga’s election. Masebo polled 6,798 votes against Kamanga’s 16,058. She alleges that false and defamatory statements were circulated against her, including claims that she lost the UPND adoption process and was only picked because of her position in the party, statements she says were intended to prejudice her candidature and influence voters by portraying her as unfit to lead.

Meanwhile, United Party for National Development candidate Sunday Chanda has challenged Sampa Muswema’s election in Kanchibiya on the National Restoration Party for Unity and Progress ticket, alleging violence, intimidation, corruption, procedural breaches and widespread non-compliance with the Electoral Process Act. In Milanzi, UPND candidate Tylad Lungu is challenging independent candidate Lumankio Zulu, who polled 5,004 votes against Lungu’s 4,424, alleging that Zulu and his supporters disrupted a campaign rally and citing irregularities recorded at three polling stations.

In Chitambo constituency, UPND’s Remember Mutale is challenging Nelson Kabanda’s victory, alleging that Kabanda, of NRPUP, accused him of stealing Constituency Development Fund resources meant for co-operatives, women and youth clubs. In Nyimba South, UPND candidate Olipa Phiri has challenged NRPUP’s Mackson Kapantha’s victory, alleging vote-buying, bribery, violence, corruption and the irregular invalidation or swapping of votes.

The petitions extend well beyond these cases. In Mwandi, UPND’s Sibeso Sefulo lost to independent candidate Iris Kaingu by fewer than 500 votes and has petitioned the result, alleging Kaingu’s agents engaged in vote-buying and interfered with the electoral process. Sefulo has also accused the Electoral Commission of Zambia of failing to properly supervise how results were counted and announced, and is seeking either a full re-run of the election or a recount.

In Ndola Central, former minister Frank Tayali lost by just 819 votes to Resolute Party’s Emmanuel Mulenga and has filed his own petition contesting the result. On the Copperbelt, UPND’s Joseph Kazhila has challenged the outcome in Chingola Central, alleging NRPUP supporters were seen handing out food and money to voters, with one incident reportedly sparking a physical altercation at a polling station. In Kabushi, UPND’s Emeldah Mpumpuni has gone further, alleging that agents for NRPUP’s Tillas Sichinga concealed cash inside pens to distribute to voters undetected.

Further petitions have been lodged in Mwense, Nchanga, Nkana, Kalabo South, Bangweulu, Siavonga and Zambezi Central, while even Lusaka Mayor Simon Mwewa’s own election is now being challenged. Beyond these, independent candidate Clive Miyanda has challenged Emelda Munashabantu’s re-election in Mapatizya before Livingstone High Court, after Munashabantu won with 14,812 votes against Miyanda’s 14,330, a margin of fewer than 500 votes.

Taken together, the total number of parliamentary and local government petitions filed since polling day now runs into the dozens, a scale of litigation that legal observers say will keep Zambia’s High Court and Livingstone High Court registries occupied for months. The petitions span both ruling party and opposition candidates, spread across provinces as far apart as Mwandi in the west and Ndola on the Copperbelt, suggesting the disputes are not confined to any single party’s grievances.

With the presidential inauguration taking place today, attention is expected to shift toward how quickly and fairly the courts can process these cases, several of which involve serious allegations of bribery, intimidation and procedural failure that go to the heart of electoral integrity. For voters in the affected constituencies, the outcome could mean a fresh look at who actually represents them in the National Assembly, adding a layer of uncertainty to the post-election period even as the country marks a new presidential term.

With so many parliamentary results now being formally contested across the country, do you think Zambia’s courts can resolve these petitions quickly enough to give affected constituents clarity on their representation?

World.title: HH To Be Sworn In As Mundubile Sits In Mukobeko
World.content:
President Elect Hakainde Hichilema will be sworn in for a second term at Heroes Stadium in Lusaka today, at a ceremony taking place just days after his closest rival, Brian Mundubile, was moved into Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison on a treason charge. The two developments, separated by little more than 48 hours, capture the sharply divided mood surrounding Zambia’s political transition.

Chief Justice Dr Mumba Malila is expected to administer the presidential oath, with Vice-President Mutale Nalumango taking hers alongside him. Botswana President Duma Boko is among the confirmed foreign dignitaries attending, with his government citing a commitment to strengthening bilateral relations and regional cooperation with Zambia. China’s President Xi Jinping has sent his special envoy, Xian Hui, Vice-Chairperson of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, to represent Beijing at the ceremony.

Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu were transferred to Mukobeko on Sunday morning, lawyer Chifumu Banda has confirmed, following their treason charge on Saturday. The pair are among 16 Tonse Alliance members implicated in the case. Their continued detention has drawn criticism from opposition-aligned voices, who argue the timing, days before the swearing-in, points to political persecution rather than ordinary due process.

Political analyst Dr Lawrence Mwelwa has gone further, urging the ruling UPND to abandon its own wave of election petitions against opposition winners. He argues that having declared the presidential poll free and fair, consistency demands the party respect parliamentary, mayoral and council results too, warning that “justice should never appear selective.” Roughly 30 parliamentary election petitions are now before the Lusaka High Court, filed by losing candidates including former ministers Paul Kabuswe and Sylvia Masebo, who allege bribery, violence, intimidation and non-compliance with the Electoral Process Act.

Adding to the tension, Socialist Party president Dr Fred M’membe has warned that Zambia’s standing as a trusted contributor to United Nations peacekeeping and military observer missions is now at risk. He pointed to the military raid connected to the death of former Lunte member of parliament Mutotwe Kafwaya, arguing that soldiers acting against civilians during the election period undermined the constitutional boundary between the army and party politics. He said commandos entering polling stations and interfering with opposition representatives at Mulungushi International Conference Centre amounted to an unacceptable overreach of state power.

Against that backdrop, an independent post-election assessment by PARI-Africa has concluded that Hichilema’s victory itself is not seriously in dispute. The report states that two separate parallel-vote-count exercises, run by the Christian Churches Monitoring Group and a civil society consortium, both independently placed Hichilema above the 50 percent threshold required to avoid a run-off, with estimates of 56 percent and 57.9 percent respectively. PARI-Africa says the highest published estimate of discrepancy between presidential and parliamentary turnout falls well short of Hichilema’s declared margin of roughly 1.1 million votes, and that Zambia’s priority should now shift toward institutional reform ahead of 2031.

That call for a reset echoes across commentary published today, including analysis describing the inauguration as a chance to convert political stability into tangible delivery, jobs, agricultural productivity, energy security and industrial growth, over the next five years. The commentary argues that political power is a public trust rather than an entitlement, and that the President must govern for every Zambian, including those who did not vote for the ruling party.

Not every story competing for attention today sits inside the political spotlight. Kapoche member of parliament Enock Kaimba says he is still fielding complaints from farmers about suspected corruption among Food Reserve Agency depot clerks, and has promised that any culprit will be reported to law enforcement once sufficient evidence is gathered. It is a reminder that, even as national attention turns to Heroes Stadium, grassroots economic grievances persist alongside the bigger political drama.

For a country that prides itself on peaceful transitions, today’s split-screen of celebration and confinement, mandate and mistrust, leaves an open question hanging over the next five years of Hichilema’s presidency.

Do you think Zambia can hold a credible inauguration and a fair legal process for its opposition figures at the same time, or are the two now on a collision course?

World.title: Baby Born With Teeth: How Mundubile’s Alliance Shook HH But Couldn’t Bite!
World.content:
By Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Part 1

After suffering a shock defeat in the August 2021 general elections, Lungu abruptly announced his retirement from active politics. However, he soon reversed that decision and sought to reclaim leadership of the party.

Like any party recovering from an electoral loss, the PF was expected to hold a convention, usher in new leaders, and focus on rebuilding. That did not happen. Instead, the party inflicted injuries on itself that caused it to hemorrhage, leading to a split into several factions.

The crisis began with a controversial convention in October 2023 that installed Miles Sampa as party leader. A High Court ruling in March 2024 reaffirmed Sampa as PF president for the 2023-2028 term.

Soon after, the Robert Chabinga faction emerged. It was recognised by the Registrar of Societies and in Parliament, positioned itself as a reformist group, and aligned with the ruling UPND.

Once Lungu had gathered enough courage, he declared his return to politics and effectively took over what was left of the former ruling party.

He remained in the background while Given Lubinda held the fort as Acting President, with the firebrand Raphael Nakacinda serving as Secretary General. The group presented itself as the bridge between the Lungu era and the future. It immediately began pushing for an Extraordinary Convention to elect new leaders, even as it fought running legal battles with the Chabinga camp in court.

Following the Constitutional Court’s decision to disqualify Lungu from contesting the 2026 general elections — and of course his eventual passing — the faction eased Lubinda out of leadership and moved to crown Brian Mundubile, the Mporokoso MP, as its new leader.

Positioning itself as election-ready, the group embarked on serious mobilization, particularly on the Copperbelt and in Lusaka. Sensing that the PF would not appear on the ballot papers, Mundubile opted to contest under a little-known political party, the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity — NRPUP. He would eventually enter into a marriage of convenience with several small political parties and form the Tonse Alliance.

In no time, prominent Lusaka lawyer Makebi Zulu, who had assumed the role of the Lungu family spokesperson after Lungu’s death, joined the fray and launched his own Resolute Party. It became the anchor of the PF Pamodzi Alliance.

Before long, Mundubile and Makebi formed an alliance that would later prove to be “a baby born with teeth.” Almost overnight, the partnership turned the political landscape upside down, drawing massive crowds to rallies and record followings on social media platforms.

One thing was clear: although PF had lost the 2021 general elections, its support base had remained intact and was eager to reclaim power by all means.

Frustrated with Hichilema over load shedding, the soaring price of the staple food mealie-meal, and the cost of fuel, the electorate along the line of rail seemed to be drawn to what Mundubile was offering.

World.title: M’membe Lays Out Sweeping Reform Agenda Ahead of Hichilema’s Second-Term Inauguration
World.content:
On the eve of President Hakainde Hichilema’s inauguration for a second term, Socialist Party president Fred M’membe released a wide-ranging policy manifesto calling for structural reforms across government, mining, taxation, and urban planning, framing Zambia’s economic and social system as afflicted by what he termed “high viscosity syndrome” — a condition in which upward mobility is blocked, merit is undermined by patronage networks, and public resources are consumed by an oversized state apparatus.

In a post on his Facebook page, M’membe urged the incoming administration to move decisively from what he described as bureaucratic consumption toward grassroots wealth creation, presenting the proposals as a “loyal opposition” manifesto for the new term.

Cutting the size of government

M’membe called for parliamentary and local council business to move to a fully digital model, arguing this would eliminate the recurring cost of centralized physical sessions in Lusaka and in council chambers nationwide. Under his proposal, members of Parliament and ward councillors would work from constituency-based digital hubs, attending live virtual legislative sessions while being required to spend a statutory minimum number of days each year physically present in their constituencies, except during declared national emergencies.

The manifesto also calls for the permanent abolition of political advisor positions across government ministries and of the office of District Commissioner, with local district administration handled instead by professional, merit-based civil servants. It proposes consolidating Cabinet into a smaller, non-duplicative executive team, with Permanent Secretary appointments made strictly on technocratic grounds and governed by performance-based delivery contracts. M’membe additionally proposed eliminating all Deputy High Commissioner and Deputy Ambassador posts across Zambia’s foreign missions, saying missions should be staffed leanly and focused on trade and commercial diplomacy.

Settling 500,000 youths on productive land

M’membe proposed that savings from downsizing government be redirected into large-scale youth settlement and vocational programs rather than general spending. The plan calls for settling 500,000 trained youths as commercial producers on state-allocated agricultural land across all provinces, with settlement packages that go beyond land titles to include mechanized land preparation, solar-powered boreholes, starter seed and input packs, and training in commercial crop production, poultry, aquaculture, and horticulture.

A parallel vocational track would provide young bricklayers, mechanics, plumbers, and electricians with professional toolkits, equipment-leasing credit lines, and guaranteed access to local public maintenance contracts. M’membe argued this would expand the domestic tax base, strengthen food security, and connect GDP growth more directly to household incomes.

Expanding state equity in mining

On the mining sector, M’membe’s manifesto calls not for privatization but for an expanded state ownership stake. It proposes requiring a minimum 51% equity stake for ZCCM-IH in all new mining licenses, with existing mines offered a 30% state equity option. Dividends from these holdings would flow into a proposed Copper Revenue Stabilisation Fund, which the manifesto models on Chile’s FEES fund and Botswana’s Pula Fund.

The plan also calls for a dedicated Transfer Pricing Enforcement Unit, supported by GPS-enabled monitoring of mineral exports and mandatory quarterly revenue reporting, which M’membe said would close loopholes that have allowed mineral wealth to leave the country undertaxed.

Tax changes

The manifesto calls for the immediate repeal of taxes on mobile money transactions, arguing they function as a barrier to financial inclusion for micro-merchants, market traders, and rural households, and proposes shifting that tax burden onto service providers instead of users. It also calls for widened Pay-As-You-Earn tax brackets to increase disposable household income.

Separately, the plan proposes a new wealth tax targeting luxury real estate, offshore assets, and unproductive domestic capital, along with an escalating land holdings tax on any landholding above 200 hectares. Under the proposal, that land tax would be waived only if the titleholder can show active commercial use of the land through filed turnover tax, income tax, and VAT returns.

A cess on commercial frontage properties

M’membe’s manifesto describes a spatial divide in Zambian cities, where malls, office parks, and commercial plazas sit along main roads while the compounds directly behind them lack paved roads, drainage, water, and sanitation. To address this, it proposes a mandatory Municipal Community Cess applied nationwide to commercial properties on primary and secondary road frontages, including retail malls, corporate offices, fuel stations, banks, distribution yards, and private health facilities.

City, municipal, and town councils would set the rating schedules based on local valuation rolls, traffic volume, and commercial footprint. By law, all cess revenue would be ring-fenced into a Compound Infrastructure and Human Development Fund, barred from covering council salaries or general administrative costs, and instead used to pave internal compound roads, install stormwater drainage, extend treated water networks, install street lighting, build solar-powered digital learning hubs, and construct electrified market stalls for informal traders.

Mining sector labor and environmental provisions

The manifesto proposes a statutory windfall profit-sharing mechanism requiring mining companies to distribute a set percentage of excess revenue to mine workers during periods of high global metal prices, along with mandatory inflation-indexed hazardous duty allowances for underground and high-risk personnel. It also calls for higher, differentiated road tolls on mining transport fleets to offset road wear caused by heavy mineral haulage, which M’membe said currently falls on regular motorists.

On the environment, the plan calls for mining houses to pay a fixed statutory charge per metric tonne of ore extracted — or a set percentage of gross export value — into an independently audited Environmental Remediation and Resettlement Sinking Fund. It calls for real-time, progressive ecological rehabilitation of land, rivers, and vegetation as mining advances, rather than remediation deferred until mine closure, and for immediate resettlement of communities living in industrial pollution zones, with new housing, water access, and soil detoxification. The manifesto further proposes giving the state a statutory first lien over mining companies’ physical assets, processing plants, and export receivables until independent auditors certify environmental reclamation is complete.

M’membe’s framing

M’membe said maintaining the current system — protecting redundant offices, insulating politically connected insiders, and taxing the poor while rewarding speculators — would not break what he called Zambia’s cycle of generational poverty. He said the combined package of measures was intended to “dissolve systemic friction and unleash the latent energy, talent, and enterprise of every Zambian.”

— Based on a policy manifesto released by Fred M’membe, President of the Socialist Party of Zambia.

World.title: North Chief hails HH leadership
World.content:
Chief Mwamba of the Mambwe people of Mbala district has expressed optimism that President Hakainde Hichilema’s administration will continue to roll-out development, following his re-election in the August 13, general elections.

The traditional leader says he remains hopeful that the government will accelerate development in Mbala district, particularly in the road sector.

Chief Mwamba cited the road leading to the Zombe border, as well as the road connecting Kawimbe through Mwamba chiefdom to Kaka, as some of the developmental projects that need urgent attention.

He said improved road infrastructure will boost economic activities and make it easier for people in the area to access markets and essential services.

Chief Mwamba said this in an interview with the media in Mbala today.

“Improved roads will not only enhance connectivity, but will also open up opportunities for our people to participate more actively in economic activities,” Chief Mwamba said.

The traditional leader has also appealed to UPND Member of Parliament for Saise, Remmy Sikazwe, to help facilitate the completion of his palace.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 1, 2026
World.content:
Kenya Aviation Workers Call Off Strike, Resume Duties

Kenya's aviation workers have called off their strike and resumed normal duties after reaching a return-to-work agreement with employers. The deal provides for the immediate remittance of agency fees owed to the Kenya Aviation Workers Union and clears the way for fresh negotiations with the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority over a new collective bargaining agreement. The union has raised concerns about new pay guidelines issued by the Salaries and Remuneration Commission but will seek to address them through the negotiations. The agreement also covers a long-running recognition dispute between KAWU and Jambojet, which will be resolved through the courts. Workers who took part in the strike will be protected from victimisation, intimidation or disciplinary action. Both sides have committed to resolving future disputes through negotiations and established mechanisms.

Namibia Rejects US Health Data-Sharing Proposal

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Namibia has rejected a United States proposal involving the sharing of health data and biological specimens, citing concerns that the agreement could undermine the country's sovereignty, privacy laws and control over its biological resources. The dispute has complicated negotiations over more than N$730 million in potential funding for the country's HIV and tuberculosis programmes. The US said that the proposed agreement would only involve aggregate rather than personally identifiable data. Namibia is exploring alternative funding options to ensure the continued delivery of essential HIV services if a mutually acceptable agreement cannot be reached.

Gabon Victims Demand Accountability a Decade After Post-Election Violence

A decade after violence erupted following former president Ali Bongo's disputed re-election in Gabon, survivors and relatives of those killed are still demanding the truth and accountability. The unrest began after Bongo was declared the winner of the 2016 election. Security forces launched an assault on opposition leader Jean Ping's headquarters, marking the beginning of several days of unrest, looting and violent repression. The true death toll remains unknown. Survivors are now calling for a full investigation. Questions persist over the possible involvement of French nationals and whether French authorities fully cooperated with investigations into allegations of crimes against humanity.

South African Airline Defends Low Flypast Over Cape Town Stadium

South African airline Airlink has defended a dramatic low-altitude flypast involving two aircraft over Cape Town's packed DHL Stadium before the Springboks' rugby match against New Zealand. Flight tracking analysis suggested the lead aircraft passed less than 50 feet above the top of the stadium, prompting criticism and concerns about the risks of the manoeuvre. However, Airlink said the stunt was carefully planned and approved by aviation authorities, with highly experienced crews after rehearsing safety and speed limits. Many South Africans have praised the pilots' precision and skill.

Close 

Niger Uprising Exposes Cracks in Military, Russia Ties

Niger's failed military uprising has exposed deepening frustration within the armed forces, where many soldiers face poor pay, inadequate equipment and dangerous conditions while battling persistent Islamist insurgencies. The unrest has also raised questions about the stability of President Abdourahamane Tchiani's military government and its reliance on Russia's Africa Corps, which reportedly helped suppress the uprising. Analysts said that the events highlight underlying structural problems within Niger's military. They said that Russian support may help stabilise the junta in the short term without addressing the grievances and security challenges threatening its long-term survival.

World.title: South Africa: Limpopo Village Cut Off as Bridge Collapses - South African News Briefs - September 1, 2026
World.content:
Limpopo Village Cut Off After Makeshift Bridge Collapses

The community of Mafarafara village in Limpopo has once again been cut off from a nearby clinic after a makeshift bridge across the Tubatse River collapsed following recent heavy rains, reports EWN. The bridge, built from wooden logs, sticks and corrugated iron sheets, provided a vital but unsafe link between remote villages. Residents must now either swim across the swollen river or pay more than R100 for transport to and from the clinic.

Hawks Officer Questioned Over R3 Million Cash Deposits

The Madlanga Commission has questioned KwaZulu-Natal Hawks Lieutenant-Colonel Deenadayalan Govender over more than R3 million in cash deposits made into his bank accounts between August 2022 and December 2023, reports SABC News. The commission said that the deposits far exceeded his monthly take-home salary. He is being investigated to determine whether the movement of the funds could indicate possible money laundering. Govender has also faced questions about his relationships with tow-truck businessman Clive Naicker and convicted drug dealer Timmy Marimuthu.

Cape Town Signs Cheaper Solar Power Deals

Cape Town has signed two solar power purchase agreements that will add 70 megawatts of electricity from plants in Atlantis and Philippi to the city's grid at prices below Eskom's tariffs, reports EWN. The city said that the future price increases will be linked to inflation rather than Eskom's tariff hikes. This might potentially help to limit electricity costs for residents. Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis said the 20-year contracts are expected to provide R8 billion worth of electricity and reduce the city's reliance on Eskom.

World.title: Uganda: Tooro Kingdom At Crossroads Over Succession
World.content:
Fort Portal, Uganda — The Tooro Kingdom is at a crossroads as some questions arise over the choice of the heir to King Oyo Kabamab Iguru Rukiidi IV, who passed away last Thursday in the United States where he was undergoing medical treatment.

The death has sparked a debate about the future of the kingdom's leadership amid conflicting information about the existence of a successor.

In an official statement, the Prime Minister of Tooro, Calvin Armstrong Rwomire, announced that the late King Oyo left behind a son who could potentially inherit the throne.

President Yoweri Museveni also echoed this claim, stating that the Queen Mother had informed him of the child's existence.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

However, this revelation has been met with skepticism by some royal insiders.

Charles Kamurasi, the Omusunga or head of the Tooro Royal Clan, expressed doubts about the story of the heir. Having known King Oyo since childhood, Kamurasi says he was surprised by the announcement of a son and questioned its authenticity.

He says the claim might be fabricated and emphasized that if no clear heir emerges, the succession should follow traditional lineage, specifically reserving the throne now for the lineage Rukidi III.

In an effort to manage the transition, a 21-member committee comprising elders from the Babiito clan has been established to oversee the traditional succession process. Led by Musuga Charles Kamurasi, the committee includes prominent Babiito elders such as Dr. Isaac Mayombo, Fr Dr. Charles Oyo, Dr. Kagoro Kaijamurubi, Job Karamagi, and Gilbert Mujogya.

The committee is tasked with planning and executting the kingdom's next steps to find a new ruler.

Kasaija Ernest Kusemerera, who is in charge of the Omukama's local security (Omukumirizi), says that as the kingdom awaits clarity, the focus remains on ensuring that the succession process respects tradition and maintains stability within the Tooro monarchy.

David Baguma, one of the ritualists at the Tooro Kingdom, states that if King Oyo's son indeed exists, his grandfather on the mother's side must first present him to the Babiito clan elders. Following this, the clan heads would conduct specific traditional rituals to prepare the heir for his future role before any formal procedures for his succession are undertaken.

Baguma emphasized the importance of maintaining calm during this uncertain period. He reassured the public that even if no clear heir emerges, the kingdom remains a well-established institution with clear protocols and structures to determine the next ruler.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Zimbabweans Abroad Raise Alarm Over Political, Economic and Human Rights Crisis
World.content:
Zimbabweans living abroad have raised fresh concerns over worsening political, economic and human rights conditions in the country, warning that mounting pressures are increasingly forcing citizens to seek opportunities and sanctuary outside Zimbabwe.

The civic movement Citizens Watch Zimbabwe, based in South Africa, has called for urgent action on issues ranging from constitutional changes and the rule of law to the high cost of passports and the decline in public services.

The movement held a media briefing in Johannesburg on Saturday.



Key issues on the agenda included human rights, the rule of law, governance, economic hardship, public service delivery and challenges facing Zimbabweans in the diaspora.

Speaking on the sidelines of a delayed press conference, the movement's president, Patience Chard, said Zimbabweans were increasingly feeling that their rights were being eroded and that Government needed to listen to their concerns.

"The reason why we've gathered here is because the Zimbabweans are going through a lot of difficulties here and back home. So, we're here to speak about all these things. Maybe the government can hear us when we gather together in our numbers. We've got issues of passports. Our passports, their prices are ridiculous.

"And we also got a challenge of our constitution that was recently amended. And that was the main reason why we formed our organisation because of the constitution, we are against the president. Because our rights have been violated as citizens. So that means we no longer Zimbabweans. If we cannot vote, what is the reason for us being Zimbabweans if we can't vote."

The movement has also criticised Zimbabwe's 2030 Agenda, describing it as unconstitutional and arguing that it does not reflect the views and concerns of ordinary Zimbabweans on the ground.
