Lois Uttley, a New York City-based researcher and activist who has worked with communities facing hospital consolidation, said Troy's success reflects a growing bipartisan suspicion of big corporate healthcare organizations.

"The executives of these health systems will tell the community that joining a big health system will be good, that the quality of care will improve, that efficiencies will mean they can keep the costs low," Uttley said. "But what I have seen over the last 30 years of work is that those promises often are broken."

As hospitals close or downsize, she said, communities are catching on. "They're becoming more skeptical."

There's another, more hopeful lesson in Troy's success, said McDonald, the state assemblyman.

"If we take down our swords," he said, "and put out our arms, maybe we can get something done."



KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Judge to decide if Tyler Robinson will go to trial in Charlie Kirk murder case
World.content:
Judge to decide if Tyler Robinson will go to trial in Charlie Kirk murder case

toggle caption Rick Egan/Pool/Getty Images

A Utah judge is slated to hear arguments Tuesday to decide whether there is probable cause to justify a murder trial for Tyler Robinson, who is accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk last fall.

The hearing comes after months of legal wrangling, in a case where prosecutors are seeking the death penalty for Robinson, 23.

District Judge Tony Graf Jr. is scheduled to begin hearing oral arguments at 10 a.m. local time in the courthouse in Provo, Utah. The proceeding is due to be livestreamed by Salt Lake City TV channel KUTV , despite objections from Robinson's lawyers, who say such coverage jeopardizes his right to a fair trial.

Kirk was killed nearly one year ago

Kirk was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, at a rally held at Utah Valley University. The 31-year-old was in Orem, Utah, to kick off his American Comeback Tour. Some 3,000 people were on hand, and were listening to Kirk speak when he was shot, police said.

Sponsor Message

Authorities said video footage showed Robinson, who then lived in Washington County, Utah, arriving and moving around on the campus, as member station KUER reported. They also say he mentioned needing to retrieve his rifle in messages with his then-roommate, with whom Robinson had a romantic relationship.

On the morning after the killing, investigators found a Mauser .30-06 caliber bolt-action rifle that they believe to be the murder weapon.

Prosecutors say Robinson has confessed to killing Kirk, citing a note he left for his roommate and other interactions. Robinson was arrested after a relative turned him in to police, saying the young man "had confessed or implied that he was the shooter," as NPR reported.

Prosecutors are likely to seek the death penalty

Robinson faces one charge of aggravated murder and six other serious counts, including tampering with a witness. Ahead of Tuesday's hearing, the defendant had not yet entered a plea. His attorneys also were urging the judge not to allow video recordings and broadcast of the proceeding, saying it could prevent the pool of potential jurors from being impartial.

Aggravating circumstances will likely play a key role in the case, as they could be used to justify imposing the death penalty for Robinson if he is found guilty. Prosecutors say there is evidence to support a victim targeting enhancement in the case, saying Robinson's alleged motive was political, as KUER reports. They cite evidence such as bullet casings bearing anti-fascist messages, such as "Hey Facist! CATCH!" [sic].

Sponsor Message

The possibility that the shooter endangered thousands of people at the rally is also an important distinction under Utah law. Police say the sniper's bullet that killed Kirk was fired from a rooftop some 150 yards away from the spot on a campus courtyard where Kirk was killed, as NPR has reported. Defense attorneys contend that because only a single bullet was fired — and struck its target — the crowd was not at risk.

Last month, hundreds of people who attended the rally in Utah where Kirk was killed filed requests for victim benefits from the state, seeking mental health and trauma support.

World.title: Made in America: How AI is keeping this U.S. factory competitive
World.content:
Made in America: How AI is keeping this U.S. factory competitive

toggle caption Julie Holder for NPR



LAFAYETTE, Ga. — Inside Roper Corporation, a GE Appliances-owned plant in rural northwest Georgia, autonomous vehicles deliver parts to assembly lines. Robots attach glass cooktops to metal frames. And deployed throughout are AI-powered cameras and sensors, trained to catch mistakes.

"We have these things everywhere out here," says Tony Gabbert, the plant's director of manufacturing operations.

If a camera spots an anomaly — the wrong gasket installed on an oven, for example — the system will shut that part of the line down and start playing loud music.

Sponsor Message

"If you hear AC/DC, you know to come running down here," says Gabbert. "The quicker we know what the problem is, the quicker we can fix it."

Pressure to be perfect

toggle caption Julie Holder for NPR

Today, American factories are under extraordinary pressure to perform perfectly. They must turn out flawless products, efficiently, in order to compete with imports from rivals overseas. It used to be up to people to achieve good results. Now, manufacturers are leaning heavily into advanced technology and artificial intelligence to up their game.

The goal at GE Appliances has always been to minimize errors, equipment downtime and scrap — and to ensure every appliance produced passes inspection and gets sent out to the consumer, problem-free.

Now, with AI bringing its analytical prowess to troubleshooting, perfection seems tantalizingly within reach.

"We're not shooting for 97. We want to run 100 every day," says Gabbert, referring to a performance metric used in manufacturing.

Already, the gains made are significant. GE Appliances' vice president of manufacturing Bill Good estimates the company saves between $1.5 to $2 million per year with every percentage point of improvement.

Data-driven transformation

toggle caption Julie Holder for NPR

GE Appliances has worked on collecting data through cameras and sensors for more than a decade. With millions of lines of data now generated every day, the company's data platform Brilliant Factory can provide a real-time view into how each of its nine major appliance plants is running, down to the workstation.

Sponsor Message

That means from company headquarters in Louisville, Ky., Good can see which machines are down and why, how many appliances are going to the repair bay and why, which parts are getting scrapped and how much that scrap is costing the company.

"In the old days, I would call my plant manager, and I'd say 'How you running today?'" he says. "Now I'll call them and say 'Why are you running so poorly?'"

As powerful as visualizing that data is, having AI analyze the data and figure out where problems lie has been transformative, Good says.

Plant managers can now start their days with AI-generated reports on not just where there might be problems, but how to solve them.

AI will flag if the data shows that a motor is running hot, a sign it may soon give out. The plant can then schedule a repair and avoid an unexpected and costly breakdown. Halting just one assembly line can cost the company between $300 and $500 per minute, Good says.

"The name of the game in manufacturing is speed — speed at which you see the problem, speed at which you solve the problem," he says. "Literally, minutes matter."

'It can outthink me'

toggle caption Julie Holder for NPR

Good says AI has shrunk the gap between manufacturing veterans like him, who have seen every problem in the book, and those who may only have five years on the job.

"It can outthink me," says Good, who's been in manufacturing for nearly 40 years.

Still, he doesn't worry that AI will replace him.

"At least in the foreseeable future, I don't see AI replacing large populations of humans," he says.

In fact, the way he sees it, AI is enabling GE Appliances to manufacture in the U.S. The more efficient they are, the better positioned they are to compete with factories overseas that can pay their workers lower wages. GE Appliances, which in 2016 was acquired by the Chinese conglomerate Haier, recently added 600 jobs in Georgia as part of a $180 million expansion.

Sponsor Message

The company has started using AI to optimize staffing. Currently, if they find they don't need as many workers in one part of the plant, they'll move them to other tasks. They're also using AI to forecast market demand. This allows them to make last-minute decisions about what products to make on any given week.

Good says all of this is helping GE Appliances thrive despite the cutthroat competition.

"You have to be faster, better, more flexible. That's the only thing that neutralizes the threat," he says.

World.title: AI wealth is creating a 'mansion shortage' and upending San Francisco's housing market
World.content:
AI wealth is creating a 'mansion shortage' and upending San Francisco's housing market

toggle caption Heather Diehl/Getty Images

SAN FRANCISCO — On a recent Sunday, 30-year-old Collin Russell was desperately visiting open houses, looking to buy a place in the city that his wife is from. They left two years ago so he could go to graduate school, and they moved back to San Francisco in June, just as the housing market here has exploded.

"I couldn't have timed it worse, honestly," he lamented after touring a condo in the affluent neighborhood of Presidio Heights.

His new job is in tech investment banking — a solid income. But finding a two-bedroom home within their budget these days has felt impossible.

Sponsor Message

"Maybe every two weeks, a new one comes on and then it's just a feeding frenzy. The last place I saw today had 10 people, and I got there two minutes after it opened," he said.

San Francisco is the epicenter of the boom in artificial intelligence, and it's intensifying competition in an already pricey housing market. AI companies are expanding fast as the tech industry brings many workers back to the office. Startups Anthropic and OpenAI are also preparing to go public, a process that has sparked a flood of wealth already, with a bigger one to come.

The jump in demand is a sharp turnaround after a pandemic slump, and it has sent home and rental prices skyrocketing. It's also raising fears of more displacement in a city where previous tech booms and a longtime housing shortage have already driven out many who could no longer afford to stay.

Record-setting sales and a "mansion shortage"

Inside the condo that Russell toured, a steady stream of people checked out the modern three-bedroom with big windows facing a shared garden. At 1,600 square feet and an asking price of $2 million, it qualifies as entry level for families here and is a steal in the current market, said Paul Kitchen, a real estate agent with Compass brokerage.

Sponsor Message

"We've done more business this year than we've done ever, setting records throughout," he said.

Compass finds that the median home sales price in San Francisco has skyrocketed 25% from a year ago. Kitchen has seen some properties pushed even higher than that as sales frequently turn into bidding wars.

"We've had clients who've bid, and it turned out there were 50 offers," he said, which takes an emotional toll on the many who lose out. "That's 49 agents who've talked through the night with their clients, people that have envisioned themselves there — they've talked to their banker, their loan officer."

toggle caption Jennifer Ludden/NPR

At the highest end, even all-cash offers of $25 million and more have gotten outbid. "You have to laugh just because it is so ridiculous and so beyond the pale," he said.

This new demand with a lack of supply, especially of single-family homes, has been dubbed a "mansion shortage" by Compass and others.

"In June, there were 44 home sales that went at least a million dollars over the asking price," said Mike Simonsen, who tracks citywide sales as chief economist for Compass.

Many AI executives are in their mid-30s or early 40s with young kids, he said. "This group is like, 'We got to put the kids in kindergarten next week, right? So we need to get a home now,'" Simonsen added.

So far, the price spikes are concentrated in a few upscale neighborhoods. But history shows that over time there will be a ripple effect across the Bay Area and beyond, as people priced out look elsewhere.

"You can't buy in California — you got to move to Texas. And that drives home prices up in Texas," Simonsen said. "So a shortage in California drives home prices up in a lot of the rest of the country."

Renters also face bidding wars

The wave of AI wealth is also upending San Francisco's rental market, as real estate agents say there's an influx of highly paid 20-somethings not yet looking to buy who can easily afford $10,000 a month in rent.

Sponsor Message

Ally Alessio, 27, and Aidan Cahill, 31, felt the pressure when they decided to move to San Francisco from San Diego and faced a brutal monthslong search online. An apartment listing on Zillow "would be posted four hours ago, and it already had 200 contacts," said Alessio. "It's crazy to see how quickly things are coming off the market."

When the couple did apply for places, they sometimes got notified that a person ahead of them had bid the rent higher. "And so it creates this competitive nature of almost, like, homebuying, but for rental markets, which is odd," said Cahill.

toggle caption Jennifer Ludden/NPR

Even though they were still in San Diego, they realized they needed to move faster. When a listing for a two-bedroom with wood floors and high ceilings went online in the middle of a weekday, they jumped on it. Within hours, they'd reached out, applied and — after a friend in the city visited the apartment the next day — took it sight unseen.

They feel lucky to have snagged it in the current market, despite the $5,200 rent that feels more like a mortgage. "You do basically have that feeling when you pay your rent — 'Yeah, I could probably buy a home right now,'" said Alessio.

In the Mission District, at a hillside park with a view of downtown, 29-year-old Alex Brenner described the stressful apartment search that he and his fiancée just went through, including lines at open houses.

"Best-case scenario, there's five people there. Worst-case scenario, there's a line of 25," he said. "Just down the street over there, we looked at a place, and were waiting in line, and it didn't even have a living room."

Before they even saw one apartment, the rent was bid up by $500, then another $500. They'd been hoping to find a two-bedroom since they both work from home, but settled for a larger one-bedroom.

Sponsor Message

"It's actually ridiculous," he said, "and making it hard for people like me and my fiancée who work in healthcare, who don't work in the tech industry, and like our jobs. We don't want to, you know, jump ship just to afford rent."

Brenner has a brother here and a new baby nephew, and he loves the outdoorsy lifestyle. But the dramatic price spike has given him pause about the high cost of staying long term.

toggle caption Jennifer Ludden/NPR

Even for many who live in rent-controlled buildings, this sudden price spike will have an impact. "A teacher, a service worker or a nonprofit employee or family trying to move today, they become financially trapped in place," said David Blosser, who directs leasing at the apartment agency RentSFNow.

Blosser's agency does not allow bidding wars. But he hears from real estate agent friends about the lengths that potential renters are going to.

"They have told me someone offered them a brand-new Samsung television, if they give them this unit at this rate," he said.

Luxury housing is expanding across the U.S.

San Francisco's AI wealth is adding to a nationwide boom in luxury housing "over the last decade across the country, in line with the expansion of the wealth gap," said New York-based market analyst Jonathan Miller.

Such buyers are more likely to pay with cash or other income, rather than a mortgage, and they've benefited greatly from the rising stock market.

For a dozen years, Miller has tracked U.S. home sales in what he calls the "super-luxury" market — $50 million or higher. When he started, "there might be one every three months," he said. Now he counts "something like 45 last year nationwide, and this year we're on track to tie it."

That will include a Bay Area estate sold in August for $70 million to someone the listing agent said was in AI, according to The Wall Street Journal. The home had originally been listed for significantly more.

Sponsor Message

But such ultra-high-end sales generally have little to do with local markets, Miller said, as "the high end is getting further away from everything else."

Instead, he sees what's happening with San Francisco's growing AI industry as the "New York-ification" of real estate.

"It's like buying a one-bedroom apartment without great views in Manhattan and it costs you $3 million, and you tell that to somebody in Des Moines, Iowa, and they're like, 'There's something wrong with you,'" he said.

But the price isn't really about the property. It's based on the value of being in a specific location.

"This is the sort of repricing that San Francisco is going to go through for the next bunch of years, just because of this economic driver," he said.

World.title: Days after Trump announces Venezuela oil deal, White House fills in some of the details
World.content:
Days after Trump announces Venezuela oil deal, White House fills in some of the details

toggle caption Matias Delacroix/AP

WASHINGTON — The White House on Monday said it's partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners as part of President Donald Trump 's push to tap into Venezuela's oil industry, setting up a deal that will give the Pentagon a stake over roughly a fifth of the country's vast oil reserves.

The Trump administration released more details on Monday night, days after Trump announced what he described as the biggest oil deal in history. The sweeping agreement has been met with skepticism from analysts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela's production, but Trump and his aides are pitching it as a chance to develop a new oil giant in the Western Hemisphere.

As part of the deal, the U.S. is creating a private company as a joint venture with NABEP — a detail the White House had withheld for days. NABEP, owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, is already the second largest operator in Venezuela, behind Chevron.

Sponsor Message

Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez is giving the company 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels. Many of those fields were previously owned by Russian or Chinese firms, the White House said.

In a statement Monday, Betancourt said Venezuela is "blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential," adding that the deal will "unleash that potential to the great benefit of both Venezuelans and Americans."

The company said Betancourt had been involved in the Venezuelan oil industry for more than 15 years and said the company has more than 5,000 employees and more than 10,000 contractors.

The deal will give the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital a 35% ownership stake in the company, the White House disclosed Monday. The U.S. will also be guaranteed a right to purchase 20% of the output at cost, orchestrated through the State Department.

The agreement was signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Betancourt's company has agreed to put up $100 billion in new oil infrastructure investments.

The deal won't affect US gas prices anytime soon

Trump has been pushing to boost oil production in Venezuela since the January military mission that captured then-President Nicolás Maduro on federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.

Sponsor Message

The White House claimed the deal would be "at zero cost" to the U.S., and said the government would have veto power on board members — the majority of whom would be U.S. citizens.

"NABEP will have reputable U.S. auditors, lawyers, and advisers and the U.S. government's agreement with NABEP is governed by U.S. law and is subject to the jurisdiction of U.S. courts," the White House said in a fact sheet about the deal.

Former U.S. government energy advisers have cautioned that the deal comes with political risk, since future administrations in Venezuela or the United States could challenge the deal. Even if the agreement holds, analysts say it could take years to turn around Venezuela's dilapidated energy sector.

Trump, who says the plan will reduce gas prices, acknowledged Monday that Americans won't see change right away. Asked about a timeline at the White House, Trump said "it could be a little bit" for prices to fall, and he played down analyst predictions that it could take years.

"If it was two years, you know, that's a short period of time," he said.

Trump said the deal will provide a source to help refill America's strategic oil reserves, which have been drawn down as the Iran war chokes global oil shipments. He added that Venezuela's heavy oil will also go toward producing asphalt and other goods.

"It was this unbelievable value that was sitting dormant," Trump said of Venezuelan oil. "But we're going to be taking all of that."

Rodríguez has also spoken in favor of the deal, describing it as a chance to modernize the Venezuela's oil industry and accelerate its revival. Facing criticism that the deal cedes Venezuelan resources to the U.S., Rodríguez insisted her country's sovereignty remains secure.

Sponsor Message

Questions remain on Capitol Hill

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill said Monday that they were looking for more information about the agreement.

Rep. Rick Crawford, the Republican chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, said he wanted to hear details from the Trump administration "hopefully sooner rather than later."

Sen. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said a deal that uses the military to boost a private oil venture should be rejected and said he wanted a full accounting of the legal authority for the agreement.

"President Trump's effort to turn the U.S. military into an investor in Venezuelan oil is a blatant abuse of power and taxpayer dollars," Reed said in a statement.

The new details were released a day before Trump plans to meet with a group of large and small oil refiners to discuss ways to increase America's capacity to refine oil into gasoline.

The meeting occurs as the Iran war has driven prices at the pump to a national average of $4.08, a 28% increase over the past year, according to AAA.

The White House has said that increasing the number of refineries and expanding the capacity at existing facilities would eventually reduce prices for consumers. The administration also sees the need for more refineries to process oil from Venezuela.

Also attending the meeting will be Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Jarrod Agen, the director of the White House National Energy Dominance Council.

World.title: Hindu pilgrims, on arduous trek, among Nepal's missing
World.content:
Hindu pilgrims, on arduous trek, among Nepal's missing

toggle caption Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP

SOCORRO, India – Two sisters sit on chairs, apparently stunned.

In halting sentences, in an Instagram post , they explain: "Our parents Shubhakshi and Sumit were in Nepal," one young woman, who introduces herself as Varnika says, "when the floods hit."

Since the devastating floods in Nepal last Wednesday, social media has been awash with appeals from people searching for their loved ones. Most posts include photographs of those missing people, with phone numbers to call for more information.

Many had one thing in common: they were pilgrims on a sacred journey to Mount Kailash, a Himalayan peak located in Chinese-held Tibet, and at the moment of disaster they were at, or near to, a once-popular border crossing, one of the worst impacted locations.

Sponsor Message

Deadly incidents at pilgrimages are not unusual: from a stampede at a religious gathering known as the Kumbh Mela in India that killed more than 30 people in 2025, to a panicked crush in the Muslim holy city of Mecca during the Hajj that killed more than 2,400 people in 2015 .

But a flood sweeping away worshippers on pilgrimages centered in the Himalayas is rare. Even more so that it was triggered, in part, by climate change—an ominous sign for the future of pilgrimages in the region.

It's unclear how many pilgrims remain unaccounted for by local authorities, but they appear to be a large cohort among the 853 foreigners that China and Nepal have reported as missing.

Indeed, according to posts on social media and interviews with journalists, they may represent many of the 287 missing Indian nationals reported by the Indian government on August 29th—the most recent date such figures were released—as well as the 80 missing U.S. citizens.

They include Vivek Srivastav, according to his brother-in-law Guarav Khare, who initially posted about Srivastav on X. He told NPR that Srivastav had settled in Atlanta decades ago.

A biotech scientist, he became an American citizen 5 years ago; the kind of person who believed that "life is all about serving people." Since the floods, "we have been in search for him," Khare says, of Srivastav's wider family.

Sponsor Message

Holy mountain draws devotees

Srivastav had been on a pilgrimage alongside 10 others to the same Himalayan mountain, Mt. Kailash, which is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and indigenous Tibetan religions.

Visiting Mt. Kailash for the faithful "is one of the most important things that they will do as they approach the last leg of their life," says Hindol Sengupta , a historian of religion.

Hindus believe Mt. Kailash "is the ultimate abode of Lord Shiva," one of the most important deities in Hinduism and a god associated with power and destruction.

"Gods walk among men in these mountains," Sengupta says. "This is very deeply embedded in what I would call the Hindu imagination of the world."

Mt. Kailash is considered so sacred that scaling this mountain is prohibited, according to Sengupta. For generations, pilgrims have instead walked some 33 miles around its base. It's a roughly 3 day trek that is made harder by the extreme altitude.

The physical exertion required is why Shubham Kumar says he and his wife had begged his parents-in-law not to go. Sanghamitra and Debarshi Banerjee were in their sixties, and part of a group of 32 pilgrims who are now missing. "It is a very difficult route," he recalls telling the older couple. "But they were destined to go."

As is the case with many of the missing pilgrims, Sanghamitra and Debarshi Banerjee's last contact with Kumar came as they reached a border crossing between Nepal and Chinese-held Tibet. "After that, there is no communication," he says.

That crossing was close to where part of a glacier broke away and smashed into a river valley 4,000 feet below . Fast-flowing water pushed forward the ice and accompanying rock. Footage from that border area captured Wednesday showed a furious wave of material engulfing a multi-story border facility known as the Gyirong Port Immigration Office .

Sponsor Message

Pilgrimage group confronts disaster and mourns

"A well-constructed concrete building just vanished," lamented Jagadish Vasudev , widely known as Sadhguru, who leads a global spiritual group known as the Isha Foundation .

That foundation lost contact with 3 guides and 77 pilgrims from 19 countries, including the U.S., Canada and European nations.

During a solidarity event with Nepalis in Kathmandu on Sunday , Vasudev said the Foundation's tours functioned with a "silly discipline," he said: "we have to be the first group, because at the immigration center between Tibet-Nepal border." This was all about avoiding delays, he explained: "If you come a little later, it'll take hours to pass through."

So when Praven, the volunteer guide leader for the Foundation's group, reported they had reached the border crossing at 9:05am, "I said: good," Vasudev recalled. "I only wish we didn't have so much discipline."

He urged followers to accept that their fellow pilgrims had died. "Death is a resounding silence," he said. "The only thing left right now is rescue, relief, reconstruction."

Vasudev also encouraged people to accept why the pilgrims had died. "Don't try to find mystical solutions to this," he said. "This is the reality of our existence right now."

"It's important we understand," he said, that "human activity" had caused "all this," and he called on countries that straddle the Himalayas to save the mountain range.

Global warming has been causing the glaciers to lose ice at a rate that has doubled in the past quarter century, according to ICIMOD, an environmental advocacy organization that focuses on the high mountains of Asia, including the Himalayas.

At stake, warned Vasudev, wasn't just the physical mountain range, but the heart of Hindu culture and civilization. "Going to Kailash is not a death wish," he said. "It's important for our culture, it's for our civilization." It is also, he added, "very important for Nepal's economy."

Sponsor Message

Awareness of climate change's role in Himalaya disaster

But the increasing popularity of the pilgrimage now forms part of the broader pressures on the Himalaya range, says Sengupta, the historian of religion. For generations, he says, "people have had to go through a lot of arduous trekking," he says, to reach the base of Mt. Kailash. "Part of devotion was this journey."

But as Hindus grow wealthier, particularly in India, "obviously many more people now wish to go there and therefore roads have to be built and faster and bigger cars go through those roads," he says.

Such infrastructure is popular with long-deprived locals and, he says, it has allowed "tens of thousands of more people to go to these shrines." But perhaps not all are meant to come, Sengupta says. "The ecology is getting destroyed."

It was not over-tourism, per se, that triggered the collapse of a glacier and the subsequent flash floods that have so far killed hundreds of people. But the way tourism numbers are managed could benefit from a broader respect for the fragile mountain ecosystem, says Sengupta—and perhaps for the pilgrims too.

With something that is genuinely sacred to so many, visitors and locals alike may need to do a better job, he argues, "ensuring that pilgrims don't have to die when they march out, as it were, to fulfill their devotion."





Omkar Khandekar in Mumbai, India contributed reporting.

World.title: To shelve or not to shelve: How the American alcohol response varies widely by province
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the trade dispute with the U.S. drags on after a deal recently fell through, the availability of American alcohol in Canada remains largely unchanged.

While it's sometimes reported there's a ban on American alcohol in the country, the reality is more complicated.

"Embargo doesn't fit. It's not a tariff, it's not a blockade and it's not a boycott," said Robert Huish, a Dalhousie University professor in Halifax who studies sanctions, tariffs and economic weapons.

"It's almost like a flex move, really, where the provinces are able to say, 'Hey, look, we're making this choice for the short term,' and there seems to be a lot of public support for that choice there," said Huish.

The reality is that the availability of American alcohol varies widely across the country — from full availability in Alberta to unavailable at the LCBO, Ontario's Crown-run liquor retailer, which happens to be one of the largest purchasers of alcohol in the world.

Many other provinces, including Nova Scotia, happen to be somewhere in the middle.

"That choice to not shelve product, that's been a very powerful symbolic message, right to the Trump White House," Huish said. "He's reacted to it personally."

What follows is a province-by-province look at the availability of American alcohol across Canada.

British Columbia

While American alcohol has remained off the shelves at the Crown-run B.C. Liquor stores since early last year, warehoused American product can still be purchased by private liquor stores, restaurants, bars and pubs from the province's Liquor Distribution Branch.

Alberta

Alberta, which has a private liquor retailing system, has a public liquor importer, Alberta Gaming, Liquor & Cannabis (AGLC). In March 2025, the importer announced it would no longer accept American alcohol imports, though retailers were permitted to sell existing inventory.

In June 2025, Alberta lifted the import ban.

Saskatchewan

Saskatchewan uses a model similar to Alberta's. The Crown-run Saskatchewan Liquor and Gaming Authority acts as the main distributor, while retail stores are privately owned.

In March 2025, Saskatchewan Liquor announced it would stop purchasing U.S. alcohol, but resumed imports three months later.

Late last month, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe announced a 50 per cent retaliatory levy on American alcohol products.

Manitoba

Manitoba's Crown liquor retailer, Manitoba Liquor Mart, removed American alcohol from store shelves in March 2025, while the Crown-run distributor halted imports at the same time.

In December, warehoused American alcohol went back on the shelves.

After the breakdown of the U.S. trade deal and resulting imposition of tariffs on Canadian goods, Manitoba Liquor pulled the remaining U.S. alcohol off the shelves late last month.

Ontario

Ontario has maintained the strictest boycott of American alcohol of any province.

After removing American alcohol from LCBO shelves and halting U.S. imports in March 2025, the province has refused to sell off any of its roughly $80 million in warehoused stock, unlike most other jurisdictions.

The province has also resisted calls to sell the product for charity.

Quebec

Quebec has maintained the second-strictest boycott, stopping imports of American alcohol and pulling stock from the SAQ in March 2025.

However, in February, the province resumed selling roughly $9 million worth of American product that was at risk of perishi ng, such as ready-to-drink beverages and sake.

New Brunswick

New Brunswick's Crown-run alcohol retailer and distributor, ANBL, stopped purchasing American alcohol in February 2025 and pulled existing stock from shelves a month later.

In May 2025, ANBL resumed selling American alcohol to select buyers, such as private agency stores. By January 2026, American alcohol had returned to all ANBL retail channels.

Nova Scotia

Nova Scotia's Crown-run alcohol retailer and distributor, NSLC, stopped buying American alcohol in January 2025 and pulled it from the shelves in March 2025. In December, it resumed selling the warehoused product.

Prince Edward Island

P.E.I.'s Crown-run alcohol retailer and distributor, the P.E.I. Liquor Control Commission, stopped buying American alcohol in March 2025 and pulled it from the shelves that same month. In December, it once again began selling its warehoused stock.

Newfoundland and Labrador

The Crown-run Newfoundland and Labrador Liquor Corporation removed American alcohol from its shelves early last year and has not ordered additional inventory since the trade dispute began.

In December, sales of the existing American stock resumed.

Yukon

The Yukon Liquor Corporation stopped placing orders for U.S.-made alcohol products in March 2025. While existing stock is not available in the six corporate stores, private licensees can sell from their existing inventory and the corporation's warehoused stock.

Northwest Territories

The Northwest Territories Liquor and Cannabis Commission stopped buying American alcohol in March 2025. Existing stock was never removed from the shelves and continues to be sold through regular retail and wholesale channels. As of the middle of last month, the commission said there was less than $5,000 worth of U.S. alcohol on the shelves.

Nunavut

The Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission stopped purchasing American alcohol in March 2025 and pulled it from the shelves at the same time, but resumed some sales in July 2025.

"American alcohol products are held in NULC inventory, but are not currently being sold in NULC stores," a spokesperson wrote to CBC News.

Even with American alcohol available for sale in many parts of the country, interest remains tepid as Canadians seek out local alternatives, said Huish.

"That's something that is sort of growing out of the disdain for this consistent belligerent behaviour from the U.S.," he said.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Used bookstores navigate 'suspicious' bulk orders amid AI book-shredding fears
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Used booksellers in Canada are navigating how to handle mysterious bulk orders, as suspicions grow that companies are buying up their old books so they can be scanned for AI training — and then trashed.

Their concern stems from a U.S. copyright lawsuit brought against AI giant Anthropic, which revealed the company was spending millions on physical books, chopping off the spines to quickly scan the pages to train its large language model Claude, and discarding the remains.

A 404 Media investigation revealed two weeks ago that large orders of books are also going to an Amazon facility in Las Vegas to undergo "destructive scanning" for LLM training, offering further evidence that the practice may be widespread. Similar concerns are being raised by bookstore owners in Australia and elsewhere.

Physical books, particularly those published before OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, are in demand for AI companies. That's partly because some experts say the language models degrade when repeatedly trained on their own output, so they need to be fed with content that is guaranteed to be free of AI-generated text.

Some AI companies have also encountered legal issues using copyrighted digital content.

'There's something not right here'

Peter Sellers, proprietor at Sellers & Newel bookstore in Toronto, says bulk book requests in the past have come from designers staging homes or film sets, and typically are accompanied by colour and size requirements.

But around June, he started getting "very suspicious" calls for bulk orders for seemingly random lists of books, he told CBC News in an interview.

"It's kind of tempting, because I can unload a lot of stuff that may otherwise be unsaleable," he said. "And then you start thinking about it — no, no no, there's something not right here."

WATCH | More about Anthropic's destructive scanning: The facts about AI companies destroying books | Duration 2:40 Anthropic bought millions of physical books to train its AI chatbot Claude. Here are the facts about the books that were ‘destructively scanned.’

On June 10, he received a message on LinkedIn from someone claiming to represent data engineering company Innodata, saying they were "currently looking to purchase large volumes of secondhand books" and "exploring potential sourcing partners."

Sellers said he ignored the request and thought little of the message until he later read an article about AI book scanning. Suddenly, he said, all those "odd" requests seemed to make a lot more sense.

"My whole staff is now attuned to this," he said.

"If somebody wants stuff in bulk, the answer's no — unless you're a designer that we know or someone we've dealt with, or you've got some kind of legitimate credentials and you want these books for a legitimate reason," he said.

Innodata, based in Ridgefield, N.J., offers "data and domain expertise" for AI projects, according to its website, which says it works with "seven of the world’s largest tech companies." Innodata recently posted a senior book buyer job on LinkedIn.

CBC News has requested comment from Innodata but has not heard back.

B.C. company named as suspected supplier

Other booksellers told CBC News they have received similar requests in recent months, often for obscure educational books that sat unsold for years. Some say it's hard to turn down those requests, especially in an industry that's not exactly booming.

The names of the companies making these requests seem to change quickly, sellers say, and none of the buyers have publicly admitted to supplying AI companies.

Zoom Books, a company based in Pitt Meadows, B.C., that says it resells and recycles secondhand books, has been frequently mentioned in online bookseller forums and on Reddit for making large numbers of perplexing bulk orders.

Booksellers in Spain , Germany , Australia , New Zealand and elsewhere have raised suspicions that Zoom's orders are intended to be resold for AI scanning, though none have shown proof that this is the case.

WATCH | Authors and creators on AI: AI-written books divide publishing world | Duration 2:13 Generative AI is making its way into publishing, leaving authors and creators with differing views on the technology. The CBC's Ben Dornan reports. Correction: A previous version of this story said that MacIntyre Purcell Publishing used AI to generate and scramble words in some puzzles in a puzzle book. MacIntyre Purcell Publishing says they do not publish AI-generated material and the information was provided to Nimbus in error.

Patrick Hempelmann, the owner of a BMV Books in Toronto, told CBC News that Zoom started buying hundreds of books from him about six months ago.

The orders were primarily for specialized technical books with small print runs, typically selling for between $5 and $30, he said. Some were old medical texts or graduate student-level math and physics books that had sat on shelves for a decade.

"We couldn't really figure out what their motivation was or what their specialty was, because they were kind of buying things all over the place. There seemed to be no real rhyme or reason," he said.

Hempelmann said Zoom Books made the purchases online through AbeBooks, a third-party seller, and BMV fulfilled the orders.

The orders were shipped to Wood Dale, Ill., care of PrepFort, a third-party logistics and fulfilment centre that works with major companies including Amazon, Walmart and Shopify.

Hempelmann says he was unaware of the AI book scanning controversy until CBC News contacted him, but after reading about it, he says it's "just sad."

BMV Books owner Patrick Hempelmann says he was 'sad' to learn about destructive book scanning. (Submitted by Patrick Hempelmann)

"I mean, we are booksellers. Books shouldn't be destroyed," he said.

Another Canadian bookseller who did not want to be quoted in this article told CBC News they received similar orders from Zoom Books several weeks ago.

Until mid-March, Zoom Books' chief growth officer, Reed Pannell, was a business development director at U.K.-based World of Books , according to his LinkedIn account. Court documents reported on by The Washington Post named World of Books one of the companies that Anthropic purchased from for its secretive destructive scanning project.

In an email to CBC News, Pannell said that Zoom does not sell to Anthropic, but he did not directly confirm that the company hasn't dealt with any other AI companies or shipped books to companies that may have scanned and destroyed them.

Pannell would not disclose Zoom's customers, citing confidentiality.

He said Zoom collects and processes more than three million books each month and that its mission is to keep books in circulation.

"We acquire secondhand books and resell them intact. We do not digitize books," Pannell said. "Our priority is always reuse, and when a book can no longer be rehomed, it is responsibly recycled."

PrepFort co-founder Sufyaan Kalota said in an email to CBC News that the company "cannot share any details regarding our customer agreements due to our confidentiality commitments."

Buyers may be 'cat's paw': store owner

Chris Brayshaw, owner of Pulpfiction Books in Vancouver, says he saw a two-week "sales bump" several weeks ago where he was making about a dozen sales a day of primarily non-fiction books that he considered "dated" and had been sitting for years.

The books were purchased at prices between $10 and $80 US each and shipped to various locations across North America and Europe, he told CBC News.

Brayshaw would not provide the names of the buyers, but says he suspects they were "limited liability companies created specifically for this purpose, maybe as kind of a cat's paw to disguise the ultimate source of where the items were going."

Pulpfiction Books owner Chris Brayshaw, pictured in 2023, says he was getting unusual bulk orders for a two-week period this summer. (Baneet Braich/CBC)

He says he has refused sales of valuable books in the past when the purchasers had destructive or esthetic reasons for buying.

Although Brayshaw has strong negative feelings about AI, the books purchased by the mysterious bulk buyers were ones he was generally "delighted" to finally move.

"I don't think it was a great loss to civilization," he said.

World.title: More than 1,000 dead from catastrophic Nepal-China floods as rescuers search for survivors
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

CBC News accompanies residents from one town in Nepal as they return to see what's left of their homes and salvage anything they can, all while surrounded by evidence of the hundreds who didn't escape in time.

The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China passed 1,000 on Tuesday, authorities said, as rescue teams worked to reach communities cut off by the disaster.

Nepal's disaster agency said Tuesday that 987 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners. Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing.

At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities. Emergency crews have been using helicopters and other aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.

The disaster began Wednesday with a chain of events high in the Himalayas. A glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.

Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.

A health-care worker holds his colleague's head during a break after handing the bodies of victims who perished in the flash floods and a mudslide, in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, on Tuesday. (Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters)

The resulting surge of water and debris entered rivers that flow through valleys in Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly. Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges and carried mud and rocks downstream.

Authorities are still searching for thousands of people who remain unaccounted for on Tuesday. Rescue teams are also working to provide assistance to survivors in areas where roads and other transportation routes have been damaged or cut off.

For rescuers, the immediate priority remains finding at least 900 workers who are missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods, about 500 of whom are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.

Visuals released by Nepal's army showed rescue teams entering dark, debris-filled tunnels, wading through mud and water and climbing over rocks as they searched for signs of life.

Nepal's disaster agency said Tuesday that 987 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners. Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing. (Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images)

Bimal Sharma, a helicopter pilot who has been flying rescue missions since the disaster began, said he was shocked to see the devastation in Timure, a border town close to Tibet that he has known for years.

"It felt like I was flying over an entirely different landscape," he said.

Sharma said he has had little opportunity to speak with the people he rescued, but their expressions told him how deeply the disaster had affected them.

"I can see the pain in their eyes. It's heartbreaking," he said.

World.title: Blue Jays get a shot at gaining ground on Guardians with 3-game series in Cleveland
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Like Yogi Berra once said, "It ain't over till it's over" — a truism that's providing some positivity for the Blue Jays and their fans, as Toronto makes a late-season drive for a playoff spot.

Toronto's 2026 season has been a bumpy ride, as the defending American League (AL) champions have battled injuries and shown inconsistent play on the field. The team has not played to expectations, and has held a losing record for much of the year — including at present.

Yet the Blue Jays are, improbably, still in the mix of teams that could claim a playoff spot.

Toronto begins a three-game series in Cleveland on Tuesday that will give the Blue Jays a shot at moving up in the standings at a critical time.

"You have a chance to leave Cleveland with a playoff spot," said Sho Alli, a host with Sportsnet 590 The Fan, underlining the importance of the next three games.

Here's a look at how the Blue Jays have stayed in the hunt for a post-season berth.

Eyes on a wild-card

Major League Baseball's current playoff format sends 12 teams to the playoffs each year — six from the AL and six from the National League.

WATCH | Fan favourites leave Toronto at the trade deadline: Blue Jays lose fan favourites in big trades | Duration 2:09 Less than a year after competing for the MLB championship, the Toronto Blue Jays made some big trades ahead of the deadline, including fan favourites Daulton Varsho and pitcher Kevin Gausman.

The six post-season teams, in each of the respective leagues, will be made up of three division winners and three so-called wild cards (the teams with the best overall records, outside of the division winners).

The Blue Jays play in the AL East division, which is currently led by the Tampa Bay Rays. The New York Yankees and the Boston Red Sox are next in the standings.

If the season ended today, the Rays would be in the playoffs as a division winner. But the Yankees and the Red Sox, with the next-best records in the wider AL, would hold two of the three wild-card spots, accordingly.

The Cleveland Guardians lead the chase for the third wild-card spot at the moment.

Trying to move up

Along with Toronto, the Baltimore Orioles, Texas Rangers, Minnesota Twins and Seattle Mariners are within five games of Cleveland. All are vying for that same wild-card spot — despite the fact they are mostly underwater in the standings.

"It's kind of crazy just how bad the American League has been," said Bob Nightengale, MLB columnist for USA Today, who says it shouldn't be the case that sub-.500 teams could be headed to the post-season.

Ernie Clement, Myles Straw, Andrés Giménez and Brett Bateman celebrate Toronto's win over Seattle at Rogers Centre on Saturday. (Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press)

The Jays, at least, are doing better lately, having played strong baseball in August, going 17-11 and pushing their overall record on the season to 68-70 ahead of Tuesday's games.

The Guardians, meanwhile, went 13-13 during the month of August. Cleveland had been in a tie for the third wild-card spot when the month started and now stands marginally ahead of Baltimore and Toronto as September begins.

Alli said that Cleveland has a strong starting rotation, including Gavin Williams — a pitcher with one of the highest strikeout totals in the majors, who's slated to start Tuesday's game against Toronto.

He also points to the Canadian closer they have at the back end of their bullpen, Cade Smith, as a concern if the Blue Jays see him on the mound at the end of a game.

Nightengale said the Guardians are serious about competing for a post-season opportunity, having made moves at the trade deadline to bring in outfielder Jo Adell and pitcher Foster Griffin — among others — to make their team better.

But he noted it's not only a one-on-one fight the Jays face as they try to climb up in the standings.

"Don't forget Baltimore is in there, too."

The Jays and Orioles will face each other in a separate three-game series later in the month.

Toronto will also have a September series with the Rangers, who pulled even with the Blue Jays in the standings on Monday night.

Keeping the pitching going

Toronto's own starting pitching ranks have thinned this year, with injuries derailing and disrupting the seasons of multiple hurlers — including Shane Bieber and Trey Yesavage.

Blue Jays starter Max Scherzer delivers a pitch during Sunday's game against the Mariners. The game saw Scherzer put on his strongest performance of the season, striking out 10 across seven innings of work. (Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press)

At the moment, the Blue Jays are banking on ace Dylan Cease, the recently acquired José Soriano and veteran Max Scherzer to keep the team in contention. The remainder of the rotation is in flux, amid injuries on the pitching staff.

Cease is in a chase for a Cy Young Award, and has been dominant when on the mound this season. Soriano has been solid during his brief Jays tenure to date and Scherzer has been heating up in August.

Recent addition Spencer Arrighetti, who has struggled in his first two starts with Toronto, will be on the mound for the series opener on Tuesday. Cease and Soriano will also get starts against Cleveland.

Toronto will also rely on the Louis Varland-led bullpen to prevent close games from slipping away to the Guardians.

Power flicker or signs of a surge?

The Blue Jays have lacked power at the plate this season, with the team ranking near the bottom of MLB in terms of home runs hit.

Blue Jays outfielder Nathan Lukes hits a home run against the New York Yankees during an Aug. 22 game at Yankee Stadium. (Jim McIsaac/Getty Images)

But a few of the Jays' hitters have started to send the ball out of the park more regularly, in recent games — and that hasn't been happening prior to this point in the season.



Outfielder Nathan Lukes hit five home runs in August (including four in his last nine games), as did catcher Alejandro Kirk. Slugger George Springer had two homers, with the round-trippers coming in back-to-back games at the end of the month.

Franchise star Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has had a difficult year at the plate, hitting just seven homers this season. But a ball he hit to the outfield at 116 miles per hour on the weekend suggests his power hasn't deserted him — even if his homer total is not where he wants it to be.

A continued power surge could be plenty helpful for a Blue Jays squad that has also scored among the fewest runs of any MLB ballclub this year.

World.title: ‘It is Lake Ontario and it won’t change,’ business owners in Niagara region respond to Trump renaming lake
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Now that Google Maps has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America for users based in the U.S., the owners of one Niagara Falls restaurant decided to take a similar approach to their menu.

The move comes after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change the name of the lake, amid escalating tensions and a brewing trade war.

“If you can rename whatever you want for your country, well then, we can do the same thing over here,” said Richard Carpenter, co-owner of Carson’s Pizzeria.

What was once their Buffalo chicken sandwich is now listed as their "Ontario wing sauce chicken sandwich."

“Also, the same thing with the Chicago Deep Dish, he named it the Thorold-style Deep Dish Pizza,” said co-owner Jonathon Olszewsky.

The pizzeria's Facebook post, announcing their “little name change,” has gathered concurring reactions from Canadians across the country, though Carpenter said the menu change is temporary and more “humour-based.”

Carson's Pizzeria is just one business in the region using small gestures like this to respond to the name change.

Katherine McMichael, owner of the shop Lady Lou Collective in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont., said “it is Lake Ontario and it won’t change.”

“It’s quite silly that somebody thinks they can change the name of the lake, especially when it was made way beyond any of us were ever here,” McMichael told CBC Niagara.

McMichael owns and curates Canadian-made art work and gift items for her store Lady Lou Collective.

She keeps a sign in her shop's door thanking her customers for supporting Canadian businesses and Canadian-made goods.

A sticker thanking customers for purchasing Canadian goods at Lady Lou Collective, a gift shop in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. (Diona Macalinga/CBC)

She said while the impact of the Canada-U.S. trade war on her own business pales in comparison to those in many other industries, particularly the automotive sector, she's still affected, as she no longer ships orders to the U.S.

“It’s sad that we can’t do that anymore,” said McMichael, fearing that her American customers would get hit with duties. “I used to say that we’re two countries that support each other … We’re all just trying to make ends meet.”

Across the street, Shauna Dickson, owner of mom-and-pop shop Irish Design said she often uses Lake Ontario as a landmark to help customers and businesses overseas find her boutique.

Dickson, who was born and raised in Niagara-on-the-Lake, said the move to change the name of Lake Ontario “felt really close to home.”

Over the years, she said she felt a shift in her interactions with customers visiting from across the border, she told CBC News. But, despite the growing tensions between the two countries she wants to make sure her American customers still feel welcome in her store.

“We had a lot of customers come in and apologize when the conversation gets brought up about where they’re from,” Dickson said.

“It feels like we’re trying to comfort people a lot to make sure they know they're welcome here,” Dickson added. “We’re not blanketing you with one bully.”

World.title: North of North is back for Season 2: Here's what we know so far
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

CBC News sits down with Anna Lambe (Siaja) and Maika Harper (Neevee) ahead of Season 2. They discuss how their mother-daughter bond turns 'raw' as Siaja’s world begins to unravel, and they tease what’s next for their characters' love lives.

Grab your parkas — North of North takes us back to Ice Cove for Season 2.

The critically acclaimed comedy series, a co-production involving APTN, CBC and Netflix, follows Siaja (Anna Lambe), a young Inuk woman rebuilding her life after a very public breakup with her husband.

Season 1 became a global hit, landing on Netflix's Top 10 in 33 countries and earning praise from critics for its ability to balance sharp comedy with heavy subject matter.

"We love comedy with heart. We love to laugh, but we also love to cry," co-creator and executive producer Stacey Aglok MacDonald told CBC News.

The show also racked up major recognition, winning nine Canadian Screen Awards, including best comedy series and best lead performer in a comedy (Lambe).

Co-creator and executive producer Alethea Arnaquq-Baril said the team couldn't quite predict the size of the success.

"We knew something special was happening, but you still can never be sure how big it's going to go," she said. "We were shocked at how successful it was."

MacDonald added, "We were extremely, just, elated by it all."

WATCH | North of North Season 2 trailer:

'A very messy place'

Season 2 picks up right where Season 1 left off. Nearly one year into her new life, Siaja is juggling motherhood, a full-time job and dating — while dealing with complicated relationships with her mother, Neevee (Maika Harper), and her estranged father, Alistair (Jay Ryan).

The season begins as Siaja tries to process her mother's confession that she has an older sister. Still, she's determined to rebuild her life and figure out who she wants to be.

Her journey is rooted in the Inuktitut concept of ᐱᓕᒻᒪᒃᓴᕐᓂᖅ (pilimmaksarniq) — mastering skills through observation, practice and effort.

Lambe said her character's life "basically implodes" this season, and no matter how hard she tries, things keep unravelling. By the end, Lambe described Siaja as being in "a very messy place … that's so raw" in her relationship with her mother.

Meanwhile, Neevee — described by Harper as "a hard woman to crack" — begins to open up. She tells her daughter she has moved on from trying to find her eldest child.

Anna Lambe as Siaja, left, and Maika Harper as her mother, Neevee, right, look at paperwork for Neevee's expanding store in the second season of North of North. (Marni Grossman/APTN/CBC/Netflix)

Siaja grapples with the tension between respecting her mother's wishes and wanting to meet her sister, as well as help her mother find "peace" and "get closure."

At the same time, Neevee's store continues to expand. She and Alistair also try to figure out what their relationship is meant to be.

"I want my parents to be happy so bad," Lambe said.

Making the show 'authentic and real'

Season 2 brings Iqaluit back on screen, standing in for the fictional town of Ice Cove again. MacDonald said filming on location helped the show feel grounded and "magical."

Arnaquq-Baril says production in the Arctic tundra — where temperatures can regularly drop below –30 C — can be unpredictable.

"We had four blizzards this season in prep and production," she said.

WATCH | North of North set tour: Behind the scenes with North of North ahead of Season 2 | Duration 3:46 CBC News visits the set of the hit comedy series to chat with Anna Lambe, who stars as Siaja, and co-creators Stacey Aglok MacDonald and Alethea Arnaquq-Baril, who share their favourite costumes and set pieces that bring North of North to life.

The creators point to Inuit cast and crew as essential to making the series. MacDonald said the team relies heavily on its community to keep the show "as authentic and real as possible."

Arnaquq-Baril added, "It's incredibly important to us to have Inuit be part of the process of making this show right from the very beginning."

She and MacDonald say the show's fashion pulls from Inuit styles across different Arctic regions, celebrating variety rather than pushing one standardized look. The aim was to create outerwear that feels lived-in and recognizable as true to the culture and place.

Because so many of these pieces are handmade by individual artists, co-ordinating shipping and construction details from afar created logistical hurdles.

Arnaquq-Baril said they had to get someone to physically carry a custom parka between communities. They also had to figure out how to measure people without traditional measuring tape since some designers measured by eye or by hand.

"Our costume department that are from Toronto had to learn a little bit of a different way to work and trust the process," Arnaquq-Baril said.

WATCH | The inspiration behind North of North's fashion: North of North co-creators discuss the show's handmade costumes | Duration 2:27 Stacey Aglok MacDonald and Alethea Arnaquq-Baril explain how North of North celebrates Inuit fashion from across the Arctic with custom outerwear and the logistical challenges involved.

MacDonald says that even when costumes didn't arrive assembled the way the team had hoped, the production team adapted fast — leaning on expertise from the community

One standout example was a parka that required a "sunburst" fur detail — a traditional Arctic hood ruff that encircles the face in a radiating pattern. MacDonald turned to her sister and others on set who then called family members for instructions so the team could assemble it correctly.

"It was so worth it; it's spectacular," Arnaquq-Baril said.

Season 2: 'Bigger and crazier'

So what comes next?

Arnaquq-Baril said fans can expect "unexpected twists and turns," including new characters, while the season also digs deeper into the lives of the people viewers already know.

"People love the humour and heart [in Season 1]," she said. "We're definitely trying to do more of that and go even bigger and crazier."

Lambe teased "so many quests, so many adventures," and said viewers will get to know the community centre and its people more. "It's so much fun," she said.

Harper offered a short warning: "It's a rollercoaster. Get ready."

In addition to Lambe, Harper and Ryan reprising their roles, returning cast members include Braeden Clarke (Kuuk), Mary Lynn Rajskub (Helen), Zorga Qaunaq (Millie), Bailey Poching (Colin), Nutaaq Simmonds (Elisapee) and Keira Cooper (Bun).

Meanwhile, Canadian actor and comedian Bruce McCulloch will guest star as Military Mitch, a first-aid instructor, while acclaimed Inuk singer-songwriter Elisapie will appear alongside online personalities and content creators Ashley Callingbull, Braden Kadlun, Chelazon Leroux, Kairyn Potts, Kayuula Nova, Shina Nova and Scott Wabano.

North of North Season 2 premieres in Canada on Sept. 1 on APTN+, followed by a larger premiere on CBC TV, CBC Gem and APTN TV on Sept. 8. After its Canadian premiere, Season 2 launches globally on Netflix later this fall.

World.title: Inadequate cell service is 'jeopardizing people’s lives' in emergencies, N.L. woman says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Even a decade removed from the event, Amanda Howse remembers Jan. 20, 2016 clearly.

After hitting a snow drift and veering off the road, she managed to pull herself out of her wrecked car — alone, hurt and stuck down the side of the highway near Charles Brook in central Newfoundland. She reached for her phone, ready to dial 911 but couldn’t. There was no cell service.

“It’s jeopardizing people's lives by not having adequate cell service across this province,” Howse told CBC News.

The issue of connectivity and access to emergency services was raised last week, after a fisherman died off Westport on the Baie Verte Peninsula. A firefighter in the community told CBC News connectivity issues are a problem in emergencies.

Howse received help when another driver saw tire marks lead off the embankment, and with the help of another resident's two-way radio, they were eventually able to contact emergency services.

She’s since been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder from the experience. However, Howse considers herself to be one of the "lucky ones.”

WATCH | What do you do when you can't dial 911?: Cellular coverage, or lack thereof, raises concerns about ability to reach emergency services in N.L. | Duration 3:12 Concerns among residents across Newfoundland and Labrador are growing once again over unreliable cellphone coverage and its effect on reaching emergency services in a timely manner. This after a small boat capsized near Westport on the Baie Verte Peninsula, killing one fisherman. Local firefighters in that community told CBC News connectivity issues make responding to emergencies difficult. And as the CBC’s Madison Taylor reports, the problem isn't isolated.

Connectivity struggles feel like ‘déjà vu’

On the other end of the line, first responders say connectivity is a problem that needs to be solved.

“It seems like we're repeating ourselves, déjà vu, every couple of years,” said Deer Lake Fire Rescue fire chief Stephen Rowsell.

“I’ve talked to other chiefs around the province. They seem to have the same concerns,” he said.

Fire chief Justin Bolt says sometimes his crew has to go to nearby a home to make calls. (CBC News)

More than a 600-kilometre drive from Deer Lake, in Marystown, Marystown Volunteer Fire Department fire chief Justin Bolt said there are some parts of his area where service is “inadequate” or not available at all.

Though Bolt’s department has purchased additional resources to try to stay connected —including three cell phone boosters — sometimes it’s not enough and his crew has to go to a nearby home to connect.

“It could be in another community where they [firefighters] have to actually go in and use a resident's phone in order to make that call,” said Bolt.

The fire chief hopes to see improvements in his community’s connectivity in the future.

“We're in an age of technology, but technology is not advancing to keep us connected. But all the tools are there,” Bolt said.

Work ongoing to 'close gaps'

In a statement to CBC News, Buckley Belanger, federal Secretary of State for Rural Development, said the federal government is “working to close gaps in mobile coverage in several ways.”

These include the Universal Broadband Fund, where up to $50 million is available to improve cell service in rural areas and along roads. The federal government has also asked provinces and territories to identify “shovel-ready” projects that could expand cell coverage.

The province's Department of Jobs, Growth and Rural Development said it’s looking to “identify potential partners and solutions to improve mobile connectivity throughout the province.”

The province also said it is continuing to advocate to both the federal government and telecommunications companies to increase coverage.

During last year’s election, the PCs promised it would spend an extra $3 million a year to increase cellular coverage in the province.

In a statement, telecommunications giant Bell spokesperson David Marcille said improving connectivity in rural and remote areas remains a “shared challenge,” that often requires collaboration between industry and governments, and that it “remains committed to working with partners to help address remaining coverage gaps.”

World.title: I’m a good listener but no one ever asks about me. Am I missing something? | Ask Rebecca
World.content:
Article content

I have so many people in my life who express what a good listener I am and what a great time or conversation we have together. These comments leave me feeling confused. About a year ago, I started to pay attention to whether our dialogue, whether one-to-one or in a group, was reciprocal. It is not. No one asks me a single question. If I ask, “Would you like to hear about my darling, or my grandchildren, or where my time is spent?” they will say “yes.” However, no one, and I mean no one, asks.
