World.title: Route 32 Closures Will Keep Coming and Here Is What Drivers Should Do
World.content:
Costa Rica said today it will spend $100 million to take the roundabouts out of Route 32, the highway that connects San José to the Caribbean coast. President Laura Fernández announced the plan during a visit to Limón. She said the highway’s original design was flawed, that the roundabouts were never the right fit for a road like this one, and that the money from the national roads council, Conavi, will pay for 10 overpasses to replace them. She framed it as a promise the previous government made to Limón and this one is keeping.

None of that helps you this year as Route 32 closed at least three times in August, and it will close again before the rainy season ends. The problem is not the road surface and the mountainside above it. Through the Braulio Carrillo stretch, rain soaks the slopes, the water has nowhere good to go, and dirt and rock slide down onto the lanes. Crews clear it, the road reopens, and the next storm starts the cycle over.

August showed how that works as earlier this month as crews reopened the highway after clearing six separate points between kilometers 28 and 38. In mid August it shut for about four hours after another slide. Days later a run of tropical waves closed it again, with the Cerro Zurquí sector flagged for saturated soil and continuing slide risk. Then two earthquakes near Coronado on August 24, magnitude 5.0 and 4.5, shook more material loose around kilometer 30.

The four-lane expansion itself is done and MOPT opened the full 104-kilometer (65-mile) stretch between the Río Frío junction and central Limón last December, eight years after work started. Almost everything around it is no as an audit published by Lanamme, the UCR engineering lab that reviews public roadwork, found more than 157 outstanding items on that stretch. They cover road safety, slope work, materials that failed quality requirements, and gaps in supervision.

Two slope sectors near Siquirres, at kilometers 100 and 112, are still eroding and shedding material with no good drainage. At some critical points, Lanamme found, nobody is pursuing a permanent fix at all. Inspectors also found crews working with no supervisor or quality-control staff on site.

Fixing a slope is slow, and it costs you time behind the wheel. The job at kilometer 27, started in March, used anchored bolts, sprayed concrete and new drainage. It meant at least three months of one-lane traffic, every day from 6 a.m. to 5 p.m. Unfortunately, expect more of that since two additional stabilization walls are planned this year at critical points.

The roundabouts are the other reason your trip runs long. Seven of them, plus two at-grade right turns, replaced six overpasses and three interchanges from the original design after the government moved to cut costs and avoid buying out landowners. Lanamme later found they were too small to meet international standards, and the Constitutional Court ordered the MOPT and Conavi to fix them. Official estimates put the added driving time across the seven roundabouts at roughly 26 minutes.

Four replacements are already contracted, at La Trocha (km 61), Calle 1 (km 64), Jiménez (km 67) and Siquirres (km 96), for ₡7,349,760,000. The MOPT published a tender for more overpasses and pedestrian bridges in July and has said construction should start in October or November. The project is now meant to finish with 44 pedestrian bridges, up from the 20 in the original contract. Fernández also said Monday that highway lighting is nearly finished and that the dead zones with no cellphone signal, a real problem if you break down, are being fixed.

Until that work lands, plan around the road. If Route 32 closes, you have three alternatives. Vara Blanca takes light vehicles only. Route 10 runs between Siquirres and Turrialba. The Bajos de Chilamate–Vuelta de Kooper road is the northern option. All three add serious time, and none is a quick detour.

So check MOPT channels the morning you travel. Do not book a tight connection between the Caribbean coast and a flight out of San José, and in heavy rain, give yourself an extra day. If you are already driving when a closure is announced, turning back early usually beats waiting for a clearance that can take hours.

Route 32 carries most of what Costa Rica imports and exports, plus everyone moving between the Central Valley and the Caribbean. The money is identified and the contracts are moving. But the work runs across several years, and the rain does not wait for it.

World.title: Argentina’s Navone Hands Djokovic His Earliest Grand Slam Exit in 20 Years
World.content:
Novak Djokovic’s bid for a record 25th Grand Slam title ended almost as soon as it began Sunday night, with Argentina’s Mariano Navone pulling off the biggest win of his career in the first round of the US Open. Navone, ranked No. 49 in the world, defeated the fourth-seeded Djokovic 7-6(5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 in a four-hour, 36-minute battle inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The result was historic. Djokovic had never lost in the first round in 20 appearances at the US Open, and he had not been beaten in the opening round of any Grand Slam tournament since the 2006 Australian Open.For much of the night, it appeared the 39-year-old Serbian might escape.

Navone won a tight opening set in a tiebreak before Djokovic fought back to take the next two. Djokovic then broke serve early in the fourth set to take a 2-1 lead and appeared to be moving toward the second round. Instead, the match changed dramatically.

Djokovic had been struggling physically throughout the night and his condition worsened as the match stretched past three hours. He vomited during the match and later said he was dealing with cramping as well as pain in his back and shoulder. Navone immediately broke back in the fourth set and began taking control. The 25-year-old Argentine won five of the next six games to force a deciding set, while Djokovic’s movement and energy continued to fade.

The fifth set quickly became one-sided. Navone broke Djokovic repeatedly and closed out the biggest upset of the opening day with a 6-1 final set.Djokovic finished with 70 unforced errors and converted only four of his 12 break-point opportunities. Navone converted six of 17. Afterward, Djokovic acknowledged that the physical problems were not limited to Sunday night. He said he has been dealing with vomiting and other issues during matches throughout the year and that his body eventually begins to break down.

“I’m trying, man. I’m trying,” Djokovic said when asked whether the problem could be fixed.The defeat continued a troubling North American hard-court stretch for Djokovic. He also lost his opening match at the Cincinnati Open earlier in August, falling to another Argentine, Thiago Agustin Tirante.

New York appeared to offer Djokovic a chance to reset. He entered as the No. 4 seed and was chasing the one major milestone still hanging over his career: a 25th Grand Slam singles championship. Instead, his tournament lasted one match. Djokovic remains tied with Margaret Court at 24 major singles titles and will now have to wait until at least the 2027 Australian Open for another opportunity to reach 25. For Navone, the night represented the opposite end of the tennis spectrum.

The Argentine arrived in New York better known for his results on clay than hard courts. He entered the match with one ATP Tour title and only two previous US Open victories. Facing one of the most successful players in tennis history under the lights at Arthur Ashe Stadium, he refused to go away even after Djokovic took control in the middle of the match.

“It is a dream come true,” Navone said after the victory. Navone now moves into the second round, where he will face the winner of the match between three-time Grand Slam champion Stan Wawrinka and Matteo Berrettini. Djokovic, meanwhile, leaves New York after the earliest Grand Slam exit of his career in two decades and with renewed questions about whether his body can continue to withstand the demands of five-set tennis.

World.title: Stopped by police for circling around in ski masks: ‘Button-would-be bandits’ busted before burglary
World.content:
Stopped by police for circling around in ski masks: ‘Button-would-be bandits’ busted before burglary

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two Belize City men were fined $1,000 each on Monday after pleading guilty to going equipped to commit burglary following an early-morning police interception in the Buttonwood Bay area.

Josh Nicholas Flowers, 28, and Mauricio Antonio Cherrington, also 28, appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where both admitted to the offence.

Police say the men were intercepted at around 4:37 a.m. on Saturday, August 29, while travelling together on a red Lifan motorcycle near the intersection of Buttonwood Boulevard and Bay Street.

According to police, both men were wearing ski masks when officers stopped them. A subsequent search reportedly led to the discovery of a pair of pliers and a screwdriver beneath the motorcycle seat.

Police alleged that the items, along with the masks, were intended to be used in the commission of a burglary. The motorcycle reportedly had no licence plate.

Flowers and Cherrington were taken into custody and later charged with going equipped to commit burglary.

After accepting their guilty pleas, Senior Magistrate Dennison fined each man $1,000 plus $5 cost of court. They were given until November 3, 2026, to pay their fines, or face five months in prison in default.

The court heard that Flowers has a previous conviction for handling stolen goods, while Cherrington was treated as a first-time offender for the offence before the court.

World.title: Charles Carr remanded after allegedly holding baby mother hostage at gunpoint and assaulting her
World.content:
Charles Carr remanded after allegedly holding baby mother hostage at gunpoint and assaulting her

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 23-year-old Belize City man employed as a technician at Belize Water Services has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being charged with aggravated assault with a firearm following allegations made by his ex-girlfriend.

Charles Carr appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, where he pleaded not guilty to one count of aggravated assault with a firearm. He was remanded until November 3, 2026.

The charge stems from an alleged incident at a residence on Electric Avenue on August 28.

According to the police report, Carr’s 22-year-old ex-common-law partner visited the residence with their three-year-old daughter so Carr could spend time with the child.

The woman alleged that when she told Carr she was ready to leave, he became upset and told her she would not be allowed to leave until she had sex with him “one last time.”

She further alleged that Carr locked the front door, kept the key and later pointed a firearm at her after she began packing her child’s belongings.

The woman told police that she feared for her life and asked Carr to put the firearm down, but alleged that he refused and struck her several times to the forehead.

She reportedly managed to knock the firearm from his hand and kick it toward a couch, but said Carr retrieved it. She further alleged that he later removed the magazine, causing a bullet to fall to the floor.

The woman told police she continued asking to be allowed to leave but Carr refused. She eventually managed to send text messages to an aunt asking for help, and police arrived at the residence about 15 minutes later.

Following her report, Carr was arrested and charged.

During his arraignment, Carr reportedly told the court that the complainant was outside the building and intended to withdraw the charge. The court did not entertain a withdrawal at that stage.

Because the charge involves an alleged firearm offence, the Magistrate’s Court did not grant Carr bail, and he was remanded to prison pending his next court appearance.

World.title: Police detain 18-year-old for theft of $4,500 motorcycle
World.content:
Police detain 18-year-old for theft of $4,500 motorcycle

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained an 18-year-old man in connection with the theft of a motorcycle from Belize City over the weekend.

A 21-year-old man told police that at about midnight on Sunday, August 30, he parked his black Lifan motorcycle outside a friend’s residence near the corner of Elston Street and the George Price Highway because the motorcycle could not fit through the property’s gate.

When he prepared to leave at approximately 3:30 a.m., he discovered that the motorcycle was missing.

The motorcycle, fitted with a black storage box behind the seat, is valued at approximately $4,500.

Police say an 18-year-old Belize City mechanic has since been detained in connection with the investigation.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: 15-year-old robbed of iPhone and injured in Belize City alley
World.content:
15-year-old robbed of iPhone and injured in Belize City alley

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the robbery of a 15-year-old student who was attacked while walking through an alley in Belize City on Sunday night.

According to police, the student was walking from Kut Avenue through an alley leading to Fairweather Street at about 7:50 p.m. when two unidentified men dressed in dark clothing attacked him from behind.

The teenager reportedly suffered an injury to the right side of his head and scratches to his right hand during the attack.

His red iPhone 11, valued at approximately $400, was stolen before the attackers fled.

The teen ran to the Fairweather Street police booth for assistance and was later taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital.

Police noted that both residential and police surveillance cameras are located in the area and investigations are continuing.

World.title: Woman charged for bursting sanitation worker’s lip after swinging machete through window louvres
World.content:
Woman charged for bursting sanitation worker’s lip after swinging machete through window louvres

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City woman, Angelique Mejia, has been charged with aggravated assault and wounding following an altercation at a Cet Site residence over the weekend.

According to police, 38-year-old sanitation worker reported that at about 7:30 a.m. on Saturday, August 29, Mejia, whom he knew, arrived at his home carrying a machete and confronted him over allegations concerning a missing laptop.

He told police that Mejia initially rode away but returned shortly afterward and began swinging the machete outside his house.

He said he attempted to speak with her through a front window to de-escalate the situation when she allegedly pushed the machete through an opening created by two missing louvres, striking him on the upper lip.

Perez suffered a bleeding injury which was later medically classified as wounding.

Police subsequently arrested and charged Mejia with aggravated assault and wounding.

World.title: Police investigate suspected arson after SUV set on fire on Rasta Street
World.content:
Police investigate suspected arson after SUV set on fire on Rasta Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a suspected case of arson after a vehicle was damaged by fire early Monday morning in Belize City.

At about 5:00 a.m. on August 31, police responded to Rasta Street, where they found a black 2011 Nissan Rogue with fire damage to its rear passenger compartment, including the rear seat and passenger-side window.

The vehicle’s owner, a 26-year-old security officer, told police that he had parked the SUV in front of his yard at about 9:00 p.m. Sunday before going to sleep.

Initial investigations indicate that at approximately 4:15 a.m. Monday, a grey Caravan van without licence plates arrived in the area. Shortly afterward, the Nissan Rogue was seen engulfed in flames, and an individual was reportedly observed entering the Caravan before it sped away toward Central American Boulevard.

The Belize Fire Service extinguished the blaze. The value of the damage has not yet been determined.

Police are investigating.

World.title: 30 Years Later: Keefe D found guilty of murder in 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur
World.content:
30 Years Later: Keefe D found guilty of murder in 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly 30 years after the fatal shooting of rap legend Tupac Shakur, a Las Vegas jury has found Duane “Keefe D” Davis guilty of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon.

The jury returned the unanimous verdict Monday after less than three hours of deliberations, marking the first conviction in one of the most notorious murder cases in hip-hop history.

Prosecutors argued that Davis, 63, orchestrated the September 7, 1996 drive-by shooting in retaliation after Shakur and members of his entourage attacked Davis’ nephew, Orlando Anderson, at the MGM Grand earlier that night. While Davis was not accused of firing the fatal shots, prosecutors said he obtained and provided the gun used in the attack. Under Nevada law, a person can be convicted of murder for aiding or facilitating the killing.

The prosecution relied heavily on Davis’ own accounts of the shooting, including statements made during interviews with investigators, media appearances and his 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend. His defense maintained that those accounts were exaggerated or fictionalized and argued there was insufficient physical evidence tying him to the murder.

Shakur was shot while riding in a BMW driven by Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight near the Las Vegas Strip. He died six days later at the age of 25.

Davis now faces a potential life sentence. His sentence will be determined by a judge at a later date.

World.title: Belize mourns the passing of longtime children’s healthcare advocate Milagro Garel
World.content:
Belize mourns the passing of longtime children’s healthcare advocate Milagro Garel

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Milagro Garel, the woman behind two decades of children’s medical missions in Belize, has died.

Her family confirmed her passing in a statement, saying she went peacefully with her loved ones at her side.

“It is with broken hearts that we share that our beloved Milagro passed away peacefully this afternoon, surrounded by love.”

Garel collapsed on July 28 with a ruptured cerebral aneurysm. Doctors stabilised her here before an air ambulance took her to Guatemala, where surgeons operated and she remained in intensive care for weeks. Her husband Joe kept the country updated as she regained consciousness in stages.

Belizeans raised the money that made the treatment possible, covering transport, surgery and hospitalisation costs running between $95,000 and $140,000.

As country director for World Pediatrics, Garel spent more than twenty years getting Belizean children onto operating tables they would never otherwise have reached, working alongside Friends of Pediatrics and other groups.

“Your beautiful smile, your incredible spirit and the light you brought into so many lives will remain with us forever,” her family wrote.

World.title: Tents? No Way!
World.content:
The tent at Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth where some classes were held

MIDDLE QUARTERS, St Elizabeth — Describing tents as heat traps, Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School Principal Pauvine Watson-Barrett is insisting that all of her 252 students must be housed in ventilated classrooms when the new academic year opens next Monday.

“The tent cannot be used; it is extremely hot. We tried to use the tent last academic year. We had grade one initially in the tent and after the [Primary Exit Profile] exam we had grade six going to the tent and giving grade one a feel of a classroom space,” she told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“However, due to the heat the children were not able to use the tent for the entire day. They had to be out of it by midday. Right now it is hotter than what we were experiencing last academic year, so I don’t see where I can use that tent to host the classroom,” she added.

Last week, the Caribbean Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology and The University of the West Indies Climate Studies Group Mona advised governments, businesses, farmers and households across the region to step up preparations for potentially severe climate extremes as El Niño conditions are and set to intensify the hot and dry conditions already affecting parts of the Caribbean.

Both entities warned that the region should remain particularly vigilant as August to October marks the peak of the Caribbean’s heat season.

This year’s El Niño is on track to be the strongest on record, threatening to unleash extreme weather across the globe and make 2027 the hottest recorded year by far.

Under such severe heat, tents would not be suitable to serve as classrooms for children.

On Monday, when asked how all her students would be accommodated, Principal Watson-Barrett said the National Education Trust (NET) had promised to deploy temporary wooden classrooms, but up to Monday afternoon there was no structure or even foundation to give assurance of the buildings.

“I am yet to see them. Between the Ministry of Education, NET, and the contractor, they promised that we would be getting two buildings each holding two classrooms, so that would be a total of four classrooms. Up to this morning (Monday) there was no updated information. The contractor said he is waiting on NET to give approval for the building of the [wooden] classrooms,” Watson-Barrett told the Observer.

She said the school is exploring two options to accommodate students if the temporary buildings are not erected in time.

“We will have to look at rotation and/or merging of classrooms into one room. For instance, last academic year I had a classroom with two grade two classes and they were placed in one room and then the teachers team-teach,” she said.

“Because of the heat, also, I am not considering a shift system. Imagine coming to school at 12 o’clock to start classes in this heat on a shift system,” added Watson-Barrett.

She said the school is expected to have seven accessible classrooms based on ongoing construction work.

“Currently, we have one block that is 85 per cent complete. That block can host two classrooms. The other two blocks that are available are currently being worked on and we are hopeful that by this Friday those two blocks will be completely cleaned and ready for the opening of school, September 7,” she said.

A deteriorating building had to be demolished last week at the school.

“That would leave me wanting five more classrooms to accommodate the other students, because as of last week I lost a building that had four classrooms, the guidance counselling room and the library on it,” said Watson-Barrett.

She said Middle Quarters Primary and Infant will be receiving students from the now shuttered Giddy Hall Primary School, three-and-a-half kilometres away.

“Even without the inclusion of the Giddy Hall Primary children I would be short of classrooms. I have 170 students expected to attend school in the primary department with an additional 29 from Giddy Hall Primary School, seeing that the school was consolidated and we are the receiving school,” she said while pointing out that five academic and two auxiliary staff were moved to her school from Giddy Hall.

“The ministry has made the decision to close down smaller schools based on the enrolment there… For the infant department we are expecting to have about 52 students,” she added.

When asked about the availability of potable water, Watson-Barrett said the school has been getting reliable water supply from the National Water Commission.

“Currently, I am seeing where improvement has been made on the water system; it is still being worked on, but whenever it is locked off we purchase water,” she said.

“During Hurricane Melissa [last October] the drums were blown off the building. However, we have a large metal tank that we store water in. Those drums that were blown down are yet to be replaced,” she added.

World.title: Tough guardrails
World.content:
Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen (second left) gestures while speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. Flanking him are CGC executives (from left) Caleigh Reid, legal officer; Damion McKenzie, senior director, investigations and enforcement; and Shainee Myles, director of human resource. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

WITH Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator set to commence operations by March next year, once all outstanding conditions are met, the Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) is assuring that stringent guardrails are in place to keep criminal elements out, with operators required to verify players, monitor suspicious transactions, and protect vulnerable gamblers.

Speaking during this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange, both CGC Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen and Senior Director of Enforcement and Investigation Damion McKenzie outlined a multi-layered system of checks that will follow casino operations from the moment a player registers to the regulator’s ongoing monitoring of the business.

The safeguards include know-your-customer (KYC) checks, scrutiny of suspicious transactions and sources of wealth, anti-money laundering controls, surveillance systems, responsible-gaming interventions, and direct regulatory access to the casino’s operations.

The officials were speaking as Adamas Grand Casino Limited, Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator, moves towards opening at Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover. The CGC granted the operator its licence on July 29, but the licence is conditional and does not yet authorise the casino to begin operations.

CGC Legal Officer Caleigh Reid said the operator must first satisfy all remaining requirements, with March 31, 2027 set as the deadline to commence operations.

“They have a specific time frame in which to open. There are certain deliverables that they have to satisfy us with, certain things that they have to provide us with before they get the go-ahead. Right now they have the licence, but they are not authorised to begin operations until all of those other deliverables are satisfied, which is all outlined in their conditions of licence,” she said.

The safeguards are intended to address several risks associated with casino gaming, particularly money laundering, organised crime, problem gambling, and the potential exploitation of vulnerable players.

At the heart of the CGC’s financial crime controls will be requirements for casinos to know who their customers are and to scrutinise the money moving through their operations.

According to McKenzie, the regulator will not simply assess an operator’s anti-money laundering system once and walk away.

“A part of our legislation requires us to do ongoing monitoring as it relates to money laundering and proceeds from illicit means. We will continue to monitor, but the training that we provided to our officers… allow them to understand the different typologies that are related to money laundering in the gaming sector, to understand the myriad things that happen that can be classified as money laundering,” McKenzie said.

The commission will also examine whether an operator has properly carried out those checks and whether the financial profile of a player makes sense.

“Our audit plan also allows us to go in and check on persons who have signed up, if you did the proper KYC and anti-money laundering check against this person: What does this person do? How did they come about the cash? The source of wealth? So all those checks continue throughout the lifecycle of the licence,” McKenzie added.

Furthermore, Allen noted that the commission is designated as the competent authority for casino gaming under the Proceeds of Crime Act, with responsibility for anti-money laundering, counter-financing of terrorism and counter-proliferation financing compliance in the casino sector.

He explained that casino gaming in Jamaica is restricted to approved Integrated Resort Developments, meaning a casino cannot operate as a stand-alone gambling establishment.

Therefore, this creates a two-stage screening process.

“At the first stage of the development of it, the Government wants to be satisfied that the operators, the financiers, their funding is from good sources, they have good standing in other jurisdictions, not just for the development but for the operations of the casino… and when you come to stage two, when you come to us, we then conduct our own due diligence, specifically in respect to the conduct and operations of a casino,” Allen said.

He also noted operators will be required to maintain surveillance systems capable of supporting regulatory monitoring, as well as provide space for commission officers at the premises.

“In Las Vegas, on any one casino property, there are about 5,000 cameras. These cameras can zoom in and read the serial number on a note at a table four miles down the road. We have similar surveillance and monitoring requirements for the casino. More than that, the operator is required to have facilities on its premises for the commission and our officers to be able to have access to and at any time go on site and monitor,” Allen said.

The CGC’s guardrails are not limited to criminal activity. Allen explained that the regulator’s responsible-gaming framework is designed to identify people who may be developing harmful gambling habits and provide avenues for intervention.

That framework includes staff training, player information, behaviour monitoring, exclusion and self-exclusion mechanisms, as well as controls on advertising. The commission has worked with the Responsible Gaming Council of Ontario and signed an MOU with RISE Life Management, which has experience in counselling and self-exclusion relating to gambling.

“The mechanism behind responsible gaming is that the staff will be trained to spot persons who have a problem, persons who sit all day and gamble. There’s some form of intervention from the staff to allow some kind of cooling-out period for this individual. Also, because Jamaica will be a cashless system, they’ll also be able to track the pattern of a player to see his betting patterns and some form of intervention can be implemented because of that pattern of constant gambling, constant topping up, constant chasing, constant losses,” he added.

Allen also assured that responsible-gaming controls will extend to how casinos advertise and promote their services.

He said s should not target children or young people and should not rely on influential figures who children might look up to.

He also noted that the CGC intends to leverage existing responsible-gambling programmes, including initiatives involving schools, while keeping casino-related promotion within the resort environment.

World.title: 60 years of Tastee: A celebration of food, music and Jamaican legacy
World.content:
Patrons enjoy the free concert hosted by Tastee Jamaica as part of their 60th anniversary celebrations.(Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FOR 60 years, Tastee Jamaica has commanded the support of Jamaicans, becoming as synonymous with the island as the patty itself. But the company’s legacy stretches far beyond food. Having established itself as a key contributor to the discovery of some of Jamaica’s most talented entertainers, Tastee has firmly cemented its place in the hearts of Jamaicans globally. On Friday night, the company showed its appreciation to its local fanbase, treating scores of Jamaicans to a free concert of the highest entertainment quality.

With Emancipation Park transformed into a sprawling celebration of music and memories, the event was far more than an anniversary concert. Hosted by veteran broadcaster Jennifer “Jenny Jenny” Small, it was as much a celebration of Jamaican music as it was a birthday party for the company. Agent Sasco, Tarrus Riley, King Yellowman, Nadine Sutherland and a host of others created an atmosphere that reflected both legacy and loyalty.

For some of the night’s performers, however, appearing on the Tastee stage carried even greater significance, having gained their break in the industry decades ago through the talent search spearheaded by the company.

“We a eat patty over 60 years. Big up Tastee. Tastee is the one that make people know me international,” said King Yellowman as he paused his set to remind the audience of his third-place finish in the inaugural Tastee Talent Contest in 1979.

Giving a commanding performance, Yellowman treated the crowd to a short yet energetic set, which included songs such as I’m Getting Married in the Morning and Zungguzungguguzungguzeng.

Also turning in a vibrant performance was the 1979 competition winner, Nadine Sutherland. She performed hits such as Action, Starvation — which she released a year after her win — and Babyface. In what she described as a full-circle moment, Sutherland recalled how Tastee changed her life when she was just 11 years old.

“I’m still in disbelief that it’s been 46 years since the 11-year-old me was brave enough to get on that stage. I was known as ‘the little girl from Above Rocks’ who was brimming with confidence. I had to draw back for that little girl tonight and just soak it all in. I’m grateful that I’m still here, and I still love this,” she said.

Tastee’s own story began in 1966 when Vincent and Valerie Chang opened the company’s first operation at Union Square in downtown Kingston. As demand grew, the business expanded, eventually establishing its headquarters in Cross Roads and developing a footprint across the island. Somewhere along that journey, Tastee’s relationship with Jamaica began extending beyond what it served across the counter.

Over its decades-long run, the Tastee Talent Contest — later known as the Tastee Talent Trail — became an important proving ground for emerging Jamaican performers, including Beenie Man, Papa San, Cobra, Mr Vegas, T.O.K., Glacia Robinson, Brian and Tony Gold, and several others.

It was therefore little surprise that the company received an abundance of praise from the night’s performers.

That spirit of giving was not confined to Tastee’s entertainment history. After the company awarded 13 students $60,000 each towards tuition through its back-to-school initiative, Agent Sasco extended the gesture from the stage, committing to cover the tuition of another high-school student.

Sasco’s giveback didn’t stop there, as he treated patrons to a delightful set, which included spirited performances of crowd favourites such as Winning Right Now, Hand To Mouth, Hand Inna Di Air, Idiot Thing Dat, Banks of the Hope, and others.

Alaine also turned in a quality set, performing songs such as Dreaming, Rise In Love, Bye Bye and Ordinary Love.

Abijah, Carey Sayles, Tony Rebel, Sista Pat, Tarrus Riley, Richie Stephens and saxophonist Dean Fraser were among the evening’s other performers, rounding out a musical package that traversed generations and genres.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer following the concert, patrons sought to explain Tastee’s longevity. Noting that not many companies would think to give back to their supporters in such a tangible way, concertgoers said Tastee’s knack for recognising the support of its consumers has helped establish its 60-year legacy.

“Tastee is not just about the patties. They’ve always been about giving back in some way, shape or form. If it weren’t for Tastee, Jamaica and the world would not have discovered talent such as Beenie Man, Yellowman, Nadine Sutherland, and so many others,” said Suzette Morgan.

“Their dedication to the Jamaican people has always been evident and it was proven again tonight when they hosted this free concert. The fact that we didn’t have to pay anything didn’t take away from the quality of the show. We got solid performances while we nibbled away on patties. It was a perfect way to celebrate their anniversary.”

Marcia Stewart agreed.

“Tastee is big in Jamaica because it’s big on supporting Jamaicans. We love our patty and the company has proven over the years that they value the support of their consumers. Hosting a free concert showed exactly how much they appreciate Jamaicans, and I hope they last another 60 years,” she said.

Friday night proved that while patties built the Tastee name, the company’s legacy has also been shaped by the love of the Jamaican people.

For decades, Tastee fed Jamaicans more than simply food. Through its talent competition, it also helped feed an entertainment industry that would eventually send some of the artistes it discovered onto stages around the world.

Behind the songs, the memories and generations of performers sharing one stage was the story of a Jamaican institution that has managed to remain part of the country’s everyday rhythm for six decades.

At 60, that relationship remains as much a part of Tastee’s legacy as the patties themselves.

World.title: Sheree Martin named first female CEO of NCBJ, effective Sept 1
World.content:
She will be the first woman to hold the post.

Martin served as interim CEO since January 19, 2026, leading the bank’s strategic and operational priorities with a focus on efficiency, governance and the customer experience.

In a statement, the bank said her appointment provides continuity as it continues to work on the same priorities. Group Chief Executive Officer of NCB Financial Group Limited and Chairman of NCBJ Robert Almeida said Martin’s leadership during the interim period reinforced the board’s confidence in her ability to lead the bank.

“Sheree brings deep institutional knowledge, a strong understanding of our customers and a clear appreciation of how the different parts of the Bank must work together to deliver,” Almeida said.

“She combines strategic judgement with practical, hands-on leadership and a strong focus on execution. These qualities will serve NCBJ well as it builds on the progress already underway.”

Martin said she was honoured by the appointment and energised by the opportunities ahead.

“NCBJ has an extraordinary legacy, talented people and a vital role in the lives of our customers and in Jamaica’s development,” she said. “I look forward to working with our board and teams to build on that foundation – accelerating our progress, strengthening the customer experience and bringing the full capabilities of the bank together more effectively.”

She added, “Our priorities are clear: empower our people within the right culture, improve the way we deliver and earn our customers’ confidence through the quality and consistency of the service, financial solutions and platforms they experience every day.”

Martin brings more than 20 years of executive leadership experience across the financial services and energy sectors. Before assuming the role of interim CEO at NCB, she had leadership responsibility for several functions including retail banking, operations, credit underwriting, marketing and enterprise information management.

World.title: Former gang member found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
World.content:
Rapper Tupac Shakur attends a voter registration event in South Central Los Angeles, August15, 1996. (AP Photo/Frank Wiese, File)

LAS VEGAS, United States (AFP) — Duane Davis, a former Los Angeles gang member, was found guilty on Monday by a Las Vegas court of the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur.

Thirty years after the rap legend’s death at a Las Vegas casino, the jury found Davis, 63, guilty of murder after just a few hours of deliberation.

World.title: Crackdown on care
World.content:
TUFTON...people must play their part...or they make way for someone else to do itPhoto: Garfield Robinson

SPURRED by more than 1,000 patient complaints in the Ministry of Health and Wellness’s Client Care Connect report, portfolio Minister Dr Christopher Tufton says efforts to expose system failures and hold negligent medical professionals accountable will intensify.

The move comes as the ministry prepares to publish its accountability data in September, which Tufton says highlighted various client complaints of poor communication, professional conduct, and overall patient experience.

“We’re looking to transform the health workforce. We are taking an inward look, recognising that a highly qualified health system cannot exist without sound governance, and that transformation requires effective leadership, which will be essential to managing the critical components of health.

“So when we speak about an accountability framework, it’s about delivering service with compassion, with empathy and, of course, ensuring that every patient is treated with dignity, respect, and fairness at every point of care,” said the minister as he delivered the keynote address at the Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston in St Andrew last Friday.

According to him, the report’s data aims to isolate departments and individuals responsible for poor patient experiences rather than allowing the failures of some to tarnish the reputation of the wider health-care system.

“Where there is a problem, we need to identify the institution, the department, and who is in charge. You have to start with all the names, because you can’t allow one bad apple to spoil the whole lot…Tell me where the worst experience takes place, the bad experience; tell me which department, and tell me who is in charge.

“And what leadership ought now to do is to address the specifics of a problem. Stop generalising the problem, because we’re letting down people who make sacrifices every day to do the work, and that’s a new modus operandi…People must play their part, and we must emphasise and insist on it, or they make way for someone else to do it,” charged Tufton.

The minister’s push for greater accountability comes amid heightened public scrutiny of the health-care system after the death of 33-year-old Kenise Dunn gained widespread media traction. The eight-month pregnant mother of three passed away at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital five days post-delivery.

When asked if his call for accountability extended to the contentious incident, Tufton told the Jamaica Observer that he cannot comment conclusively while the investigation is ongoing. Still, he emphasised that health-care professionals are always bound by a duty of care. “What I’ve heard, preliminary, is that, clinically, there was a diagnosis of the problem, but it appears, based on some of the feedback — including from persons who are on the ward — that maybe the management of the customer care and the empathy to the patient may have been less than desired. Now, I don’t have the final report, so I prefer not to conclude on that,” he said. “But the truth is drawn from what I said about the complaints report, the 1,000, which I spoke to, it’s quite clear that while we have excellent health workers, we have to work harder at delivering service with compassion and with empathy. And it’s not good enough to just have technical competence. If you treat people badly, if you don’t listen to them, if you don’t respond to them, if you don’t give them a sense of comfort when they’re in distress, then it hampers the healing process,” said the minister. In the meantime, Tufton urged the 141 recipients of the Barry Wint medical grant, valued at over $190 million, to be the difference once they enter their respective fields of practice. “I say this at the risk of offending some, that money is not the primary issue in health care, currently public health; the primary issue is how we conduct ourselves within the system. People who are in the system only for a pay cheque are not sufficiently willing to give the commitment and show care. You cannot afford to be like that. You have to show a better way, and that’s what Barry Wint is investing in. Not just in your capacity as a technical and competent person, but in moving the process forward,” the minister said. Pointing to what he identified as the major weaknesses of the system, Tufton noted that health care in Jamaica lacks a sufficient number of practitioners — specifically specialised individuals — and professionals with the capacity to show empathy to patients. He reiterated that that was not the type of behaviour that he expected from recipients of the Barry Wint scholarship, and challenged them to become “a catalyst for change”. “If you just want to be a nurse, a doctor, a biotech engineer because at the end of the month you’re going to get a fat pay cheque, and that’s the only driving motivation to apply and to pretty up the application for this money, do not accept it. There are too many people in the profession who see the profession only in financial terms, and not enough as a passion and commitment to enhance service delivery for those who need it, Jamaicans who are in distress,” he said firmly.

World.title: Jamaicans loud and proud!
World.content:
Trinidad and Tobago’s High Commissioner to Jamaica Deborah Thomas-Felix shares her admiration for the manner in which Jamaicans display pride in their country while speaking at the Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday. Photo: Naphtali Junior

FROM schoolchildren in the country’s colours to packed cultural events, Trinidad and Tobago’s new High Commissioner Deborah Thomas-Felix says the unapologetic pride Jamaicans display in their identity is one of the things that has impressed her most since taking up her post.

Having lived in several Caribbean countries, Thomas-Felix said Jamaica’s expression of national pride stands out to her because of how openly it is displayed in everyday life, from the workplace to sporting and cultural events.

She was particularly struck by the way Jamaicans embrace national occasions, including Jamaica Day, when people turn out in the country’s colours, adding that the celebration of national identity extends beyond the traditional observances of Independence and Emancipation.

“You all have a national day — schoolchildren, big people going to work in Jamaica colours. I was so struck by that when I experienced it… Don’t get me wrong, because Trinidad and Tobago has a deep sense of pride and love, but it’s the way, the open way in which it’s displayed in Jamaica,” she expressed during the a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s Beechwood Avenue, St Andrew, headquarters last Friday.

For Thomas-Felix, the pride is also visible in how Jamaica celebrates its culture, with Reggae Month — commemorated in February — providing an entire month of activities centred on one of the country’s most recognisable cultural exports.

She said that visible enthusiasm has helped her better understand Jamaicans in the Diaspora.

“Everywhere you go within the country, they say, ‘Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica,’ and I think that is so encouraging, and it gives me a better understanding of the Jamaicans I know who don’t live in Jamaica,” she said.

Thomas-Felix, whose parents are Grenadians and who has lived in St Vincent, Barbados, and Trinidad and Tobago, stressed that she was not suggesting that Trinbagonians lack national pride, but said she was particularly impressed by how visibly Jamaicans express theirs.

“There’s this open display of pride, and I think you all should keep that. I think that is just an excellent way to let [future] generations inherit that and continue with that, because I really, really like that,” she said.

Her comments come as Thomas-Felix seeks to strengthen ties between Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago across areas including trade, culture, and people-to-people relations.

She said the relationship between the two countries extends well beyond governments, pointing to Trinidadians who have built lives and careers in Jamaica and Jamaicans who have done the same in Trinidad and Tobago.

For Thomas-Felix, those personal connections are part of the Caribbean relationship that she wants to strengthen during her tenure.

“So the relationship is way beyond government to government, it’s really about people, and we interact through music, we interact in terms of culture, and so I want to really strengthen those bonds,” she said.

World.title: Slow movement on Spring Mount road repairs
World.content:
Residents of Spring Mount listen keenly as manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw (left) provides an update on plans to rehabilitate collapsed roads in the area.

SPRING MOUNT, St James — A soil test is among the items to be done before the State-run National Works Agency (NWA) can finalise a design to rebuild Spring Mount road in south St James. Last October’s Hurricane Melissa caused two major breakaways on the heavily trafficked route, leaving commuters with the choice of engaging in risky road use or a much longer, more costly journey.

With schools about to reopen, residents of Spring Mount and neighbouring areas have become increasingly anxious for an update on what is being done to fix the road. They were given the clearest signal, Thursday evening, that the road will likely be rebuilt in the same location; but there was no timeline on when work will start.

“We are looking to build back the road. We have looked at different possibilities and I can tell you straight up, one of the things that we are looking at is to take down the hillside and acquire [those] two houses on top of the hill,” manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw told residents during a meeting held at Spring Mount Basic School.

He said the goal is to rehabilitate the roadway as soon as possible, restoring the vital connection between the north and south of the parish. The damage has made safe passage by vehicular traffic impossible just beyond Spring Mount Police Station. Residents have established a pedestrian path which is sometimes utilised by motorcyclists.

Shaw made it clear that there will be challenges in executing the project, given its scope and magnitude.

“It is not the normal run of the mill [approach of] looking at it as a breakaway, put up a wall, backfill it, and move on. No. We are going to have to do what are called bore hole tests,” he warned, adding that this falls outside the technical capabilities of the NWA and a private sector firm would have to be engaged.

These tests, he explained, will provide laboratory-based information on the soil in the area that will guide the designs on which work has already started.

“That testing of the material beneath there will inform us as to what else, if required, needs to be done to ensure that… when we build up that road, you have it longer than all of us inside here will live,” Shaw told the audience.

“Based on the survey that was executed, a design is being worked on but that design will not be finalised until the boreholes are done,” he added.

He explained the importance of the soil tests.

“A crucial factor in this area is the springs. It’s called Spring Mount for a reason. We have to design with that in mind to ensure that we don’t see a situation where we build a big wall, costing a lot of money… and then, [as seen in other locations] rain came, and the entire retaining wall just moved like… it was plastic,” Shaw outlined.

“We have that kind of experience and historical knowledge on which to build or not to build. We are not taking anything lightly in ensuring that the design solutions that we come up with, they are adequate, they are appropriate, are sufficient, and necessary for the particular areas that we are going to be working,” he added.

Responding to residents’ questions about timelines, the NWA representative said he was unable to provide one as it depends on the soil testing which is being done outside of the agency. He did, however, promise to explore ways in which alternate routes — such as the journey through Kempshot, up the treacherous Charlie Mount — may be improved.

Councillor Uvel Graham (Jamaica Labour Party, Spring Mount Division) was at the meeting and while he acknowledged that the project is complex he expressed frustration that it is moving too slowly.

“To be honest, I was looking for more of a timeline and that these tests would be done already and people would be hearing that the next two to three months, the work would start,” he told the

Jamaica Observer after the meeting.

World.title: Burnham enters the political bearpit
World.content:
Parliament is back and the honeymoon is over – Andy Burnham now faces his first major test as prime minister.

The PM will make his Commons debut as he promises to “bring back hope” and make life more affordable. But with pressure on public finances, can he deliver on his promises to cut energy bills, cap bus fares and slash business rates?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy examine the gap between Burnham’s ambitious promises and the tough reality facing the government.

And the duo look at how Kemi Badenoch plans to puncture the Burnham bounce with her shadow cabinet reshuffle.

World.title: Europe gears up for its China counterpunch
World.content:
Brussels is getting increasingly worried about its economic relationship with Beijing … but the bloc doesn’t want to bring out the big guns just yet.

While the EU already has the infamous ‘trade bazooka’ at its disposal, the Commission is considering a new tool to address Chinese overcapacity and dangerous dependencies. Our colleague Camille Gijs has spoken with EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to learn more. Hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart discuss what he said in the interview.

Next, EU defense ministers are meeting in Ireland today, and Ukraine is right at the top of the agenda. The big question will be whether the bloc can help ease Kyiv’s shortage of missile interceptors.

And finally, is Europe’s most prominent right-wing think tank, MCC Brussels, imploding … or is it morphing into something new?

World.title: Labour’s new housing model comes from California’s backyards
World.content:
Experts think the tweaks could help the government stretch towards its target of building 1.5 million new homes before the next general election, but note the risk of a political backlash among local residents worried about their neighborhoods losing their character and green spaces and becoming overwhelmed.

“It could be significant and it’s certainly creative,” said Simon Creer from the Royal Town Planning Institute. “But it’s hard to say definitively what the increase in housing delivery could be, and whether it will be popular. There’s always a fundamental tension between the need for more homes and the potential local backlash about where those homes are and what they look like, which is why early, meaningful communication with communities matters.”

Indeed, planning changes around garden use during the previous Labour government in the 2000s led to public outrage about homes being demolished so speculators could cram properties into available land, as well as fears about destruction of green spaces. Labour was forced to intervene on what was dubbed “garden grabbing” as the 2010 election loomed, then the successor Conservative-Lib Dem administration was quick to change the rules.

Now the government has tweaked them again to fuel development on and around existing buildings, instructing planning committees via national guidance to favor upward extensions to homes and commercial buildings and filling gaps around houses.

The aim is densification: increasing the number of homes on a designated land mass.

“These changes are in line with our push for urban and suburban intensification, aiming to unlock private land and speed up small-scale construction alongside major transport-hub and grey-belt redevelopment,” said a government official who was granted anonymity to speak about the plans.

World.title: Britain’s Liberal Democrats get a new think tank
World.content:
The think tank is not formally affiliated to Ed Davey’s party, but at least 50 of his 71 MPs attended a presentation promoting its work during one of their regular parliamentary meetings in July — with many indicating they want to get involved.

Tim Leunig, the group’s policy director, who recently became a Liberal Democrat peer in Britain’s unelected House of Lords, said: “We are here to help them.”

“But we’re also here to ask them tough questions because: who knows? They might be a minister one day, and then the civil service will ask them tough questions.”

While in public the Lib Dems refuse to countenance any future deal with Burnham’s Labour, in private their MPs are frank that the opinion polls — which anyone can read — point to the two parties’ combined seat totals being an obvious route to a post-election majority.

Luke Tryl, executive director of More in Common, a think tank which tracks public opinion, said the “ever more acrimonious” battle for the right now makes a pact between the Conservatives and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK “less likely.”

“The Burnham bounce and consolidation of the progressive left vote makes a Lib-Lab pact a more likely prospect,” he said.

World.title: Marine Le Pen’s risky economic gamble
World.content:
She also said she would soon present a plan to cut some €125 billion in spending, including on budget items associated with migration, “useless” public agencies, and France’s contribution to the EU. Le Pen will present her detailed platform in the fall, but Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a member of Parliament for the National Rally, told POLITICO this would be accomplished in “less than five years.”

But Le Pen has yet to explain in detail how those savings would be achieved, and rivals are already questioning whether the numbers add up. “Marine Le Pen will ruin France,” Bruno Retailleau, a conservative candidate from Les Républicains, told reporters shortly after the Medef event.

Marine Le Pen and François Durvye visit the VivaTech technology startups and innovation fair at the Paris Expo Porte de Versailles, in Paris on June 19, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images

The tension has also surfaced inside her own camp. As Le Pen was outlining her economic agenda at the Medef event, news broke that François Durvye, one of her key economic advisers and a leading advocate of greater fiscal discipline, was leaving the campaign.

Internal cracks

Durvye, who has informally advised Le Pen for five years, has been credited with building bridges between her party and the business world. A former fund manager, he was a key voice in the party on economic issues.

But his push for more fiscal discipline and economically liberal policies ran against the instincts of the party’s old guard, which remained wedded to the party’s populist positions. He was also a special advisor to National Rally President Jordan Bardella, Le Pen’s protégé who was expected to take the campaign’s reins if Le Pen had been judged ineligible to run because of her guilty verdict for embezzlement of EU funds.

Bardella has been working to move the party toward the center on economic issues, including softening Le Pen’s pledge on the pension age — something that Durvye had been advocating for internally.

World.title: What 248 books reveal about Kaja Kallas
World.content:
EU's top diplomat is a noted bookworm. But what can her bookshelf tell us about the politician leading Europe's diplomacy?

While actively running the EU’s foreign policy on the world’s most demanding issues, Kaja Kallas still finds time outside work to read about … more foreign policy.

The top EU diplomat and former Estonian prime minister frequently talks about her love of reading, citing her favorite authors in speeches and meeting with them privately to discuss their work. Since taking up her most recent post in December 2024, she has read at least 52 books she has shared publicly — all of which she has posted on her Instagram — most of them related to international affairs. In total, she has shared more than 200 titles since 2017.

“You know, my reading list is quite long,” said Kallas, who officially serves as the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, at a press conference in January. “By the end, when I finish this job, I will be very smart,” she joked.





The collection closely tracks the subjects Kallas is most involved with in her role, evolving alongside her professional remit: 24 books on Russia and Ukraine, nine on China, and seven on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Further-flung regions pop up only rarely, with just three books on the rest of East Asia and none on South American politics beyond Venezuela.

“Reading books is a valuable advantage, especially as it is not so common nowadays,” an official from Kallas’ team told POLITICO. “The Middle East wars, Russia’s aggression and China’s growing influence are major geopolitical issues, so naturally they feature on the High Representative’s reading list.” Noting that she meets with ministers, officials, staff and experts daily and receives countless briefing papers, memos and other sources of information, “books are a nice addition on long-distance flights,” the official added.

The reading lists alone have not shaped the full contours of Kallas’ foreign policy, of course. But they provide a view into which political subjects Europe’s chief diplomat is interested in learning more about and where she goes looking for answers.

So, what does Kallas’ bookshelf reveal about the person shaping Europe’s diplomacy? To find out, POLITICO reviewed the 248 titles she has included on public reading lists since 2017 and spoke to 24 of the authors.

Noted bookworm

Kallas is not the only avid reader in Brussels, but few politicians talk about their love of literature quite as often. Since 2023, she has released reading lists twice a year on Instagram, and before that, she blogged about her latest reads monthly.

“I read a lot, but you’re always influenced by the books you’ve read most recently,” Kallas told POLITICO in 2025.

Political scientist Ivan Krastev, who co-authored 2019’s “The Light That Failed: A Reckoning” on why liberalism failed to spread in Eastern Europe, said Kallas had reached out to him after reading his book. She was trying to find a publisher to translate it into her native Estonian, he told POLITICO. The translation was eventually released in 2022.





While Kallas was prime minister, her government had similarly pushed for the translation of political scientist Mark Leonard’s “The Age of Unpeace: How Connectivity Causes Conflict,” which she said she would “often cite.”

“It’s interesting, particularly when a politician in a high position reads a book,” said Krastev. “They’re trying to make sense of their own experience” and “trying to answer some of the questions that [they] are struggling with.”

Indeed, Kallas’ book choices appear to closely reflect her scheduled diplomatic trips. Visiting Montenegro for the EU-Western Balkans Summit in June this year, the top diplomat had read the memoirs of Richard Holbrooke, architect of the 1995 Dayton Accords in Bosnia, and Martti Ahtisaari, the former Finnish president and mediator of the 1999 Kumanovo Agreement forcing Serbia’s withdrawal from Kosovo.

“A lot to learn also today, and actually a lot of parallels,” said Kallas of Holbrooke’s book in July.

Ahead of her trip to Sarajevo a month later, she then contacted former Swedish Prime Minister and High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina Carl Bildt about his 1998 book “Peace Journey: The Struggle for Peace in Bosnia,” a memoir about his work in the region.

“She sent me a text and said, ‘I’m reading your book, and I like it very much.’ And I said, ‘How on earth did you get hold of that one?'” Bildt told POLITICO, joking that the book was published nearly three decades ago. “She wanted to go down into the weeds of the history … and that could be useful.”





Earlier in the year, after the U.S. forcibly captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Kallas picked up two books about the South American country, too: “Comandante: Hugo Chávez’s Venezuela” and “Things Are Never So Bad That They Can’t Get Worse: Inside the Collapse of Venezuela.”

“She is one of the best-read people I know,” said Marietje Schaake, a friend and former liberal MEP who served with Kallas in the European Parliament. “That depth has shaped her thinking and her career.”

What’s in the library?

Six of the authors who spoke to POLITICO for this article specifically cited Kallas’ hawkish stance on Moscow as echoing the messages in their books — perhaps unsurprising given Kallas warned of Russia’s threat to Europe back in 2021, during her first term as prime minister.

“What is happening in Ukraine right now is what I was reading about in our own history books,” she told Vogue Greece in 2023.

Sylvie Kauffmann, author of 2023’s “Blindsided” (Les aveuglés) — which argues that Germany and France failed to recognize the Russian threat — told POLITICO her book “confirms everything that Kallas thinks” about how others downplayed Moscow’s aggression.





Speaking to POLITICO about his 2018 book “Identity,” famed political philosopher of liberal democracy Francis Fukuyama said the work contained “a kind of ideological roadmap to be able to better explain what it is that … we’re fighting for.” Noting that Ukraine’s fight against Russia was one of the reasons he wrote it, Fukuyama then praised the chief diplomat’s support for the country.

Kallas has also read extensively on Israel-Palestine, a conflict on which her stance has attracted both attention and controversy in Brussels.

Far more critical of Israel than her peers in the European Commission, Kallas reportedly compared the situation on the ground to South Africa under apartheid during a closed-door meeting in June, causing Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar to sever contact.

Kaja Kallas at the E5 defence ministers meeting in Krakow, Poland on Feb. 20, 2026. | Omar Marques/Getty Images

Two of the authors on the subject who feature on Kallas’ reading lists told POLITICO her reported comparison mirrored the arguments made in their books, with 2024 Pulitzer Prize winner Nathan Thrall saying his “aim in writing [“A Day in the Life of Abed Salama: Anatomy of a Jerusalem Tragedy”] was to influence people like her.”

“The fact that she has come to the conclusion that Israel is practicing apartheid is most welcome as far as I’m concerned,” he said.

“I explain the aspects of apartheid, and I hope she’d see that her judgment is well founded,” echoed Michael Scott-Baumann, author of “Palestinians and Israelis: A Short History of Conflict.”





But not every author on Kallas’ lists approves of her foreign policy decisions when it comes to their topics of specialization.

Kim Ghattas, who wrote her book “Black Wave” on the Middle East, for example, said Kallas has been too passive on the Israeli-U.S. war with Iran. “That is not good policymaking. I would hope that reading books like mine can help prepare policymakers like her, specifically for moments like the one that we find ourselves in right now.”

Former U.S. National Security Adviser John Bolton, who has long advocated for regime change in Iran, said he, too, wished Kallas had become more involved — though in support of President Donald Trump’s military operation.

He also noted that Kallas’ blunt style risked further alienating the U.S. from the EU, with her comments advocating for the bloc’s sovereignty “giving [Trump] the excuse to do what he probably wants to do anyway.”

Criticism extended beyond the Middle East as well. Robert D. Kaplan, author of 1993’s “Balkan Ghosts” — which heavily influenced former U.S. President Bill Clinton’s initial reluctance to militarily intervene in the region, according to his biographers — told POLITICO that Kallas’ impolitic moments “may be things that she’ll come to partially regret over time.”

“When you get far quick, you tend to make mistakes. Because you’re confident, you’re even arrogant,” said Kaplan.

Booking ahead

It’s not all about world affairs and global diplomacy, though — some of Kallas’ more recent political predicaments lie a little closer to home.

Recent months have seen the top diplomat losing a turf war with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over the bloc’s foreign policy, while her diplomatic service, the European External Action Service, has struggled to build consensus across a divided Europe.

So with the rentrée almost upon us in Brussels, there may be no better time for Kallas to get through a few more books — a strategy she has turned to previously.





While serving as prime minister, during a 2023 podcast, Kallas recalled how she once considered foreign policy to be her greatest political weakness — until she turned to books.

“It’s not my weakness anymore because I’ve read so much about this,” she said.

Perhaps this time it will be Brussels that sends her back to the stacks.

World.title: Trump vows US will take 'all' of Venezuela's oil as deal details emerge
World.content:
Days after announcing what it calls the largest oil deal in history, the Trump administration has filled in the details.

 

A fact sheet released on Monday night by the White House named North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) as the operator at the centre of the arrangement, disclosed the ownership structure for the first time and set out what Washington gets in return.

Venezuela's interim authorities have granted NABEP 100-year concessions over 17 fields with the agreement signed by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.

The Venezuelan reserves dwarf America's own, as the 65 billion barrels covered by the concessions compare with roughly 46 billion across US territory.

Speaking in the Oval Office on Monday, US President Donald Trump called the reserves "unbelievable value that was sitting dormant" and added that the US is "going to be taking all of that. We're going to be taking that oil out."

The US president also reasserted that American majors were queuing up to be a part of the takeover of Venezuelan oil fields.

"We have Exxon going in, we have Chevron going in, we have our big oil companies going in, and everybody's bidding," Trump stated.

FILE. A pedestrian walks past a mural featuring oil wells in Caracas, Venezuela, 29 Aug. 2026 AP Photo/Pedro Mattey

What Washington gets

In exchange for the inclusion in the deal, NABEP has given the US Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital a 35% equity stake in its corporate parent, which the White House says is worth up to hundreds of billions at zero cost to taxpayers.

The US State Department also secures the right to buy 20% of output from all current and future NABEP fields at production cost, intended to partly refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, plus right of first refusal on the remaining 80%.

Washington holds a veto over board appointments, a majority of directors must be US citizens and the agreement falls under US law and courts.

NABEP has committed to investing up to $100 billion (€86bn) in Venezuelan oil infrastructure and is expected to pay around $200 billion (€172bn) in royalties and taxes over 25 years.

Most of the fields were previously run by Russian or Chinese firms, which the White House casts as a reassertion of the Monroe Doctrine.

Signatures expected, questions unresolved

Further energy contracts are due to be signed this week, but reports suggest the arrangement is causing unease among the very majors that Trump says are queuing.

NABEP is controlled by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, investigated by US and European authorities over past dealings with the Venezuelan government, though never charged, and who denies wrongdoing.

Reportedly, oil majors negotiating their own contracts want assurances they will not find themselves seated alongside him.

Exxon and ConocoPhillips both left Venezuela in 2007 after their assets were nationalised, and each says its requirements on legal certainty and contract sanctity remain unmet.

Former US energy advisers have warned of political risk, since a future government in Caracas or Washington could challenge the terms. NABEP reportedly produces between 170,000 and 200,000 barrels a day, second among private operators behind Chevron.

Betancourt said Venezuela is "blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential," and that the deal would "unleash that potential to the great benefit of both Venezuelans and Americans."

Venezuela's Acting President Delcy Rodríguez has also backed it as a chance to modernise the industry, insisting in the face of criticism that the country cedes nothing of its sovereignty.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill said on Monday they were seeking further information about the agreement, which was negotiated without congressional involvement.

Whether the majors share the Trump administration's confidence should become clearer within days, when the contracts are due to be signed.

World.title: We need to use Russian assets to fund Ukraine, Swedish Foreign Minister says
World.content:
Russia has become "more desperate" in recent weeks, and is stepping up its hostile activity towards NATO, Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard, told Euronews.

 

Speaking on Euronews' flagship morning Europe Today show, she said European unity was key to deterring Russia from further aggression on NATO territory.

The minister was responding to reports of a significant uptick in hybrid-war activities across Europe in recent weeks. The most significant was the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport, Germany in early August.

"We see a more desperate Russia," she said.

"Russia is losing territory, losing influence, losing men, and now they are obviously more desperate testing us and testing our unity," she told Euronews correspondent, Shona Murray.

"We have seen a lot of incidents lately and we have seen united response from NATO," she said.

Meanwhile, German Chancellor Frederic Merz is due to announce he is to formally accuse the Kremlin for the drone incident in Leipzig and vowed to respond accordingly.

It'll be the first time a European country has formally accused Russia of such aggression, and it's likely his response will raise tensions further.

Malmer Stenergard spoke to Europe Today ahead of a gathering of EU defence and foreign affairs ministers to be held in Ireland this week.

EU foreign affairs ministers are also meeting in Wicklow for the so-called Gymnich informal session Wednesday. They’ll be joined by their Ukrainian, British and Canadian counterparts where European and transatlantic security is top of the agenda.

Meanwhile, Stockholm is calling for the European Commission to revisit the issue of using frozen Russian state assets – most of which are held in Belgian financial repository, Euroclear - to fund Ukraine.

Leaders of Sweden, Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands want to reopen the issue and pledge to accommodate Belgium’s concerns.

The Belgium government put up the strongest resistance to the measure late last year saying it would create too much risk to the financial sector.

Prime Minister Bart de Wever insisted on limitless guarantees in exchange for his government’s imprimatur. "We cannot stay in the same position as we were before Christmas," said Malmer Stenergard.

"We have to move on because this is what is fair to Ukraine, it's what is fair to the taxpayers," she said.

"And we have to find a way to make sure that Belgium feels comfortable with this," said Malmer Stenergard.
