World.title: Air conditioners save thousands of lives every year in the US
World.content:
As rising temperatures take a toll on human health, air conditioning at home is about more than comfort. A recent study published on Monday in Nature Health found that it also saves thousands of lives.

 

Over 5,260 heat-related deaths are prevented every year in the US, reducing heat-attributable mortality by more than half, according to a new study by Yale School of Public Health and the Yale School of the Environment.

“Everyone agrees that air conditioning works, but knowing that it works for one person is not the same as knowing how much death it prevents across an entire population,” Kai Chen, senior author of the study and an associate professor of epidemiology at Yale School of Public Health, said in a press release.

But turning the air conditioning up to maximum does not necessarily save more lives, the study found. Maximum cooling offered no additional health benefits compared with average use, highlighting the need to balance the health benefits of air conditioning against the environmental costs of excessive use, including higher energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions.

Lower-income and heat

The researchers analysed nearly 30 million death records from 2010 to 2020, matching each death with the daily temperature in the county where it occurred. They then compared those patterns with estimates of household electricity consumption for cooling in each county.

The researchers focused on actual cooling use rather than air-conditioning ownership. Knowing whether a household has an air conditioner says little about whether residents can afford to run it, or how often they do so, Chen said.

The findings shed light on how lower-income households cope with extreme heat, said Narasimha Rao, a study co-author and professor of energy systems at the Yale School of the Environment.

“While some choose to turn on their ACs, others make the uncomfortable choice of bearing the heat to save money for food,” Rao said.

Furthermore, the findings could also have implications for housing policy, said Robert Dubrow, a study co-author and founding faculty director of the Yale Center on Climate Change and Health.

“Landlords in the United States are required to provide heating in the winter, and our study contributes to a compelling body of literature that indicates they also should be required to provide cooling in the summer,” Dubrow said.

The study comes as, across the Atlantic, in Europe, the question of air conditioning has become a political battle. French politicians have drawn ideological battle lines over air conditioning as Europe struggled with record-breaking temperatures, reaching over 40°C.

Meanwhile, the European Commission advocates a "holistic" approach that combines passive and efficient cooling technologies. Rather than encouraging mass installation of air-conditioning units, Brussels wants Europe to prioritise cooler buildings and cities through design, insulation and passive measures, using efficient air conditioning where it is genuinely needed.

World.title: Eurozone inflation jumps to 3.3% in August as energy prices surge
World.content:
Eurozone inflation climbed to 3.3% in August 2026, up from 2.9% in July, according to a flash estimate from Eurostat, the statistical office of the European Union.

 

The increase was largely driven by energy, as global oil and gas prices surged amid the war in Iran and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Energy prices rose by 14.3% in the year to August, accelerating from 10.3% in July.

Leo Barincou, senior economist at Oxford Economics, said: "This was driven by a rebound in fuel prices following the renewed closure of the Strait of Hormuz, while underlying price pressures remained contained as services inflation came down. Inflation should remain well above target into next year, as higher gas and food prices put additional upward pressure on the index."

Food, alcohol and tobacco prices rose by 1.2%, unchanged from July.

Services inflation — a more persistent measure closely watched by the ECB — eased from 3.3% to 3.0%.

On a monthly basis, overall prices in the eurozone rose by 0.4% in August, with energy prices alone increasing by 2.9%.

At the same time, core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, edged down from 2.5% to 2.4%. This suggests that the rise in energy costs has not yet spread extensively to services and other prices.

Among eurozone members included in the August flash estimate, Lithuania recorded the highest inflation rate, at 5.8%, while Estonia had the lowest, at 1.3%.

Among the largest economies, inflation in France and Germany, at 2.7% and 2.9% respectively, remained below the eurozone headline rate. France, however, recorded a noticeable increase from 2.4% to 2.7%.

Spain stood out with inflation of 4.5%, well above the eurozone average, while Italy's rate reached 3.2%.

Eurozone inflation is considerably above the European Central Bank's 2% target. Markets expect the ECB to raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points at its meeting on 10 September as policymakers seek to contain price pressures.

"With inflation still accelerating, the ECB is all but certain to hike at next week’s meeting, in line with our expectations," Barincou said.

"However, unlike markets, we think it is too early to pencil in a third hike, especially given that underlying price pressures remain contained for now," he added.

World.title: Solar outpaces coal for the first time in China: How does Europe compare?
World.content:
China's solar energy capacity has surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time ever.

 

"As of the end of July this year, China's installed solar power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts," China's National Energy Administration (NEA) said.

"For the first time, photovoltaic installed capacity surpassed coal-fired power, becoming the largest power source category in China," it added.

The country's coal-fired power installed capacity, the energy body said, stood at 1.285 billion kilowatts.

Solar generation rose 15.5 per cent in the first seven months of 2026 compared to the same period last year to 802.4 billion kilowatt-hours, about one-eighth of the country's total, the NEA said in another statement.

China, the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases that drive climate change, has pledged to peak carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060.

Piles of coal sit near a chemical plant in Datong, 14 March, 2026 AP Photo

It did not detail in these statements what the total generation of coal-powered energy was for the first seven months of this year.

The NEA said China's installed solar power capacity and power generation "have maintained a steady trend of rapid growth," with it playing an "increasingly prominent role" in guaranteeing electricity supply and driving the energy transition.

Coal has been China's key power generation source for decades and a key driver of planet-warming emissions.

But the country's coal-fired power generation fell by nearly two per cent in 2025, despite rising energy demand in the world's largest emitter, data reviewed by the AFP news agency showed in February.

It marked the first decline in six years, with some analysts saying it was the first time on record that coal generation dropped at the same time as power demand rose.

China has seen an explosive growth in its renewable installation, with coal's share in its energy mix edging down in recent years.

The country installed a record 315 gigawatts of solar power and 119 gigawatts of wind power capacity last year, over 80 per cent of total newly installed power generation capacity, according to the China Electricity Council.

How does Europe compare to China on energy generation?

EU countries are trailing behind China when it comes to renewables, partly because China started their transition to clean energy much sooner. As an example, in 2023 China installed between 180 and 230 gigawatts of solar, compared to 58 gigawatts in all European countries combined.

China's ownership of clean technology parts and patents makes a big difference to how quickly and cheaply they can install, as well as cheaper labour.

China's energy grid is also more efficient at handling energy from multiple sources, where as Europe's grid has been called "outdated". Hybridisation has been recommended as a solution.

World.title: Cigarettes are on the decline in the EU, but how popular are smoking and vaping still?
World.content:
It's well-known that smoking is harmful to your health, and the use of cigarettes in Europe is seeing a slow yet steady decline.

 

In 2025, one in six people aged 16 or older in the EU used tobacco and related products, such as e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, every day, according to Eurostat.

The statistics office said that 20.8% of men smoked every day, compared with 12.6% of women.

However, both shares decreased slightly compared with 2022, when 22.2% of men and 13.1% of women smoked daily.

Tobacco kills 1.1 million people in Europe each year, with 153,000 of those dying from exposure to second-hand smoke, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Furthermore, deaths from lung cancer attributable to tobacco use are 71% for men and 46% for women.

As tobacco is such a prevalent cause of cancer, the EU has brought in measures to stem its use, including a goal to reduce its use to less than 5% of the population by 2040 under its Beating Cancer Plan.

Tobacco use varies by age, although not significantly. People aged between 35 and 49 years old registered the highest share (21.3%) of daily users of tobacco, e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, according to Eurostat.

This was followed by people aged between 25 and 34 at 19.9%, and those aged between 50 and 64 at 19.8%.

Which countries smoke the most?

Among EU countries, Bulgaria (26.3%), Sweden (23.9%) and Croatia (23.6%) recorded the highest shares of the daily use of tobacco and related products.

In contrast, the Netherlands (9.9%), Ireland (11.7%), Belgium (13.6%) and Luxembourg (13.8%) had the lowest shares.

In 17 EU countries, the share of people who used tobacco and related products daily decreased between 2022 and 2025.

The largest decreases were in Spain and Luxembourg, while Croatia and Lithuania recorded the largest increases.

Are citizens aware of the smoking consequences?

Despite years of tobacco-control policies, graphic warnings and public-health campaigns about the dangers of smoking, medical journal BMJ Open found that awareness of its health consequences has barely improved over the past two decades.

More than 90% of respondents knew that smoking can cause lung cancer.

Yet, only about 80% identified heart disease as a consequence of smoking and even fewer knew about the stroke risk as well as second-hand smoke risks.

Researchers found that awareness that smoking causes lung cancer increased significantly in the Netherlands in the same timeframe, but declined in countries such as Germany, France, and Romania.

World.title: What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey
World.content:
Nearly a week after the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to dissolve, the consequences are beginning to take shape for Syria's Kurds and neighbouring Turkey. As the former US-backed force is absorbed into the Syrian state, questions remain over what the country's Kurds have secured in return – from language and political rights to protections for women – and what the end of more than a decade of Kurdish-led autonomy means for Turkey's own conflict with Kurdish militants.

Advertising

SDF leader Mazloum Abdi announced the force's dissolution last Tuesday, saying its fighters would be integrated into the Syrian army.

At its height, the predominantly Kurdish force numbered around 100,000 fighters and controlled nearly a fifth of Syrian territory in the northeast, including major oil fields and fertile land. Under SDF rule, Kurds gained cultural and political rights denied to them under previous governments in Damascus.

“It means the end of Kurdish autonomy. After more than one decade of freedom, now they are under the control of Damascus,” said Syria expert Fabrice Balanche of Lyon University, who frequently visited the region.

Kurdish rights

“There are no guarantees for the Kurdish language because it's just a presidential decree: ‘let the Kurds use their language and teach Kurdish in schools,’ but there is nothing in the constitution,” Balanche said.

The decree, issued by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January, recognised Kurdish as a national language and allowed it to be taught in schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations.

It also restored citizenship to Kurds who had been left stateless under measures stemming from a controversial 1962 census and made Nowruz, the Kurdish New Year festival, an official national holiday.

The Education Ministry followed up on 27 August with rules providing for three Kurdish-language classes a week in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with marks counting towards pupils' final grades.

‘Words and promises not enough’ as Syria’s Kurds face uncertain future

Abdi was also appointed as an adviser to al-Sharaa on Friday, days after announcing the SDF's dissolution. It remains unclear whether the role will be more than ceremonial.

But questions remain over what the end of the Kurdish-led administration will mean for women. The SDF and affiliated institutions used a system in which governing bodies were jointly headed by a man and a woman.

“During these 10 years of autonomy, men and women were equal,” Balanche said. “In the region’s administration. It was always a co-presidency. In Raqqah, for example, the mayor was Leyla Mustafa, a woman, and the co-president was a man. Now that is no longer the case.”

Balanche also said the change could threaten restrictions on polygamy introduced under the Kurdish-led administration. Another unresolved question is what will happen to female SDF fighters as the force is absorbed into Syria's armed forces, which currently have no female troops.

Shifting alliances

For years, the SDF was Washington's main partner on the ground in Syria in the fight against the Islamic State group. But its position weakened as the United States built closer relations with Syria's new rulers.

A Syrian government offensive in January seized large areas held by the SDF and pushed the Kurdish-led force back into negotiations over integration with Damascus.

Washington, meanwhile, has increasingly embraced al-Sharaa's government, dismantling broad sanctions against Syria in 2025 and last week removing the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Turkey has emerged as one of al-Sharaa's main foreign allies and has long pressed for the SDF to disarm and integrate into the Syrian state.

Ankara considers the SDF a terrorist organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which launched an insurgency against the Turkish state in 1984. The SDF has rejected Turkey's claim that it is an extension of the PKK.

A year after Assad's fall, Syrian hopes for transitional justice are fading

The United States and European Union designate the PKK as a terrorist organisation, but not the SDF.

Turkey has carried out several cross-border military operations against the SDF in northern Syria since 2016 and still has thousands of troops stationed in the country. Ankara says those forces will remain until the security threats it faces have been eliminated.

The SDF's dissolution therefore achieves a longstanding Turkish objective in Syria. Turkey's ruling AK Party welcomed the move last week as an important step towards strengthening Syria's unity.

“Stability in Syria means Turkey perhaps being able to divert some of the resources it's been spending on counterterrorism into other areas of its defense that are absolutely necessary at a time like this, a time of regional turmoil,” said Turkey expert Asli Aydintasbas of the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey's Kurdish conflict

The SDF's dissolution could also remove an obstacle to the fragile peace process between Ankara and the PKK.

The process is intended to end the PKK's decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state through the group's disarmament and dissolution.

Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disarm and disband in February 2025, and the PKK announced three months later that it would do so. A group of militants symbolically burned their weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq in July 2025.

Turkey's parliament passed a law in August establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment. Kurdish politicians have said broader democratic and legal reforms will also be needed for lasting peace.

Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria

For Ankara, however, the process does not stop at Turkey's borders. It has repeatedly insisted that the SDF must also dissolve, because it regards the Syrian force as part of the same militant movement as the PKK.

The SDF has disputed that characterisation, with Abdi saying in 2025 that the PKK's decision to disarm did not apply to his forces in Syria.

The dismantling of groups Ankara regards as PKK affiliates across the region is essential to the process, said Middle East expert Serhan Afacan of Istanbul's Marmara University.

“The PKK should not exist anywhere in the region. This is what Ankara has been saying for more than a year,” Afacan said.

“If there is going to be any kind of peace process or reconciliation, the PKK is not supposed to exist anywhere in this region, in Turkey, in Iran, in Iraq, Syria.”

World.title: US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans
World.content:
Russia's finance minister is at the G20 meeting in Asheville but some key US press corps members are not. The mood was already tense amid the lengthy Iran war and Trump's renewed beef with neighbor Canada.

G20 finance ministers and central bank heads gathered in Asheville, North Carolina for two days of talks.

The session is being overshadowed by dissatisfaction over the White House welcoming Russia to the meeting but not some critical reporters, the war with Iran and its economic fallout, and Donald Trump's latest trade dispute with Canada.

Who is representing Russia at the meeting?

Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov made an unexpected appearance as talks opened late on Monday. He held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

"We like getting along with everybody," Trump told reporters when asked about the first in-person Russian invite since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The US currently holds the rotating G20 presidency and so is hosting the session.

The US government told several news agencies on condition of anonymity that Bessent used the meeting to tell Siluanov that the US would not give Russia economic relief until it brings its four-and-a-half-year invasion to a close.

Anton Siluanov appeared at the summit but not in the 'family photo' amid European resistance Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

How did European delegates respond?

"Receiving the Russian finance minsiter here sends a troubling signal," German Finance Minsiter Lars Klingbeil said.

He said he and his European colleagues made clear that they would not appear in the traditional "family photo" alongside the Russian media, saying this was a common EU position.

The photo was ultimately taken without Siluanov and away from the media.

Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told the Reuters news agency that he recognized the right of the G20 hosts to invite guests, but that he was unhappy to see Moscow represented.

"We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them," he said. "So for me it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia."

Klingbeil was critical both of inviting Russia and of excluding reporters Image: Amrei Schulz/BMF/photothek.de/picture alliance

Which reporters and outlets were excluded?

As leaders gathered in Asheville, three giants of the US media landscape complained of either no or limited access toe the meeting.

The business-focused Bloomberg News said that its team was not allowed access, while the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both complained that certain journalists who would typically cover such events were refused media credentials.

Following a challenge from the DJV German journalists' union on Monday, Klingbeil was critical on the matter.

"I believe the press has a completely legitimate interest in reporting openly and freely on this G20 summit," he said. "I consider it unacceptable for journalists or entire editorial teams to be excluded."

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has the unenviable task of trying to sell Donald Trump's trade and economic policies to allies Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

Intractable Iran war weighing down global economy

Klingbeil had also said in a German political podcast last week that he would bring a simple message to the US regarding what he called Donald Trump's "irresponsible" war in Iran — that it needed to come to an end.

Host Bessent, however, was trying to drum up support among allies for the US plans for what it calls "Operation Economic Outcast," an intensified sanction regime against Iran reliant in no small part on third parties outside the US who still do business with Tehran.

Iran has withstood decades of extensive Iranian and western sanctions, but Bessent tried to argue when asked by reporters that it could swiftly be made to collapse if its remaining trading partners joined in.

"I think it could be within weeks or months — and the economy doesn't have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses," he said.

Why Canada rejected Trump's terms despite economic risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump's latest Canada meltdown unsettles allies

The other major source of strain at the meeting was last week's sudden deterioration in trade talks between the US and Canada.

This quickly descended into the tit-for-tat imposition of tariffs, and President Trump launching various social media jabs before unilaterally redesignating Lake Ontario as Lake America, at least on the books in the US.

Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne sought to stress that even the recent friction did not impact his participation.

"Canada has always been at the table and constructive, ready to discuss," he told reporters, stressing the need to ensure continued economic growth and "bring back some stability in trade."

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin would offer a measured response to last month's discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport.

The German government has not officially said who it believes was behind the August 4 incident, although there has been widespread speculation that Moscow was responsible. Russia's embassy in Berlin has denied involvement.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said an investigation into the incident was nearing completion and vowed to provide a clear-cut response in coordination with NATO and EU allies.

News outlets Welt and Politico reported on the weekend that the German government was preparing to announce that Russian intelligence was behind the attempted drone attack.

German media have reported on Tuesday that the federal government would issue an announcement later Tuesday.

When asked to comment, Foreign Minister Wadephul said Germany would not overreact and that its response would be "firm."

"Germany must position itself in such a way that anyone who attacks us knows we will respond. And we are now preparing that response carefully," he told journalists at a press conference in Algiers.

"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said. "Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated."

World.title: Iran says it will return to ceasefire if US does
World.content:
Speaking on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan, Iran's president Pezeshkian called on the US to return to the terms of an interim ceasefire deal.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday said Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal.

"I state explicitly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the ... memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action," Pezeshkian said on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

Pezeshkian accused the US of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms.

At the time, the US carried out strikes on Iranian targets after what it called "continued aggression" against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, with an Iranian drone striking a Panama-flagged tanker.

Tehran has repeatedly said it ⁠will ​allow free navigation through the Strait, but on its terms. A diplomatic solution to the conflict remains elusive.

Pezeshkian's comments come shortly after the US and Iran traded fire for the first time in over a month. The US said it struck Iranian minelaying forces on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday and Iran targeted US forces in the Middle East in response.

US President Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday that there will be a "response" to the Iranian attacks, but said the latest strikes did not mean a return to full-scale war.

Putin and Xi meet at SCO summit

Pezeshkian is due to have talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin later Tuesday.

The meeting takes place as Russia's full-scale invasion into Ukraine continues to rumble on for more than four years.

Earlier, Putin met Chinese President Xi Jinping, who has provided Russia with implicit economic backing during the Ukraine war.

According to Xi, the China-Russia pact has become "more solid" and that its "prospects will be even brighter."

On his side, Putin said the two countries' cooperation was "successfully developing on all fronts."

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping met and discussed relations between the two countries Image: Kristina Solovyova/Sputnik/REUTERS

The SCO is a bloc promoted by Russia and China as an alternative to Western power, which has in the past mostly served for economic discussions, with Moscow and Beijing pushing its significance in recent years.

Its 10 members also include India and Pakistan, while its 15 "dialogue partners" being Turkey and Qatar, amongst others.

World.title: Apple's new CEO John Ternus makes AI top priority
World.content:
John Ternus is just the third Apple CEO in 30 years. His primary challenge is to correct the company's faltering AI strategy to preserve its position as a big tech leader.

On September 1, a new era begins at Apple as John Ternus becomes just the third man to hold the CEO role at the tech giant since 1997.

Ternus was announced as Tim Cook's successor back in April, bringing Cook's 15 years at the helm of one of the world's biggest companies to an end. Since then, Ternus, a leading hardware engineer at the company, has been working closely alongside Cook in preparation for the big job.

Just as Cook had when he took over from the iconic Steve Jobs, Ternus has big shoes to fill. Apple's share price has increased by more than 2,000% since Cook took over in 2011 and the company has sold more than 3.1 billion iPhones in that time.

Ternus faces a range of challenges at Apple, but his ability to keep the company at the top will hinge on how he reshapes its AI strategy.

Apple has struggled to successfully embrace the technology so far, with critics saying it has fallen far behind its rivals.

September 9: John Ternus makes public debut

Ternus will make his public debut as CEO at Apple's Autumn product launch event on September 9. Dubbed "Surprise and Shine," Ternus is expected to announce the company's first foldable iPhone as well as a new version of an AI-powered Siri, Apple's virtual assistant.

John Ternus made his name as a key engineer at Apple Image: Mason Trinca/REUTERS

Francisco Jeronimo, VP for Data and Analytics at tech research group IDC, said Apple's forthcoming announcements were planned during Cook's time in charge and that it will be 2027 before the direction Ternus wants to take the company in becomes apparent.

"Of course, September 9 will be quite an important milestone for the company around foldables and around innovation," he told DW.

"But I don't think we have seen anything that could indicate that Apple is behaving in a different way or is showing a different kind of strategy because Tim Cook is not in the job anymore — yet."

Apple's huge AI challenge

What observers will be looking out for from Ternus on September 9 is the extent to which he focuses his remarks on AI.

While it was already undeniable when he was announced in April that the artificial intelligence boom would be pivotal to his time at the helm, it has become even clearer in the five months since the unveiling that the AI revolution is here to stay.

"It's becoming clear that AI is not a fad, is not something that will go away in the next two or three years," said Jeronimo. "It's something that will dictate the future of most tech companies and indeed all companies."

He reckons AI could be "the most consequential technology" for Apple because it could either help it maintain its lofty position or create a set of daunting challenges.

The biggest challenge he sees is that Apple doesn't "control" AI infrastructure the way it could previously in terms of designing and controlling both the hardware and software for its key products.

"Maybe that will be what John Ternus will be doing differently from Tim Cook, because at the moment, even if Apple built their own AI technology, the reality is that they still depend on someone else," he added.

Apple's reliance on other companies in the AI realm has led it into unfamiliar territory. It struck a deal with OpenAI in 2024 to integrate ChatGPT into the iPhone, but that has led to a bitter dispute between the companies. Apple sued OpenAI earlier this year, alleging that the AI company stole its trade secrets.

Earlier this year, it announced a deal with Google, whereby the search giant's Gemini models would be used for Apple's own AI models and its new AI-powered version of Siri.

"The risk for Apple is to become less relevant in a world where companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are leading in terms of technology, in terms of awareness, in terms of services and potentially in terms of hardware," said Jeronimo.

For decades, Apple's success has been built on its physical products, from the iPad to the iPhone.

"If devices from OpenAI become available, that could be very, very risky for Apple. They could completely disrupt the experience and the way we interact with technology. And if Apple is not on the front of that innovation, that is a big risk," he said.

A combination of Jobs and Cook?

Ternus' background as an engineer who worked on Apple's core products, as well as innovations such as the Apple Watch and AirPods, means he will be expected to lead the way on new AI-driven products for the company.

He also played a central role championing Apple's shift to designing its own chips instead of relying on external suppliers like Intel — precisely the kind of independence Apple would like to achieve when it comes to AI.

The role of Apple CEO is in itself iconic, in part due to Steve Jobs' tenure Image: Kristy Macdonald/picture alliance/AP

Jeronimo thinks Apple still has big advantages, given its massive volume of users as well as the company culture of having dominated innovation in tech for decades. He thinks if Apple can get to grips with AI under Ternus, it could lead to huge success: "What we will see in the next years will dictate whether Apple is on the right track or if they are really struggling."

For Ternus, the first task will be to simply fit smoothly and convincingly into a role that both Jobs and Cook undeniably made their own. "Steve Jobs was the guru of innovation and disruption and Tim Cook was the guru of execution," saidJeronimo.

"I think John Ternus can be a combination of both."

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: Times Square stabbing in NYC leaves 1 dead, assailant killed
World.content:
A woman armed with two kitchen knives killed one person and wounded another in New York City's Times Square before police fatally shot her. Authorities said the attack was random and unprovoked.

A woman with two kitchen knives fatally stabbed one person and wounded another in New York City's popular Times Square on Monday before police shot and killed her, officials said.

The knife attack occurred just before 4:30 pm near a police substation outside One Times Square, the building known for hosting the city's annual New Year's Eve ball drop.

What do we know about the Times Square knife attack?

New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the 49-year-old suspect from the borough of Queens pulled the knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man in the abdomen as he exited a subway station with his wife. She then attacked a 32-year-old woman, stabbing her in the abdomen. Both victims were hospitalized, with the young woman dying of her wounds. The older man is currently in stable condition, police said.

Authorities recovered two knives from the scene of the fatal stabbing incident Image: Kyle Mazza/Anadolu/picture alliance

Officers surrounded the suspect and attempted to get her to drop the knives before deploying a Taser, which also failed to stop her, according to Tisch.

The suspect reportedly told officers, "I'm not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you," before advancing toward them with the knives raised.

Multiple officers then opened fire, with bystander video showing her falling to the ground, where officers handcuffed her and administered first aid. She was later pronounced dead.

What did the authorities say?

"This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world," Tisch said.

She added the attack was random and unprovoked.

Tisch said the suspect had a documented history of mental health contacts with police, including incidents in 2018 and 2019, but no prior arrests.

Investigators do not believe the attack was terrorism-related, and police have not released the victims' identities pending notification of family.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch addressed the press in the aftermath of the attack Image: Kyle Mazza/Anadolu/picture alliance

Mayor Zohran Mamdani, told a news conference, "We know that those families' lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment."

Both Mamdani and Tisch credited the responding officers, saying their actions likely prevented further casualties.

The incident marks the second fatal stabbing in Times Square this year, following a similar attack in May, even as the New York City's overall homicide rate has dropped sharply to one of its lowest totals in decades.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn
