World.title: AfD's Ulrich Siegmund has plans for Saxony-Anhalt and beyond
World.content:
The AfD's lead candidate in the upcoming election aims to turn his small federal state into a blueprint for right-wing extremist politics across Germany.

All eyes are on Saxony-Anhalt this week, ahead of a state election on Sunday that could trigger a political earthquake across Germany.

Though the state is small, with a population of just 2 million — and with economic strength and life expectancy the lowest of any of Germany's 16 federal states — a victory for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could usher in the first far-right government in the history of post-World-War-II Germany.

The AfD's lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, and polls show him well in the lead. The only open question seems to be whether the AfD will be able to secure an absolute majority of the seats in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which would allow it to govern alone. This would appear to be Siegmund's only path to the state premiership, as the other parties have said they will not enter a coalition with the AfD.

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Things are going well for the 35-year-old Siegmund. As he tours his state on the campaign trail, he draws crowds — even in small towns. He's often surrounded by a swarm of international journalists: from Canadian and Danish television, Swiss broadcasting, the BBC and the British magazine The Economist, alongside dozens of reporters from across Germany. Everyone wants to know: Who is Ulrich Siegmund?

The candidate was born in the small town of Havelberg, Saxony-Anhalt, in 1990. He joined the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at age 19, only to leave the party five years later and join the AfD. A former perfume salesman, he cuts a dynamic and athletic figure: slim, handsome and fresh-faced.

Above all, he is cheerful — playing the role of a charismatic charmer in his public appearances. When he steps into town squares to a cheering crowd, he beams back, shaking hands and cracking jokes. Nothing about him seems forced; he visibly enjoys the campaign grind.

"I don't know when there was last such a high approval rating, even among young people," Siegmund told DW. "It's simply enormous." He speaks quickly, articulately and with practiced ease.

AfD, right-wing influencers battle for young voters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD campaign pushes policies with 'high-gloss marketing'

Even critical observers in Saxony-Anhalt can't help but admit that the AfD has all the momentum in this election.

"The AfD's campaign events run like clockwork, both logistically and in terms of political strategy," observed David Begrich of Miteinander , an organization based in the state capital of Magdeburg that fights right-wing extremism. "It is high-gloss marketing of their own policies."

But what exactly do the AfD's policies aim to achieve? To judge by Siegmund's campaign speeches, the goal is a return to a bygone era — a time before Germany viewed itself as a country of immigration, when electricity came from nuclear power plants rather than wind turbines, and when LGBTQ+ rights were not yet recognized. Siegmund wants to pursue, as he says in his campaign speeches, politics "from the people, for the people!"

Apparently, that doesn't include all the people living in the state. The AfD's "100-day immediate action plan" contains some radical policies, including a key promise to "deport from minute one" foreign nationals who have no legal right to stay, but whose presence is tolerated for humanitarian reasons, many of whom have found work and established their lives in Germany.

Germany's freedom of art under threat? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The action plan also calls for funding cuts to pro-democracy NGOs, forcing refugees to work and prioritizing a love for the German homeland over social diversity. There are significant legal doubts, however, about whether a state government actually has the authority to implement all these pledges.

Controversial figures behind the scenes

There are also doubts over the "clean" image that Siegmund has cultivated. He has not been able to escape the allegations of cronyism that have dogged the AfD, after it was reported that several of the party's state and federal lawmakers secured well-paid jobs for their friends and relatives in the offices of other AfD officials.

Siegmund himself found a position for his own father. While not illegal, the move was poorly received, even within his own party.

Then there are the people behind Siegmund, those who support him as leader of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt. According to the daily newspaper Die Welt, the group employs four former members of a now-banned neo-Nazi organization, the Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend (German Youth Loyal to the Homeland). Before it was outlawed, the group openly admired Adolf Hitler's Nazism and adhered to his racial ideology, one that led to the murder of 6 million Jews and hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma in the Holocaust.

German activists target neo-Nazis with trademark law To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Siegmund himself appears to have no qualms about associating with supporters who have tattoos or clothes with neo-Nazi symbols. DW observed him appearing arm-in-arm with men wearing neo-Nazi attire and sporting tattoos such as the Black Sun, a recognized symbol among neo-Nazis.

AfD wants to 'turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground'

But what would all this mean if the AfD actually did take power after the September 6 election?

"There are clear indications that if the AfD were to enter government, it would turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground for the whole country," said Begrich. "Just how far can one go in overriding the written — and perhaps even more importantly, the unwritten — rules of democratic culture in a federal state?"

For that reason, many churches, trade unions, civil society organizations and political parties have warned against an AfD victory. Begrich shares their concerns.

AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund is using social media and merchandise to push his message in Saxony-Anhalt Image: Heiko Rebsch/dpa/picture alliance

"Naturally, things will become difficult, above all, for those in society who either belong to minorities or do not fit into the AfD's ideological worldview," he said. "The social climate would inevitably shift to an authoritarian regimentation — and that poses a problem for people who need liberal openness in society as they need air to breathe."

Like many critics, Begrich believes that winning Saxony-Anhalt is only the first step for a party that wants to take over the entire country.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis guilty
World.content:
The jury reached a verdict in less than three hours in a case that had been unsolved for nearly 30 years. Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison.

A Las Vegas jury on Monday found former gang leader, Duane "Keffe D" Davis, guilty of orchestrating the killing of hip hop artist Tupac Shakur, following nine days of testimony.

Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.

Shakur was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.

Verdict reached in under three hours

It took jurors less than three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that has, up until now, been unsolved for almost three decades.

Sixty three-year-old Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison.

Davis, a one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips gang, is the only person ever to have been charged in Shakur’s murder.

In closing arguments, Clark County Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that Davis acquired a gun and “went hunting” for Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight after they beat up Davis’ nephew earlier that night.

Palal said that Davis’ accounts of the killing evolved over the years but maintained that those differences showed Davis’ changing motivations and efforts to protect himself.

Palal argued that a key detail remained consistent throughout and that was that Davis repeatedly placed himself inside the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired.

Tupac Shakur died six days after he was shot in September 1996 Image: Kathy Hutchins/ZUMAPRESS/picture alliance

Davis, the sole surviving suspect

Davis is the only person still alive among the four men prosecutors say were in the Cadillac from which shots were fired. The man who prosecutors say originally gave the gun to Davis is also dead.

Police ​had long suspected Davis of involvement in Shakur's murder but could not charge him due to a lack of concrete evidence.

That was until Davis went public with his version of events in media appearances and a memoir, which along with recordings of his secret meetings with investigators, made up the bulk of the prosecution’s ​case.

Davis told the judge that he planned to appeal the verdict. He had pleaded not guilty to the single count of murder using a deadly weapon.

Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison Image: Bizuayehu Tesfaye/Las Vegas Review-Journal/dpa/picture alliance

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Marruecos observa como una provocación una visita real a Ceuta en medio de su campaña electoral
World.content:
La presencia de Juan Carlos I en ambas ciudades autónomas fue recibida en 2007 con un mensaje de condena de Mohamed VI y la retirada del embajador marroquí en Madrid

Marruecos no se ha pronunciado oficialmente ante una eventual visita de Felipe VI a Ceuta, aunque los medios de comunicación se han hecho eco del anuncio efectuado este lunes por el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, en la Cadena SER. Un responsable político y analista de las relaciones bilaterales, que prefiere no ser citado ante la sensibilidad de la cuestión, ha asegurado tras la entrevista del jefe del Ejecutivo que “una visita del rey de España a Ceuta en estos momentos solo serviría para reavivar la crisis”. “Ahora hay que reducir la tensión, intentar encontrar soluciones para el retorno inmediato de las personas que han atravesado la frontera [en la avalancha migratoria del 30 y el 31 de julio]. Eso es lo importante: encontrar salidas pragmáticas a estos graves problemas, vista la situación que se vive en Ceuta”, ha destacado la fuente política marroquí consultada en Rabat.

También considera que “frente a una política de símbolos y de escalada nacionalista, es mejor calmar los ánimos”, concluye en su análisis ante las elecciones legislativas convocadas en Marruecos el 23 de septiembre. “Una visita del Rey español va a ser vista siempre como una provocación que no va a servir para arreglar nada”, advierte. “Marruecos ha expuesto su posición sobre Ceuta y Melilla y España también. Pero este diferendo no debe impedir que sigamos trabajando juntos”.

Coincide en alertar sobre el clima de hipersensibilidad política marroquí el arabista y experto en las relaciones bilaterales con Marruecos Bernabé López García. “A tres semanas de las elecciones legislativas, la coyuntura es muy peculiar. Marruecos anda con pies de plomo”, sostiene este profesor honorario de la Universidad Autónoma de Madrid.

“La respuesta de Marruecos sería en todo caso muy medida, pues hay muchas susceptibilidades en juego”, explica. “A Mohamed VI ya le han contado una lección de historia en un acto religioso para expresar veladamente la posición oficial sobre Ceuta y Melilla”, puntualiza en alusión al discurso del ministro de Asuntos Islámicos, Ahmed Tufiq, quien se refirió a las “ciudades ocupadas” durante una velada religiosa presidida por el monarca en la que aludió a la histórica reivindicación marroquí sobre Ceuta y Melilla. “El rey de Marruecos puede verse obligado a recurrir de nuevo a algún subterfugio en caso que quisiera advertir contra una visita Felipe VI a las ciudades autónomas”.

Mohamed VI fue más explícito en 2007 cuando Juan Carlos I viajó a Ceuta y Melilla, y condenó mediante un comunicado oficial “la lamentable visita” como un “paso contraproducente” y contra “los sentimientos patrióticos (…) del pueblo marroquí”, en un “acto nostálgico de una era sombría y decididamente superada”. La declaración se produjo poco antes del discurso público del monarca con motivo del 32º aniversario de la Marcha Verde sobre el Sáhara Occidental, en el que no hubo mención expresa a la visita del rey Juan Carlos a Ceuta en esa misma fecha.

El comunicado del soberano de la dinastía alauí se difundió en paralelo a la retirada del embajador de Marruecos en Madrid, un gesto que sorprendió tanto al entonces presidente del Gobierno, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, como a su ministro de Asuntos Exteriores, Miguel Ángel Moratinos, ambos conocidos por su estrecho entendimiento con el país magrebí.

El ministro de Justicia, Abdelatif Uahbi, ha estado llevando hasta ahora la voz cantante en nombre del Gobierno marroquí durante la crisis de Ceuta para reclamar un proceso de negociación sobre su soberanía, lo que ha sido rechazo de plano por el ministro de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares. El jefe de la diplomacia española enfatizaba en 2022, tras el giro dado por el Gobierno de Sánchez sobre el Sáhara Occidental, que Rabat y Madrid habían alcanzado “el compromiso mutuo de evitar el uso de reclamaciones unilaterales de soberanía y de acciones que puedan ofender a la otra parte”.

World.title: El curso escolar comienza con un sistema educativo al límite: huelgas, protestas docentes y conflictos en nueve autonomías
World.content:
El curso escolar comienza oficialmente este martes ―las clases lo harán en casi toda España la semana que viene― en un clima de alta presión. Hay huelgas anunciadas en tres comunidades autónomas: indefinida en Madrid (a partir del 14 de octubre) y de una jornada, de momento, en Cataluña (el 8 de septiembre, coincidiendo con la vuelta a las aulas) y Andalucía (el 11 de noviembre). El mapa de conflictos docentes que señalan los sindicatos es, sin embargo, más amplio. Abarca otras seis autonomías y en algún caso también puede desembocar en paros: Comunidad Valenciana, Cantabria, Aragón, Baleares, Navarra y Castilla y León. Coincidiendo con la vuelta a las aulas, la OCDE presentará, además, el informe PISA, la mayor evaluación internacional, cuya publicación suele generar sacudidas en algunos sistemas educativos, como ocurrió hace tres años con el hundimiento de los resultados de Cataluña, que este año ha sido excluida de la prueba por incumplir los requisitos de la muestra de alumnos examinados (generando un efecto de maquillaje en los resultados). Un escándalo que este lunes le costó el puesto a la secretaria general de Educación de la Generalitat.

La alta conflictividad del inicio de curso refleja, afirma Fernando Villalba, portavoz del sindicato STES, el malestar que acumula buena parte de los 806.000 profesores españoles de las enseñanzas de régimen general. Villalba lo atribuye a la combinación de unas aulas cada vez más diversas, unos recursos que no han crecido lo bastante para atender el cambio en el alumnado, una temporalidad muy elevada (ronda el 30%) y la erosión de su poder adquisitivo, debido “especialmente al aumento del precio de la vivienda y el carburante”.

Al cabreo real, que tiene más causas, como la carga de papeleo que soportan los docentes, se suma, apunta Francisco Venzalá, presidente del sindicato ANPE, que en la mayor parte de España se celebrarán elecciones sindicales entre finales de 2026 y principios de 2027. Un contexto en el que las organizaciones tenderán, previsiblemente, a mostrarse especialmente exigentes en sus reivindicaciones. Y más en un contexto en el que su representatividad y margen de negociación ante la administración se está viendo cuestionada por movimientos de base, articulados en asambleas y reforzados por las redes sociales, como han puesto de manifiesto las huelgas docentes que ha habido en Asturias, Cataluña y, en menor medida, la Comunidad Valenciana, a lo largo del último año y medio. En 2027 habrá, además, elecciones en una decena de comunidades autónomas y comicios generales ―si no hay adelantos―, lo que también puede incentivar las exigencias de las centrales.

Cambios en la escuela

No hay un indicador específico que mida el incremento de la complejidad de las aulas del que hablan la mayoría de los docentes. Pero algunos datos dan pistas sobre la velocidad con la que crece. El curso pasado, en los centros públicos de 17 provincias, al menos uno de cada cinco estudiantes era extranjero. En la Comunidad Valenciana, escenario de una huelga especialmente dura, la tasa fue del 24% en primaria y del 23% en la ESO, 11 y 9 puntos más respectivamente que hace una década. En Alicante alcanzó el 30%, el nivel más alto de España. Y la estadística del Ministerio de Educación solo recoge una parte del fenómeno. No muestra, por ejemplo, el peso de los estudiantes migrantes de segunda generación que son españoles, pero cuyos padres nacieron en otro país y, según evaluaciones como PISA, también presentan en promedio una desventaja educativa.

El alumnado migrante a menudo se incorpora a los centros desconociendo la lengua del aula (que en media docena de comunidades autónomas no es el castellano, al menos en parte de su red escolar) o desde sistemas educativos más precarios. Muchos de ellos, además, señala Teresa Esperabé, secretaria general de la federación de Enseñanza de CC OO, viven en hogares vulnerables. Un tercio de los menores que viven en España están en riesgo de pobreza o exclusión social, según el INE, y la mayoría asiste a la escuela pública, en un país que lidera en el mundo desarrollado la segregación escolar por motivos socioeconómicos entre esta red educativa y la concertada, según mostró en 2024 un estudio de Save the Children.

Los centros educativos también se han vuelto más diversos (y complejos), por el aumento en las aulas ordinarias del alumnado con necesidades específicas de apoyo educativo. Una categoría amplia que engloba desde chavales con discapacidad o TEA hasta estudiantes con trastornos de la atención o incorporados tardíamente al sistema educativo español. En el curso 2024-2025, último disponible, los centros públicos acogían a 422.631 de ellos en Primaria y a 298.915 en la ESO. Cuatro años antes eran 272.398 y 183.549, respectivamente. El dato hay que tomarlo con precaución, porque parte del crecimiento se debe a una mejora en los sistemas encargados de emitir los dictámenes. Pero muchos docentes coinciden en que en los últimos años han visto un verdadero salto en el número de alumnos con este perfil en sus clases.

Refuerzo insuficiente

Esperabé subraya que el problema no es que haya más estudiantes migrantes o con necesidades especiales, sino que no hayan crecido en la misma medida los recursos para atenderlos. Como las aulas de acogida que les ayuden a salvar cuanto antes el obstáculo lingüístico, los programas de refuerzo, o el profesorado especialista en Pedagogía Terapéutica o Audición y Lenguaje. Las ratios máximas de alumnos por clase apenas han cambiado en décadas en la mayor parte de España, aunque ahora por fin, admite la responsable de CC OO, el Ministerio de Educación está pisando el acelerador para bajarlas. El número de profesores sí ha crecido (un 1,6% el curso pasado, mientras el alumnado se reducía un 0,8% en el conjunto del sistema), pero no en la cantidad que Esperabé considera necesaria.

La mayor parte de las competencias educativas están transferidas a las comunidades autónomas. Pero los sindicatos también plantean exigencias al ministerio, que Esperabé concreta en cuatro: completar la bajada de las ratios en todas las etapas educativas (las de Primaria y la ESO se tramitan por ley, así que el Gobierno necesitará reunir apoyos en el Congreso); aprobar la anunciada normativa para exigir a los centros privados de FP unos parámetros mínimos de calidad; regular la IA en educación y facilitar a alumnado y docentes una plataforma pública que puedan usar, e impulsar un gran plan financiado junto con las comunidades autónomas para climatizar las aulas en un contexto de veranos cada vez más largos. CSIF, por su parte, va un paso más allá en su exigencia al Gobierno y ha convocado una campaña de movilizaciones en toda España para reclamar mejoras para el profesorado y la escuela pública, “sin descartar la convocatoria de huelga”, que empezará el 16 de septiembre con una concentración ante el Ministerio de Educación.

World.title: Leucemia linfocítica crónica: cuando la investigación equivale a supervivencia
World.content:
Del total de personas a las que se diagnostica leucemia linfocítica crónica, un tercio no necesita tratamiento y la decisión de aplicarlo depende de que la enfermedad esté activa o no, según establecen las guías clínicas de esta patología. /GETTY IMAGES

La supervivencia a cinco años sitúa la leucemia más habitual en adultos entre los cánceres con mejor pronóstico. La incorporación de tratamientos de duración limitada ha permitido, además, reducir la toxicidad y facilitar una mejor calidad de vida a los pacientes

La historia de la oncología se ha escrito con avances paulatinos que han supuesto un aumento en la supervivencia del cáncer en general, y además con grandes saltos terapéuticos, como la medicina de precisión, que han marcado un antes y un después en el abordaje de algunos tipos de cáncer. Uno de ellos es la leucemia linfocítica crónica (LLC). Los datos de supervivencia a cinco años de los pacientes con LLC revelan ese impacto: ha pasado de un 59% en 2005 a un 85% en la actualidad, según datos recogidos por la Sociedad Española de Hematología y Hemoterapia en su informe Avance en los cánceres hematológicos.

Francesc Bosch, jefe del servicio de Hematología del hospital Vall d’Hebron de Barcelona, sitúa el punto de inflexión definitivo en la última década: “El conocimiento de la biología de la LLC se ha traducido en el desarrollo de medicamentos muy dirigidos que van a buscar las debilidades de la enfermedad”.

La combinación de mutaciones que se registran en un cáncer es única en cada persona y la medicina de precisión aplicada a la oncología se basa en buscar esas alteraciones genéticas tumorales para predecir la respuesta al tratamiento. En la LLC ha supuesto, en la práctica, pasar de la quimioterapia que se aplicaba a todos los pacientes a un tratamiento personalizado. Los avances terapéuticos han supuesto, además, menos efectos secundarios y, como consecuencia, mejor calidad de vida para los pacientes.

En qué consiste la leucemia linfocítica crónica Fuente: Instituto Nacional del Cáncer (NIH) de EE UU y elaboración propia a partir de las fuentes consultadas.

Las leucemias se clasifican según la rapidez con la que se desarrollan y la célula en la que se originan. Francesc Bosch explica que “la leucemia linfocítica crónica afecta a los linfocitos y a los órganos donde se ubican estas células y, a diferencia de la leucemia aguda, que se manifiesta de forma abrupta, la LLC aparece lentamente, por lo que muchos pacientes no van a necesitar tratamiento para su enfermedad”.

Cuando una persona escucha en la voz de su médico la palabra leucemia, no espera que la indicación sea una cita a los tres o a los seis meses. En la mente de esa persona se instala la idea del cáncer, un diagnóstico que todo el mundo asocia automáticamente con recibir tratamiento urgente. Pero, en el caso de la LLC, la espera activa forma parte del proceso. Jesús Pérez Viejo, psico-oncólogo y profesor de la Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia (UNED), ha comprobado esa perplejidad inicial en numerosos enfermos: “A veces es difícil integrar palabras como cáncer y enfermedad crónica porque el paciente no espera convivir con la leucemia de por vida; la idea generalizada que tenemos de un proceso oncológico es que, si no te curas, te mueres”.

“La leucemia linfocítica crónica es de los cánceres con mejor pronóstico y la incertidumbre del diagnóstico desaparece si sabes que estás en buenas manos y si hay información sobre el camino por el que vas a pasar” Julio González González, presidente de la Asociación de Pacientes con Leucemia Linfocítica Crónica (ASPALLC)

Cómo gestionar esa incertidumbre es, según los clínicos y las asociaciones de pacientes, uno de los retos en la LLC. Julio González, presidente de la Asociación de Pacientes con Leucemia Linfocítica Crónica (ASPALLC), convive con ella desde hace 12 años y pone especial énfasis en la importancia de que la persona diagnosticada conozca lo mejor posible la enfermedad para despejar las nubes oscuras que tienden a instalarse en la mente y hallar respuesta a las docenas de preguntas que le surgen: “La leucemia linfocítica crónica es de los cánceres con mejor pronóstico y la incertidumbre del diagnóstico desaparece si sabes que estás en buenas manos y si hay información sobre el camino por el que vas a pasar”.

Un paciente implicado y una responsabilidad compartida

Los propios equipos sanitarios, cada vez más multidisciplinares, propician la implicación del paciente. Les corresponde ese protagonismo y asumirlo repercute, entre otras cosas, en la adherencia terapéutica. “Cuanto más formado e implicado esté el paciente, mayor es la adherencia”, señala el doctor Bosch. Jesús Pérez Viejo, por su parte, incide en que los beneficios alcanzan a todos los implicados en la LLC: “La participación de los pacientes, sobre todo en la toma de decisiones, mejora su capacidad de afrontamiento de la enfermedad y ayuda al personal sanitario a que su responsabilidad sea compartida”.

“Con los tratamientos que tenemos, basados en las características genéticas de la enfermedad en cada paciente, la respuesta es muy rápida: al cabo de un mes o dos desaparecen los síntomas y el paciente nota que mejora mucho” Francesc Bosch, jefe del servicio de Hematología del hospital Vall d’Hebron de Barcelona

Del total de personas a las que se diagnostica LLC, un tercio no necesita tratamiento y la decisión de aplicarlo depende de que la enfermedad esté activa o no, según establecen las guías clínicas; es decir, que el paciente presente síntomas asociados a la leucemia, como crecimiento de los ganglios, anemia o descenso de las plaquetas. Si se ha iniciado el tratamiento, la adherencia es muy importante porque hay un grupo de enfermos en los que la terapia será de por vida, igual que ocurre en enfermedades como la diabetes o la hipertensión.

Aunque los efectos adversos de estas terapias están lejos de los que producía la quimioterapia, siguen existiendo, como en cualquier tratamiento crónico. De ahí que los especialistas ponderen el valor de uno de los cambios que se ha registrado en los últimos años: la incorporación de tratamientos limitados en el tiempo a partir de la combinación de diferentes terapias ya existentes. “Con un terapia de duración fija se ahorra toxicidad para el paciente y se evita la posibilidad de que genere resistencias al tratamiento”, apunta Bosch.

La leucemia linfocítica crónica (LLC), en datos Fuente: Fuente: Elaboración propia a partir de las fuentes consultadas.

De la mano de los avances terapéuticos en los últimos años ha llegado también una atención cada vez más integral a los pacientes. Jesús Pérez Viejo precisa: “El cáncer afecta a todas las áreas de la vida, desde la familiar a la laboral y hay momentos en que los tratamientos o el avance de la enfermedad requiere un soporte emocional especializado”.

Los profesionales de la psico-oncología tienen cada vez mayor protagonismo en ese acompañamiento. Se trata de vivir y hacerlo con calidad de vida, y en el logro de ese objetivo el bienestar emocional es fundamental. Pérez Viejo comenta que el psico-oncólogo puede resolver muchos de los temores que viven el enfermo y su entorno: “La LLC conlleva síntomas que generan retos psicológicos, pues hay inmunosupresión y se deben cuidar las infecciones. A veces, esto genera inseguridad en muchos pacientes porque tienen miedo a contagiarse y eso les hace evitar determinados lugares y el consiguiente aislamiento”.

“La participación de los pacientes, sobre todo en la toma de decisiones, mejora su capacidad de afrontar la enfermedad y ayuda al personal sanitario a que su responsabilidad sea compartida” Jesús Pérez Viejo, psico-oncólogo y profesor de la Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia (UNED)

Con la experiencia de 12 años conviviendo con la LLC, Julio González recomienda disponer de “una caja de herramientas propia” para afrontar una relación no querida pero inevitable, como es la de la leucemia. Esa caja le sirve para afrontar las repercusiones de la enfermedad en todos los ámbitos en los que se desenvuelve. Así, para las personas que todavía están trabajando recomienda tener claro que “el diagnóstico forma parte de la información médica privada y es el paciente quien decide qué compartir, con quién y cuándo hacerlo”. Si se necesita flexibilidad para revisiones o pruebas, señala que lo mejor es ser práctico: “Necesito tal día o tal franja horaria. Hay que proponer soluciones. Menos drama, más claridad”.

Los pacientes, las asociaciones como ASPALLC y los profesionales que atienden a las personas con LLC consideran que todavía quedan necesidades no cubiertas, que tienen que ver, sobre todo, con la falta de equidad en el acceso a un soporte integral. “Hay sitios donde la posibilidad de recurrir a un psico-oncólogo simplemente no existe y la información para los pacientes se limita a una consulta cada cuatro meses aprisa y corriendo”, apunta Julio González. Las otras necesidades por cubrir alcanzan a otros ámbitos muchas veces ignorados, pero importantes, que precisa Jesús Pérez Viejo: “Tienen que ver con el trabajo, el gasto económico que supone una enfermedad oncológica o incluso con problemas sexológicos que pueden aparecer y que en un primer momento no son prioritarios, pero afectan a la calidad de vida”.

Todo suma en el abordaje integral de una enfermedad, la LLC, cuyo horizonte se tiñe cada vez más de verde. La investigación y los profesionales implicados en el proceso oncológico han conseguido prolongar drásticamente la supervivencia y mejorar la calidad de vida de los pacientes, pero no se han olvidado del objetivo final, que apunta Francesc Bosch como médico: “Se investiga mucho la LLC porque no deja de ser la leucemia más frecuente en adultos, pero nuestro fin último es curarla”.

World.title: ¿Puede el casero subirme la renta un 20% a pesar de estar el piso en una zona tensionada?
World.content:
Pregunta. Mi madre, de 79 años, es inquilina desde hace 16 años de un piso en Barcelona. El próximo 31 de octubre vence el contrato y el arrendador nos ha comunicado su intención de no renovarlo en las condiciones actuales. Nos propone una subida del 20% y un plazo de prórroga de tres años con subida del IPC. ¿Existe alguna forma de evitar una subida tan elevada? ¿Se puede exigir un plazo más largo? Actualmente el importe del alquiler es inferior a la referencia correspondiente a zona tensionada, pero la subida es brutal. J. Marín

Respuesta. Si la inquilina lleva 16 años en la vivienda, lo más probable es que el contrato se encuentre en situación de tácita reconducción civil, al haber agotado el periodo del contrato y las sucesivas prórrogas previstas legalmente. Esto significa que el contrato se prorroga en las mismas condiciones mientras el arrendador no comunique su voluntad de ponerle fin, ya sea anualmente (si se pactó una renta anual abonada por mensualidades) o mensualmente (si únicamente se estableció una renta mensual).

En caso de que el arrendador haya efectuado dicha comunicación, el contrato finalizará en los términos indicados y la única posibilidad será formalizar un nuevo contrato en las condiciones que arrendador y arrendatario acuerden de mutuo acuerdo.

En todo caso, el arrendador deberá ajustarse a las disposiciones de la Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos (LAU), que reconocen el derecho del inquilino a una prórroga obligatoria de hasta cinco años, y no de tres años, como se plantea en la consulta.

Por otro lado, dado que el inmueble se encuentra ubicado en una zona declarada tensionada, resulta de aplicación el artículo 17.6 de la LAU, que establece lo siguiente:

En los contratos de arrendamiento de vivienda sujetos a la presente ley en los que el inmueble se ubique en una zona de mercado residencial tensionado dentro del periodo de vigencia de la declaración de la referida zona en los términos dispuestos en la Ley 12/2023, de 24 de mayo, por el derecho a la vivienda, la renta pactada al inicio del nuevo contrato no podrá exceder el de la última renta de contrato de arrendamiento de vivienda habitual que hubiese estado vigente en los últimos cinco años en la misma vivienda, una vez aplicada la cláusula de actualización anual de la renta del contrato anterior. No se pueden fijar nuevas condiciones que establezcan la repercusión al arrendatario de cuotas o gastos que no estuviesen recogidas en el contrato anterior.

Por lo tanto, la propuesta de un nuevo contrato por parte del arrendador, sometida a la legislación vigente, debería firmarse por un periodo que permita al inquilino disfrutar de una prórroga inicial obligatoria de hasta cinco años, así como respetar la limitación de la renta a la vigente en los últimos cinco años, una vez aplicada la cláusula de actualización anual prevista en el contrato anterior.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Groningen University launches Frisian language degree
World.content:
Groningen University has launched a bachelor’s degree programme in the Frisian language, the first standalone course in the country’s second official language for 15 years.

Three students began the course this week, which covers linguistics, history and Frisian culture. Frisian was taught as a degree in its own right until 2012, when it was absorbed into a broader programme on Europe’s minority languages, Minorities & Multilingualism.

That programme drew too few students to survive and the university said it would phase it out from the 2025/26 academic year, leaving the academic study of Frisian at risk of vanishing altogether.

A rescue from The Hague

The course was saved after the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (KNAW) recommended, in a report on the future of Frisian studies, that the state pay for a dedicated bachelor. The government agreed to put in €340,000 a year, with further provincial money.

For legal reasons the new degree sits as a Frisian track within the university’s Dutch Languages and Cultures programme, though the focus is now entirely on Frisian.

Professor of Frisian Arjen Versloot said he was happy with the intake, even though a course usually needs around 20 students to break even. “There are often only five students in French and German too, so as a small language we can’t complain,” he told regional broadcaster Omrop Fryslân.

Teachers in demand

The degree is also meant to supply qualified teachers. Since August, schools in Friesland have been required to use more Frisian in the classroom under new curriculum rules, and Versloot expects strong demand for teachers able to deliver it at the highest level.

Frisian is spoken by around 470,000 people in Friesland and is the closest living relative of English.

Reading and writing proficiency in Frisian has risen sharply over the past two decades, despite fewer people speaking the language at home, according to a recent survey.

Around 58% of residents in Friesland now say they can read Frisian well or very well, up from 46% in 2007. Self-reported writing proficiency nearly doubled over the same period, from 9.6% to 18.9%.

World.title: Man cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia
World.content:
A man has been cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia, the eldest daughters of king Willem-Alexander and queen Máxima, after a court ruled he was suffering from a psychosis at the time.

Anne Romke van der H., 33, believed he was in a relationship with Amalia, 22, and fantasised about marrying her before living in the wilds in Poland with her and her 21-year-old sister.

He bought items from a hardware store designed to use as a survival kit, including knives, cooking equipment and two hatchets, one of which he inscribed with Alexia’s name.

The prosecution service said he intended to abduct or attack the two princesses if they were unwilling to go along with his plans.

But a court in The Hague ruled there was no evidence that van der H., from Groningen, was preparing an actual attack on Amalia and Alexia or intended to threaten them.

A psychiatric assessment found he was schizophrenic and had become obsessed with the royal family, particularly the two princesses.

He was found guilty of insulting six police officers and smashing a window, but the court did not impose a fine or punishment because he was in psychosis at the time.

The court said the offences were not severe enough to justify a compulsory treatment regime (tbs), but Van der H. told the judges at an earlier hearing that he was willing to undergo voluntary treatment.

World.title: Housing minister announces sites for 30,000 new homes by 2035
World.content:
Housing minister Eleanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan has identified five new sites around the country to build 30,000 new homes by 2035.

The five urban locations in Friesland, Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Limburg have been designated National Large-Scale Housing Locations (NGWs) as part of the cabinet’s plans to build 400,000 houses in the next 10 years.

Between 5,000 and 6,000 homes are planned at four of the sites in Haarlem, Deventer, Weert and Leeuwarden, while 8,000 houses are due to be built in Maastricht. All the sites apart from Haarlem are close to main railway stations.

The sites are the first to be identified by the current government under the NGW scheme, a €5 billion fund first announced in 2023 to speed up development in urban areas and relieve the pressure on housing.

It takes the total number of NGW areas to 26. However, last month plans to develop four sites nominated by the previous housing minister, Mona Keijzer, had to be put on hold because there was no money to build road and railway connections.

Boekholt-O’Sullivan said in a letter to parliament that the locations had been chosen because they could be easily connected to services such as water and electricity, allowing the areas to be developed quickly.

“In choosing these five new NGW locations we explicitly looked at locations where no extra measures are needed for availability to realise these homes,” she said. “That means we can use our joint efforts to realise new neighbourhoods at speed.”

World.title: VVD MP quits lobby group board over conflict of interest claims
World.content:
VVD MP Renate den Hollander has resigned from the management board of a vets’ lobby group after facing questions about her role as the party’s spokesman on animal welfare.

NOS reported that some of Den Hollander’s comments in parliament were almost identical to statements made by the BPW, an organisation representing owners of veterinary practices.

Den Hollander, 49, spent 22 as a vet and ran her own practice in Drenthe before being elected to parliament for the first time last November. She was a member of the BPW before becoming an MP, but only joined the board this year.

NOS reported that her response to a report by the consumer markets watchdog ACM that criticised high vets’ bills and unnecessary procedures was strikingly similar to the BPW’s official line.

Den Hollander said the VVD did not share all the ACM’s criticisms, stressed the need for veterinary staff to be paid properly and suggested alternative solutions to deal with rising costs such as encouraging people to take out more insurance.

Identical language

Although she was not a member of the board at the time, Den Hollander used almost identical language to the BPW in its response, such as comparing vets to other business owners such as bakers and garage owners.

A month later she was taken on as a member of the management board with an allowance of €1,000 a year.

In a written reply to NOS, she said she was stepping down from the board with immediate effect after the national broadcaster compared her speech with the BPW’s statement.

“The similarities to a contribution I later made as an MP, which you have rightly asked questions about. have made me realise that my membership of the management board of the BPW could lead in future to (the appearance of) a conflict of interests,” she said.

World.title: Cabinet agrees 11th-hour budget deal without opposition support
World.content:
The coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD have agreed a draft budget package after a marathon weekend of “tough” and “intensive” talks.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen said the negotiations had produced a “budget for 10 parties”, but the minority government was unable to secure the approval of opposition parties before the plans are presented to parliament on September 15.

Instead the three coalition partners had to resolve their own differences on issues such as welfare cuts, changes to the system for taxing wealth and assets and the higher excess charge on health insurance.

Heinen and prime minister Rob Jetten did not disclose what concessions had been made during the negotiations, but party leaders said they had produced a balanced package designed to appeal to both left and right.

Jetten acknowledged the negotiations had been “tough” at times. “Occasionally there was a bit of friction, but that gave us a more polished budget,” he said.

Dilan Yesilgöz, leader of the VVD, said in a post on X that the cabinet had produced a budget “that can take the Netherlands forward”, while emphasising her party’s campaign points.

“The VVD wil always stand for lower taxes, room for economic growth and a government that spends less,” she said. Earlier Yesilgöz described the negotiations as “long and intensive”.

We zijn eruit. Na lange en intensieve onderhandelingen ligt er een begroting waarmee Nederland vooruit kan. De VVD staat daarbij altijd voor lagere lasten, ruimte voor economische groei en een overheid die minder uitgeeft. In een kabinet betekent verantwoordelijkheid nemen ook:… — Dilan Yesilgöz – Zegerius (@DilanYesilgoz) August 31, 2026

Henri Bontenbal, leader of the CDA, said: “My aim was to come up with a good offer to the opposition. I think we’ve managed that.”

Minority government

Jetten and Heinen spent two weeks talking to opposition party leaders behind closed doors to try to secure their support for the budget before the draft package was sent to the Council of State.

But those negotiations broke down at the end of last week without producing a formal deal, meaning the cabinet will have to find the votes as the bills pass through parliament in the autumn.

The government is 10 seats short of a majority in the Lower House and 16 short in the smaller Senate, where it needs the support of at least two opposition parties.

The original deadline of last Friday was extended over the weekend and into an extra cabinet meeting on Monday afternoon as the divisions within the coalition became harder to reconcile.

The centre parties, D66 and CDA, wanted to scrap some of the proposed €6.5 billion budget cuts planned for the next four years to appeal to Progressief Nederland (PRO), the largest opposition party, which was previously the left-wing alliance of Labour (PvdA) and GroenLinks.

“Problems delayed”

But the VVD favoured a different package of measures designed to bring on board right-wing parties such as JA21 and the SGP, who wanted to see tax cuts instead.

The parties also had different visions of how to reform the “box 3” income tax module, which covers assets and savings, with the VVD arguing for a more generous deal for investors.

The VVD justice minister, David van Weel, said “nobody is proud of this process, nobody is happy with it” ahead of Monday’s meeting, where the draft budget was agreed.

Pro leader Jesse Klaver said he feared that the coalition parties had “not made choices” and “the problems have been delayed” until after the budget is presented on September 15.

World.title: Footage shows armed group at deadly Gelderland shooting
World.content:
One person has died and two police officers have been injured in a suspected gang-related shooting in Overasselt, a village in Gelderland, in the early hours of Tuesday. A large number of arrests have been made and the village has been cordoned off.

Unverified images shared by the Telegraaf shows a group of at least 20 armed men – some carrying what appear to be automatic rifles – shooting outside a property. The paper says the men were storming a farmhouse that was previously used as a drugs lab and the shots killed a security guard.

Officers were initially called to the Ewijkseweg road in the village at around 4.20am and police later confirmed that one person was dead and two officers injured. Their condition has not been released, and no details have been given about the person who died.

The owner of the farmhouse allegedly did business with Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, in the past and the attack on Tuesday morning was part of a long running dispute over large quantities of cocaine, the Telegraaf reported.

The same house was shot at with an AK-47 last year, according to police, by a young man from Amsterdam who was paid 2,500 euros. He never said who paid him, and received a year in prison.

A large scale police operation is now underway in Overasselt, with helicopters, dogs and arrest teams scouring the area around the farm for evidence. Several of the people arrested were found hiding in bushes.

World.title: Rotterdam medical students offer cash to jump training queues
World.content:
Medical students in Rotterdam are offering each other thousands of euros to move up the queue for the hospital training they need to qualify as doctors amid a shortage of spaces.

The bids – one as high as €2,000, according to news website NU.nl – after the lottery system for places at Erasmus MC left hundreds of students waiting months, some more than a year, to begin.

The medicine master’s is built mostly around clinical placements in hospital departments. Each department can take a limited number of trainees, so start dates are drawn by lottery, and pulling the short straw can cost the better part of a year.

This time the draw went badly for a lot of them. Of the roughly 380 students who entered, about a quarter can’t start until autumn 2027 and 35% not until 2028, NU.nl reported, citing an email sent to students.

Richer students paying ahead

Students have bought and sold Rotterdam start dates before. Medisch Contact, a medical journal, documented the trade in 2020, when the medical faculty’s student council warned it let wealthier students buy their way ahead.

Erasmus MC told NU.nl it did not want money deciding who trains first, and said it would look at tightening the rules on swaps. It called the shortage of places temporary: extra students are graduating amid a switch to a new curriculum.

Students who wait longest can sometimes claim compensation from a university fund that covers study delays outside their control. The Netherlands is already facing a shortage of doctors, particularly neurologists.

World.title: Former CDA leader Elco Brinkman dies aged 78
World.content:
Elco Brinkman, the Christian Democrat minister and party leader whose 1994 election defeat pushed the CDA into opposition for the first time in decades, has died aged 78. He died on Monday in Leiden after a short illness, his family said.

Brinkman became minister of welfare, health and culture in 1982, aged 34, serving seven years under Ruud Lubbers.

As minister he coined the phrase “caring society”, arguing that people had grown too dependent on the welfare state. He pushed through cuts to welfare and the arts and steered a new media law that opened the Netherlands to commercial television.

He took over as CDA leader in parliament in 1989 and was earmarked as Lubbers’s successor, but his 1994 campaign collapsed after Lubbers publicly withdrew his backing. The CDA fell from 54 seats to 34, and Brinkman left national politics in 1995.

He later chaired the construction federation Bouwend Nederland and returned as the CDA’s senate leader from 2011 to 2019.

A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B., has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. Na miejsce przybyły tłumy. „Nie chcemy bać się chodzić po chodnikach” – apelują.@RadioKrakow pic.twitter.com/DlOn5GvyL5 — Elżbieta Raczyńska (@_eraczynska) August 25, 2026 Acting mayor Stanisław Kracik said that an inspection of the street carried out after the accident had not shown any problems with the existing signage or need for traffic-calming measures. He added, however, that the city would be installing a speed bump. “I believe that this is simply what we should do…as a kind of expression of solidarity with the victims of this tragedy,” he said, quoted by broadcaster TVN. City police said they had been monitoring and taking action about road safety issues in the district for years, but that the street in question had not previously been reported as a particularly dangerous place, with just one incident causing one injury in the five years before the fatal accident. MPs from The Left have called for tougher rules on illegal street racing, saying police currently do not have sufficient legal tools. World.title: Polish student accused of planning Islamist terrorist attack on Christmas market to stand trial

We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State. On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law. Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”. Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then. Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned. However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause. “Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office. In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”. Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison. Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”. In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”. Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect. World.title: Polish WWII massacre victims reburied in Ukraine at ceremony attended by officials from both countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of 55 Poles – around half of them children – massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, many of whose bones show signs of brutal deaths, were exhumed this summer after Ukraine recently ended a moratorium on searches for tens of thousands of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres who are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. “This is an important moment for [the victims’] families, but also the Polish state, because this funeral follows decades of waiting,” said Polish culture minister Marta Cienkowska at the ceremony in Ostrówki (Ostrovky in Ukrainian), a depopulated former village that, before the war, was part of Poland and now lies in Ukraine. “Poland has the right and obligation to speak about the crimes committed against its citizens. It has the obligation to commemorate the victims, search for their remains, and provide them with a dignified burial…We will continue this work…everywhere that the graves of the victims of the Volhynian crimes still remain.” Pogrzeb ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej Na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach na terytorium Ukrainy odbyła się uroczystość pogrzebowa 55 ofiar zbrodni dokonanej 30 sierpnia 1943 roku. W uroczystości, zorganizowanej w 83. rocznicę tragicznych wydarzeń,… pic.twitter.com/4dXPOj4m7y — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) August 30, 2026 Others to attend the reburial included deputy Ukrainian culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi; Vitaly Skomarovsky, the bishop of Lutsk and president of Ukraine’s Roman Catholic episcopate; Piotr Zgorzelski, the deputy speaker of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament; and former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. Karol Polejowski, the deputy head of Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which led the exhumation work, said that the presence of Ukrainian representatives “fills me with optimism for the future”. While Polish President Karol Nawrocki did not attend, one of his advisors, Jakub Banaszek, read a letter on his behalf, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will never forget those who died in agony simply because they were Poles,” wrote Nawrocki. “We will not cease our efforts to ensure that all our compatriots murdered by members of the OUN-UPA are properly buried and commemorated.” ✝️ W 8⃣3⃣. rocznicę zbrodni dokonanej przez ukraińskich szowinistów, na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach pochowaliśmy ofiary ludobójstwa na Wołyniu. 🔻🔻🔻 pic.twitter.com/5oh3uiCKX4 — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 30, 2026 The Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Poles were killed, were led by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was a partisan group founded by a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) faithful to nationalist leader Stepan Bandera. They sought to ethnically cleanse areas that they saw as Ukrainian territory by wiping out other ethnic groups, in particular the large Polish population. Massacres took place in dozens of villages, including Ostrówki and the neighbouring Wola Ostrowiecka (Volya Ostrovetska in Ukrainian), where on 30 August 1943 the UPA killed over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Exhumations previously took place on the site of the two villages in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Earlier this month, the IPN announced the results of that work. They uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during WWII have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools https://t.co/LbLPzJcG1b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 8, 2026 The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit. Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where Zelensky’s counterpart Karol Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest honour. In his letter read at Sunday’s ceremony, Nawrocki warned those who “continue the tradition of Banderite ideology” that they “place themselves outside the community of citizens of the free, civilised world” and are sending “a clear sign of hostility towards Poland and Poles”. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Since the crisis broke out in May, there have been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Earlier this month, Zelensky signed a law establishing a new national pantheon of Ukrainian heroes. Poland has warned that the inclusion of figures associated with the massacres could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. A survey conducted this month by Rating Group, a Ukrainian research agency, which asked Ukrainians to name their country’s greatest hero found that Bandera was the fourth most popular choice, having been chosen by 11% of respondents. World.title: Poland is terrible at promoting itself – but has never had better press
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Two incidents this month have highlighted how state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad often disappoint. Yet, at the same time, the country has never had better international press. Politicians should let Poland’s successes speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story. Poles care a lot about what the world thinks of their country. Major Polish media outlets regularly devote entire articles to what Western journalists, commentators and influencers are saying about Poland. “A German showed what he saw on the streets of Poland,” read one typical recent headline by Onet, Poland’s biggest news website, which devoted an entire report to one video by a German-speaking TikToker with around 7,000 followers. One rarely sees such reports in more self-confident Western countries. Given Poland’s history, such sensitivity regarding the country’s status is not surprising. Poland was, up until the 18th century, a major European country. But, for most of the last 250 years, it has been under foreign subjugation. Only since 1989 has it been able to develop independently, and Poles are understandably keen for the world to take note of their return to the top table. Poland has emerged as Europe’s undisputed growth champion over the past 35 years. In the first part of a new series of articles and podcasts, @AlicjaPtak4 explores the reasons behind Poland's rapid economic development, and the dangers that may lie ahead https://t.co/bW3bnV7Ozn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2025 Polish politicians are also inevitably eager to capitalise on such sentiment by showing voters that they are making an effort to promote Poland abroad. The problem is that such efforts are often poorly conceived and executed – as two examples this month have shown. In mid-August, the sport and tourism ministry launched a new advertising campaign intended to attract visitors from western Europe and the United States. However, the first advert – featuring Polish football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, and actor Nikodem Rozbicki playing Fryderyk Chopin – was widely panned in Poland. Res Futura, an organisation that monitors social media sentiment, found that 85% of comments about the advert were negative. The campaign’s slogan – “Poland. More than you expected” – is negative and lacking confidence. The Polish Tourism Organisation says it is based on research showing that visitors to Poland are often positively surprised by how nice it is. Yet, while that is undoubtedly true, it does not mean it is a good idea to try to attract potential tourists by focusing on their low expectations. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The video also has no narrative, with the creators seeming to think that showing famous faces will be enough. Rubik does not speak a single word, while Eisenberg says only “Poland” and Lewandowski “More than you expected”. The film itself does nothing to show that Poland is more than anyone expects. In fact, its depressingly colourless palette and focus on Warsaw’s Stalinist Palace of Science and Culture actually reinforce (false) stereotypes of Poland as grey, dull and post-communist. The country has so many interesting and colourful places that could have been showcased instead. The advert is also a wasted opportunity to tell a story about the film’s stars, especially Eisenberg, who has reconnected with his family’s Polish roots, produced a critically acclaimed movie set in Poland, and last year obtained citizenship. Instead, Chopin dominates the film, but his dialogue is incoherent. When he says, “Warsaw is where my heart is”, almost no potential visitors would understand that this is a reference to the real Chopin’s heart being transported from Paris, where he died, to Warsaw, where it is now entombed in a church. Not long after that advert launched, another controversy emerged around a state official, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, who had been appointed only weeks earlier by the government to lead the promotion of Poland. It quickly transpired that a report she had authored last year on creating a national brand – and which appeared to have played a big part in her getting the new job – contained significant errors, questionable methodology, and bizarre language. Many parts showed signs of being AI-generated. Mróz-Gorgoń, who has now resigned, insists that the report was the genuine product of work by her and her team at Marka Polska (Brand Poland), a think tank she leads. However, that is not particularly reassuring given the report’s content. Many parts are simply obvious: at the end of the 26-page text, the three recommendations for the government are to “develop a coherent, long-term national branding strategy”, “invest in promotional campaigns in key markets”, and “coordinate between ministries and other entities”. Other sections are very strange, such as noting that “Germany does not build its brand on the Holocaust”. But perhaps the most telling aspect is that, although the introduction claims it is “a comprehensive report on building…a coherent, long-term branding strategy in the international arena”, the document focuses entirely on how Poles themselves view their own country (its title is even A Self-Portrait of the Poles). It includes no research into what foreigners know or think about Poland and what could interest or attract them. While any national branding exercise should of course take account of the views of the native population, it is clearly incomplete without research into the target of such a campaign, the outside world. Yet that is sadly typical of many state-led efforts to promote Poland, which focus more on pleasing a domestic audience – the voters that politicians want to keep happy – than on being truly outward looking. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland's brand abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing major errors, bizarre language, and signs of being generated by AI https://t.co/9fpfzFCFuI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 It should be noted that such failings are nothing new. Successive governments have been responsible for botched efforts to promote Poland. The uninspiring slogan “Poland. More than you expected” has been used since 2021. A previous one, “Polska. Spring Into”, launched in 2014, was simply bizarre and quickly disappeared. In 2016, the former Law and Justice (PiS) government established the Polish National Foundation (PFN), which was pumped full of money from state-owned companies and tasked with promoting Poland abroad. Instead, it focused much of its efforts on domestic activity, often intended to support PiS’s political agenda. The work it did do internationally was often of questionable efficacy, such as spending millions on buying a yacht, naming it “I Love Poland”, then attempting to sail it around the world (before it ended up breaking down and getting stuck in port). A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Yet, despite woeful state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad, the country has in recent times been enjoying a soaring international reputation. Western media have been full of articles about the country’s economic success; about how not only are Polish emigrants returning from the UK, but many Brits are moving to Poland too; about how Poles are becoming major buyers of property in Spain; about how companies with roots in Poland, such as InPost and ElevenLabs, are pioneering their industries. Social media feeds are full of influencers extolling Polish cities, with their safe, clean streets; the beauty of Polish nature, with its mountains, lakes and beaches; and the sense of dynamic development that you can feel as soon as you set foot in the country. Last weekend,@thetimes reported on how Brits are moving to Poland. This weekend, on how Poles are replacing Brits as property owners in Spain. pic.twitter.com/IDDdDlluTE — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) June 21, 2026 This positive publicity is largely organic – it is the product of Poland’s own actual successes, not of artificial efforts to create an image of success. It is generated from the bottom up, not from the top down. While the state can play a role – for example, by arranging visits for foreign journalists and influencers and supporting media and institutions that are already telling Poland’s story – it would be better for politicians to focus on creating the conditions for those successes, rather than concocting cockeyed schemes to promote them. World.title: Polish government sets out draft 2027 budget with deficit remaining at 7.1% of GDP
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
