Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead. The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger. In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine. The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered. Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later. “It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN. The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning. “In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living. However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element. Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin. “The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023 Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death. However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown. The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks. This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community. Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth. Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose. “It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.” A team of scientists has reconstructed the face of a 400-year-old woman, once believed by her neighbors to be a vampire, revealing the human story buried by supernatural beliefs https://t.co/Q6sipo7h4O pic.twitter.com/0gLVIEfaZi — Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. A dispute has emerged between Poland’s government and the office of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over whether Poland would be willing to host allied nuclear weapons. Deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski announced on Thursday that Poland wants to participate in the US-led NATO nuclear sharing programme, but without actually hosting warheads. That prompted criticism from Nawrocki’s senior foreign policy aide, Marcin Przydacz, who says Poland should host such weapons. Jedno zdanie wiceszefa MON wystarczyło, by wywołać polityczną burzę wokół kwestii broni jądrowej w Polsce. Paweł Zalewski stwierdził w Kwaterze Głównej NATO w Brukseli, że Polska nie chce głowic nuklearnych na swoim terytorium. Kilka godzin później zareagował szef MON Władysław… pic.twitter.com/EqjTPKqidg — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) August 28, 2026 Zalewski met on Thursday with Elbridge Colby, US under secretary of defence for policy, at NATO’s headquarters in Brussels. Afterwards, he was asked by reporters if an expanded future US military presence in Poland might include nuclear weapons. “No. I would like to say this very clearly and openly: Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory,” replied Zalewski, quoted by broadcaster TVN. The minister added that Poland still wants to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme. However, he said that this could be achieved without hosting the weapons themselves. Those remarks triggered criticism from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. Former PiS defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak said that refusing to host warheads “in practice means renouncing participation in nuclear sharing”. “Poland should strive for full participation in nuclear sharing,” added Błaszczak. “This is not a matter of Poland possessing its own nuclear weapons, but of strengthening NATO’s nuclear deterrence on the eastern flank.” Criticism also came from other sources, including retired Brigadier General Stanisław Koziej, who served as head of the National Security Bureau (BBN) of former President Bronisław Komorowski, who is an ally of the current government. Koziej called Zalewski’s announcement “an incomprehensible strategic mistake in the field of deterrence”. He said that, to deter Russia, Vladimir Putin must know that there is the possibility Poland could host nuclear weapons. Chęci nie odstraszają. Odstraszają realne zdolności – własne i sojusznicze. A przede wszystkim takie, o jakich użyciu sami decydujemy. To elementarz, który warto przypomnieć https://t.co/Nc3xXnA7bU — Paweł Zalewski (@ZalewskiPawel) August 27, 2026 Late on Thursday, Zalewski commented on the controversy. He rejected Błaszczak’s claim that refusing to host warheads would effectively exclude Poland from nuclear sharing. “We want to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme without wanting the stationing of nuclear weapons in Poland,” he wrote. “Thanks to our efforts, NATO has opened up precisely such a possibility.” In response to Koziej, Zalewski argued that “intentions do not deter, real capabilities do…above all, those whose use we ourselves decide upon”. Meanwhile, defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also weighed in, declaring that “Poland remains strongly interested in participating in the NATO nuclear sharing programme” and is also “conducting talks regarding the proposal for participation in a European nuclear protective umbrella”. Kosiniak-Kamysz did not, however, comment on the issue of Poland potentially hosting warheads. Rozwiewając wszelkie wątpliwości: Polska jest niezmiennie zainteresowana udziałem w programie NATO Nuclear Sharing. Prowadzimy także rozmowy na temat propozycji uczestnictwa w europejskim nuklearnym parasolu ochronnym. Stanowisko naszego rządu jest w tych kwestiach… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) August 27, 2026 On Friday morning, Przydacz, who is the head of President Nawrocki’s International Policy Bureau (BPM), joined the criticism of Zalewski, calling his comments “bizarre, absurd and completely inconsistent with what Poland has been saying so far and what the policy of the Polish state is”. “Both the presidential palace and the executive branch of the government have so far supported Poland joining the nuclear sharing programme as part of its deterrence policy,” he continued. Przydacz added that “it is not true” the country wants to participate without actually hosting warheads. “Poland also wants to have warheads on its territory,” he said. Nawrocki, who is a close ally of President Donald Trump, has made clear his support for Poland seeking a nuclear sharing arrangement with the United States. But it remains unclear exactly what the government’s plans are. Earlier this year, Poland entered discussions with France over the extension of the French “nuclear umbrella” over Europe. Later, however, Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated that Poland would not want to actually host French nuclear-armed aircraft. Both last year and this year, Tusk has also hinted that Poland could seek to develop its own independent nuclear deterrent. However, Colby made clear that the US would “strenuously oppose” European countries such as Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian states seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has regularly clashed with the government, including vetoing a record number of laws. However, the two sides have sought to present a more united front on issues of national security. The United States would “strenuously oppose” Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian countries seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons, says a senior Pentagon official. His comments come amid discussions in Poland and Europe over nuclear deterrence https://t.co/e9J8tNxcc9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: September 19: Celebrate South Africa’s Heritage Braai Day in Prague
World.content:
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.

The event is organized by Saffa Maso.



From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.

Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.

In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.

Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can also choose a braai package, which includes 500g of traditional boerewors sausage and 150g of biltong.

On-site, guests will also be able to purchase Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices and other South African products.

Visitors should not bring their own drinks, as a selection of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available at the venue. Guests should bring their own plates and cutlery, although disposable options are also allowed.

Tickets are available via SMSTicket at this link. Children under 12 enter free.

World.title: Prague Philharmonic Could Begin Construction in 2028. New Visuals Reveal Design
World.content:
Prague has taken another step toward building the long-planned Vltava Philharmonic.

The Prague Development Company (PDS) submitting an application for planning permission and new visualizations revealing the project in greater detail.

The application covers not only the Philharmonic building but also the surrounding public spaces, transport infrastructure and connections to the existing metro, tram, road, cycling and pedestrian networks.



If the permitting process stays on schedule, the city expects to receive the necessary approval in the first quarter of 2027. A tender for the construction company would then follow, with building work potentially starting in the first quarter of 2028.

The project is planned for the Bubny-Zátory district, near the existing Vltavská metro station. The new cultural complex is expected to be completed in 2033, when trial operations could begin.

The building was designed by Danish architecture studio BIG – Bjarke Ingels Group, which won an international competition in May 2022. Preparation of the detailed permit documentation began in 2025.

The complex will have three underground levels and six floors above ground. It will contain five music halls, creative spaces, restaurants and other facilities.

The project is also intended to provide new premises for the Prague Symphony Orchestra FOK and music collections belonging to the Municipal Library of Prague. The Czech Philharmonic is also expected to gain additional facilities, addressing the limitations of its current premises.

Construction could start in early 2028

The current estimated cost of the Philharmonic building is around CZK 12.33 billion, including equipment but excluding VAT. The surrounding infrastructure and public spaces are expected to cost an additional CZK 5 billion, also excluding VAT.

World.title: Tiny Steps, Big Milestones: What Really Matters When Toddlers Start Preschool
World.content:
For a one-year-old, starting preschool is not about learning letters or sitting through lessons.

It is about feeling safe without Mum or Dad nearby, discovering the joy of playing alongside other children, and slowly gaining the confidence to explore the world independently. At Tiny Tots in Prague, these small everyday moments are at the heart of the programme.

A favourite toy clutched tightly in one hand. A cautious look back at Mum or Dad from the classroom door. Perhaps a few tears (from either side).

For families with children aged one or two, the first experience of leaving a little one in someone else’s care can feel like a very big step.

And for the child, it is one too.



At this age, development happens through moments that can look almost insignificant to adults: reaching for a spoon without help, joining another child in play, recognising a familiar song, saying a new word, or feeling comfortable enough to wander a little further away from a trusted adult.

These are precisely the moments that Tiny Tots, a programme for children aged 1–2 at Nessie English Preschool, part of Park Lane International School, is designed to encourage.

Before learning comes feeling safe

For very young children, a good first preschool experience begins with something much more fundamental than an academic curriculum: trust.

“Parents often want to know how their child will cope with separation, whether we can follow the rhythm they are used to at home and, above all, whether their child will really be seen as an individual,” says Catalina Gonzalez-Got, who leads the Tiny Tots programme.

Catalina knows the feeling from both sides. An early-years educator with international experience, she is also a mother herself. Becoming a parent, she says, gave her a much deeper understanding of how emotional it can be to entrust a young child to somebody else for the first time.

That is why settling in is treated as a process rather than a test that a toddler is expected to pass on day one.

Some children may quickly become curious about their new surroundings. Others need more time, reassurance and proximity to a familiar adult before they are ready to explore.

Both are perfectly normal. The goal is to allow each child to find that confidence at their own pace.

For toddlers, play is serious business

Adults sometimes separate “playing” and “learning”. Toddlers do not.

When a child squishes playdough between their fingers, listens to a story, sings along to a familiar song, explores the garden or watches another toddler build something, they are constantly learning.

They are practising movement and coordination. They are discovering cause and effect. They are learning how to communicate, negotiate space with other children, manage emotions and make choices.

Tiny Tots therefore follows a play-based approach inspired by the English Early Years Foundation Stage framework, with activities designed around the developmental needs of one- and two-year-olds.

There are no miniature school desks or pressure to perform.

Instead, children encounter language, movement, music, creative activities, sensory experiences, stories and outdoor play as a natural part of their day.

The programme keeps the class to a maximum of eight children, allowing teachers to pay close attention to individual personalities, routines and developmental stages.

English without the flashcards

The same philosophy applies to language.

At one or two years old, learning English does not mean memorising vocabulary lists. Children absorb language through relationships and repetition: hearing the same words during snack time, listening to songs, following simple instructions, sharing a picture book or hearing an adult describe what is happening during play.

Tiny Tots provides an English-language environment, giving children regular, natural exposure to the language throughout their day.

Catalina, who raises her own child in a multilingual family, sees communication as something that should grow out of connection rather than performance.

Toddlers often understand far more than they can say, she explains. What matters is creating a positive environment in which language is associated with people, experiences and emotions that make sense to the child.

Learning to do things “all by myself”

Anyone who lives with a toddler knows how powerful those words can be.

Between one and two, children increasingly want to try things independently — even when the result is a spoon on the floor, mismatched shoes or a task that takes considerably longer than if an adult simply did it for them.

Tiny Tots gives children safe opportunities to practise that emerging independence while knowing that an adult is close by when they need help.

The milestone may be eating more independently, choosing an activity, joining a group song, approaching another child or simply becoming comfortable enough to explore a new corner of the room.

For a toddler, these are significant achievements.

And independence does not mean pushing children away from adults. In fact, the opposite is often true: children are more willing to explore when they know they have a trusted person to return to.

A small community for Prague’s smallest residents

For international families in particular, early-years programmes can provide something else that is easy to overlook: a sense of community.

Many parents raising children in Prague live far from grandparents, siblings and the wider family network that might otherwise form part of everyday life.

A nurturing preschool environment can therefore become more than somewhere a child spends part of the day. Familiar teachers, other children and their families can gradually become part of the support network that makes a new city feel more like home.

Tiny Tots is based at Nessie English Preschool in Prague 5, in a quiet residential setting with its own garden. The programme combines experienced early-years teachers, personalised attention and structured routines with plenty of room for children simply to play, discover and be little.

Because at one or two years old, success does not need to look impressive.

Sometimes it is a child who cried at the door last week walking in happily today.

Sometimes it is making a first little friend.

Sometimes it is a new word, a messy painting, a favourite song or the confidence to let go of a teacher’s hand and go exploring alone.

Those tiny steps are exactly where the big journey begins.

Tiny Tots at Nessie English Preschool is designed for children aged 1–2 years. Families interested in the programme can arrange a visit to the Prague 5 campus to see the environment and meet the team.

Enrolment for the 2026/27 school year is now open.

World.title: Wine Harvest Festivals in Prague in September: The Full Guide
World.content:
Every September, Prague celebrates vinobraní, the traditional wine harvest festival marking the end of the grape season.

Visitors can look forward to concerts, dance and theatre performances, food stalls, and tastings of young wine and the seasonal favorite burčák (partially fermented grape juice). The festivals are family-friendly, offering children’s theatre, horse rides, folk craft demonstrations, competitions, and workshops.

World.title: Czechia Spent CZK 19 Billion on COVID Vaccines and Used Less Than Half
World.content:
The Czech Republic has spent roughly CZK 19 billion on COVID-19 vaccines since 2020, but fewer than half of the 41 million doses supplied under its pandemic-era procurement agreement were ultimately used in the country.

More than 18 million doses expired and had to be destroyed, representing a value of about CZK 8 billion.

A further four million doses were donated to other countries, according to information provided by the Czech Ministry of Health in response to a request from the Czech Technical Committee.



For the 2026-27 vaccination season, around 900,000 doses will be available in the country. By comparison, fewer than one-third of that number was administered during the previous season. The vaccination season runs from September through the end of August the following year.

Demand for COVID-19 vaccination has fallen sharply since the initial rollout. More than 15 million doses were administered during the first year vaccines were widely available. A year later, demand had fallen to roughly one-fifth of that level. Between 2022 and 2023, interest dropped by more than 80 percent, followed by further declines of about one-third in subsequent years.

Only about 1,500 doses had been administered by July 26 this year. Most vaccinations, however, take place during the autumn months.

The low demand has contributed to substantial vaccine waste. When the original purchases were made, authorities faced considerable uncertainty over how the pandemic would develop, how many booster doses would be required and how many people would seek vaccination.

Maintaining sufficient supplies was considered necessary in case the epidemiological situation deteriorated.

The Czech Republic is now considering a different approach to future procurement. The Ministry of Health is negotiating with vaccine manufacturers, health insurance companies and medical organisations over supplies and financing for the 2027-28 season. The talks are taking into account both the expected demand and the cost-effectiveness of vaccination.

World.title: Foreign Pupils on the Rise in Czech Schools — Nearly One in Five in Prague
World.content:
Of the nearly one million pupils attending Czech primary schools last academic year, almost 8% were foreign nationals, most commonly from Ukraine.

According to the Czech Statistical Office (CSO), Prague recorded the highest proportion, with foreign pupils making up 18% of all children in its primary schools.

Compulsory education is mandatory for Czech citizens as well as citizens of other European Union member states who reside in the Czech Republic for more than 90 days. The requirement also applies to foreign nationals with long-term residence permits.

Their children therefore have the same rights as Czech children, including access to free education, school meals and extracurricular activities.



The number of foreign pupils increased significantly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, nearly doubling that year. Their numbers have continued to rise ever since. Today, children from Ukraine account for 5% of all pupils in the Czech Republic.

The trend is similar in secondary schools, where the proportion of foreign pupils reached its highest level in the past 10 years, at almost 5% of the total.

Although the number of children in primary schools has remained relatively stable at just over one million in recent years, a sharp decline is expected in the coming years due to the falling birth rate, according to Vendula Kašparová of the CSO’s Social Development Statistics Department. The office said the birth rate has been falling continuously for the fifth consecutive year.

The decline is already visible at the kindergarten level. The number of children enrolled in kindergartens fell below 350,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, the first time this has happened since 2013. Over the past three years, enrolment has dropped by more than 21,000 children, or around 5.8%.

Fewer Children Receiving Deferrals From Starting School

Kašparová identifies another clear trend: fewer children are being granted deferrals from starting compulsory school. Since the 2021/2022 academic year, the proportion of six-year-olds whose school entry was deferred has fallen from 24.1% in September 2021 to 17.7% in September 2025, representing just under 21,000 pupils.

Furthermore, an amendment to the Education Act is expected to reduce the number of deferrals even further. Under the new rules, deferrals will only be granted when justified by a medical condition that prevents a child from attending school.

This could include a serious medical condition following surgery, cancer treatment or a moderate intellectual disability.

World.title: Czechia, the Land of Burgers. More Fast Food Chains Enter the Market
World.content:
The Czech fast food market is expanding beyond its established players, with new international brands entering the country and existing chains opening restaurants in smaller cities.

McDonald’s and KFC continue to build their networks, while brands from Germany, the United States and Poland are looking for opportunities in the Czech Republic.

The expansion is increasingly moving beyond Prague and other major cities, with retail parks becoming an important location for new restaurants.



Burgermeister prepares Czech debut

One of the newest international brands preparing to enter the Czech market is Germany’s Burgermeister. The Berlin-based burger chain plans to open its first restaurant on Wenceslas Square at the beginning of next year.

The company already sees its Prague location as more than a single restaurant. It is also considering further locations across the country.

Popeyes and Burger King continue expanding

Burger King entered the Czech market 18 years ago and now operates around 70 restaurants. Popeyes arrived much later but has expanded quickly, opening 19 locations during its first three years in the country.

The companies are building a network that stretches from smaller regional towns to central Prague. In Králův Dvůr, a town of around 11,000 people, both Burger King and Popeyes operate at the Litavka Retail Park.

Popeyes is preparing additional restaurants at the Eden shopping centre and in the Budějovická area of Prague. The chain is also expanding into regional cities, with planned locations in Klatovy and Písek.

Five Guys adds another international brand

The Czech burger market gained another major international name last December when U.S. chain Five Guys opened its first Prague restaurant.

The restaurant is located in the former Máj department store on Národní Street. Five Guys is known for burgers prepared to order and a wide range of toppings, allowing customers to customise their meals.

Its prices, however, are generally higher than those of traditional fast food chains.

Another U.S. brand, Dave’s Hot Chicken, is also expected to enter the Czech market this year, according to consulting firm Cushman & Wakefield.

The chain specialises in spicy fried chicken and will therefore compete directly with established players such as KFC and Popeyes.

Czech chains are looking beyond their home cities

The expansion is not limited to international companies.

Czech burger chain Mama’s Burger is also developing its network. Originally based in Ostrava, the company has expanded into several larger Czech cities and operates a restaurant at Prague’s Arkády Pankrác shopping centre.

The company is also seeking franchise partners as it looks to increase the number of locations.

World.title: Slavia Prague to Face Bayern Munich, Arsenal and Porto in Champions League
World.content:
Slavia Prague have learned their eight opponents for the 2026/27 UEFA Champions League league phase following Thursday’s draw in Monaco.

Slavia will play four matches at home at Eden Arena and four away.

At home, Slavia will welcome Arsenal, Aston Villa, Villarreal and Lens. Their away fixtures will take them to Bayern Munich, Porto, Fenerbahçe and Sabah Baku in Azerbaijan.



The most high-profile home fixture will be against Arsenal, the reigning Premier League champions. Slavia also faced the London club in last season’s Champions League campaign, making the return meeting at Eden Arena particularly notable.

The toughest away assignment is likely to come in Munich, where Slavia will face six-time European champions Bayern at the Allianz Arena. The team will also travel to Portugal to meet Porto and to Istanbul for a match against Fenerbahçe.

The longest trip of the league phase will be to Baku to face Azerbaijani champions Sabah, who are making their debut in the Champions League league phase.

How the Champions League league phase works

The 2026/27 competition is being played under UEFA’s new league-phase format for the third consecutive season. Instead of a traditional group stage, all 36 teams are placed in one league table.

Each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents, with two opponents drawn from each of the four seeding pots. Every team has four home and four away games.

The top eight teams in the final standings will advance directly to the round of 16. Teams finishing ninth to 24th will enter a knockout playoff for the remaining eight places, while clubs finishing from 25th to 36th will be eliminated.

The league phase begins on September 8–10, with six rounds taking place before the end of 2026. The final two matchdays will be played in January, with the league phase concluding on January 27. UEFA will announce the exact dates and kick-off times for each individual match later.

World.title: Extraditing Hungarian MOL’s head to Croatia? Péter Magyar gives cryptic answer at Bled forum
World.content:
Hungary and Croatia could be preparing for a new round of high-level talks over the long-running dispute surrounding Croatian oil company INA and Hungary’s MOL Group.

Péter Magyar was asked about oil giant MOL’s chief

Speaking at the Bled Strategic Forum in Slovenia, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Hungary was ready to negotiate with Croatia and that a “new chapter” could begin in relations between the two countries.

Magyar said he had held a brief meeting with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković in Bled. The two leaders agreed that their foreign and economic ministers should begin talks on the relationship between INA and MOL. Magyar also suggested that a meeting between the two prime ministers could take place in the foreseeable future.

“We are ready to negotiate. Naturally, everyone will defend their own national interests, but that is normal. At the same time, we all see that there is an opportunity to open a new chapter in relations between the two countries,” Magyar said, according to Croatian outlet Jutarni List.

What about Zsolt Hernádi ?

The issue of MOL chairman and chief executive Zsolt Hernádi remains one of the most sensitive aspects of the dispute. Magyar was asked directly whether Hungary would be prepared to extradite Hernádi to Croatia, where a European arrest warrant has been issued against him. However, the Hungarian prime minister did not give a straightforward yes or no answer.

Instead, he referred back to his comments about opening a “new chapter” in Hungarian-Croatian relations. “I have already answered the question by saying that there is an opportunity to open a new chapter between Croatia and Hungary. Both countries have their own obligations that need to be settled. That is my answer,” Magyar said. His response leaves unclear whether Budapest’s position on Hernádi could change. For now, there is no explicit confirmation that Hungary intends to extradite the MOL chief.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

INA dispute has strained relations for years

The relationship between MOL and INA has been a major source of tension between Hungary and Croatia for more than a decade. MOL acquired 25 per cent plus one share of INA in 2003 and subsequently increased its stake. It now holds 49.08 per cent of the Croatian oil company, while the Croatian state owns 44.84 per cent.

The dispute has centred on control of INA, corporate governance and the possibility of Croatia buying back MOL’s stake. The two sides have also been involved in arbitration proceedings. Plenković said the unresolved INA-MOL issues had held back wider Hungarian-Croatian relations, despite strong economic, tourism and energy links between the two countries. “I think we are now in a position where we can try to resolve this issue, and afterwards move on,” the Croatian prime minister said.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar in Bled about crisis management, budget deficit, EU affairs, illegal migration, regional cooperation

Hernádi case remains unresolved

Croatian authorities have accused Hernádi of bribery in connection with MOL’s acquisition of management rights at INA. He has rejected the allegations. His legal case has become closely linked to the wider political and corporate dispute between Budapest and Zagreb.

The latest statements from both prime ministers could signal a renewed attempt to resolve the INA conflict. Whether the proposed talks can deliver a lasting settlement — and whether Hernádi’s case will form part of any broader agreement — remains uncertain.

World.title: Police aircraft spot wanted man hiding in woodland and suicidal missing man in cornfield in Hungary
World.content:
A police helicopter and a thermal-imaging drone helped officers locate two men in separate incidents in northeastern Hungary last week: one a wanted man attempting to hide from police, the other a missing 28-year-old who had reportedly threatened suicide.

Helicopter tracks down wanted man

The two incidents took place on 25 August during a policing operation carried out by the Rapid Response Police in Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg County.

In the first case, officers were searching for wanted individuals in Tiszavasvári with support from a helicopter operated by the Rapid Response Police’s Air Policing Service. The helicopter crew spotted something suspicious as officers approached a house. A man was seen moving towards a wooded area at the back of the property, apparently attempting to escape.

The helicopter operator immediately directed the camera towards the man and continuously relayed his location to officers on the ground. The 55-year-old suspect attempted to hide beneath the trees, but the aerial surveillance allowed officers to locate him within minutes.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Police subsequently established that two warrants had been issued against the man by Tiszavasvári Police Station. One was issued in March after he failed to pay a HUF 65,000 (EUR 178) fine, while the other followed an unpaid HUF 52,000 (EUR 142) fine issued in August.

Both fines had been converted into custodial sentences of 10 and eight days respectively. The man told officers that he was still unable to pay the fines, and he was taken to Tiszavasvári Police Station.

If you missed it: Hungarian man beats and tortures partner, forcing her to dig her own grave

Thermal drone finds missing man in cornfield

Later that same day, the Rapid Response Police’s Nyírbátor unit received a report about a different man who had left his home after allegedly threatening to take his own life.

The man’s father, from Besenyőd, told police that his 28-year-old son, who was receiving medical treatment, had run into a cornfield behind their home. He said he could no longer find him and was concerned because his son had threatened suicide.

Officers deployed a drone equipped with a thermal-imaging camera to search the area.

The technology quickly revealed the man’s location, allowing patrol officers to reach him without difficulty. Given his confused state, officers called an ambulance to provide him with medical assistance.

The two cases show the important role of aerial technology in police operations, from tracking suspects attempting to evade arrest to locating vulnerable people who may be difficult to find from the ground.

World.title: Hungarian man beats and tortures partner, forcing her to dig her own grave
World.content:
A 49-year-old man allegedly beat, threatened and tortured his partner before forcing her into a forest to dig what was intended to be her own grave. He is now facing charges that could carry up to 12 years in prison.

Woman allegedly forced to dig her own grave

Prosecutors in Győr have charged a 49-year-old man who allegedly subjected his partner to a brutal attack, including forcing her to dig her own grave in a nearby forest.

According to the indictment cited by the Győr District Prosecutor’s Office, the man and the woman had been in a relationship for around a year and a half when they had an argument at their home in Győr in November 2025.

The man allegedly slapped the woman several times before threatening her with a handgun and ordering her to take a shovel with her. He then took her to a forest and forced her to start digging a grave for herself.

The prosecutor’s account says the attack then escalated. The man allegedly pushed the woman to the ground, sat on her chest and forced soil into her mouth until she lost consciousness.

Alleged torture continued at home

When the woman regained consciousness, the man allegedly took her back home, where the abuse continued.

According to prosecutors, he pressed a hot spoon against her body and extinguished cigarette butts on her.

The woman eventually managed to end the relationship, but the alleged abuse did not stop there. The man reportedly threatened her repeatedly after their separation.

If you missed it: Man in life-threatening condition after huge fall near Budapest’s Chain Bridge

Unlicensed shotgun seized during search

A subsequent search of the man’s residence uncovered weapons, according to the prosecutor’s office. Authorities allegedly seized a gas alarm gun as well as an illegally held hunting shotgun and ammunition.

The man, who is currently in custody, has been charged with an aggravated form of unlawful deprivation of liberty, an aggravated form of relationship violence, and the unlawful possession and misuse of firearms and ammunition.

Taking the offences together under Hungary’s sentencing rules, he could face up to 12 years in prison if convicted. The Győr District Court is expected to make the substantive decision in the case.

World.title: Gas “terrorism” against Hungary: Serbian authorities investigate group of suspects
World.content:
Seven people are under investigation in connection with an organised group suspected of procuring and storing explosives, explosive devices and drones in Serbia before sending them to predetermined locations in European Union countries. The group is also believed to have planted explosives near gas infrastructure linking Hungary and Serbia in April, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Subotica said on Monday.

Did they want to blow up the essential Serbian-Hungarian gas pipeline?

According to a statement, proceedings have been launched against the seven suspects on suspicion of the illegal manufacture, possession, carrying and trafficking of weapons and explosives, MTI wrote.

The group was uncovered during an investigation into explosives found on 5 April in the municipality of Kanjiža/Magyarkanizsa. The inquiry was conducted by Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency (BIA), Military Security Agency (VBA), the Interior Ministry’s criminal police and military police. While monitoring the suspects’ activities, the authorities discovered further explosives, explosive devices, drones and other equipment needed to operate them.

The prosecution said the investigation would continue in co-operation with law-enforcement authorities in the European countries concerned. Investigators are seeking to establish the suspects’ precise roles, as well as the intended purpose of the seized equipment.

Former PM Orbán suggested the action was part of an “international narrative”

On 5 April, only 7 day before the Hungarian general elections, about four kilograms of a substance suspected to be explosive were found in two black rucksacks near a road between Felsőhegy (Gornji Breg) and Ilonafalva (Vojvoda Zimonjić), in the municipality of Kanjiža. The Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Subotica said at the time that the material was believed to be plastic explosive, along with components that could be used to assemble an explosive device.

Russia threatens to cut oil and gas supplies to Hungary after Budapest labels Moscow a security threat

The suspicious items were found near the gas pipeline linking Serbia and Hungary. About 140 soldiers and police officers took part in the search of the area.

Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s president, said at the time that a highly destructive explosive and the detonators needed to set it off had been found in the immediate vicinity of the gas infrastructure. He also briefed Viktor Orbán, then Hungary’s prime minister, on the investigation, saying that, had the suspected operation succeeded, Hungary and northern Serbia could have been left without gas supplies.

If you missed: Suspected Russian operatives held at Hungarian border ‘may have been plotting bombing in Germany’ — authorities tight-lipped

Orbán suggested Ukraine was behind the sabotage

Afterwards, former prime minister Orbán said he would not accuse any country, but suggested that the events formed part of an international narrative. In making that enigmatic remark, he may have been referring to Russian gas deliveries to Hungary, over which he has repeatedly clashed with the EU. He mentioned the Nord Stream pipeline, which was allegedly blown up by Ukrainians, and added that Ukraine had both the capability and the intention to carry out such an act.

Orbán and FM Szijjártó holding a press conference near the Serbian-Hungarian border after news about the sabotage action appeared. Photo: MTI/Zoltán Fischer

He also referred to sabotage with potentially devastating consequences, convened the Defence Council and warned that nobody should play games with Hungary’s energy security.

Meanwhile, Serbian authorities dismissed the claim that Ukraine could have been behind the planting of the explosives, adding that the explosives were of American origin.

Orbán suggests Ukraine plotted to sabotage TurkStream pipeline — Serbia sees it differently

World.title: Internal documents show Orbán-linked politician and businessman had unlimited power over Hungary’s public media
World.content:
Hungarian public media chiefs are filing a police complaint over alleged unlawful management practices in previous years, the press office of the operator, Duna Médiaszolgáltató, said on Monday.

Orbán-linked politician ‘steered Hungary’s public media’

Internal letters, statements and other documents uncovered during a review of the then operator, the Media Services and Asset Management Fund (MTVA), reveal details of the political surveillance of the public media and the role played by Attila Várhegyi, a Fidesz-linked politician and businessman, in directing the organisation, the statement said.

According to the statement, the public media was effectively managed by Mr Várhegyi, who had been contracted as an adviser. He assumed the powers of media executives, making decisions on content, staffing and financial matters. “In many cases, those in charge of the institution did not even dare to make a decision without his consent,” it said.

The 20 August broadcast of the renewed Hungarian public media. Source: Facebook/Közmédia

Link between politicians and public media

The statement also suggested that Mr Várhegyi acted as a link between the political leadership and the public media, conveying the wishes of government ministers and Fidesz politicians.

“Várhegyi’s conduct clearly shows that the public media, which is legally required to be independent of political influence, was in fact under close political control,” the statement said.

According to the statement, not only was Mr Várhegyi’s informal influence unlawful, but so were “the benefits he accepted”.

If you missed: Why is it a problem if Péter Magyar decides who can lead Hungary’s public media?

For years, for example, the public media provided him with a driver, who was employed as an event organiser “to conceal the truth in official documents”.

PM Orbán (left) and propaganda minister Antal Rogán (right). Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Mr Várhegyi also held weekly meetings with public media executives, at which “director general Dániel Papp and other leaders informed him about even the smallest matters”, consulted him on planned decisions and acted on his instructions, the statement said.

The document added that Mr Várhegyi had received a monthly salary of HUF 3.5 million since 2023.

Owner of Hollóháza porcelain brand

Mr Várhegyi owns 100 per cent of the shares in Hollóháza Porcelain Manufacturer, a world-renowned Hungarian brand that he bought in 2020. He paid HUF 175 million for the company at the time.

New chapter may begin in history of public service media on 20 August

World.title: PM Magyar: Hungary has met all conditions to access frozen EU funds
World.content:
Hungary has met all the European Union’s requirements to access “thousands of billions” of forints in EU funding, “in line with its commitments and by today’s deadline”, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Facebook on Monday.

“Now the funds from Brussels are welcome to arrive,” Magyar said, thanking everyone who had contributed to the Government’s efforts. Hungary has reportedly completed the measures required to unlock around €10 billion from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility, while a total of €16.4 billion in previously frozen EU funds is at stake.

Magyar talks about a more constructive role

Hungary had become a more constructive player within the European Union under the new Government, Magyar said at the Bled Strategic Forum. “But that does not mean that we would not defend Hungarian interests every minute of every day,” he added.

PM Péter Magyar and FM Anita Orbán in Bled, Slovenia. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Magyar also spoke of the need to strengthen the EU’s political leadership, improve its competitiveness and harness the potential of Central European co-operation. He said Hungary was ready to play a more constructive role in the European Union than it had in the past.

‘We have come for our money’

“It is not a great challenge to be more constructive than we were before,” he remarked.

Magyar stressed that the Prime Minister’s duty was to represent the interests of the Hungarian people, just as every EU member state was required to defend its own interests.

If you missed: Hungarian Parliament clears fiscal reforms to unlock additional EU funds

Recalling his first meeting with Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, in Brussels, Magyar said he had made Hungary’s position clear: “We have come for our money.”

Photo: Anadolu/Dursun Aydemir

He described negotiations over €16.4 billion in Hungarian EU funds, which had been frozen for three or four years, as smooth. According to Magyar, Hungary gained access to the money within a single day, although the European Commission is expected to assess the country’s compliance with the agreed milestones before funds are disbursed.

Hungary set to launch EUR 5.5 billion railway upgrade as development plan gets green light

Featured image: illustration. Facebook/Péter Magyar

World.title: Péter Magyar in Bled about crisis management, budget deficit, EU affairs, illegal migration, regional cooperation
World.content:
Hungary’s government has already solved several crisis situations since coming to power in May, Prime Minister Péter Magyar told the Bled Strategy Forum in Slovenia on Monday, adding: “I am proud of my government.”

He cited the energy supply crisis due to extreme weather conditions as an example, saying that the solution was provided by “a huge, unprecedented cooperation.” He also said that while his government had inherited a significant deficit, they have managed to shrink it by 2.5 billion euros.

PM Péter Magyar and FM Anita Orbán in Bled, Slovenia. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Straightforward dialogue

A straightforward dialogue is crucial when it comes to resolving problems facing the European Union, Magyar said. Concerning the fight against illegal migration, Magyar said “it is hard to explain to Hungarians why Hungary receives unfair treatment in Brussels.”

Under a European court ruling, Hungary has to pay a significant amount a day “just because we protect the common EU borders … this is not fair,” he said, adding that border control was “one of the most important tasks” of EU member states.

Tisza government ‘more constructive’ than predecessor

The Tisza government is “more constructive than its predecessor in the EU, but it does not mean that we would not promote the Hungarian interest day and night,” the prime minister said at the Bled Strategy Forum on Monday.

The European Union needs to focus on such issues as economic cooperation and competitiveness, he said. “It is not too late for change … we need to decide if the EU just wants to survive or win,” he said, adding that the two ways required two different approaches.

He said “the latter is still not the goal” in Brussels, but added that central Europe “must work to become a winner” and highlighted the importance of regional cooperation.

Regional cooperation important for Hungary, FM Anita Orbán highlighted

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán underscored the importance of regional cooperation ahead of the Bled Strategic Forum, which begins on Monday. Hungary’s security, competitiveness, transport and energy connections, and the European integration of the Western Balkans all depend on how well the country can cooperate in the region, Orbán said in a post on Facebook.

If you missed – Péter Magyar’s government promises a new era for Hungarian schools: should pupils and teachers be celebrating?

The minister is attending the forum in Slovenia, which she described as “one of the most important foreign policy meetings in central and south-eastern Europe”, where political and diplomatic leaders gather to discuss the region’s most pressing issues.

She said the Bled Strategic Forum had “tangible stakes” for Hungary. Orbán said she would discuss regional cooperation with her counterparts on Monday and hold several bilateral meetings.

The 21st Bled Strategic Forum, which begins on Monday, will focus on Europe’s future, European Union enlargement, European security, and the Western Balkans. The two-day event will bring together heads of state and government as well as foreign ministers from central and south-eastern Europe, EU commissioners and economic and policy experts.

New home-building programme in Hungary may reshape property market

World.title: Another Budapest city centre district may ban Airbnb – referendum on the horizon
World.content:
Buda Castle District council is launching a poll on short-term rentals (Airbnbs), allowing residents’ views to inform decisions on future regulation, the council told Hungarian news agency MTI.

Mayor wants a vibrant and attractive residential district

The issue is particularly timely because the statutory moratorium on registering new short-term accommodation will expire at the end of the year. The council must therefore decide what rules should apply in District I, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

Short-term rentals are a particularly significant issue in District I, one of Budapest’s main tourist destinations, especially in and around Buda Castle. Short-term rentals generates tourism revenue, but residents’ associations and property owners have also raised a number of concerns about such rentals.

Buda Castle District: operating short-term rental(s) here can be a gold mine for families, companies. Photo: PrtScr/Youtube

“There are markedly different arguments and interests at stake in the debate, and all of them deserve consideration. As mayor, I believe it is right that we should not make decisions over the heads of the people who live here,” László Böröcz said, according to the statement.

The Fidesz mayor added that the council wanted to preserve Buda Castle as a vibrant and attractive residential district, while recognising that tourism and short-term rentals are important to many people and local businesses.

Buda Castle district may ban Airbnb

Residents aged 18 or over who have a permanent address in District I will be eligible to take part in the poll. They will be asked two questions.

The first will ask whether they support a complete ban on Airbnb. The second will ask whether, if Airbnb were not banned, they would support the council imposing conditions on the provision of short-term accommodation.

Airbnb restrictions in Budapest could deter tourists

In response to a question from MTI, the council said that District I currently has more than 400 licensed private accommodations and other properties, typically operated as commercial businesses.

The first Budapest district to ban Airbnb rentals was the capital’s 6th district following a referendum, which had a very low turnout.

World.title: VGP acquires 294,000 sqm plot for new industrial park in Oradea
World.content:
Pan-European real estate developer VGP announced that it acquired a 294,000 sqm land plot near Oradea in western Romania for a new logistics and industrial park. VGP Park Oradea is planned to offer an initial lettable area of 133,000 sqm for logistics, light industrial, and commercial activities.

The site is located close to the DEx16 expressway and the Borș border crossing with Hungary. It also offers access to Oradea International Airport and the city’s railway station.

VGP said the location would provide connections to major European transport routes for companies involved in cross-border distribution, manufacturing, and regional supply chains.

The planned park will be designed to accommodate different technical requirements from prospective tenants. It is targeting BREEAM Excellent certification and compliance with the EU Taxonomy. Sustainability features are expected to include photovoltaic panels, electric vehicle charging stations, smart metering systems, and measures to improve biodiversity at the site.

The acquisition expands VGP’s Romanian portfolio, which also includes industrial and logistics parks in Arad, Brașov, Bucharest, Timișoara, and Sibiu. The company said demand in Romania was being supported by manufacturing growth, e-commerce expansion, and the diversification of regional supply chains.

VGP entered the Romanian market in 2007. Since then, it has acquired more than 1.7 million sqm of industrial space, representing nearly 900,000 sqm of potential lettable area.

World.title: Romanian-made watch enters major watchmaking competition Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève
World.content:
A watch created in Târgu Mureș, central Romania, is set to take part in Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève 2026, one of the most important watchmaking competitions in the world.

Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève is considered one of the major benchmarks of contemporary watchmaking and is frequently dubbed the “Oscar of watchmaking.” Every year, the competition brings together creations by renowned manufacturers and independent watchmakers from around the world.

The 2026 edition marks the first year with Romanian participation in the competition. Genesis, the watch created by Romanian watchmaker Alin Constantin Mureșan and entered in the competition, is inspired by the vaults of Transylvanian fortifications and local craftsmanship.

The Genesis dial is inspired by the vaults and arches of Transylvanian fortifications. The brass piece was processed, engraved, finished, and colored in the workshop in Târgu Mureș. The hands of the watch were also made in the same place. Their shape refers to the weapons that defended the fortresses and fortifications of Transylvania, while the finish was designed to reproduce the shine of the metal. The strap is made by a Transylvanian artisan. The watch uses a Swiss movement, according to the same source.

The model is entered in the Challenge category and brings international attention to Romanian independent watchmaking. For Alin Constantin Mureșan, founder of Constantime Watches, participation in Geneva is also a way of making elements related to Romania's history and identity known around the world.

“We have many things in Romania, and especially in Transylvania, that deserve to be shown to the world: architecture, symbols, crafts and stories. I don't just want to make watches in Romania. I want them to speak about Romania,” he said.

World.title: Romania among top beer producers in EU in 2025
World.content:
Romania was the ninth largest beer producer in the European Union in 2025, according to data published on Monday, August 31, by Eurostat.

Germany was the main beer producer in the EU the same year, with 7.4 billion liters of beer (21.6% of the EU's total production). Spain ranked second (5.3 billion liters; 15.5%), followed by Poland (3.5 billion liters; 10.2%). The list of the top five producers was completed by the Netherlands (2.4 billion liters; 6.9%) and France (2.1 billion liters; 6.0%).

The next places were occupied by Belgium (1.992 billion liters of beer), Czechia (1.922 billion liters), Italy (1.725 billion liters) and Romania (1.594 billion liters of beer).

Most of the beer produced last year in the EU, 32.3 billion liters, contained more than 0.5% alcohol, while low-alcohol beer (below 0.5%) and alcohol-free beer accounted for 2.1 billion liters.

In Romania's case, most of the beer produced in 2025 (1.491 billion liters) contained more than 0.5% alcohol, while low-alcohol beer (below 0.5%) and alcohol-free beer accounted for 103.954 million liters.

Aside from producing, Romanians also enjoy drinking beer. According to Visual Capitalist, Romanians drank 87.4 liters of beer per capita in 2024, ranking ninth in the world. The Czech Republic (148.8 liters per capita), Lithuania (110.6), and Austria (104.6) took the first three spots in the ranking. European countries dominated the list, accounting for 25 of the 35 highest beer-consuming nations.

Earlier this summer, Romania’s Chamber of Deputies approved a bill allowing for the sale of beer and even wine in stadiums during competitions and public gatherings. The project was mainly initiated by deputies from the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and far-right representatives from the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) and United for Romania parliamentary groups.

World.title: Romanian security chief Lucian Pahonțu rejects accusations of involvement in communist-era suppression
World.content:
Lucian Pahonțu, the longtime head of the Protection and Guard Service (SPP) and alleged backroom political powerbroker, rejected the findings of a journalistic investigation regarding his involvement in the suppression of the anti-communist December 1989 Revolution and the protests during the June 1990 Mineriad.

In a series of clarifications made on Monday, August 31, Pahonțu claimed that he did not participate in violence against protesters and that the statements concerning him are untrue and unfounded. “My position is simple: I have never carried out activities aimed at violating or restricting fundamental rights and freedoms and which could be classified as acts of ‘political police’,” he said, cited by Digi24.

To construct his defense, Pahonțu went through his professional biography, starting with his graduation from the Military School for Active Officers in Sibiu, specializing in communications. After his graduation, Pahonțu said he worked as a platoon commander within the Security Troops between 1987 and 1989. According to the security chief, his duties were limited exclusively to the field of communications.

In December 1989, Pahonțu, 25, was a lieutenant and commander of a communications platoon within the combat support and transport company of Military Unit 0305, Security Troops. The official insisted on the difference between the Security Troops and the structures of the former Securitate with intelligence-operational duties.

“At the time, the Security Troops were the equivalent of today's Romanian Gendarmerie and should not be confused with the Securitate structures with intelligence-operational and criminal investigation duties,” he said. According to his account, the company he was part of consisted of a communications platoon, an anti-aircraft defense platoon, a logistics platoon, a drivers' platoon and another logistics platoon.

On the evening of December 21, 1989, the company allegedly received successive orders to move to Casa Scânteii, another square and, subsequently, to the blocking position on 13 Decembrie Street, currently Ion Câmpineanu Street.

Pahonțu said that he remained in position until he received the order to withdraw. In this time, “neither the soldiers under my command nor I changed our position, and we had no direct contact with the revolutionaries,” he said. He also claimed that the soldiers under his command did not have ammunition with them, as it was kept in sealed boxes in the unit's trucks.

Pahonțu explicitly rejected the accusation that he participated in suppressing the demonstrations in the Intercontinental area, in central Bucharest. According to his version, on the morning of December 22, he and the soldiers under his command re-entered the deployment at the intersection of 13 Decembrie and Academiei streets. Later in the morning, he and his troops allowed the protesters access to Republicii Square, today's Revolution Square.

Subsequently, the soldiers allegedly withdrew toward the trucks and returned to the unit. Pahonțu said that upon arrival, the ammunition was checked and handed over and that not a single cartridge was missing. In his defense, Pahonțu cited general Cătălin Ranco Pițu, former chief prosecutor of the Military Prosecutor's Office Section and one of the investigators of the Revolution file.

Lucian Pahonțu also denied involvement in the violence against protesters in University Square on June 13 and 14, 1990. “During the two days, the soldiers under my command and I did not participate in the events in Bucharest. During that period, we remained in the barracks, according to the documents in the archives of the Romanian Gendarmerie,” he said.

He also said he did not leave the barracks until June 15, 1990, when he allegedly received an order to participate, together with 72 soldiers, in maintaining public order in University Square. “On that day there were no demonstrations in University Square, no violence was recorded, and the miners withdrew from the area and left for the Jiu Valley," the official argued.

Pahonțu also claimed that his activity was repeatedly checked, including before he was appointed director of the SPP.

Recorder’s response

Recorder published a response to Lucian Pahonțu's defense, following the investigation into his alleged involvement in the events of December 1989 and June 1990. The journalists claimed that several documents from the archives and statements given before military prosecutors contradict the version presented by the head of the SPP.

In their argument, the journalists cited three former soldiers under Pahonțu's command, namely Ianțuc Cristian Gheorghe, Ianțuc Daniel Ioan and Spătariu Iulian. In handwritten statements given before military prosecutors, the three conscript soldiers stated they participated in the events of June 13 and 14 and were present in the Television area and in University Square, contradicting Pahonțu’s account, according to the same source.

The publication also disputed Lucian Pahonțu's account of the position occupied by his unit on the night of December 21-22, 1989. Pahonțu acknowledged that he was then part of the Security Troops and was present on the streets of Bucharest. However, he claimed that the platoon he commanded entered the deployment on 13 Decembrie Street, in the area of the intersection with Academiei Street, and that it did not reach the barricade at the Intercontinental hotel.

According to Recorder, this version is contradicted by major Gheorghe Rădulescu, who allegedly recorded in his statement in the Revolution File that he had the platoon commanded by Pahonțu under his command, and that the unit was positioned at the intersection of 13 Decembrie Street and 1848 Boulevard, today's Nicolae Bălcescu Boulevard, in the area of the Intercontinental barricade.

In the published response, Recorder announced that it will present additional documents from the archives concerning Lucian Pahonțu's actions during the Revolution and the Mineriad.

World.title: Romania completes PNRR-backed integrated digital system for forest monitoring, ministry says
World.content:
Romania has completed an integrated digital system for monitoring forests and combating illegal logging, the Environment Ministry announced. The RON 272.6 million project, financed through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), combines satellite imagery, AI-assisted video monitoring, and LiDAR scanning.

The Environment Ministry developed the system in partnership with the Special Telecommunications Service (STS). All its components have been completed and accepted, it said.

The platform provides forestry personnel with digital tools to monitor and inspect forests and timber shipments. It is connected to Romania’s SUMAL timber-tracking system, allowing authorities to identify risks, generate alerts, and better target field inspections.

“Through the PNRR, we have created tools that allow us to see more quickly what is happening on the ground, identify suspicious changes, verify timber shipments, and obtain much more precise data about the state of forests,” interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said.

“Technology does not replace field inspections, but it makes them much more efficient,” she added.

One component uses Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from the EU’s Copernicus program to monitor changes to forest canopies across approximately 70,000 square kilometers. The system compares images and generates alerts when it detects changes that cannot be explained by authorized logging or natural disasters.

Machine-learning algorithms help locate and assess vegetation loss, while a mobile application allows forestry personnel to investigate alerts in the field, the ministry explained.

A second component monitors timber shipments at 350 locations selected in areas with significant timber traffic. It comprises 700 license-plate recognition cameras, 350 cameras for advanced analysis, and 11 control centers.

The video system compares information captured by the cameras with data registered in SUMAL. It can identify undeclared shipments, deviations from approved routes, multiple transports using the same permit, and discrepancies between cargoes and accompanying documents.

The third component uses aerial and terrestrial LiDAR technology to create a digital model of Romania’s forests. It includes an airborne hybrid sensor, 30 mobile sensors, and high-performance computing infrastructure for processing and storing the data.

The resulting model can provide detailed information about selected forest areas, including timber volumes, tree heights, tree numbers, and affected surfaces, according to the Environment Ministry.

Of the project’s total value, RON 262.2 million represents investment expenditure, while RON 10.4 million covers goods and services. The project fulfills milestone 167 under Romania’s PNRR.
