World.title: Romania switches to new portal for medical services starting September 1
World.content:
Starting with September 1, 2026, patients in Romania can access the new “eSănătateaMea” portal to manage their interactions with healthcare providers. The digital services included in the new platform will be gradually rolled out, according to the authorities.

The new portal, integrated into the IT Platform of the Social Health Insurance System, is administered by Romania's National Health Insurance House (CNAS). According to CNAS, the development of the portal aims to simplify the circulation of medical documents, reduce administrative burdens, and facilitate patients' access to the information they need.

Through the platform, insured persons will be able to securely consult data and documents recorded in the public health insurance system, according to official information cited by Digi24.

CNAS head Horațiu Moldovan assured that the new platform has a superior architecture, capable of handling the data flow, having been developed alongside cybersecurity experts.

“The platform cannot crash in the first days because it is already functioning and we have not had any negative signals in recent weeks. We completely changed the hardware and software infrastructure through the PNRR project for resizing, optimization, and standardization. The problems that caused the failures over the past 20 years have been solved. The update was carried out by some of the most important players in the field in Romania, with the support of the most competent state institutions in terms of cybersecurity,” concluded the CNAS president.

A new digital health wallet

The CNAS president described the portal as a “digital health wallet.” According to him, the platform is structured into 12 modules or submodules and was designed so that information can be easily found and consulted.

Among the components presented by the CNAS management was the “My Package” module, intended for the medical history available in the system, as well as a section dedicated to prescriptions and records of their dispensing.

The portal will also include the reimbursement history, through which the patient will be able to check consultations, investigations and other medical services paid for from the National Unique Health Insurance Fund.

Another component, called “My Health Status,” will bring together useful information for health monitoring. At the same time, the “You Are Not Alone” section will provide users with answers to relevant questions about medical services. The system will also contain information concerning providers under contract with health insurance houses.

However, the displayed data should not be confused with a complete archive of all medical documents ever prepared for a person. The information available will depend on what has been recorded and transmitted to CNAS systems, as well as on the operationalization of each module.

Gradual rollout of services

Not all digital services announced as part of the “eSănătateaMea” portal will be available initially. CNAS announced that starting September 1, 2026, the component concerning medical forms will come into use. The component includes the referral form to other clinical specialties or for hospital admission; the referral form for paraclinical investigations; the medical letter; the recommendation for medical care at home; the recommendation for palliative care at home; the care plan for palliative care services at home; the plan for specific physical medicine and rehabilitation procedures; the recommendation for medical devices; and the medical leave certificate.

As such, a referral form issued by a doctor will be available for consultation in the patient's account if the document has been properly transmitted to the system. Eventually, the new portal will allow patients to book appointments with doctors.

The implementation of the new system does not mean that all printed documents will automatically disappear on September 1. The functioning of the new services depends on providers being connected and on the updating of the IT programs they use.

Moreover, the National Health Insurance House reminded healthcare providers who use their own or third-party-developed IT applications of the need to ensure that these are updated and prepared for the use of the new functionalities available through the “eSănătateaMea” portal. For medical forms to be visible in the eSănătateaMea portal, the third-party applications used by providers must be appropriately adapted.

Healthcare providers will be required to use this component starting in the fourth quarter of 2026, namely during October-December. Until then, a pilot project must be carried out to operationalize the service.

How to use the portal

Patients will need a secure account to consult their medical data and documents available in “eSănătateaMea.” CNAS president Horațiu Moldovan explained that users' identities will be able to be verified through ROeID, the official digital identity system administered by the Authority for the Digitalization of Romania.

To create a ROeID digital identity, the user must install the application on a mobile phone (Android or IOS) and complete the enrollment procedure. According to the official information published by ROeID, this stage involves entering personal data, photographing the identity card, taking a selfie, and recording audio-video sequences through which the identity of the applicant is verified. Approval usually takes between 24 and 72 working hours, but the period may increase during periods with a large number of requests.

After the digital identity is validated, ROeID can be used for authentication in public services that have integrated this system.

Importantly, registration with “eSănătateaMea” will not be mandatory. People who do not use a smartphone, do not have internet access, or do not wish to use the portal will continue to be able to interact with the healthcare system through the usual procedures, according to CNAS management.

The “eSănătateaMea” is also designed to work in sync with the new electronic identity card. The latter will serve as the national social health insurance card, replacing it in the end.

“We can get rid of the health insurance card. We go to the Population Records Office and change our ID card and get the new electronic identity card, which also becomes a health insurance card. Let's be clear: it does not store any information either for the health component or for the other component, except for a digital signature and a few facilities that allow communication with the Population Records Office,” CNAS president Horațiu Moldovan said.

World.title: Slovakia to send low-altitude radars to Romania, defense minister says
World.content:
Slovakia will send low-altitude radars and personnel to operate them to Romania, Romanian defense minister Radu Miruță announced. The deployment is intended to strengthen surveillance along Romania’s eastern border amid repeated Russian drone attacks in neighbouring Ukraine and unauthorized incursions into Romanian airspace.

Radu Miruță thanked his Slovak counterpart, Robert Kaliňák, and the Slovak government for approving the deployment.

“This is a response to the appeal I made at both NATO and European Union level to strengthen surveillance capacity at our eastern border,” the Romanian minister wrote on Facebook.

Miruță said the decision followed meetings in which Romania presented and argued its need for additional surveillance equipment. He also linked Slovakia’s response to the work carried out by the Romanian Defense Ministry under the EU’s SAFE programs.

The Romanian minister personally thanked Robert Kaliňák during the informal meeting of EU defence ministers in Ireland.

“I stressed once again how important it is to demonstrate in practice how cooperation between states works,” Radu Miruță said.

He e added that Romania had shown it was a reliable partner by fulfilling its own responsibilities before requesting support from its allies.

Low-altitude radars are designed to detect and track targets flying close to the ground. They can help identify drones that are more difficult for some conventional radar systems to detect, according to Biziday.ro.

According to Defense Ministry data updated on August 31, Romania recorded 65 drone attacks near its border in 2026. Military aircraft were scrambled in 50 cases, while 25 unauthorized incursions into Romanian airspace were reported and four drones were shot down. The most recent major incident occurred in August, when a NATO F-18 operated by a Spanish contingent shot down a drone that had entered Romania from Moldova in the Galați area.

In another major incident in May, a drone entered Romanian airspace during a Russian attack on targets in Ukraine. Romanian military radar systems tracked it to Galați, where it crashed onto the roof of an apartment building.

World.title: Former Bucharest district mayor Clotilde Armand receives deferred one-year prison sentence, ruling not final
World.content:
Former Bucharest District 1 mayor Clotilde Armand was handed a one-year prison sentence on Monday, August 31, in a case concerning her appointment as manager of an EU-funded project. The District 1 Court postponed the application of the sentence, while the ruling can be appealed, Agerpres reported.

The court found Armand guilty of using her position to favor certain individuals in a continued form involving four acts. The case concerns allegations that, while serving as mayor, she appointed herself manager of the EU-funded project.

Judges ordered a two-year supervision period, which would begin when the ruling becomes final.

The court also imposed a three-year ban on Clotilde Armand being elected to public office or holding a position involving the exercise of state authority. However, this additional penalty would apply only if the postponement of the main sentence were annulled or revoked.

Clotilde Armand said she would appeal the ruling and maintained that she had acted legally and in good faith without seeking any undue benefit.

“The ruling is not final. We will challenge it on appeal,” she wrote on Facebook. “I have maintained from the beginning that I acted legally, in good faith, and without seeking to obtain any undue benefit.”

She also stressed that the court had not established any financial damage in the case and that she would not serve a prison sentence under the current decision.

“There is no damage established in this case. Zero lei,” Armand said. “We are not talking about the execution of a prison sentence.”

The former mayor argued that the case had been used against her politically and raised questions about how the investigation and trial had been conducted. She claimed the proceedings began following a complaint linked to the Social Democratic Party (PSD).

Clotilde Armand also said the current ruling did not prevent her from standing in elections or holding elected office.

“I am continuing my work and my fight on appeal with the same determination as before,” she added.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Former Interim PM Andrey Gyurov Confirms Presidential Bid
World.content:
After months of speculation, Bulgaria’s former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov announced on Tuesday that he will run in the presidential elections on October 25. He will likely be the main rival to acting President Iliana Iotova who will be seeking a full mandate.

“The answer is yes, I will run, but the more important question is ‘why’… I don’t dream of a career, I dream of us leaving our children a united, honourable and modern Bulgaria, which is centred around the economy of knowledge and its biggest asset – the people,” said Gyurov.

“We can’t let our differences turn us into mutual enemies. Bulgaria can do so much better,” he added.

His two-month stint as caretaker prime minister in early 2026 was marked by a crackdown on fraudulent voting ahead of the general elections in April and the signing of a cooperation agreement with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in March.

Gyurov will run with the former chief secretary general to the Interior Ministry, Georgi Kandev, as his designated vice-president.

The duo – expected to lead a pro-EU and reformist campaign in opposition to the government of current Prime Minister Rumen Radev – announced their campaign in their common home town of Gotse Delchev in south-west Bulgaria, named after a revolutionary Ottoman-era hero celebrated in both Bulgaria and North Macedonia.

The announcement ended months of speculation over their political futures. Rumours started as early as April, while Gyurov was still interim prime minister, with his name widely mentioned as a potential presidential candidate by analysts and fellow politicians.

Since his caretaker term, Gyurov has been noticeable for his carefully curated social media and public presence: from visiting festivals and endorsing cultural events to running in marathons and reuniting with his baseball youth team – moves seen as aimed at engaging pro-EU, liberal, urban voters.

Born in 1975, he built a career spanning banking and financial academia, moving from work as an analyst and credit-risk expert in Vienna to lecturing and directing financial programmes in Bulgaria.

He entered parliamentary politics in November 2021 as a member of the reformist and then newly-founded We Continue the Change party, which the won the general elections. He left the party in 2023 and was then appointed deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank.

In 2026, he left that position to become interim prime minister, chosen by President Iliana Iotova – herself in a new role after Rumen Radev left the president’s office to successfully run in the general elections with his Progressive Bulgaria party.

Now, Gyurov and Iotova, supported by Progressive Bulgaria and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, will be the main opponents in the 2026 presidential elections.

Gyurov’s designated vice-president, Kandev – also born in 1975 – has held various positions in the Interior Ministry since 1999. He left his last position as chief secretary in June, claiming he had been subjected to political pressure by Radev’s office, but the issue was ultimately left unexplained.

A month and a half before the elections, it’s unclear whether the two men will be supported by the otherwise fragmented centre-right. The Democratic Bulgaria party and Gyurov’s former partners from We Continue the Change have previously stated that they will support their bid.

The lack of a candidate from the longstanding dominant party GERB might also be to their benefit, but Boyko Borissov’s party has yet to make its opinion public.

World.title: Russian Suspected of Triple Homicide in Montenegro Dies by Suicide
World.content:
Montenegro police officer. Photo illustration: EPA/Boris Pejovic.

A Russian citizen suspected of killing three people at a shooting range in Danilovgrad, central Montenegro shot himself dead on Tuesday after opening fire on police when he was found near the coastal town of Herceg Novi, authorities said.

The victims, killed by the Russian national on Monday, have been identified as Podgorica residents Nemanja Kapor, 20, and Petar Globarevic, 24, and Danilovgrad resident Momir Radonjic, 67.

Police identified the suspect as 30-year-old Russian citizen Mikhail Nikolaevich Shabunin.

Police Director Lazar Scepanovic said on Tuesday that officers had located Shabunin in a wooded area above the Topla neighborhood of the coastal town of Herceg Novi.

“After the suspect was surrounded and found himself in a hopeless situation, he opened fire in the direction of police officers and then committed suicide using a firearm,” Scepanovic said.

Police said Shabunin had visited the Ceska Zbrojevka shooting range in Danilovgrad in the days before the killings.

“He carried out a test shooting at the range, entered the building and committed the killings,” Scepanovic said. “After that, he drove away in one of the victims’ vehicles.”

Police later found the vehicle that Shabunin allegedly used to leave the crime scene in Rogami, near Podgorica. They believed Shabunin later travelled by taxi from Podgorica toward Herceg Novi.

Scepanovic had described the suspect as dangerous and said he had taken a firearm and ammunition with him after the killings.

The Ceska Zbrojevka shooting club told state broadcaster RTCG that the three victims were its employees and had been at work without weapons and without the possibility of defending themselves.

Police initially urged residents to remain indoors while the suspect was at large and warned people to avoid contact with unknown persons and report any suspicious behaviour.

Authorities have not disclosed a possible motive or provided further details about the circumstances leading up to the killings.

“Police officers are continuing their activities in cooperation with the Higher State Prosecutor’s Office in Podgorica to establish all the circumstances of the incident, including its cause and motive, and to fully clarify the entire situation,” the statement said.

Prime Minister Milojko Spajic expressed condolences to the victims’ families. He said September 1 and 2 would be declared days of mourning in Montenegro.

World.title: Animals in Tirana Zoo Struggle in Sweltering Summer Heat
World.content:
In Britain, the BBC reported that some zoos were using paddling pools, iced water and iced fruits to keep animals cool.

Iced fruits have also been deployed at Tirana Zoo, said zoo director Evis Rrahmani.

Rrahmani said the zoo has plans to enhance its enclosures, “to make them more diverse to provide mental stimulation for the animals”.

“We intend to improve it, but it takes time,” she acknowledged.

Research-based news website The Conversation recently raised the issue with an article under the headline ‘Are Zoos Ready for the Changing Climate’. It argued that extreme heat should be treated as a “foreseeable animal welfare risk”.

“This might involve expanding shaded areas, creating climate-controlled refuges, improving ventilation, installing misting systems and water features, and monitoring temperature and humidity in real time,” it suggested.

“But infrastructure alone will not be enough. Zoos may also need to adapt their daily management practices, adjusting feeding and enrichment schedules and modifying routines to minimise heat exposure during the hottest parts of the day,” it cautioned.

“To be honest, we don’t have [enough] water in Tirana; everyone struggles to get it, not just us. But since our water consumption is higher, it stands out more in our case,” wildlife veterinarian Vasili said.

Indrit Osmani from Animal Rescue Albania, ARSA, said securing enough water and shade was only the bare minimum.

“If an animal is kept in captivity, the responsibility extends far beyond merely providing the minimum conditions for survival,” said Osmani, who stressed that ARSA opposes keeping animals in captivity.

“A modern zoo should not be judged solely by the quality of its infrastructure or the fact that the animals have access to water, food, and shade,” he said. “It must be evaluated based on whether the entire living environment is adapted to the biological, social, and behavioral needs of each species and the individual animals housed there.”

“Extreme temperatures can cause heat stress, dehydration, fatigue, and behavioural changes. Naturally, the impact varies depending on the species, age, and condition of each individual.”

“Modern animal welfare standards require that animals have the ability to make choices and exercise some control over their environment, including access to varied microclimates, shaded areas, and indoor spaces, as well as the opportunity to escape continuous exposure to heat.”

World.title: Montenegro Greenlighting Solar Plants Despite Warnings of Biodiversity Damage
World.content:
In ratifying the Paris Agreement in 2017, Montenegro committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 per cent by 2030 and raising the share of renewables to 50 per cent of gross final energy consumption.

Renewables accounted for 41 per cent in 2024, while solar plants generated 4.51 per cent of Montenegro’s electricity in 2025.

Documents analysed by BIRN show that since March 2023 the Montenegrin government has issued private investors with more than 40 sets of urban and technical requirements for solar power plants.

The Ministry of Spatial Planning, Urbanism and State Property has meanwhile issued construction permits for six projects.

The government issues the urban and technical requirements after consulting relevant institutions. Investors may then be required to prepare an EIA assessing the project’s potential environmental impact and setting out measures to prevent or reduce damage.

For projects under state jurisdiction, the Environmental Protection Agency approves the EIA, while local authorities decide on municipal projects, based on the findings of an assessment commission.

Once the final design has been prepared and reviewed, the investor can apply for a construction permit.

BIRN found that the company Obnovljivi Izvori Energije received a construction permit for the Predis solar power plant in Cevo, near Cetinje, even though its EIA warned that the project could permanently destroy black hornbeam and manna ash scrub, as well as two proposed Natura 2000 habitats.

The assessment argued that the habitats were widespread and that their eradication at the project site “would not have significant negative consequences for their distribution or survival”.

Likewise, MEnergy received a construction permit for a 385-megawatt solar plant on the border between Cetinje and Niksic, even though four prospective Natura 2000 habitats and 70 species on the IUCN Red List were recorded at the site.

The EIA says the project will have a major negative impact on habitats and plant and animal species, while noting that the biodiversity is not unique to the area. “Some habitats will be destroyed, others degraded,” the assessment reads.

“The composition of existing plant and animal communities will change.” Avramoski said areas containing proposed Natura 2000 habitats, endemic species and IUCN Red List species require particular caution.

“The fact that an area is not yet formally protected does not mean that it is ecologically low- value or automatically suitable for development,” he said. “At the same time, the presence of important biodiversity values does not automatically mean that every project is impossible.”

But, he added, such projects must undergo “rigorous, transparent and science-based assessment”.

“Where significant impacts cannot be avoided or adequately mitigated, the project should be redesigned, relocated, or not proceed in its proposed form.”

Government speeds up permitting

World.title: Women Survivors of Bosnia’s War Watch Tributes to Mladic with Despair
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

"I do not hate them," 82-year-old Kada Hotic tells BIRN over the phone. "I am just wondering what kind of person you have to be to celebrate a war criminal."

Hotic was answering the call from hospital, where she was undergoing medical checkups while trying to follow the reactions to the death last week of Ratko Mladic, the convicted war criminal who was serving a life sentence for the Srebrenica genocide.

Hotic lost her husband, a son and two brothers in the genocide in July 1995. More than 50 other members of her extended family were killed in a series of systematic killings executed after Mladic’s forces overrun the UN-declared “safe zone” of Srebrenica, committing crimes which were classified as genocide by international and domestic courts.

World.title: Montenegro Opposition Seeks Parliament Speaker’s Dismissal Over Mladic Condolences
World.content:
Parliament speaker Andrija Mandic addresses parliament in Podgorica, October 2023. Photo: EPA/BORIS PEJOVIC.

Montenegro’s main opposition party, the Democratic Party of Socialists, said on Monday it will seek the dismissal of parliamentary speaker Andrija Mandic over his decision to express condolences to the family of Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb wartime commander convicted of genocide and other war crimes.

Danijel Zivkovic, the leader of the Democratic Party of Socialists, DPS, said the party would send an initiative to all parliamentary groups and independent lawmakers before formally submitting it to parliament.

Zivkovic said Mandic “had crossed a line that could no longer be ignored by expressing condolences following Mladic’s death”.

“For a long time we have been told that a distinction should be made between his personal political views and the office he holds, that we should show understanding for the stability of the government and that difficult issues should not be raised because of the European path,” Zivkovic told reporters in parliament.

“But there are moments when silence ceases to be political wisdom and becomes acquiescence. This is one of those moments,” he said.

Zivkovic said the initiative was not simply about Mandic, but a test for the other lawmakers in the ruling majority.

“We are not asking them to support the DPS, change the government or change their political relationship with Andrija Mandic,” he said.

“We are asking only one question – can a man who, from the position of parliament speaker, expresses such an attitude toward a legally convicted war criminal and a man responsible for genocide have their confidence to represent the parliament of a country that wants to become the next member of the EU?”

The initiative comes amid renewed controversy and divisions in Montenegro following Mladic’s death.

Mandic, the leader of the ruling pro-Serb New Serb Democracy party, said last week that he had sent condolences to Mladic’s son, Darko, “in his own name and in the name of New Serb Democracy”.

President Jakov Milatovic sharply criticised the move, saying that respect for Mladic’s family could not be used to play down war crimes.

His office said Mladic had been convicted of genocide in Srebrenica and other serious crimes by an international court and that this “must not be subject to political relativisation”.

Several other pro-Serb politicians also praised Mladic. Milan Knezevic, leader of the opposition Democratic People’s Party, posted a photograph of Mladic saying that “every Serbian household has one Ratko.”

The Serbian Orthodox Church’s Metropolitan Metodije of the Budimlje-Niksic Eparchy also praised Mladic, saying that Serbs had recognised in him “not only a great Serb and a man worthy of respect, but all the beautiful and holy qualities of the holy Serbian warriors and knights”.

Metodije said Mladic had “stoically” borne his conviction and that his death should serve as a lesson to Serbs not to abandon the path of their “holy ancestors”.

Montenegro’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic, who leads the Bosniak Party, another coalition member, took a sharply different position, saying a convicted war criminal, “both alive and dead, deserves only contempt”.

The Bosniak Party later said Ibrahimovic had received death threats and calls for his expulsion from Montenegro, torture and violence on social media. It urged the police and National Security Agency to assess and strengthen security for Ibrahimovic and his family.

Islamic Community leader Rifat Fejzic said Montenegro “cannot move forward while some officials glorify Mladic”, urging the government to “decisively put its house in order”.

Human Rights Action, a prominent Montenegrin rights group, meanwhile warned that there was no “military or human honour” in war crimes, and recalled that Montenegro’s criminal code punishes certain forms of public approval, denial or minimisation of genocide and war crimes established by final court judgments when they can incite violence or hatred.

Zivkovic said the DPS would proceed with the initiative regardless of whether it secures enough votes to remove Mandic, arguing that the vote itself would show where each lawmaker stands on the issue.

The positions of the Europe Now Movement and the Democrats, allies of Mandic’s party in the governing majority, are not yet known, but the motion is unlikely to pass in the 81-member parliament, as the three groups hold a majority even without the Bosniak Party.

“If there are 41 votes for his dismissal, Montenegro will say that, regardless of political differences, there are lines that must not be crossed,” he said. “If there are not, citizens will at least receive a clear answer about who considers preserving the majority more important than those lines.”

Political analyst Stefan Djukic told BIRN that a similar initiative had previously been launched over similar actions by the parliament’s speaker in 2014, but failed to result in his dismissal.

“I do not expect that to happen this time either,” Djukic said briefly.

The European Commission last Friday told Vijesti, responding to Mandic’s condolences to Mladic’s son, that “glorification of war criminals was contrary to fundamental European values and had no place either in the European Union or in candidate countries seeking membership.”

The Commission also recalled that Mladic was serving a life sentence for crimes against humanity and genocide in Srebrenica. “He was a war criminal,” the Commission said.

World.title: Kosovo’s Vetevendosje, LDK Agree on Ex-Judge as Joint Presidential Candidate
World.content:
Kosovo presidential candidate Bekim Sejdiu (C) at a joint press conference with (L-R) former President Vjosa Osmani, LDK leader Lumir Adbixhiku, LDK MP Lutfi Haziri, and Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti in Pristina on August 31, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Vetevendosje and the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK party agreed on Monday on a joint presidential candidate – a move that could end the country’s long-running political crisis.

Following a meeting between the respective party leaders, Albin Kurti and Lumir Abdixhiku, the latter announced Bekim Sejdiu, a former judge at the Constitutional Court and a former diplomat, as their pick for the vacant post.

“The talks were not easy, but they were exhaustive; we held long meetings and engaged in continuous, quite intense discussions. Both sides were committed to finding a consensus candidate for the president of Kosovo,” LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku told media at a joint press conference with acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti and MPs from the LDK and Vetevendosje.

“Various names were considered during the discussions. Ultimately, we agreed on one name: Professor Doctor Bekim Sejdiu,” Abdixhiku said.

“It is a great mark of trust and a great honour,” 51-year-old Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court and ambassador, who currently lectures in law, told the press conference.

“Although my ambitions have always leaned more towards the academic and professional spheres, I have – fully aware of the burden and responsibility entailed by the office of the president, and mindful of the current political context in the Republic of Kosovo – placed myself at the service of the republic, its citizens, and our state,” he added.

The agreement is a move towards ending the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June. Parliament has yet to be inaugurated since then, as political parties disagreed over who should be the next president – a position whose incumbent is elected by MPs. Without an agreement, new elections seemed inevitable.

Amid the institutional logjam, the provisional parliament speaker, Avni Dehari from election-winning party Vetevendosje, refused to resume the inaugural session that started on August 6. Vetevendosje also refused to submit a name for the new parliament’s speaker, as it first demanded an agreement with other parties on the election of a new president.

When announcing the deal on Monday, Abdixhiku called for the inauguration of parliament “without delays” and a vote for a new government before the vote for the new president.

In elections in June, Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, putting it well ahead of the PDK, which won 22. The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) won 18 seats.

Kurti is likely to obtain a simple majority in the assembly to form a new government by again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

In the presidential election, Sejdiu must receive at least 80 MPs’ votes in the first two rounds of voting to be confirmed in the role. In a potential third round, he would need a simple majority of 61 votes.

Sejdiu is a former judge of the Kosovo Constitutional Court and served as as ambassador to Turkey from 2008 to 2012, and as Kosovo’s consul general in New York from 2012 to 2014.

Since 2002, he has worked as an assistant professor in the Department of International Law at the University of Pristina’s Faculty of Law.

Sejdiu was also the rapporteur judge in the December 2020 Constitutional Court ruling that the government led by the LDK’s Avdullah Hoti was illegitimate because it was voted in with an invalid vote from a MP who had been convicted of a crime.

Most recently, he served as an adviser to then President Vjosa Osmani. Osmani returned to political activity with the LDK after her presidential mandate ended.

World.title: Two Kosovo Serbs Plead Guilty to Participating in 2022 Unrest
World.content:
Dusan Dobrac (R) and Milos Radosavlevic (L) at the Pristina Basic Court on August 31, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Dusan Dobrac and Milos Radosavlevic were given prison sentences of one year and nine months respectively at Pristina Basic Court on Monday after pleading guilty to violating the constitutional order by participating in setting up roadblocks in the north of Kosovo in December 2022.

Dobrac was convicted of activity that breaches the constitutional order and obstruction of an official in the performance of their duties, and Radosavlevic of violating the constitutional order.

The indictment charged six Kosovo Serb men – Dusan Maksimovic, Dusan Drobac, Milos Radosavljevic, Nemanja Jolovic, Nenad Orlovic and Srdjan Vucinic – with staging organised, coordinated and violent activity to subvert the constitutional order by blocking public roads to two border crossings with Serbia: Jarinje and Bernjak.

While Dobrac and Radosavlevic have been sentenced, the trial of Maksimovic, Jolovic, and Vucinic will continue, as they have not pleaded guilty. The sixth defendant, Orlovic has not been arrested yet and the judge announced that Kosovo will seek his arrest internationally as he has failed to appear in court for two hearings in a row.

The charges relate to unrest in December 2022, when Serbs in northern Kosovo were setting up barricades at the two border crossings with Serbia, parking trucks, ambulances, diggers and other vehicles across access roads in what was cast as a ‘spontaneous’ outpouring of popular anger. It began after the arrest of a Kosovo Serb on suspicion of attacking election facilities.

The prosecution file, seen by BIRN, claims the unrest endangered the lives of police and customs officers. Those involved also allegedly participated in creating “a tense security situation through the opening of fortified positions and the presence of uniformed and armed persons”, according to the prosecution.

During questioning, Maksimovic, Jolovic, and Vucinic denied any role in organising the barricades, saying they were only part of a protest by local residents. Orlovic refused to answer the prosecutors during questioning.

However, the police discovered a Viber group named ‘Barricades December 2022’ on Maksimovic’s phone, suggesting the incidents were organised and coordinated.

They acquired the phone in September 2023, after Maksimovic was arrested over his involvement in an armed attack on Kosovo police in the northern village of Banjska, in which one Kosovo Albanian officer was killed and a cache of military-grade weaponry was seized. He was sentenced in the first instance to 30 years in prison over the Banjska incident,

The contents of his phone helped prosecutors investigating the unrest in Serb-majority municipalities and the setting up of the barricades of December 2022. The messages it contained included “Today we’ll all receive ammunition” and “In the afternoon we could try the weapons in Suvi Dol [local village] with two or three bullets each.”

Prosecutors stated that the phone evidence undermined claims that local Serbs had spontaneously set up the barricades and sparked the unrest.

World.title: 35 Million Euro Croatian Football Federation Camp Progressing Well
World.content:
September the 1st, 2026 – The 35 million euro Croatian Football Federation camp in Velika Gorica not far from Zagreb is progressing well and according to plan.

The construction of the new Croatian Football Federation (HNS) camp in Velika Gorica is progressing according to plan, and the project worth more than 35 million euros is taking its final shape. It will be the new base for Croatia’s national teams and one of the most important football projects in Croatia. Poslovni reports that the camp is being built on land covering 92,206 square metres, which the state donated to the HNS after the administration in Velika Gorica re-designated the area as a sports and recreation zone. The government is investing 15 million euros in the project, while it is also being financed with the help of the HNS, UEFA and FIFA.

The new complex will boast four football pitches. The central one will have a covered stand with around 1,500 seats, while the remaining three are intended for training. Two will have natural grass and one artificial turf. A particularly important part of the project will be the modern HNS business building, into which the Federation’s administration will move. In this way the HNS will for the first time have business and sports facilities combined at one location.

The camp will also have changing rooms for all age categories, restaurants and a kitchen, spaces for coaching staff, analysis and the media. In the second phase the possibility has been left for the construction of a multi-purpose sports hall, gym, wellness centre and medical centre for players’ recovery. The new complex will not be intended only for the senior national team. Younger men’s and women’s national teams as well as futsal selections will also prepare there, and the space will also serve for the education and licensing of coaches and referees. Works should be completed and the camp put into operation by the summer of 2027.

World.title: Split Landlord’s August Worries Point to Deeper Croatian Tourism Issues
World.content:
September the 1st, 2026 – One Split landlord has shared his August worries about reservations which point to a much deeper problem within Croatian tourism.

A discussion developed on Reddit recently under a post by a resident of Split from Varoš about the bursting of Split’s tourist bubble, prices and “nerve amortisation”.

“Basically, this is the first time it’s happened that I’ve been empty for a longer period in August. I have an apartment in Varoš. So… a week has already passed by without any check-in or reservation made, and my price is low. Is anyone else in a similar situation?” This short post, which an anonymous Split landlord shared on Reddit, instantly laid bare the anxieties that have for some time been creeping among Split’s hospitality workers and property owners. Morski reports that Varoš, a traditional old Split neighbourhood, has experienced unexpected silence right in the very heart the middle of the peak summer season.

stuck between a rock and a hard place – market reality and harsh algorithms…

Many people in the comments immediately pointed out that the problem may not be in Split itself or a general crisis, but in the fact that supply has long exceeded demand. One user vividly explained the situation with the following words: “Supply and demand. In Split there are 15-20% more apartments on the market at any given moment than the city has guests.”

Others located the problem within the digital platforms themselves and suggested the landlord check how the apps treat him at all: “Try searching for your apartment on the site where you rent it out as a guest, preferably in an incognito window… Maybe it’s not even about the price but the algorithm. Most guests don’t scroll past the first 10-15 apartments before booking something.”

A particularly sharp discussion arose around the definition of what exactly a “low price” is, and the mentality of newly minted landlords. Workers from the tourism sector warn that guests have become more cautious and no longer accept just any conditions. “As an employee in a tourist agency, I completely agree with this. All clients who have realistic prices from the start fill up much better, with longer reservations and generally better guests, fewer cancellations, and of course fewer problems.”

Another user described how his family manages to stay competitive, but with enormous effort: “A studio for two 100 euros a night, it’s been full from the May onwards… When Airbnb takes its commission what’s left is quite a bit less than 100, but the occupancy rate is excellent. We clean the place ourselves, greet our guests, wash the bedding… Unfortunately, today everyone would rent out apartments and have a cleaner come, a laundry service… and still make a big profit.”

In contrast to that, landlords from the same neighbourhood appeared on the same post, claiming they have no problems if they position their accommodation well: “I also have an apartment in Varoš… my prices range 150-220 euros and around 400 for Ultra, everything is filled within one day.”

what is the situation with foreign nationals renting purchased properties?

Among the slew of comments, an interesting theory about long-term changes in the structure of guests also stood out. Split and its surroundings are slowly ceasing to be a destination where foreigners exclusively rent accommodation, because many of them have become property owners themselves.

“They count the entry of foreigners into Croatia as visitors, but they don’t count how many of those foreigners already have their own properties located in Croatia. People around Omiš tell me that everything has been bought up by Slovenians, Poles and Austrians. Everyone has sold everything and that’s why the apartments are less filled up. The only ones left are the party crowd that comes to Split every now and then.”

This Reddit post from Varoš actually served as a microcosm of Split’s housing and tourism reality at the moment. While some consider a “week-long hole” in August an anomaly or a bad algorithm, others see it as a fair sobering of a market that has grown for too long on unrealistic foundations. The conclusion of the discussion remains open, but the message is clear: the time when it was enough to “just open the doors” and wait for filling at maximum prices is slowly passing. Split must face the fact that without a sustainable strategy and balancing between the needs of the local population and the real possibilities of supply, empty apartments in August will no longer be a surprise, but the rule.

World.title: Less Heat, Less Crowds, Lower Prices – Croats Travel More in Post-Season
World.content:
September the 1st, 2026 – Less heat, less crowds and generally fairer prices are leading more and more Croats to opt to travel during the post-season.

With the first days of September arriving, the tourist off-season practically officially begins for Croatia. Booking.com has therefore published its 11th annual research report on consumer attitudes and understanding of the social and environmental impact of travel, with insights from 32,500 travellers across 35 markets worldwide. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that according to that data, the majority of Croatian travellers – 58 percent of them in total, plan to travel during the post-season. Both Croatian and European accommodation providers are trying to make use of this period, while the latter want to monetise the remaining demand and attract bookings in the later part of the season.

less heat, less crowds and (sometimes) better value for money

Speaking further about Croats who decide to travel during the off-season, 80 percent of them stated in the research that they do so in order to avoid destinations with large numbers of visitors, while 55 percent are motivated by the possibility of savings. The results indicate that travelling in the off-season has its advantages: besides smaller crowds, there is also a more price-accessible experience, and 53 percent of Croatian travellers plan to avoid overcrowded tourist destinations, which represents an increase of 11 percent compared to the previous year. This part of the season also reflects a more thoughtful approach to travel, as 65 percent of our travellers state that they want to avoid contributing to mass tourism, while 45 percent of those who travel in the off-season are motivated by the desire to reduce pressure on destinations.

the weather is in charge…

As many as 68 percent of all respondents globally say they actively avoid destinations known for extreme weather conditions. Speaking solely about Europeans, research by the European Travel Commission shows that September stands out as an important month for travel, with 22 percent of residents of the Old Continent planning trips in 2025, compared with 25 percent who do so in July and August.

When it comes to owners of accommodation facilities, attention is focused on more commercial tactics with which they can attract demand. Namely, data from the European Accommodation Barometer for 2026 are based on a survey conducted among 1,240 executives and managers from the European accommodation sector, including representatives of hotels and alternative accommodation facilities, and they state that discounts stand out as the most frequently used tool for attracting guests.

In view of this, 79 percent of Croatian accommodation facilities state that special prices or packages for the off-season bring positive results. Accommodation facilities also rely on broader distribution strategies, with 87 percent of them considering online platforms an effective channel for generating bookings in the off-season. The report states that event-driven tourism is another popular way of attracting alternative demand among accommodation facility owners; 37 percent of them stated that they had benefited from event-motivated travel over the past 12 months.

one third cancelled a planned trip

Nevertheless, the weather is increasingly influencing travel, so Booking notes that extreme weather conditions are actively changing travel choices and travel times. Almost three quarters of all respondents said they take into account the risk of extreme weather conditions when choosing a destination (74 percent) and the time of travel (74 percent), while 68 percent say they actively avoid destinations known for extreme conditions.

Interestingly, 31 percent of travellers stated that they had cancelled or changed their travel plans in the past year due to extreme weather conditions or natural disasters.

World.title: Croatia Introduces Life Imprisonment for 15 Criminal Offences
World.content:
September the 1st, 2026 – Croatia is set to introduce life imprisonment for 15 criminal offences as of the 1st of January 2027.

The liability of companies, i.e. legal persons, for criminal offences committed through them by responsible persons will be sanctioned significantly more severely than before. From the 1st of January 2027, life imprisonment in Croatia will be able to be imposed on perpetrators of 15 types of the most serious criminal offences, including those related to irreversible or long-term environmental pollution.

Poslovni reports that the harshest penalty will be able to be imposed on all persons who were 18 or older at the time of committing the offence, which means that younger adults will not be spared either, writes Kristina Turčin for Jutarnji. However, all those sentenced to life imprisonment, regardless of age, will have the right to conditional release after serving 25 years of the sentence.

Specifically, for offences that have caused the most severe environmental pollution, i.e. ecocide, fines will rise to as much as 50 million euros.

Reports (including statements linked to the Ministry of Justice and coverage of the reforms) highlight that life imprisonment will apply to the most serious offences currently punishable by long-term imprisonment. Specific examples repeatedly cited include aggravated/serious murder, femicide, certain forms of genocide, serious forms of human trafficking, sexual abuse and the exploitation of children, terrorist attacks and terrorism-related offences and the aforementioned ecocide.

World.title: Rijeka Becomes a Key Regional Hub as Rijeka Gateway Welcomes 100th Vessel
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – Rijeka has become a key regional hub as the Rijeka Gateway facility welcomes its 100th vessel.

Rijeka Gateway successfully tested parallel ship operations for the first time back in April, as this operating model enables better utilisation of the operational quay, shorter waiting times for ships and greater efficiency of terminal operations. Poslovni reports that Rijeka Gateway is currently the technologically most advanced container terminal in this part of Europe, marked the arrival of its 99th and 100th ships just a few days before the first anniversary of the start of commercial operations at the terminal. The feeder ships Moraga and Conship Luv berthed at the terminal almost simultaneously, after which terminal operations of unloading and loading cargo began.

The ships Moraga and Conship Luv, which have been calling at Rijeka in a regular weekly rotation since the end of July, have further strengthened the role of Rijeka Gateway and cooperation with the global shipping companies Hapag-Lloyd and Maersk. After the successfully established cooperation model with Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd has also started using the terminal as a transhipment hub for import and export cargo from neighbouring Italy, just across the Adriatic.

In this way, Rijeka Gateway has further confirmed its role as a regional logistics hub for container traffic within the Adriatic and is currently the only terminal on the Adriatic that performs this type of operations within the Gemini network. The Gemini network is an operational cooperation between the companies Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd, which covers seven main global trade routes and serves to accelerate and optimise traffic, and Rijeka Gateway is a key port of call within the Gemini cooperation on the AE12/SE1 line that connects major Asian ports with the Mediterranean. Rijeka is now further connected with Trieste, Venice, Ravenna and Ancona over in neighbouring Italy, and the terminal has expanded its accessibility and connectivity with regional markets.

“It’s a particular pleasure for us that we welcomed the 100th ship before marking the first anniversary of commercial operations. In just one year, as a newly built terminal, Rijeka Gateway has received 100 ships, of which 47 large container ships, so-called mother vessels, on intercontinental services between Asia and Europe, and 53 feeder ships that connect Rijeka with regional Italian ports. But behind each of these numbers stand people. I am extremely proud of our team, which in a very short time has built organisational and operational capabilities comparable to the best terminals in the network. Today Rijeka Gateway employs more than 420 people, and it is precisely their expertise, dedication and professionalism that have enabled the achievement of such a significant success already in the first year of operations,” stated Peter Corfitsen, Chief Executive Officer of Rijeka Gateway.

World.title: Kucel – The Sandy Oasis Less Than an Hour from Zagreb
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – You’ll likely have never heard of it, but Kucel is a sandy oasis less than an hour from the heart of Zagreb, but it seems as if it couldn’t possibly be further away.

There’s a rather unknown touch of the tropics in a completely unexpected place not far from Zagreb, more specifically Lijevi Dubrovčak near Ivanić-Grad. Putni kofer writes that the beach is called Kucel Beach, and it’s worth discovering.

a surprise on the sava’s banks

Kucel Beach is nothing like a small accumulation of sand mixed with gravel. Instead, it’s an expansive stretch of shoreline made of the finest sand, which is quite a surprise compared to the gravel banks most are used to seeing. Almost perfect sand, together with the beautiful nature, are its main assets. The beauty of this beach also lies in its peace. You’re likely to have Kucel Beach entirely to yourself. Navigation will easily take you to this area, and it’s no more than an hour’s drive from Zagreb at most. There is no infrastructure on this beach, meaning that wild and natural is precisely what you’ll get. Nevertheless, various events are sometimes held on the beach. Kucel Beach isn’t an organised bathing area, nor is swimming actually intended on the beach. Because of the currents of the Sava, it’s safe only in the shallows, so it’s recommended only to dip your feet in and paddle. Dogs are also freely allowed on the beach.

an area for walks, bike rides and unwinding

Kucel Beach, if you don’t mind the sand, can indeed be an excellent option for a picnic and a starting point for exploring the rest of the area. In the latter case, it is enough simply to stay in the embrace of the Sava and follow its course. As you follow it you will notice that a number of places there have a left and a right version, depending on which bank of the Sava they are on. Lijevi Dubrovčak, home to the Posavina Corn Maze which we also visited that day, is just one such example. There is also Desni Dubrovčak.

The wider area is made for a relaxed road trip, cycling or walks. The region is peaceful, the fields are expansive, and although the road is quite narrow there is still room for two cars to pass. On one side of the fence there is often the steep bank of the Sava, hidden behind dense bushes and trees; on the other side it drops a few metres towards the fields. You can also “switch” sides of the Sava: you can cross the river by ferry or via the 160-metre-long bridge in Martinska Ves.

World.title: Martelovo Jezero: Meet The Strange Cave Deep Below a Town in Istria
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – Martelovo jezero lies inside a strange cave deep below a town in Istria. It is the name of an even stranger lake that lies inside it. Very strict rules apply if you want to pay it a visit…

Croatia’s main “event” is certainly the coast, but there are plenty of incredible lakes to enjoy up and down the country. From the world-famous Plitvice Lakes to the “colourful” ones near Imotski, they all share one thing regardless of their shapes, sizes and depths: supernatural beauty. Putni kofer writes that some of them hide from our view, forcing us to make a little effort and look deeper into the secrets of the earth. One such lake is found in the very heart of Istria and its administrative centre, the town of Pazin. Martelovo jezero, or Martel’s lake, is a real gem of the darkness.

pazin’s most striking feature

Martelovo jezero is located deep within the Pazin Cave. As one of Pazin’s most distinctive features, the cave dominates the town: Pazin’s buildings cluster above this abyss, which has been protected since 1964. The protected area covers the canyon and sinkhole of the little river Pazinčica, about 500 metres long and around 100 metres deep, as well as the 300-metre-long speleological object known as the Pazin Cave, in which this largest Istrian sinking river disappears. It is precisely this cave that is home to Martel’s Lake.

the cave is named after a frenchman

But let’s start from the beginning, from the very entrance to the cave. It is called Dante’s Vestibule and is a huge, rock-vaulted fissure more than 20 metres high and 30 to 50 metres wide. The fissure continues into the darkness in a south-westerly direction, first narrowing to a width of only 10 metres and then widening again. At a distance of 100 metres from the entrance begins an expansion that essentially grows into an 80-metre-long and about 20-metre-wide terminal hall. In it lies the siphon lake named Martel’s Lake. The lake is widest at the very end of the hall, where water swirling can sometimes be observed. On average it is 10 metres deep. The lake owes its name to the French speleologist Édouard-Alfred Martel, who at the end of the 19th century began exploring the Pazin Cave in cooperation with Wilhelm Putick, a forestry expert from Ljubljana. The two of them also made the first detailed plan of the cave, and it was Martel who recorded the greatest flood that has so far occurred in the cave: in 1896 the water in the cave rose to 30 metres below the walls of the Castle that stands above it. Major floods were also recorded in 1964 and 1993.

adventure deep below the surface…

Martelovo jezero itself is located in the “terminal” hall of the Pazin Cave, but it is not the only lake the cave hides. It is connected by a siphon to another lake. That second, smaller lake is called Mitar’s Lake and was discovered in 1975, when Pazin speleologist divers dove into the terminal siphon and discovered a 70-metre-long continuation of the sinkhole. The diver responsible for that discovery was Mitar Marinović, and the smaller lake bears his name. Although Martelovo jezero is at first glance hidden from view, it is still possible to enjoy the sight of it as part of a guided speleo-adventure lasting two and a half hours, with equipment provided. As part of it, visitors also get a small zipline with which they cross over to the gravel bank of the underground lake.

a descent into the bowels of the earth…

“Physically, what awaits you is a somewhat more demanding walk that is accessible to all healthy people. It is not accessible to children without parental supervision or to people with physical motor impairments. It is necessary to bring sturdy sports footwear and a change of clothes; light long sleeves are recommended because of the cooler interior (around 15°C). The minimum age for children is 8 years,” state the pages of the Tourist Board of Central Istria.

If you aren’t up for this adventurous option, the Pazin Cave can also be enjoyed in other ways. For example, on the large zipline above the canyon itself, at a height of about 100 metres. There is also the possibility of walking along an educational trail or simply enjoying the view of the Pazin Cave from the Vršić Bridge or from below the terrace of the Hotel Lovac. These two locations are considered the best viewpoints overlooking the Pazin Cave.

diving is exceptionally dangerous…

But let us return briefly, at the end, to an activity in the Pazin Cave that will truly remain beyond the reach of ordinary mortals, and that is diving, which is left to experts. And even for them it is demanding and dangerous.

“Diving in the Pazin Cave is one of the more demanding cave dives because of the poor visibility (only 0.5–1 metre), which makes orientation and exploration of new space difficult. In addition, large quantities of branches and tree trunks are packed into the lake in front of the siphon, and in the siphon itself they are jammed between the rocks. This has caused cave divers to get tangled in the branches as well as the safety line being pulled under tree trunks, which made the return from the siphon difficult in already poor visibility. On top of that, the rocks in the siphon are very smooth and compact, which prevented cave divers from attaching the safety line,” states, for example, a document on the subject of the Pazin Cave.

World.title: Serbian Influencer Detained in Split Over Chetnik Tattoos Faces Deportation
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – A Serbian so-called influencer has been arrested and detained in Split for publicly displaying his Chetnik tattoos and now faces deportation and a 5-year ban from entering Croatia.

Split police arrested a 31-year-old Serbian citizen who publicly displayed tattoos of Chetnik leaders Draža Mihailović and Momčilo Đujić, as well as a Chetnik emblem, on Žnjan and then posted the photo on Instagram. Index reports that the court ordered him held for 15 days, and after the misdemeanour proceedings are completed he will be expelled from Croatia and banned from entering the country for five years. According to earlier media reports, this is Serbian influencer Marko Stojković, who has around 90,000 followers on Instagram. Nacional reported that Stojković had been photographed in a hospitality establishment on Split’s Žnjan, where a large tattoo of Draža Mihailović was clearly visible.

multiple people reported the man

Police revealed that the incident occurred on Thursday around 18:15 on the outdoor terrace of a hospitality establishment on Šetalište Ivana Pavla II. They say the 31-year-old publicly displayed on visible parts of his body a tattoo of Draža Mihailović, a tattoo of Momčilo Đujić, and an emblem featuring a double-headed spread eagle, a skull and crossed swords. Next to the symbol were Cyrillic inscriptions reading “with faith in God” and “freedom or death”. Police note that such insignia was used by Chetnik forces. About ten minutes later the man posted the photograph taken at that location on his public Instagram profile. “The post caused unrest and outrage among the public in Croatia,” police stated, adding that they subsequently received multiple reports from distressed members of the public.

the police discovered him in a car in split

Police launched a criminal investigation and yesterday established his identity and location. Around 14:00 they found and arrested him in a vehicle in the Split area. The criminal investigation, police say, established a well-founded suspicion that by publicly displaying the tattoos he disturbed public order and peace and that, “with the aim of causing fear and creating a hostile and humiliating environment,” he violated dignity and caused public disturbance. Police are also charging him with a misdemeanour under the Law on Combating Discrimination. He was brought before the competent court today, and police requested a 30-day prison sentence and a fine of 2,000 euros. The court has so far ordered him held in custody for 15 days, while the verdict will be delivered later.

he will face a 5-year ban from croatia

Police announced that after the misdemeanour proceedings are completed he will be issued an expulsion order from Croatia and a five-year ban on entering the country. Measures were also taken against a 56-year-old Serbian citizen who was in his company. His stay in Croatia was cancelled under the Law on Foreigners. Police state that by participating in the activities he promoted behaviour which he “knew or must have known” was contrary to Croatian regulations and public order.

who were the people his tattoos are depicting?

Draža Mihailović was the organiser and commander of the Chetnik movement during the Second World War. The Croatian Encyclopaedia states that from the autumn of 1941 he openly collaborated with the Germans and their allies, and that his forces committed numerous crimes and carried out ethnic cleansing of the non-Serb population in the territories of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the war he was convicted as a war criminal, sentenced to death and executed by firing squad in 1946.

Momčilo Đujić was a Chetnik vojvoda from the Knin area and commander of Chetnik formations in Dalmatia. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon states that he collaborated with the Italian occupation authorities and, after Italy’s capitulation, with German forces. Units under his command committed numerous crimes against the Croatian population, as well as against Serbs who did not accept Chetnik ideology.

this isn’t the first such incident…

A similar case occurred back in 2004. Croatia at that time banned the entry of Serbian basketball player Milan Gurović, who had a tattoo of Draža Mihailović on his upper arm and did not intend to cover it during a Partizan vs Cibona match in Zagreb. The Ministry of the Interior explained at the time that publicly displaying such insignia expresses or incites hatred or violence on racial, national or religious grounds.

World.title: Isamaa attracts most new members, Eesti 200 least
World.content:
While 204 people joined Isamaa during the first eight months of this year, just two joined the coalition Eesti 200.

As the Riigikogu elections approach, we are certain to hear repeatedly which well-known figures have joined one party or another and plan to run on their candidate lists in next year's parliamentary elections.

Political party membership lists are available in the Business Register, making it possible to see who has joined this year. In the first eight months of the year, Isamaa gained the most new members, with 204 people joining the party.

Among the better-known names are entrepreneur Tõnis Arro, playwright Anu Tonts, publisher Mart Jagomägi, school principal Mehis Pever and basketball figure Aadu Kana. Several people who had already run for the party in local elections also joined. Isamaa has 7,347 members in total.

Among the larger parties, Eesti 200 has gained the fewest new members this year, with just two people joining — one in January and the other in February. As of Tuesday morning, Eesti 200 had 586 members.

EKRE and the Center Party gained fairly similar numbers of new members in the first eight months of the year. A total of 108 people have joined EKRE this year. The party has 9,044 members in total.

The Center Party has gained 104 members this year. Among the better-known figures to join the party this year are volleyball coach Urmas Tali and former Haapsalu Mayor Urmas Sukles. Silver Kuusik has also returned to the Center Party where he began his political career in 2004. In the meantime, he also tried out his political views in the People's Unity Party, the Free Party, EKRE and the Estonian Nationalists and Conservatives. The Center Party has 11,685 members in total.

The non-parliamentary Parempoolsed party has gained 47 members this year. Better-known names include Kalev Stoicescu, who switched from Eesti 200, as well as the party's press secretary, Ekvard Joakit. Parempoolsed has 848 members.

The Social Democratic Party has gained 43 members. New members include psychiatrist Anne Kleinberg and cultural figure Kersten Kõrge. The Social Democratic Party has 4,488 members in total.

The Reform Party has gained 29 members this year. The best-known new member is musician Ruslan Trochynskyi. The Reform Party has 8,895 members.

Among the smaller parties, eight people have joined the Greens this year, bringing its total membership to 708.

The Estonian Nationalists and Conservatives has gained 41 members this year. However, with many members having left, the party is now just one member above the minimum requirement of 500 members.

The Estonian National Liberals – Free Party has gained no new members this year. The party has 528 members in total.

Two people have joined the Koos party. The party has 726 members in total.

World.title: Estonia to raise pension age to 65 years, 4 months in 2029
World.content:
The Ministry of Social Affairs has proposed setting the old‑age pension age at 65 years and four months from 2029 — a rise of four months on the current benchmark.

Under a new system taking effect from next year, the pension age will be set annually based on life expectancy, rather than a person's year of birth.

Estonian law requires the legal retirement age for each year to be established by regulation two years in advance. The old‑age pension age is calculated on the basis of a five‑year average of life expectancy at 65 in Estonia — for 2029, this is based on the years 2021–2025.

The 2029 pension age applies to people born between October 1963 and August 1964. For those born from September 1964 onwards, the pension age will depend on the pension age established for 2030.

The Ministry says regularly hiking the legal retirement age is a widely used EU measure to ease demographic pressure on state pension systems. Nearly half of EU member states link rises in the retirement age to increases in life expectancy. In Denmark, for example, the old‑age pension age is 67 now and is set to rise to 70 by 2040.

As of January 1, 2026, there were 331,000 pensioners in Estonia, including 315,000 old‑age pensioners. According to a Ministry of Finance forecast, the number of pensioners will increase to around 340,000 by 2060.

World.title: Estonia's new expert panel to tackle online risks to youth mental health
World.content:
An expert panel convened by the Estonian government is examining online risks to youth mental health in a push for solutions to make digital spaces safer for kids and teens.

The panel will submit recommendations to the government by the end of 2026, covering measures for kids and teens, parents and guardians as well as the state that preserve the benefits of digital technology while reducing potential harms.

"Youths' anxiety and mental health issues are a serious and growing concern," said Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform). "Several countries have introduced or are considering restrictions on youths' social media use in recent years, but more crucial than bans are solutions that actually help our young people."

The panel's leading experts, he added, will work with researchers, youth workers and representatives of youth themselves to find effective ways to reduce the negative effects of social media.

Troubling studies

The move comes amid signs of growing problematic digital use among Estonian kids and teens.

A 2025 University of Tartu study found students were increasingly exposed to disturbing online content, sexually explicit messages and excessive internet use, with harmful content and cyberbullying also linked to poorer mental well-being.

A 2022 National Institute for Health Development (TAI) found symptoms of social media addiction among 8 percent of 11- to 15-year-olds, up from 6 percent in 2018.

The study also linked social media use with lower life satisfaction, less sleep, weaker school performance and more frequent depressive episodes.

Expert panel meeting in Tallinn on Monday. August 31, 2026. Source: Carl-Robert Kagge/Government Office

The researchers stressed, however, that digital technology itself does not cause mental health issues, with its effects depending on how and why it is used.

Practical solutions, not blanket bans

The newly convened panel brings together experts in media studies, psychology, neuroscience, education, mental health, child protection and youth work, along with a youth representative. University of Tartu media studies professor Andra Siibak was elected panel chair.

"Our common goal is to develop multilevel solutions based on scientific research and international best practices and tailored to Estonia's circumstances and our young people's experiences," said Siibak.

"We will be working with young people to develop and discuss these solutions to ensure our recommendations are not only evidence-based but also genuinely workable for the target group they are meant to serve," she added.

The panel will examine risks associated with both social media and online video game platforms.

Its next meeting is scheduled for September 14.

World.title: Estonia's PPA urges caution over video claiming Russian riverbank work
World.content:
Videos circulating on social media claim to show that Russia is reinforcing the bank of the River Narva, which borders Estonia, with crushed stone. The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) said it continuously monitors developments on the eastern border.

In one video, a man claims the Russian authorities dumped several meters of crushed stone along the riverbank. In another clip, a woman says it is now difficult to access the riverbank to swim.

The activity is said to be taking place in the Vasknarva area near the entrance to Lake Peipus on Estonia's eastern border.

A person living in Vasknarva confirmed to ERR that they have heard noise coming from the other side of the border for several days. However, they do not have visual confirmation of what exactly is taking place on the other side of the river.

Deputy director general of the PPA for border guard affairs, Veiko Kommusaar, said the agency cannot comment on activities taking place on the other side of the state border or on the activities of another country's authorities.

Local residents have posted videos claiming that Russia is building gravel embankments along the Narva River near a border crossing with Estonia.



I don't know how reliable these videos are. I have followers from this region - what do you think? pic.twitter.com/bk42m6YshA — Anton Gerashchenko (@Gerashchenko_en) August 31, 2026

"However, we continuously monitor developments related to Estonia's security and border safety and cooperate with other security agencies to have a comprehensive overview of the situation," he told ERR.

The PPA recommends that viewers approach information circulating on social media critically.

"It is particularly important to exercise caution with content that is emotional, provocative or may be intended to create fear, anxiety or uncertainty among people. Before drawing conclusions, it is worth checking the origin of the information, seeking confirmation from reliable media outlets and following official information from the authorities," Kommusaar said.

He added that the PPA continuously monitors developments on the eastern border.

"We are aware of developments in the border area and continuously assess their possible impact on Estonia's security and border safety. If information or activity emerges that requires informing the people of Estonia or taking additional measures, we will notify the public through official channels," Kommusaar stressed.
