World.title: ‘No irregularity’ in use of AFP certification for DepEd confi funds liquidation – defense
World.content:
TESTIFY. Colonel Manaros Boransing II takes the witness stand on Day 20 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 1, 2026.

'The certification was also issued for what legal, whatever legal purpose it may serve,' defense lead counsel Sheila Sison says

MANILA, Philippines – The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte maintained that there was “no irregularity” in the Department of Education‘s use of Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) certifications to support its confidential fund expenses.

“Of course, on our side, since we’re advocating for the client, there’s really no irregularity. But this is not advocating through the media. That has been our position in the answer,” defense counsel and deputy spokesperson Justin Nicol Gular told reporters on Tuesday, September 1.

The Senate impeachment trial is in the middle of hearing the prosecution’s evidence about Duterte’s alleged misuse of the confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President and the DepEd when she headed the agency.

On Tuesday, the prosecution presented witnesses from the AFP — Colonel Manaros Boransing II and Colenel Magtanggol Panopio — to prove that the Philippine Army conducted youth summits without DepEd’s confidential funds, and that Duterte and her office allegedly misrepresented the AFP certifications issued to the DepEd about these activities.

Boransing and Panopio issued certifications proving the success of the AFP’s youth summits in partnership with agencies like DepEd. However, DepEd allegedly submitted these certifications to the Commission on Audit (COA) for the liquidation of the agency’s P15.54-million funds.

Although he said that there was nothing irregular on the use of certifications, Gular refused to belabor on that point, explaining the recent sub judice reminder from the impeachment court. Gular, however, said that the public is entitled to interpret what happened during the trial proper.

During the trial’s 20th day, defense lead counsel Sheila Sison shared the contents of the AFP’s certifications. She noted that the certifications of Panopio and Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Sangdaan Jr. stated that the projects were done in collaboration with other agencies like DepEd.

“… The certification was also issued for what legal, whatever legal purpose it may serve,” Sison added.

“But that statement, just basically means what it says — for whatever legal purpose it may be used for. And you can find this in several documents, not only in the document tackled by the impeachment court,” Gular explained.

Play Video

DepEd’s credit notice

In the trial, the DepEd’s credit notice from COA was again brought up.

On August 11, COA state auditor Xylene del Campo confirmed that COA’s Intelligence and Confidential Funds Auditing Office (ICFAO) cleared DepEd’s P75-million confidential funds through a credit notice.

Presiding officer Chiz Escudero, on Tuesday, clarified with the parties if the P15 million DepEd funds in question were part of the P75-million cleared funds. Both defense counsel Lindon Miguel Bacquel and prosecution counsel Reynaldo Robles responded in the affirmative.

“I think what’s important is just to ensure that that document exists in public records. And we just want that public record or that document, the credit notice to be highlighted as well that it is included as one of the documents, as among those that senator-judges should consider during the impeachment trial,” Gular explained in a mix of Filipino and English, when asked about the credit notice’s relevance.

However, Robles reiterated Del Campo’s August remarks, stating that COA and ICFAO are still studying the possibility of referring the matter to its fraud audit unit. Meaning, COA’s credit notice is not yet conclusive.

Play Video

Why no cross?

Bacquel was the defense’s assigned lawyer for the supposed cross-examination of both Boransing and Panopio but he declined to cross-examine the AFP witnesses.

Gular explained that cross-examination is done by the defense to test the credibility of the prosecution’s witnesses.

Play Video

“But if we do not see any issue as to the testimony of the witness…. Lawyers sometimes do not conduct cross-examination anymore,” Gular said in a mix of Filipino and English. “That’s the reason why we don’t conduct cross-examination.” – Rappler.com

World.title: OpenAI denies Apple trade secret theft allegations, blames iPhone maker for its ‘own mess’
World.content:
APPLE VS OPENAI. Apple and OpenAI logos are seen in this illustration taken July 12, 2026.

OpenAI says Apple 'cannot use its own sloppy ​procedures to blame others for its own mess'

MANILA, Philippines – OpenAI on Monday, August 31, denied allegations it had stolen some Apple trade secrets, adding that the iPhone maker did not show former employees had taken confidential information.

Apple’s July complaint against OpenAI and Tang Tan and Chang Liu, former Apple employees and now OpenAI workers, stems from assertions that OpenAI took on a broad effort to systematically acquire and exploit Apple’s confidential information through ex-employees.

According to a Reuters report, OpenAI said Apple’s lawsuit intends to slow down a potential competitor while also discouraging Apple employees from leaving the company, with OpenAI taking on some 400 former employees of the iPhone maker to boost its hardware initiative according to filings from both companies.

OpenAI said Monday that Apple’s encouragement of the use of personal iCloud accounts to access documents and perform work tasks makes separating personal and company information difficult, adding that Apple’s policy of immediately escorting departing employees from the premises does not give them the time to return company devices, turn over responsibilities, and move over work files to the right people within the company.

Liu said in a filing that his access to Apple documents after his departure was done to help former colleagues within the company to locate files or answer work-related queries, and adding Apple employees kept contacting him for help after his departure. Meanwhile, Tan said he only kept non-confidential documents, like an employee departure checklist, after he left the company.

OpenAI on August 3 also denied wrongdoing and published messages and email correspondences on their website that support what Liu has said — that he was helping his former coworkers.

OpenAI said that employees “can leave a company like Apple that has struggled to ⁠adopt ​AI and move to an exciting startup that builds innovative products.”

“Apple may not like those choices. But it cannot claim those choices are unlawful, and it cannot use its own sloppy ​procedures to blame others for its own mess,” OpenAI added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pilandok now a tropical storm; heavy rain in 4 areas due to southwest monsoon
World.content:
WEATHER. Tropical Storm Pilandok and southwest monsoon inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of September 1, 2026, 5:20 pm.

The southwest monsoon is bringing moderate to heavy rain to Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, and Zambales. Haze due to forest fires from Kalimantan, Indonesia, is also affecting the western portions of Visayas, Mimaropa, and Mindanao.

MANILA, Philippines – Tropical Depression Pilandok intensified into a tropical storm on Tuesday morning, September 1, while the southwest monsoon or habagat is still bringing moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) to Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, and Zambales.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration’s (PAGASA) said Metro Manila, Cordillera Administrative Region, the rest of Ilocos Region, the rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of Central Luzon, Cavite, Batangas, Rizal, Occidental Mindoro, Aklan, and Antique are seeing scattered rain and thunderstorms on Tuesday afternoon, while the rest of Luzon and Visayas can expect isolated rain showers or thunderstorms.

Below is PAGASA’s latest heavy rainfall outlook due to the southwest monsoon:

Tuesday afternoon, September 1, to Wednesday afternoon, September 2:

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, and Zambales.

Wednesday afternoon, September 2, to Thursday afternoon, September 3:

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, Bataan, and Occidental Mindoro

Thursday afternoon, September 3, to Friday afternoon, September 4:

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Occidental Mindoro

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Zambales, Bataan, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas, Oriental Mindoro, and Antique

These areas should still watch out for floods and landslides.

The southwest monsoon is also bringing strong to gale-force gusts, especially in coastal and upland areas exposed to winds, over most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Oriental, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental, and Davao Oriental from Tuesday until Thursday.

Moderate to very rough seas persist in the following areas:

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Western seaboards of Batanes and Babuyan Islands; the seaboard of Ilocos Norte — waves up to 5 meters high

Seaboards of Ilocos Sur and northern La Union; the western seaboard of Pangasinan; the northern seaboard of Babuyan Islands; the remaining seaboard of Batanes — waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Seaboard of Zambales — waves up to 4 meters high

Seaboard of Lubang Islands; the western and southern seaboards of Bataan; the western seaboards of Cavite and Batangas — waves up to 3.5 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Babuyan Islands; the western seaboards of northern Occidental Mindoro, Calamian Islands, and northern Palawan; the northern and western seaboard of Kalayaan Islands — waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboard of Isabela; western seaboard of central Palawan; the eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; the remaining seaboards of Kalayaan Islands, Pangasinan, and La Union; the northern seaboard of Calamian Islands; the remaining western seaboard of Occidental Mindoro — waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboards of mainland Cagayan, northern Aurora, Romblon, Cuyo Islands, Antique, Surigao del Sur, and Davao Occidental; the western seaboard of Burias Island; the southern seaboards of Quezon, Marinduque, Oriental Mindoro, Iloilo, and Guimaras; the southwestern seaboard of Negros Occidental; the remaining western seaboard of mainland Palawan; the remaining seaboards of Occidental Mindoro and Davao Oriental — waves up to 2 meters high

PAGASA Weather Specialist Benison Estareja also said haze is affecting the western portions of Visayas, Mimaropa, and Mindanao due to forest fires from Kalimantan, Indonesia.

Tropical Storm Pilandok (international name Krovanh) was last located 1,015 km east of extreme Northern Luzon, moving northwestward at 10 km/h, with maximum sustained winds of 65 kilometers per hour and gustiness of up to 80 km/h. It still has no effect on the country.

With its current track, PAGASA said Pilandok may exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) by late Wednesday or early Thursday. It will remain over the northern Philippine Sea as a tropical storm before approaching Okinawa, Japan.

Aside from Pilandok, PAGASA is also monitoring Tropical Storm Saudel (formerly Obet) and a low pressure area outside PAR. The other tropical depression weakened into an LPA and has since dissipated.

Saudel was located 685 km west of Calayan, Cagayan, moving east northeastward at 30 km/h, with winds of 65 km/h and gustiness of up to 80 km/h.

Meanwhile, the LPA located 3,010 km east of southeastern Luzon still has a “medium” chance of developing into a tropical depression in the next 24 hours.

Estareja said two to three tropical cyclones may develop within or enter PAR in September. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Post uses AI-generated news report to falsely claim Duterte is back in PH
World.content:
Former president Rodrigo Duterte remains detained; he was not released from detention to attend his daughter’s impeachment trial, contrary to the claim

Claim: Former president Rodrigo Duterte is coming home to the Philippines to attend the impeachment trial of his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, as shown in a news report.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook reel showing the supposed news report was posted on August 10. It has already received 179,000 views, 7,300 reactions, 1,100 comments, and 1,100 shares as of writing.

The graphic shows the former president waving while a plane is seen in the background. The text on the graphic reads, “Breaking news: Rodrigo Duterte comes home to the Philippines to attend the hearing of Sara Duterte.”

The caption of the post emphasized the claim that Duterte has been released from International Criminal Court (ICC) detention: “[Confirm] nakalabas na po mahal natin [presidente] na magaling Digong Duterte.”

(It is confirmed that our beloved and excellent president, Digong Duterte, has been released.)

Some Facebook users believed the claim, leaving comments in support of the former president.

The facts: Duterte remains detained at the ICC facility in The Hague, Netherlands. The ICC website lists his current status as “In ICC custody.”

The supposed news report was generated using artificial intelligence (AI). AI image detector Sight Engine flagged the image as 99% likely to be AI-generated. Hive Detect also labeled the same image as 99.1% likely to contain AI-generated content.

Reverse image search did not show any credible news report similar to the one being shown in the Facebook reel. There are also no official announcements from the ICC stating that Duterte was released from detention to attend his daughter’s impeachment trial.

Still detained: Duterte’s counsel had repeatedly appealed for an interim release citing health reasons, but this has been denied by the ICC. The court’s latest decision was issued in May 2026, when the Trial Chamber III said the former leader is still not eligible for temporary liberty.

Under the Rome Statute, a suspect cannot be released if they present risk factors, which include the danger of fleeing, obstructing justice by intimidating witnesses, or recommitting the same alleged crimes. Article 60(3) notes that the court may modify its ruling on a person’s detention or release if circumstances have changed.

In its ruling, the chamber said, “The Chamber therefore finds no notable change in circumstances [of Duterte] that warrants the release of the accused, with or without conditions.”

Duterte was arrested in March 2025 for crimes against humanity linked to killings in his brutal war on drugs. In April 2026, the ICC’s pre-trial chamber confirmed all the charges against him, including three counts of murder, covering 49 incidents of killings and 78 victims. His full trial is scheduled to begin in November.

Impeachment: Meanwhile, Duterte’s daughter is facing an impeachment trial for her alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery, and threats to assassinate President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte)

Previous fact checks: Rappler has previously fact-checked similar false claims about Duterte:

– Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com

Angelee Kaye Abelinde is a student journalist based in Naga City, and an alumna of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Flood in San Simon, Pampanga causes heavy traffic in NLEX
World.content:
Victory Liner says some trips on Monday, August 31, took as long as 11 hours to Dagupan, 14 hours to San Fernando, Pampanga, and 10 hours to Baguio from Metro Manila

MANILA, Philippines – Many vehicles were stuck in traffic along the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) on Tuesday, September 1, due to flooding in San Simon, Pampanga.

Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation (MPTC), owner and operator of NLEX, said on Tuesday that it recognizes motorists’ difficulties and will continue working with national and local agencies to expedite flood-prevention measures.

To address the recurring flood problem in the area, MPTC said it will raise the northbound and southbound pavements in Tulaoc, San Simon, Pampanga once the Tulaoc Bridge elevation is completed.

MPTC said the huge volume of rain water caused by southwest monsoon or habagat “overwhelmed the system.”

In an advisory issued at 2:20 pm Tuesday, NLEX said heavy traffic was reported in both the southbound and northbound lane of Tulaoc and at the San Simon Interchange. Northbound Class 1 vehicles in Tulaoc and the San Simon Interchange were being diverted to Balagtas Exit.

Play Video

Traffic along the southbound lanes of NLEX in Balintawak, Valenzuela, and Meycauayan, meanwhile, was reported as “light.”

As of 2:20 pm, the following areas were also temporarily closed to all vehicles:

Libtong Exit (northbound)

Sta. Rita Northbound Entry

Pulilan Northbound Entry

Some bus operators like Victory Liner and Baliwag Transit said their operations continue, but warned the public over the heavy traffic and extended travel time.

Victory Liner said some trips from Manila on Monday, August 31, took as long as 11 hours to Dagupan, Pangasinan; 14 hours to San Fernando, Pampanga; and 10 hours to Baguio City.

Pampanga Governor Lilia Pineda said in an interview with One News on Monday, that the town of San Simon — the affected portion of NLEX — is submerged in flood. She said the the flood was caused by the overflow of Pampanga River.

Since Sunday, August 30, NLEX Corporation has issued traffic advisories warning motorists about water buildup in the San Simon and Tulaoc areas. – Rappler.com

World.title: Experts: Kazakhstan’s New Security Council Apparatus Signals Shift Toward Preventive Security
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is strengthening the institutional role of its Security Council, a move experts say could mark a shift toward more systematic strategic analysis and preventive risk management as the country’s understanding of national security expands beyond traditional defense and law enforcement.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree on Aug. 28 establishing the Security Council Apparatus as a state body directly subordinate to and accountable to the President. The move was accompanied by changes to the council’s leadership: Aida Balayeva was appointed Deputy Chair of the Security Council, while Gizat Nurdauletov was relieved of his position as Secretary.

The changes raise a question about the direction of Kazakhstan’s security architecture: whether the new structure primarily strengthens the administrative capacity of an existing institution or signals a more substantive expansion of the Security Council’s role in strategic governance.

On Aug. 31, Tokayev met with Balayeva in her new capacity and outlined several priority tasks, including those related to establishing the Security Council Apparatus. The new state body will deal with issues related to national security, legality and law and order.

A more defined institutional role

The Security Council is a constitutional collegial body chaired by the President and responsible for coordinating a unified state policy in national security, defense capability and the protection of sovereignty.

Political science expert Gaziz Abishev said the change could increase the council’s analytical and coordinating capacity. According to him, creating a separate apparatus gives the council a more clearly defined institutional structure.

“The Security Council of Kazakhstan is acquiring more specific institutional contours. President Tokayev signed a decree on establishing the Security Council Apparatus as a state body directly subordinate to the head of state. This, it should be understood, anticipates strengthening the Security Council with personnel, technical and other resources,” Abishev wrote on his Telegram channel.

Manarbek Kabaziyev, deputy chairman of the Board of the Foreign Policy Research Institute under Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry, sees the change primarily as an effort to improve strategic governance.

“The creation of the Security Council Apparatus should, first of all, be considered in the context of further improving the system of strategic governance of the state. Under modern conditions, the concept of national security has expanded significantly: it is no longer only defense and the law-enforcement sphere, but also information, technological, economic, energy, environmental and other components,” Kabaziyev told the Astana Times.

Why the security agenda is changing

The broader definition of national security reflects the increasingly interconnected nature of modern risks. For Kazakhstan, this is particularly relevant given its geographic and economic position at the intersection of major Eurasian political, trade and transport routes. Kabaziyev said the main objective of strengthening the Security Council should be to improve the state’s ability to identify risks before they develop into crises.

“In my view, the main task is to ensure more systematic and professional analysis of internal and external risks, their early identification and the timely development of government decisions,” he said.

According to Kabaziyev, legislation already provides the Security Council Apparatus with functions related to information and analytical support, organizational support, coordination and monitoring the implementation of Security Council decisions.

The current reform therefore represents, in his assessment, not the creation of an entirely new institution but its organizational and substantive strengthening in response to changing security requirements.

From reaction to prevention

One of the reform’s most important potential consequences is a greater emphasis on preventive rather than reactive approaches to national security.

“The long-term effect, in my view, is a transition from a predominantly reactive approach to security to a more preventive model,” Kabaziyev said.

Such a model requires the state to identify connections between risks that traditionally might have been considered separately. Kabaziyev said the apparatus should have strong analytical capabilities, engage with the expert community and use modern forecasting and scenario-analysis tools.

“Then its role will consist not only in responding to threats that have already emerged, but also in identifying potential risks in advance and proposing options for their neutralization,” he said.

Appointments’ role

The creation of the apparatus coincided with Balayeva’s appointment as Deputy Chair of the Security Council, adding an important personnel dimension to the institutional reform. Political analyst Talgat Kaliyev noted that Balayeva’s new position significantly expands her responsibilities.

“The election of Yerlan Karin as Vice President and the appointment of Balayeva as Deputy Chair of the Security Council are events of the same order. Essentially, President Tokayev now has two deputies, and separating the Security Council Apparatus into a separate body allows us to discuss the delineation of powers,” Kaliyev wrote on his Telegram channel.

He described Balayeva as effectively becoming a “vice president for security,” suggesting that her responsibilities could extend to oversight of law-enforcement bodies and the implementation of the Law and Order policy in everyday governance.

The precise distribution of responsibilities within the new structure will become clearer as the apparatus is organized and its institutional framework develops.

Security and international reputation

The Security Council’s institutional strengthening could also affect how Kazakhstan is perceived internationally. Kabaziyev said the development should not automatically be interpreted as a move toward greater state isolation or excessive centralization.

“On the contrary, if the new format ensures professional decision-making, interagency coordination, strategic forecasting and the rule of law, this could strengthen Kazakhstan’s international reputation as a state capable of effectively managing complex risks,” he said.

The creation of a dedicated Security Council Apparatus provides the institutional foundation for a potentially stronger role, but its ultimate significance will depend on how effectively the new structure operates. Kabaziyev emphasized that the reform’s effectiveness should ultimately be measured by its results rather than by the expansion of the institutional structure itself.

“Ultimately, the effectiveness of the Security Council will be assessed not by the number of structural divisions, but by the state’s ability to foresee challenges, make balanced decisions and ensure their consistent implementation,” he said.

World.title: Teachers at Heart of President’s Vision: NU Researchers on Kazakhstan’s Education Future
World.content:
Kazakhstan has backed its education ambitions with substantial investment in new schools, higher teacher salaries and measures to strengthen the profession. Speaking at a Republic Day event in October 2025, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said education funding had tripled over the previous five years and teachers’ salaries had doubled.

Yet investment alone cannot transform learning. As Tokayev emphasized in 2024, even the best programs and modern schools cannot succeed without good teachers. In July 2026, he described artificial intelligence as a tool that should empower teachers rather than replace them. Against this national backdrop, Nazarbayev University’s Science Café examined a timely question: what do teachers need to turn Kazakhstan’s education investment into better learning?

Three Graduate School of Education (GSE) researchers Assel Sharimova, Duishon Shamatov and Askhat Makhmetov examined teacher preparation, professional status, well-being and technology. Their research suggests that physical and digital modernization must be matched by investment in teachers’ capacity, autonomy and working conditions.

A teacher’s first year tests the system

For Shamatov, an associate professor specializing in teacher preparation and professional development, the decisive test begins after graduation. Young teachers often enter schools with limited classroom experience and little structured support. When they struggle or leave, the problem may lie less in their ability than in the conditions in which they begin. Preparation should therefore extend beyond a diploma through practical experience, systematic mentoring and opportunities to learn from experienced colleagues. Shamatov also serves on a working group of Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Science and Higher Education that is improving accreditation standards for teacher education. He cautioned against treating PISA as an exam for teachers or a competition between schools. It indicates how well an education system enables students to reason, solve problems and apply knowledge in real-life situations. Improving Kazakhstan’s performance requires investment not only in assessment, but in teachers’ preparation, continuing development and ability to create meaningful learning experiences.

Professional status, he added, cannot be reduced to salary or public recognition. Although Kazakhstan’s Law on the Status of a Teacher marked important progress, status is ultimately experienced through working conditions, professional trust, autonomy and respect for teachers’ judgment.

When high performance leads to exhaustion

Makhmetov, a postdoctoral researcher specializing in teacher well-being and educational equity, presented findings from Kazakhstan’s first study focused on teacher well-being. His analysis identified six profiles, challenging the simple division of teachers into “good” and “bad” performers. One vulnerable group consists of highly effective yet exhausted teachers, representing almost a quarter of the workforce. These educators often lead innovation, accept additional responsibilities and support school improvement. The commitment that makes them valuable can also expose them to chronic overwork and burnout.

This shifts the leadership question from how to demand more to how to retain those already driving change. Makhmetov highlighted workload monitoring, burnout prevention and conditions that keep professional motivation sustainable.

His study also revealed a “master’s degree paradox.” Holding a master’s degree was associated with lower subjective well-being, while the proportion of such teachers has risen from approximately 3.5% to 11%. Schools could respond by offering them greater autonomy and roles as mentors, curriculum developers and leaders of professional initiatives.

Support must continue inside schools

Sharimova, an assistant professor specializing in teacher preparation and professional development, emphasized that teachers’ early years are critical. New teachers learn through relationships with experienced teachers, subject colleagues and school leaders, while managing lesson preparation, assessment, reporting and class-teacher responsibilities.

Meaningful mentoring should include opportunities to observe lessons, receive constructive feedback and approach a trusted colleague when difficulties arise. Practical assistance and openness from school leaders are equally important.

The speakers also viewed digital technologies and AI as useful resources. They can support lesson planning, assessment and feedback, student engagement and the visualization of complex STEM concepts. Yet technology cannot compensate for weak preparation, excessive workloads or a lack of professional trust.

Kazakhstan’s education modernization will ultimately be judged not only by the schools it builds or technologies it introduces, but by what happens inside classrooms. The Science Café discussions point to the next stage of reform ensuring that teachers are well prepared, professionally trusted, protected from burnout and supported throughout their careers. Strong schools require strong teachers and national ambition depends on giving them the conditions to succeed.

The author is Saqib Raza, a PhD scholar in education and an MSc graduate in Educational Leadership in Higher Education from Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Education, Kazakhstan.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Historic KMG Dim Sum Bond Issue Sets New Benchmark for Yuan Financing in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – KazMunayGas’ (KMG) historic issuance of 3.5 billion yuan (US$520.3 million) in Dim Sum bonds could mark a new stage in Kazakhstan’s access to yuan-denominated financing, financial analyst Andrei Chebotaryov said.

The transaction, which includes the first 10-year Dim Sum bonds issued by a company from Kazakhstan and Central Asia, attracted more than 25 billion yuan (US$3.7 billion) in orders.

KMG closed the order book on Aug. 26, with proceeds earmarked for its investment program. The bonds are scheduled to be placed on Sept. 2.

A new benchmark in yuan financing

The issue consists of two tranches. The five-year bonds, worth 1.5 billion yuan (US$223 million), carry a 2.3% annual coupon and a 2.45% yield. The 10-year tranche totals 2 billion yuan (US$297.3 million), with a 2.8% coupon and a 2.98% yield.

According to Chebotaryov, KMG became the first company in Kazakhstan and Central Asia to issue 10-year Dim Sum bonds, creating a long-term benchmark for yuan-denominated borrowing in the region.

“KMG became the first company in Kazakhstan and Central Asia to issue 10-year Dim Sum bonds. In the region, a 10-year benchmark was formed for the first time – in other words, a long-term yuan borrowing market has opened, which we did not have before,” Chebotaryov wrote on his Telegram channel on Aug. 28.

Dim Sum bonds are yuan-denominated securities issued outside mainland China, typically in Hong Kong. For Kazakhstan, access to this market provides an alternative international financing channel.

Moody’s assigned the bonds a Baa1 credit rating, matching KMG’s rating.

Investor demand is the stronger signal

The most striking indicator was the scale of demand. Investor orders exceeded 25 billion yuan (US$3.7 billion) at the peak – more than seven times the announced issue size. According to KMG, this was the largest order book in the history of Dim Sum issues by issuers outside mainland China and Hong Kong.

Investors included banks, insurance companies, hedge funds and sovereign investment funds. A two-day roadshow in Hong Kong preceded the issue.

Chebotaryov said the combination of borrowing costs, maturity and demand points to strong investor confidence.

“Low funding costs, a long maturity and sevenfold oversubscription together say one thing: investors trust KazMunayGas and see the company as financially stable,” he wrote.

He added that the signal extends beyond KMG itself.

“Asian investors were buying Kazakhstan’s credit risk for 10 years ahead – and they were buying it willingly,” he said.

Why the deal matters for Kazakhstan

The transaction could have implications beyond KMG. According to Chebotaryov, it provides a reference point for other Kazakh issuers considering yuan financing.

The deal also broadens access to Asian capital markets and could reduce reliance on dollar financing, according to Energy Monitor.

Whether other Kazakh companies can replicate KMG’s terms will depend on investor demand. The key indicator will be whether other domestic issuers follow KMG into the Dim Sum market.

What to watch next

The immediate milestone is settlement on Sept. 2. The longer-term test will be whether other Kazakh issuers follow KMG into the Dim Sum market.

“KMG has set a trend for other domestic companies. This deal is now a natural reference point for any Kazakh issuer looking toward yuan financing: there is a price, there is a maturity, and there is confirmed demand,” Chebotaryov said.

The deal builds on Kazakhstan’s recent expansion into yuan-denominated capital markets, following KMG’s 2025 plan for a Dim Sum program of up to 15 billion yuan (nearly US$2 billion) and Samruk Kazyna’s 3 billion yuan Panda bond issued in April.

If other issuers follow, the transaction could establish a benchmark for future yuan borrowing in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Kazakhstan Has Begun Structural Shift Toward Non-Resource Economy, Expert Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has entered a new investment cycle that is beginning to change not only the volume but also the structure of capital entering the economy, according to the country’s leading financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov.

While the country remains dependent on extractive industries, growing investment in manufacturing, processing and high-technology production suggests that the long-discussed shift toward a more diversified economy is beginning to take shape.

“We can already confidently speak about the beginning of a structural shift. It is still too early to say that we are moving away from the resource-based model, but the figures show that the state is now moving toward a non-resource model not just in words, but in practice,” Rysmambetov said in a comment to The Astana Times.

From investment growth to structural change

The change is visible in investment data. Between 2019 and 2025, investment in fixed capital in Kazakhstan increased from 12.6 trillion tenge (US$27.3 billion) to 23.5 trillion tenge (US$51 billion), while investment in manufacturing tripled from 1 trillion (US$2.2 billion) to 3 trillion tenge (US$6.5 billion). The sector’s share of total investment rose from 8.1% to 12.7%, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Aug. 31.

Foreign investment is also diversifying. Gross foreign direct investment reached $20.5 billion in 2025, up 14.4%. Investment in manufacturing increased by 47.4%, or $1.4 billion, while investment in mining fell by 47%, or $3 billion. The changing composition suggests Kazakhstan is attracting more capital into activities beyond raw-material extraction.

This trend is supported by the growing pipeline of industrial projects. The Kazakh Invest portfolio currently includes 215 projects worth $78.6 billion, with more than 88,000 jobs expected to be created. Of these, 93 projects worth $32.2 billion are already being implemented, while 122 projects worth $46.4 billion remain under development.

A new system for turning capital into projects

The government is seeking to reinforce this shift through a new investment-support system. Since 2025, a three-level investment attraction model has been operating, with regions identifying priority projects and targeting investors. Fast Track mechanisms, investment headquarters and a “prosecutorial filter” are intended to reduce administrative barriers, while the National Digital Investment Platform provides monitoring and coordination.

Investment agreements are another part of the framework. Since the mechanism was introduced in 2021, 66 agreements worth more than 17.8 trillion tenge (US$38.6 billion) have been concluded. In 2025 alone, 30 agreements worth nearly 11.2 trillion tenge (US$24.3 billion) were signed. By August, another 25 agreements worth approximately 4.4 trillion tenge (US$9.5 billion) had been concluded.

The approach reflects a broader shift in investment policy: attracting capital is increasingly being linked to specific economic needs, including import substitution, exports, localization and the development of domestic supply chains.

The real test is what happens after investment

The quality of this investment, however, will ultimately matter more than the headline figures, Rysmambetov said. In his view, the next test is whether new factories generate exports, domestic value added, higher productivity and better-paid jobs.

“Investments should not simply increase gross output, but also increase labour productivity and real wages,” he said.

This distinction matters as Kazakhstan expands projects in pharmaceuticals, agricultural processing, food production and digital infrastructure. New pharmaceutical plants are expected to localize production of hundreds of medicines, while projects by international companies in agriculture and food processing are designed to create demand for domestic suppliers.

Large-scale projects such as Dalian Hesheng Holdings’ $739 million wheat-processing complex, Fufeng Group’s $340 million corn-processing plant and Tiryaki Agro’s approximately $320 million agro-industrial complex illustrate the move toward deeper processing. Rather than exporting agricultural commodities with limited processing, these projects aim to produce starches, gluten, amino acids, protein isolates and other higher-value products.

Beyond factories: building domestic technological capacity

A similar logic is emerging in digital infrastructure. The planned Data Center Valley near Ekibastuz is being developed as a major computing and artificial intelligence hub, with investment potentially reaching $30 billion and energy capacity expanding from 300 megawatts to 1 gigawatt. In June, Kazakhstan signed a $10 billion package of agreements with Firebird and NVIDIA covering AI and digital infrastructure.

For Rysmambetov, however, industrial diversification must be accompanied by stronger domestic technological capacity. He pointed to limited spending on research and development and underused laboratories at universities and enterprises as areas requiring greater attention.

“Industry often relies on ready-made engineering solutions from abroad instead of developing them internally,” he said, arguing that Kazakhstan needs greater investment in R&D, industrial analytics and applied research.

From foreign capital to domestic value

The international dimension is equally important. Kazakhstan’s ability to attract capital from the UAE, Qatar, Singapore, China, the United States and European countries gives the country access not only to financing but also to technology, markets and supply chains. The challenge is to ensure that foreign investment creates lasting links with domestic businesses rather than operating as isolated production facilities.

The emerging investment cycle therefore represents a transition rather than a completed transformation. Manufacturing’s growing share, rising non-resource investment, and the expansion of processing industries provide evidence that Kazakhstan’s economic structure is changing.

The decisive indicators over the next several years will be whether these projects reach operation, increase exports, deepen domestic value chains, raise productivity and stimulate innovation.

“The transformation has begun. But to replace the economic model, we still need some time – three to five years,” Rysmambetov said.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: First Korea–Central Asia Summit Marks New Phase in Seoul’s Eurasian Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — South Korea is moving to place its nearly two-decade engagement with Central Asia on a presidential footing, bringing the region’s five leaders to Seoul in September for an inaugural summit expected to focus on critical-mineral supply chains, energy infrastructure and artificial intelligence, Ambassador of the Republic of Korea Jung Ki-Hong said in an interview with The Astana Times, his first interview since formally assuming the post.

The gathering, scheduled for Sept. 16-17 in Seoul, will elevate a diplomatic mechanism launched at the deputy minister level in 2007 into a leaders’ platform, a shift the ambassador described as more consequential than any single agreement expected from the summit.

“I think the formation of this multilateral forum at the presidential level itself is the most important outcome,” said Jung, who presented credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Aug. 19.

Jung said the leaders are expected to discuss cooperation on critical minerals and energy infrastructure, the resilience of supply chains, artificial intelligence and digital transformation, as well as cultural and people-to-people ties.

“This is not going to be just a one-time event,” he added.

Untapped potential

Kazakhstan is South Korea’s largest trading partner and investment destination in Central Asia, but considerable potential remains untapped, Ambassador Jung said.

According to the Ministry of Trade and Integration, bilateral trade reached $3.17 billion in 2025, up 1.4% from the previous year. In the first six months of this year, trade reached $1.3 billion, while Kazakhstan’s exports to South Korea increased 17.2% to $510 million. In 20 years, South Korea’s gross investment in Kazakhstan surpassed $10 billion.

Ambassador Jung identified three particularly promising areas: critical minerals, artificial intelligence, and power generation and the transition to cleaner energy.

The 21st century is about critical minerals

“Critical minerals are not just mineral resources, they are geopolitical resources,” he added, echoing a recent assessment by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

“They say the 20th century is about oil and gas, but the 21st century is about critical minerals,” Jung said. Semiconductors, batteries, renewable-energy systems and AI infrastructure all depend on these materials, he added, making Kazakhstan’s resource base increasingly important to South Korean industry.

Jung emphasized the two economies bring complementary strengths. Kazakhstan possesses substantial critical-mineral resources in deposits, concentrates and mine tailings, while South Korea has advanced processing technologies, industrial capacity and demand as an end user.

Cooperation on critical minerals is beginning to show progress. On Aug. 5, Kazakh and South Korean institutions met at Satbayev University in Almaty to finalize arrangements for a joint research center focused on rare and rare-earth metals. The initiative brings together the Korea Institute of Industrial Technology, or KITECH, and Korea National Institute of Rare Metals, known as KORAM, with Satbayev University’s Institute of Metallurgy and Ore Beneficiation.

According to Ambassador Jung, the initiative followed two years of feasibility work supported by the two governments. The center is intended to assess Kazakhstan’s mineral resources and identify technologies that could extract and process rare metals from ores, concentrates and industrial waste.

Jung said South Korea wanted the partnership to move beyond research and development toward business partnerships and commercially viable processing projects.

“We want a business-to-business matchmaking in the critical mineral sector.”

Jung said he had raised the proposed transition toward commercial cooperation during talks with Kazakhstan’s Minister of Industry and Construction Yersain Nagaspayev on Aug. 21. The two sides would need to match South Korean processing technologies with specific Kazakh deposits and determine whether potential projects could be scaled to commercially viable production, he said. If major Kazakh mining companies, including Tau-Ken Samruk and Eurasian Resources Group, identify common interests with South Korean industrial companies, Jung said, they could potentially establish processing facilities in Kazakhstan to produce intermediate materials or higher-value finished products.

AI ‘revolution’ is underway

AI offers another area for closer cooperation, Jung said, describing South Korea as one of the few countries outside the United States and China with advanced homegrown AI capabilities. Kazakhstan, meanwhile, has positioned itself as a regional leader in the sector.

“I think we have a huge room to help each other, exchange data and exchange our technologies together,” he said.

Jung noted energy cooperation would become increasingly important. Expansion of AI and data-center infrastructure would sharply increase electricity demand, creating further opportunities for cooperation in power generation. He pointed to South Korea’s experience in gas-fired generation and nuclear energy, including small modular reactors.

That cooperation is already visible in Kazakhstan’s power sector, where South Korean companies have taken on major generation projects. Doosan Enerbility completed the 310-megawatt Karabatan combined-cycle gas power plant in the Atyrau Region in 2020 and is now the engineering, procurement and construction contractor for a 1,000-megawatt power plant in the Turkistan Region.

Cooperation is also expanding into nuclear energy. During talks in Astana on June 8, Kazakh and South Korean officials discussed a proposed memorandum covering small modular reactors, workforce training and scientific and technical cooperation. The officials said Kazakhstan was interested in drawing on South Korean expertise in reactor technology and nuclear safety.

What Korean companies want to see in Kazakhstan

Nearly 800 companies with South Korean participation operate in Kazakhstan. Yet Jung cautioned that commercial interest alone would not be enough to unlock a new wave of South Korean investment. Large energy projects carry substantial financial risks, he said, while the experience of some earlier Korean investors in Kazakhstan has made companies more cautious.

He contrasted South Korean companies’ approach to risk with that of larger American and Chinese competitors.

“I met many Korean entrepreneurs and companies who have already invested here in this country,” he said. “If you want to get more profit, you have to take the risk as well. But Korea is not the U.S. and not China, so they [companies] are very much worried about the risk factor. If the Kazakh government or the big companies can share this risk factor together with the Korean investor, I think it would encourage Korean companies to further invest.”

Rebuilding confidence, Jung said, would require projects that demonstrate that long-term investment in Kazakhstan can succeed.

“We need to create more success stories of Korean investment here in this country. (…) We need fresh investment and new success stories between our two countries. That’s our hope,” he added.

Kazakhstan’s flagship project

Jung pointed to Alatau City as both an opportunity for deeper cooperation and a test of whether the two countries can turn political ambition into commercially viable projects.

Senior Kazakh officials were in Seoul in October presenting opportunities stemming from Kazakhstan’s flagship project. In December, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Industry and Construction, the Alatau City Authority and Korea Overseas Infrastructure and Urban Development Corporation (KIND) signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a framework for cooperation on Alatau Smart City. KIND, a state-backed corporation, has worked on urban and infrastructure projects in South Korea and abroad, including in Vietnam and Indonesia.

“They are eyeing this Alatau City project with great interest, but with great prudence. They are now undertaking pre-feasibility study,” said the ambassador.

Jung expects Alatau City to feature in talks between South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev during their meeting in Seoul in September.

“We will see what the future holds,” he added.

“We found the Alatau City project fascinating, but it is also true that it entails huge risk as well. When I arrived in Kazakhstan, the first thing that I did was to go there. I made a field trip to Alatau City,” said Jung.

There, the ambassador also visited K-Park, a Korean cultural and business complex now under construction, as well as sites planned for urban air mobility infrastructure and a new science and technology university modeled on South Korea’s Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, or KAIST.

“If all these important projects are realized in the future, it is an ideal scenario,” he added.

Educational opportunities

Beyond investment and technology, Jung said South Korea’s cultural appeal among young Kazakhs had created demand for deeper educational and professional ties. South Korea remains a popular higher-education destination for Kazakh citizens, with more than 1,500 students enrolled at Korean universities as of April 2024.

Dozens of universities and secondary schools across Kazakhstan also offer Korean-language instruction, he said, while the Korean Cultural Center in Astana and the Korean Education Center in Almaty provide language courses and cultural programs.

“I feel a huge demand for and great interest in Korean culture among the Kazakh young generation. (…) You can make the most of the diverse programs that Korean institutions can offer you, so I very much encourage the Kazakh young generation to think seriously about learning Korean language,” he said.

According to the ambassador, tangible progress has also been made on the proposed Qazaqstan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, or QAIST. A feasibility study for the planned KAIST branch campus in Alatau City was completed and presented in Astana in July. The university is modeled on the experience of KAIST, Korea’s leading research university, established in 1971.

Jung said the September summit will also advance Kazakhstan’s admission to South Korea’s Employment Permit System, or EPS. South Korea designated Kazakhstan as the system’s 18th labor-sending country on Aug. 14, with the first Kazakh workers expected to arrive in 2028.

The program provides a regulated pathway for foreign workers to take jobs in South Korean industries facing labor shortages, such as manufacturing, construction, agriculture and fisheries. Kazakhstan’s participation would expand opportunities for its citizens to work legally in South Korea, acquire professional experience and receive formal labor protections.

Jung also pointed to direct air links as another factor bringing the two countries closer. Nonstop flights connect Seoul with both Astana and Almaty, placing the cities within roughly six to seven hours of one another.

A sense of familiarity

When asked what had made him feel most connected to Kazakhstan in the two months since he arrived in the country, Jung pointed first to a sense of cultural familiarity. During a diplomatic career spanning more than 33 years, he has served primarily in Europe and the United States, as well as Argentina. Kazakhstan is his first posting in Central Asia.

“Frankly speaking, I feel very much comfortable living and working in this country because people are quite similar to me. Sometimes I found many Kazakh people more similar than the Koreans in Seoul,” he said smiling.

That connection is reinforced by Kazakhstan’s community of more than 120,000 ethnic Koreans, known as Koryo-saram. In 2027, Kazakhstan will mark 90 years since Soviet authorities forcibly relocated Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia.

“We have a very strong bridge that connects our two countries already,” said Jung.

World.title: Sixth World Nomad Games Kick Off in Kyrgyz Republic
World.content:
ASTANA, BISHKEK – Following the fifth World Nomad Games (WNG) in Kazakhstan, the country has handed over the hosting baton to the Kyrgyz Republic, which holds the sixth edition Aug. 31-Sept. 6. The six-day international celebration of traditional nomadic sports to open tonight, will bring together over 100 countries, more than 2,000 representatives of sports, cultural and academic delegations.

Launched in 2014, the WNG are the world’s only multisport competition dedicated entirely to traditional sports of nomadic peoples. Held every two years, the games aim to preserve and promote the cultural heritage of the steppe. Many of the disciplines are rooted in skills traditionally essential to life on the steppe, including wrestling, bone throwing, falconry, archery and horse racing.

The idea for the WNG originated in the Kyrgyz Republic, which hosted the first three editions in Cholpon-Ata.

In 2014, the Games brought together 583 athletes from 19 countries competing in 10 sports. In 2016, participation grew to 1,200 athletes from 62 countries across 26 sports. By 2018, around 2,000 athletes from 82 countries competed in 37 sports. The games were held in Iznik, Türkiye, in 2022, attracting more than 3,000 athletes from 102 countries across 13 sports.

In 2024, Kazakhstan hosted the fifth edition, with around 2,500 athletes from 89 countries competing in 21 sports. Kazakhstan sent the largest delegation, with 195 athletes, followed by the Kyrgyz Republic with 172 and Russia with 144. Wrestling was the largest discipline at the games, attracting 266 competitors.

Horses at the heart of the games

This year’s program is built around three main areas: sports, culture and science. The sporting program features traditional ethnic sports, national games and competitions practiced by peoples worldwide.

Some of the most anticipated events will take place around Lake Issyk-Kul. At the hippodrome in Cholpon-Ata, riders will compete in events that draw on centuries-old traditions of speed, agility and horsemanship. Horse racing will have a particularly prominent place in the program. Events include alaman baige, a long-distance race in which endurance and the ability to manage a horse’s strength are crucial.

The cultural program will feature festivals and an ethnovillage, where regions of the Kyrgyz Republic will showcase living traditions through crafts, music, dance, customs, rituals and national cuisine.

Kazakhstan is also preparing for the games, with a qualifying championship in zhorga zharys, a traditional pacing-horse race, recently held at the Central Hippodrome in Almaty, reported the capital’s akimat (city administration) on Aug.20.

Riders from Astana took first and second place after completing a 9-kilometer course.

One of the notable performances came from a 13-year-old female jockey who recently joined the team. Despite her young age, she delivered a strong performance in one of her first competitions and won a silver medal.

Aliya Toktassynova, a coach and champion rider, said the competition was particularly important because it served as a qualifying event for the upcoming WNG.

Volunteering adds a new dimension to the games

Volunteers play a key role in organizing and hosting the WNG, supporting visitors and participants and helping maintain order at sporting and cultural venues.

Around 3,000 volunteers are taking part in this year’s games, including international volunteers. Kazakhstan is also represented by a delegation selected through a competitive process.

The head of the Kazakh delegation Asiya Sarbayeva from the Mangystau Region, said that she had long wanted to take part in the WNG because of their atmosphere and cultural significance.

According to her, the games bring together professional athletes worldwide to showcase their strength and skills while allowing participants and visitors to experience traditional nomadic culture firsthand.

“Holding such a large-scale event is crucial for our culture, so I wanted to contribute in some way. I especially want to see the golden eagle hunting and tayak tartysh competitions. After all, reading in a book and seeing the ancient art of our nomadic ancestors in person are two different things,” Sarbayeva told The Astana Times.

For 73-year-old volunteer Galiya Nurutdinova from Kazan, Russia, these games are far from her first experience with the event.

She attended the WNG in 2016 and 2018 in Cholpon-Ata and volunteered at the 2024 Games in Astana. This year, she has returned to Cholpon-Ata.

“The WNG are not standard sporting competitions. They are extraordinary, emotional and captivating. In addition to witnessing unique sports that are rarely seen outside their regions of origin, you can take part in master classes, try traditional crafts and taste authentic nomadic cuisine,” Nurutdinova told The Astana Times.

She noted the atmosphere of ethnic sports is different from that of conventional sporting competitions held in stadiums and sports complexes.

“It really draws you in. You have to see it for yourself. It is difficult to describe,” she said.

Nurutdinova has volunteered at various world championships and Olympic events, however, she said the WNG hold a special place for her because of their cultural dimension.

“We are united by our shared nomadic heritage. These Games bring people from around the world together while introducing them to the history and traditions of nomadic peoples. They also help revive, preserve and promote the heritage of nomadic civilizations worldwide,” she said.

She also highlighted the games as an opportunity to meet people from various regions and countries.

“During the WNG in Astana, I met the silver volunteers, volunteers like me who are older and retired. Recently, I also came to Astana as a volunteer for the World Future Games and met friends I had made during the Nomad Games. Events like these bring people together,” Nurutdinova said.

World.title: Rybakina Begins US Open Campaign With World No. 1 Ranking in Sight
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina has moved to No. 1 in the WTA live rankings as the US Open women’s singles main draw gets underway in New York, putting her within reach of becoming the first Kazakh player to top the official world rankings.

Rybakina currently leads the live standings with 7,911 points. Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus is second with 6,585, followed by American Jessica Pegula with 6,555 and Coco Gauff with 6,474. The official WTA rankings, however, still have Sabalenka at No. 1 with 8,575 points and Rybakina at No. 2.

The difference reflects points being recalculated during the US Open. Rybakina is defending only 230 points from last year’s tournament, while Sabalenka, the reigning champion, is defending 1,990 points.

A clear path to No. 1

According to the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA), Rybakina has the clearest route to the top ranking. She can become No. 1 without winning a match if Sabalenka, Pegula and Gauff do not win the title. If Rybakina reaches the semifinals, she will secure the No. 1 ranking regardless of the other results.

For Sabalenka to remain No. 1, she must win the US Open and have Rybakina lose before the semifinals. Pegula and Gauff also need to win the title and hope Rybakina exits before the semifinals.

The scenario adds significance to a tournament in which Sabalenka is seeking a third consecutive US Open title.

Rybakina focused on health

Despite the ranking implications, Rybakina said she is trying not to focus on the calculations, particularly after her recent injury.

“I don’t check the ranking exactly, the point situation. The most important [thing is to] try to stay healthy, play match at a time,” she said ahead of the tournament.

The 27-year-old sustained an ankle injury during her Cincinnati quarterfinal against Iga Swiatek on Aug. 20 and retired from the match. She has since returned to training and expressed confidence in her recovery ahead of the US Open.

Rybakina is scheduled to face 17-year-old U.S. Thea Frodin in the first round.

A symbol of Kazakhstan’s tennis growth

Rybakina’s potential breakthrough also comes as Kazakhstan’s tennis infrastructure and development system continue to expand.

In a 2025 interview with The Astana Times, Kazakhstan Tennis Federation Executive Director Dave Miley said the country had made tennis increasingly accessible beyond Almaty, with tennis centers, tournaments and junior programs developing across the country.

Speaking about Rybakina and another Kazakh tennis star, Alexander Bublik, Miley said: “Rybakina and Bublik have been very important for Kazakh tennis.” He added that when Kazakhstan’s leading players compete in the Davis Cup or Billie Jean King Cup, they spend time with juniors, helping inspire the next generation.

For Rybakina, the immediate task is simpler: win her opening match and take the tournament one round at a time.

The US Open, the final Grand Slam of the 2026 season, runs through Sept. 13 in New York.

World.title: Kazakhstan, CERN Advance Framework for Kazakh Scientists’ Participation in Research
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research and a leading global center for particle physics, are advancing a new mechanism that will enable Kazakh scientists to participate in CERN research experiments and scientific internships.

This was discussed at a meeting between acting Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek and CERN Director-General Mark Thomson, reported the ministry’s press service on Aug. 31.

The officials discussed next steps to expand scientific and technological cooperation, focusing on high-energy physics, fundamental science and training highly qualified scientific and engineering personnel.

Kazakhstan and CERN’s partnership is based on an international cooperation agreement signed in 2018. A draft protocol to the agreement has been developed to provide a practical framework for Kazakh scientists’ participation in CERN’s scientific experiments and research programs.

The proposed mechanism will allow Kazakh researchers to undertake scientific internships and participate in CERN research through the Bolashak International Scholarship Center’s Scientific Internships program.

The initiative is expected to strengthen the expertise of Kazakh specialists, expand international research cooperation and provide new opportunities for domestic scientists to work alongside leading researchers at one of the world’s major scientific centers.

The initiative also aligns with Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to connect its universities and researchers with global scientific networks. In a 2025 interview with The Astana Times, Nurbek said international and Kazakh academics were increasingly working together on joint research projects, international grant competitions and the development of new laboratories, helping strengthen the country’s access to global research networks.

“President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has set the task of training domestic engineering and technical personnel in the peaceful use of nuclear energy, taking into account the prospects for Kazakhstan’s nuclear industry,” Nurbek said.

He noted that Kazakhstan is transforming its scientific ecosystem and introducing a new model of science management focused on applying research results and their contribution to the economy.

Nurbek also highlighted Kazakhstan’s expanding international partnerships in science and higher education, including cooperation under the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation program.

“Against this backdrop, cooperation with CERN is of particular importance,” he said.

The officials reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the partnership, noting its potential to advance fundamental science, develop scientific and engineering expertise and expand opportunities for Kazakh researchers.

World.title: ‘Kocharyan’s arrest is driven by geopolitical motives’: Former Armenian president’s team speaks out
World.content:
Former president Robert Kocharyan’s team on his arrest

“President Kocharyan should be released because his detention is illegal, not at the request of President Putin,” opposition Armenia faction leader Anna Grigoryan said. In Armenia, people have spent recent days discussing whether the Russian president will ask for the release of Armenia’s former president, with whom he has friendly ties. Today, on Robert Kocharyan’s birthday, his allies and lawyer held a news conference. They said there were no legal grounds for his detention. Putin also congratulated Kocharyan, wishing him “strength in the face of adversity”.

Meanwhile, Russian officials have announced that Putin will meet Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan in Bishkek on 1 September. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the meeting would take place at a time “when opposition leaders are being arrested en masse in Armenia”.

Anna Grigoryan, who represents the faction led by Armenia’s former president, does not believe that Kocharyan’s detention should dominate the Pashinyan-Putin talks. She says the two sides should first resolve the crisis in bilateral relations to “avoid an economic collapse”. She hopes Russia will lift its restrictions on imports on Armenian food and goods, or at least refrain from introducing new restrictions.

At the same time, the opposition MP considers it natural and logical for Russia to discuss Kocharyan’s detention alongside other issues on the bilateral agenda. She notes that he is a “rational politician who supports maintaining good-neighbourly relations with Moscow”.

Former president’s lawyer Aram Orbelyan said both the criminal case against Kocharyan and the detention order were illegal.

“We have not yet received the detention order. As soon as we receive it, we will begin the appeal process,” he said.

Prosecutors have charged Kocharyan with abuse of office, accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. A court ordered the former president to spend two months in detention.

The lawyer argues that the alleged actions do not fall under the Criminal Code article cited in the detention order. He says the charges concern Kocharyan’s approval of certain government decisions while he served as president. According to Kocharyan’s defence, he had no choice but to approve them. The lawyer says the president’s office had no “tools, procedures or powers” to act otherwise.

Police detained Robert Kocharyan on 25 August. On the same day, law-enforcement officers searched companies belonging to the Kocharyan family and carried out other investigative measures. On 27 August, the Anti-Corruption Court granted the investigator’s request to detain Kocharyan. On 26 August, authorities also detained his eldest son, Sedrak Kocharyan, in the same case.

“Pashinyan is trying to minimise resistance”

Anna Grigoryan, head of the Armenia faction, believes that the case against Robert Kocharyan is not economic but political and even geopolitical. She says the fact that the issue will also come up at the Pashinyan-Putin meeting during the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit supports this view:

“If Kocharyan’s arrest were purely an economic and domestic issue for our country, would it be discussed at such an important forum? We are indeed facing a serious political and geopolitical arrest.”

She does not believe Robert Kocharyan’s “neutralisation” is accidental. She has put forward her own explanation for what prompted his arrest. In particular, she believes the Armenian authorities are preparing to amend Armenia’s Constitution and intend to “hand over territories to Azerbaijan”. She believes Pashinyan is trying to achieve “minimal resistance” in this context.

The MP says the case should also be viewed in a broader context. She believes Armenia will eventually find itself at the centre of a “clash of interests between geopolitical centres”. She says a similar process in Ukraine led to territorial losses and a mass exodus:

“But in the end, Ukraine achieved nothing. The country is still neither an EU nor a NATO member. And it remains unclear whether it will join the EU in the future. The Armenian authorities talk about diversification and reducing dependence on Russia, but they are leading the country towards Turkish domination and hostile relations with Russia.”

Lawyer says there are no grounds for arrest

Lawyer Aram Orbelyan says neither the former president nor his son committed any unlawful acts:

“They cannot fully understand what they are being accused of or what role specific individuals played in the whole process. All the processes were lawful. There were no fictitious processes carried out in the names of other people.”

According to him, the actions described in the indictment relate to the former president only through the phrase “persons associated with him”.

The lawyer stresses that the law prohibits accusing one person of another person’s actions, especially restricting someone’s freedom when “the other person’s actions are lawful in themselves”.

Orbelyan also announced that the statute of limitations for the charges had expired. In such cases, he explained, a court does not order detention, except in exceptional circumstances.

“If they saw a need to detain him, why could they not impose house arrest? It is unclear who the former president could have influenced, and what influence he could have had, if he had remained free,” he said.

Details of the case presented by the Anti-Corruption Committee

According to the Anti-Corruption Committee, Kocharyan, while serving as president, acquired several valuable public assets together with a group of people linked to him. They bought the assets at prices significantly below market value. Investigators also found that he received large bribes in some of the deals.

“According to evidence gathered during the preliminary investigation, the property was registered in the names of affiliated companies to conceal the actual ownership and the criminal origin of the assets. The acquired property was later transferred through development and sales, transfers to third parties, and the transfer of company shares, including as gifts,” the Anti-Corruption Committee said.

Investigators are also examining transactions made in the former president’s son’s name between 2001 and 2019. The investigation covers money transfers totalling around 144 billion drams (more than $397 million at the current exchange rate), $309 million, €77 million and 18 million Russian roubles during that period. It also covers the acquisition of more than three dozen properties in Armenia and abroad.

The same investigation has also opened criminal cases against nine other people. They include former Defence Minister Serzh Sargsyan, former Prime Minister Andranik Margaryan and former Yerevan Mayor Gagik Beglaryan.

In addition, the Prosecutor General’s Office has brought criminal cases against current and former directors of several local companies linked to Kocharyan. Authorities accuse them of failing to pay taxes on a particularly large scale. The total unpaid tax bill amounts to around 2.567 billion drams (more than $7 million).

Context

Opposition figures say Kocharyan’s arrest was politically motivated. They argue that the law-enforcement system is acting at the whim of a single person – the prime minister.

They also point to the heated parliamentary exchange between Nikol Pashinyan and Kocharyan’s son, Levon Kocharyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, which preceded Robert Kocharyan’s arrest.

“If the country’s prime minister says that this or that person should be sent to prison, or that this or that person should have their property confiscated, that is a political order. It is abnormal and goes against European standards, democracy and everything you fought for,” Kocharyan told Pashinyan.

The prime minister replied:

“Explain why you are a millionaire. Where did you get this property? And are you saying that you should remain a millionaire in Armenia? Are you saying that your millions should pass to your children and then from your children to their children? I’m sorry, but I’m telling you directly: that will not happen. For me, this is not a personal issue but a political one.”

Pashinyan said he had pledged to return to the people, “piece by piece”, all property that had been illegally plundered.

“In a democratic country, the court, not the country’s leader, should decide what should be returned to whom,” Levon Kocharyan replied.

Later, speaking to journalists, Pashinyan returned to the issue. He said that if Armenian citizens considered the government’s actions unlawful, they could stage a revolution.

“Let them remove us from power through a revolution. Let them bring their beloved and most honourable Robert Kocharyan, [former president] Serzh Sargsyan, [Russian businessman under house arrest on charges of calling for the seizure of power] Samvel Karapetyan, [major businessman arrested on charges of fraud, money laundering and extortion] Gagik Tsarukyan into government buildings. Let them take us to Republic Square and hang us. I’m fine with that scenario. If that is what they want, the people’s decision is not open to discussion for me,” the prime minister said.

Former president Robert Kocharyan’s team on his arrest

World.title: 1,795 applicants in Georgia to get second chance to enrol
World.content:
University admissions in Georgia in 2026

A total of 1,795 applicants in Georgia who passed the minimum threshold in the Unified National Examinations but failed to secure a place at a university will be given a second chance to enrol.

This year, the number of applicants who passed the minimum threshold but were unable to gain admission to a university increased 2.5 times compared with the previous year.

Education Minister Givi Mikanadze announced the decision, saying it had been made as a one-off exception this year because it is the first year of the higher education reform introduced by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Mikanadze said that registration for vacant places at public and private higher and vocational education institutions would open in the first half of September for applicants who had not previously secured a university place.

“As we have embarked on nationwide higher education reform, and this year is something of a transitional period, we are making an exception. Only this year, at the initiative of Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, we are giving 1,795 applicants who passed the minimum competency threshold in the Unified National Examinations the opportunity for so-called second-round admission,” Mikanadze said.

The Georgian government has radically changed the higher education system. Under the new reform, admission to public universities is organised around strict specialisation, with specific academic fields assigned to individual cities and universities.

The authorities say the measures are aimed at aligning the education system with labour market needs and concentrating resources. However, the changes have already raised questions about academic freedom, regional development and university autonomy.

More on the higher education reform can be found here.

University admissions in Georgia in 2026

World.title: Salaries rise 7% while house prices climb 12.4%: Is it worth buying home in Azerbaijan?
World.content:
Buying a home in Azerbaijan

The average price of a 65-square-metre flat in Baku is now around 178,000 manats (about $105,000). Someone earning the country’s average monthly salary of 1,174 manats (about $690) would have to save their entire income for 12 and a half years to afford it. But once the cost of food, rent, transport and other everyday expenses is taken into account, this calculation is purely theoretical.

According to an August review by the Central Bank, house prices rose by 8.6% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. Prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%, while those on the secondary market rose by 8.6%. Rents increased by 7.4%. Over the same period, average nominal wages rose by 7%.

Wage growth is failing to keep pace with house prices

In Azerbaijan, the average nominal wage rose by 7% over the year, or about 77 manats (around $45), reaching 1,174.4 manats. At the same time, prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%. This means new homes became 5.4 percentage points more expensive than the rate at which average wages increased.

The gap shows that housing affordability for potential buyers has not improved. The rise in wages increased a worker’s annual pre-tax income by around 920 manats (about $541). Meanwhile, a 12.4% increase in house prices means that a flat costing 170,000–180,000 manats would have become roughly 19,000–20,000 manats (about $11,200–11,700) more expensive over the year.

It should also be noted that 1,174 manats is the average nominal wage across the economy as a whole. The figure is calculated before taxes and social contributions and does not reflect the actual income of most workers.

How many years would it take to buy a 65-square-metre flat?

The m2map platform, which analysed more than 82,000 active listings in August, estimated the median asking price in Baku at 2,735 manats (about $1,609) per square metre. At that price, a 65-square-metre flat would cost 177,775 manats.

According to July data from the Azerbaijan Chamber of Appraisers, the median price per square metre for newly built homes was 2,812.5 manats (about $1,655), compared with 2,616.7 manats (about $1,540) on the secondary market. This puts the price of a flat of this size at roughly 170,000 to 183,000 manats (about $100,000–108,000), depending on the segment.

At the national average monthly wage of 1,174.4 manats, 177,775 manats is slightly more than 12 and a half years of a worker’s total earnings. Using Baku’s average wage of 1,487 manats (about $875), the period falls to around 10 years. But this is only a theoretical calculation, assuming a person spends none of their salary on anything else. In reality, someone on an average income would need considerably longer to save the full price of a flat.
