World.title: Powerhouse big spending is at the expense of so much else
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What people don’t see behind the eye-watering Powerhouse figures, tossed around like confetti, is the opportunity cost of missed chances (“Powerhouse joins our troubled history of building public institutions”, September 1). It’s amazing that the government can rustle up, at the drop of a hat, $70 million to spend on rugs, studio apartments, videos and other frivolities. Swept under a rug (not one of their $4000 ones) is the fact that many other worthy causes are being neglected. Take the Australian Print Museum at Penrith (recently reopened by the Hon Bob Carr) – a marvellous “working museum” that showcases the story of Australia’s print heritage. All the presses are kept running by an army of volunteers with not a penny from government. For 25 years we’ve been praised by thousands of visitors who are horrified when we explain that governments of both persuasions have ignored us. Their excuse being “we haven’t got the money”. Now, thanks to the Herald exposing what is a scandal of monumental proportions, we’ll approach the treasurer, safe in the knowledge the NSW government has bags of money. We should at least thank the Powerhouse management for alerting the rest of us to the fact that the state government is loaded with hollow logs just waiting to be prised open. James Cryer, Castlecrag A final polish for the Powerhouse ahead of opening. Steven Siewert Apparently Powerhouse Parramatta is spending $70 million on opening exhibitions (“Pressure builds on Powerhouse board”, September 1) and yet there exists a 147-year-old collection of objects across applied arts, design, fashion, craft and other areas that we rarely get an opportunity to view. One of the points of these new building projects was surely to allow more access to the collection for the public, students and academics. These collections are part of our heritage but are not even mentioned in this suite of lavish new exhibitions. Surely some of the $70 million could have been spent on supporting the Australian Design Centre in Sydney, which was unceremoniously defunded after supporting designers, makers and craftspeople for more than 50 years on a very small budget. Dr Ruth McDermott, Randwick Hypocrisy on display Pauline Hanson is absolutely entitled to protection from threats of violence, and those threats should be condemned without qualification (“Hanson security boosted amid war of words with PM”, September 1). But her hypocrisy is breathtaking. After 30 years of a political career built around division, exclusion and fear of the “other”, Hanson now accuses Anthony Albanese of inciting violence because he describes One Nation as divisive. This from a politician who has long portrayed herself as a fearless champion of free speech, prepared to say the provocative things others supposedly will not. Apparently, free speech becomes dangerous when it is used to criticise Pauline Hanson. Barnaby Joyce’s defence only adds to the absurdity. Albanese did not call One Nation “evil”. He criticised its policies and argued that it divides Australians. That is political debate, not incitement. And it just happens to be true. Threats against politicians are unacceptable, whoever the target, but Hanson’s increasingly familiar pose as the victim whenever she is challenged is becoming a little tiresome. Free speech works both ways. What’s that old saying about people in glass houses?

Denise McHugh, Tamworth I do not wish to make light of threats against politicians, but it strains credulity for Pauline Hanson to portray Albanese’s observation that she is dangerous as inciting violence. Nor should we forget that Hanson has form in exploiting threats for political sensationalism. Who could forget her extraordinary 1997 video declaration: “Fellow Australians, if you are seeing me now, it means I have been murdered”, that was deliberately broadcast when she was very much alive. Salvatore Sorbello, Campsie Talk about the pot calling the kettle black. Hanson, as usual, has a very selective memory and needs to be reminded of some of the outrageous statements, all more likely to incite violence than anything the PM has said. Her complaint is clearly just another wild thought bubble intended to gain attention. The media needs to stop giving her free publicity by quoting every ridiculous thing she says. Ian Ferrier, Long Jetty



Photo: Matt Golding Time for patients Mukul Desai’s own experience is the exception that proves the point, not a rebuttal to it (Letters, August 30). A five-minute consult after a 30-to-40-minute wait doesn’t mean his care needs were simple, it may mean anything beyond the acute complaint went unaddressed. Preventative care, medication reviews and early mental health signals rarely announce themselves; they surface only when a GP has time to ask. The data Dr Elly Goodsall cites bears this out: female GPs report substantially more psychological, women’s health and multi-condition presentations, and spend three extra minutes per patient accordingly (“I’m just one more female GP quitting”, August 29). A funding model that pays per visit rather than per minute doesn’t reward thoroughness, it punishes it. Mr Desai’s quick appointments aren’t evidence the system works; they may be evidence of exactly what’s being lost. Dr Zinnia Lo, Castle Cove Beat the cheat The NSW government is to be applauded for its changes to HSC assessment to try and combat students cheating using AI (“‘It tests you far more’: New HSC home rules combat AI”, September 1). For quite some time, schools have had the flexibility on how they administer assessment tasks, and even before AI there were problems with home assessment tasks. I’m sure I disappointed quite a few parents with the marks I’d given them for trying to pass off their own work for their children. Anyone who has been teaching a while picks up very quickly whether a submitted work is that of the student. AI is capable of writing in a person’s style, provided it has samples to work with. This makes it virtually impossible for a teacher to detect unless they are using sophisticated software, as some universities do. One thing for sure is that there will always be students who will cheat, with a few getting away with it, so the challenge remains for the government and teachers to try and keep one step ahead. This will be no mean feat as technology continues to evolve. Peter Miniutti, Ashbury Construction constructiveness If Premier Chris Minns is serious about addressing the crisis in housing supply then he needs to do much more than wring his hands in the hope of an industry white knight galloping into view with saddlebags full of restorative cash. The prospect of construction group Bathla’s collapse and the effect its financial woes are already having on its suppliers and subcontractors require decisive and immediate action (“Builder collapse risks sector-wide contagion,” September 1). It would be enough to send the housing sector reaching for its collective smelling salts, but why doesn’t the Minns government stump up what’s needed to keep the Bathla construction group afloat and take equity or perhaps even a controlling stake in the company for its trouble? Given the scale of Bathla’s woes, such a move might not only placate the industry and the legions of buyers dependent on the company’s viability, but also send a signal to the state’s construction sector that it is a partner in the struggling construction boom but not its controller. Bradley Wynne, Croydon



Unforced error The 2022 decision to grant the Aboriginal land claim over Naremburn’s Talus Street Reserve and the subsequent demand for the Northern Suburbs Tennis Association to vacate with under seven weeks’ notice is a profound miscarriage of community stewardship (“Tennis players face eviction”, August 31). For 45 years, more than $10 million in investment by the local community volunteer tennis organisation, including a recent $500,000 upgrade, has made this arguably Australia’s most well-used community tennis centre. The state minister overrode standard land-claim usage protections by exploiting a 1992 clerical oversight where a minister did not sign off on a management agreement with a private operator (a common system in tennis court facility administration). Despite early promises to engage, the Metropolitan Local Aboriginal Land Council has refused dialogue, issuing an aggressive, abrupt eviction notice instead. This is scarce public recreation land. It is also the birthplace of the Humpty Dumpty Foundation, a charity formed by the centre’s players that has raised more than $100 million for critical children’s hospital equipment. Evicting a thriving community and philanthropic hub on an administrative technicality, seemingly to bank green space for future development, defies justification. Our community assets deserve better from state leadership. Rick Anderson, Frenchs Forest The eviction notice requires current operators to vacate the site by the end of September. Sitthixay Ditthavong Cost of climate crisis The housing crisis in my part of the world has been significantly worsened by the effects of climate change, particularly in the aftermath of the disastrous 2022 floods. There are still flood-damaged, unlivable homes scattered through Lismore and surrounding townships. As reported in the Herald, in 2025 alone declared catastrophes damaged 145,392 homes nationwide – almost as many as the 172,657 new homes completed that year, according to the Insurance Council of Australia in its annual Insurance Catastrophe Resilience Report (“‘The homes we build twice’: Repair bill for climate disasters climbing faster than inflation”, September 1). No wonder the supply of new houses nationwide isn’t increasing fast enough. That huge impact on housing supply has absolutely nothing to do with immigration levels but, of course, those banging the anti-immigration drum, like Pauline Hanson and her followers, dismiss climate change as a hoax because acknowledging the real-world effects of climate change, already being experienced, would weaken their anti-immigration arguments and wouldn’t please her mining billionaire sponsors. Lynne Wallis, Wollongbar



Snow and steady Because so many weather phenomena are immediately attributed to climate change these days, I decided to analyse 75 years of Snowy Hydro’s data on snow depths at Spencer Creek (“Spring set to sizzle after warm winter”, September 1). Yes, there is a slow, long-term decrease in average snow depths and length of snow season, which may be attributable to climate change, among other factors. But what is certain is that snow depths vary widely from year to year – which may relate to the El Nino/La Nina cycles. My conclusion is that it’s just as likely that there will be bumper snow years in the decades to come, just as 2025 was, and Ms Rennie will be digging out her front door once again, and I will be digging out my car. And to put it in perspective, poor as the snow has been, 2026 is better to date than 1973 was and only marginally worse than in 1954 – both way before global emissions were anything like today. Peter Thornton, Killara I operate a lawnmowing business and always enjoy a break in the winter months. If the weather warms up permanently it might become a solid slog for 12 months a year. Michael Deeth, Como West A new threat Purely for research purposes, a one-line AI search, available to any child, negated Labor’s age verification legislation. Courts are recognising the negative addictive effects of social media on children, but the risks that AI pose will be far greater. It’s easy to imagine that you’re having a conversation with a real and helpful person, who vulnerable children could easily adopt as a cyber friend, leading them down endless labyrinthine pathways to who knows where. If social media is addictive, AI will be heroin (“How Australia’s social media ban loomed over Meta’s $24b settlement”, September). William S. Lloyd, Denistone Inspirational Tony “Stand up and fight until you hear the bell” may well have been the motto of the late former Australian boxing champion Tony Mundine (“Vale Tony Mundine, a champion fighter and a great Australian”, August 31). While the damage caused by boxing is now well known, we can still recognise how in another age it was one of the few paths out of poverty for some. In hindsight, we can see that this never should have had to be an option. However, we can still applaud the discipline and resolution shown by Mundine, for whom boxing bettered his own life, that of his family and of those boxers whom he later trained. As someone who shunned smoking, drinking, gambling and drugs, his philosophy of life and his achievements, if not his preferred sport, have been inspirational. Paul Casey, Callala Bay

World.title: The ‘lush oasis’ being built next to Sydney’s busiest motorway
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The ‘lush oasis’ being built next to Sydney’s busiest motorway Cindy Yin September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After spending years as a construction site for one of Sydney’s biggest transport projects, 2.5 hectares on the edge of Warringah Freeway will be transformed into parkland – but residents will have to wait at least another two years before they can access the space. The NSW government has unveiled draft designs for Cammeray Parklands on the lower north shore, with plans to build a synthetic-turf sporting area and courts suitable for basketball or pickleball, as well as open lawns, gardens, shared paths and an outdoor fitness station. An artist’s impression of the new Cammeray Parklands. NSW Government An artist’s impression of the new Cammeray Parklands. NSW Government Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said the parkland would be a “lush oasis” next to one of Australia’s busiest roads, the Warringah Freeway, and open at the same time as the $7.6 billion Western Harbour Tunnel project.



But North Sydney Council’s independent mayor Zoe Baker said the two road projects had created “scarring” impacts on residents and motorists who have endured years-long disruptions. Once construction finishes in late 2028, the three-lane tunnels in the 6.5-kilometre Western Harbour Tunnel motorway will link the Warringah Freeway on the north shore to the WestConnex toll road at Rozelle in the south, providing motorists an alternative to the Harbour Bridge and Harbour Tunnel in the CBD. Aitchison said the new parkland would act as a “connecting piece of landscape” linking existing green space, Cammeray golf course and the nearby Anzac Park. An aerial view of the current Western Harbour Tunnel construction site near the Warringah Freeway. NSW Government The 2.5 hectares of open space will have open lawns, gardens, shared paths, a multi-use half court for pickleball and basketball, a synthetic-turf sports area and an outdoor fitness station. NSW Government



“What this is designed to do is to really give back to the community a green space where they can enjoy their time,” she said. The government was “getting on with delivering the Western Harbour Tunnel but we are also making sure the communities hosting this major construction work see a lasting benefit”, Aitchison added. Related Article Roads ‘Every millimetre counts’: Inside the beast tunnelling under Sydney Harbour Baker welcomed the plans and said every bit of green space that facilitated passive and active recreation was “vital” in North Sydney, but stressed the new parkland did not represent a real increase in open space because it was previously green space and a golf course before it became a construction site. “Overall it’s a net loss but it is better than what we were fearing,” she said. “The Warringah Freeway upgrade meant the loss of 3000 mature trees … When those trees went, there was a loss of biodiversity, and there was a very emotional – rightly so – response from our community. I hope this project will be part of the repair.”



The government is replanting 6000 trees to offset the 3000 lost to road upgrades but workers have discovered there is not enough room to plant them, due to a shortage of land. The Cammeray Parklands are also right next to the golf course that the Minister for Lands Steve Kamper signalled his intent, in March, to hand to Golf NSW, sparking backlash from the council who wanted the land to remain in the club’s hands. Western Harbour Tunnel project operations director Tariq Macan-Markar said Cammeray Park would have a similar feel to a park above the Rozelle Interchange. World.title: Messages of hate strike wrong note at Sydney Marathon
World.content:
NationalNSWAntisemitism Opinion Messages of hate strike wrong note at Sydney Marathon Orly Lavee Doctor September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm

September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I was one of 40,000 people who ran the Sydney Marathon on Sunday. For one morning, a city of more than 5 million people becomes unusually intimate. Nobody cares what you earn, where you were born, which god you believe in or which language your grandmother spoke. It is communal joy in its purest form. Competitors in the 2026 Sydney Marathon. George Chan So perhaps that is why what happened next felt so discordant. Among all of that, I saw accusatory messages of hate directed against Israelis. I cannot know precisely who every person holding those signs intended to address. But in the current social climate, it was difficult not to understand them as being directed at Israelis participating in the Marathon, or at people perceived to be affiliated with Israel.



And for Jewish runners, particularly at a time when the distinction between criticism of Israel and hostility towards Jews is considered by many in the Jewish community as opaque, it was difficult simply to run past that language as though it existed in a vacuum. Related Article Sydney Marathon Sydney Marathon results 2026: Gobena and Jepchirchir crowned champions as thousands participate in Sydney Marathon What struck me most was not simply the politics of the signs. It was their spirit. It was inserted into an event whose entire character was the opposite of conflict: tens of thousands of ordinary people running the same course, drinking from the same cups, being cheered by the same strangers. It was immediately dispiriting not because politics should be confined to parliament, or because protest should always be polite. Some of the most important protest movements in history have been disruptive and uncomfortable. But protest is supposed to communicate something. At its best, it persuades, illuminates, demands, challenges or mobilises. It identifies an injustice and asks other people to see it. These signs seemed to ask nothing. Does telling a stranger they are hated move anyone closer to a solution?



Does importing the language of collective guilt into a community sporting event create empathy for Palestinians – or does it simply create another person who feels frightened, humiliated or despised? Political movements can become so enclosed within their own language and moral certainty that they stop noticing how they sound to everyone outside them. Slogans become articles of faith. The same ideas circulate among people who already agree with one another until expression itself becomes confused with achievement. Related Article Analysis

Antisemitism royal commission Liberals wanted to extend the royal commission. But Jewish groups did not join the call If they were protesting against the Israeli runners – most of whom would be ex-service people given Israel’s policy of conscription – who were raising money for Shalva, a disability NGO that serves Jewish, Muslim, Christian and Druze Israelis, then it highlights the futility in protest that no longer seems interested in persuasion or nuance. If the person passing you is not someone whose mind you hope to change, and not someone with power to implement the change you seek, then what precisely is the purpose of confronting them? Perhaps the answer is simply to make them feel unwelcome. If so, we should call that what it is.



It has been widely explored that criticism of the Israeli government and the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) is not inherently antisemitic but neither is there an impermeable wall separating anti-Zionism from antisemitism. There are circumstances in which the distance between them becomes for some of us very small indeed. Perhaps the most useful test is a simple one: would we apply the same principle to anybody else? Is this a world in which ordinary people may be publicly confronted with the actions of governments, leaders or countries with which they are associated? Russians for Putin. Iranians for the Islamic Republic. Americans for American wars. Chinese Australians for Beijing. Palestinians for Hamas. Israelis for Netanyahu. Australia works, imperfectly but remarkably, because people can arrive carrying different histories, religions, languages, loyalties and inherited griefs and nevertheless meet one another in a public space without demanding that every person answer for everything done by someone who shares their ethnicity, nationality or faith. That social contract is fragile. None of this diminishes the suffering of Palestinians. None of it makes criticism of Israel antisemitic. Those are lazy binaries, and this subject deserves better than lazy binaries.



In our determination to make every public space another battlefield, I wonder whether we understand what we are giving up. Orly Lavee is a doctor who lives in Sydney. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Gold Coast filmmaker to face fresh fraud trial after jury dismissed
World.content:
The trial of a Gold Coast filmmaker accused of a multimillion-dollar fraud has been delayed after the jury was dismissed and the judge ruled a mistrial. Luke Sparke, 42, will face a fresh trial at a date to be revealed in coming weeks. He was facing 17 counts of fraud in Brisbane’s District Court over offences allegedly committed between February 2017 and November 2019 when he was a bankrupt. He had pleaded not guilty. Luke Sparke (right) on the set of Occupation: Rainfall. Occupation Two The charges relate to how Sparke secured loans to make his movies, and the fact he gave personal guarantees for those loans while allegedly failing to disclose his status as a bankrupt.



But on just the second day of evidence in a case originally scheduled to take four weeks, the trial was adjourned. Judge Glen Cranny discharged the jury after the prosecution introduced some late evidence. The defence argued this was unfair and sought to have the charges dismissed. Gold Coast filmmaker Luke Sparke, who has been accused of fraud. Chris Pizzello/Invision/AP But Cranny ruled on Tuesday that there had been no improper conduct on the prosecution’s part, and that the trial would begin again with a fresh jury at a date yet to be set. Sparke still faces the possibility of prison, with non-disclosure of bankruptcy when obtaining credit of more than $3000 carrying a potential jail term of up to five years.



On the second day of the trial, in evidence heard before a jury, accountant Terence Rose – who has managed the administration of a number of Sparke-aligned failed companies through insolvency experts SV Partners – told the court that the filmmaker’s debts were well into the eight-figure range. “At one stage … it was around about $11 million, and there were some secured creditors there as well, which were about $6 million,” Rose said. “I recall by the time I did the dividend, they were probably up towards about $17 million.” The company in question was Sparkefilms Pty Ltd, through which Sparke made the science-fiction alien invasion film Occupation, released in May 2018. That company entered administration in early 2018 and was wound up in August 2020. The film was made with a reported $6 million budget, with most of the funds raised through loans from private investors. According to boxofficemojo.com, the film made just under $US22,000 at the cinema.



Four of the people who lent money to Sparkefilms were slated to testify before the court, but they represented just a fraction of those who claim to have lost money through their association with the company, of which Sparke and his wife, Carly Sparke, were directors. Terence van der Velde, who was Sparke’s bankruptcy trustee at SV Partners, told the court: “We identified a number of creditors that weren’t included in the statement of affairs … I think we ended up with about 74 creditors.” Tika Shelton, who led the investigation by the Australian Financial Security Authority that ultimately led to charges being laid by the Commonwealth Department of Public Prosecutions, also testified that Sparke had misled one of his principal backers, Jim Carney. She told the court that Carney advanced money to pay off the debt of almost $700,000 that had resulted in Sparke’s bankruptcy in 2017. “Mr Carney asked Mr Sparke for a statutory declaration declaring all of his debts that he owed at that point in time, which related to personal liabilities and … the debts associated and liabilities with all of his companies as well, so Mr Carney could make an informed decision in how to proceed,” she said.



“There were quite a few creditors and amounts missing from the statutory declaration that was provided to Mr Carney by Mr Sparke. So the true volume, or true dollar value, was not declared to Mr Carney.” The question of what was and was not disclosed by Sparke was at the centre of the case against him. The judge is expected to set a fresh date for the new trial in coming weeks. Sparke, meanwhile, is pressing ahead with plans to make more movies and a TV series called Dinosaurs of the Wild West, primarily using crowdfunding and income ostensibly received from his previous efforts. His most recent outing was the $7 million Vietnam War meets dinosaurs mash-up Primitive War, which has earned about $US1.2 million at the box office since its release in August, 2025. World.title: Family of WA man missing in Nepal ‘hoping for a miracle’ as search for survivors continues
World.content:
NationalWAFloods Family of WA man missing in Nepal ‘hoping for a miracle’ as search for survivors continues Cameron Myles September 1, 2026 — 7:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The family of a West Australian man missing in Nepal say they are hoping for a miracle after he was caught up in the glacial flood disaster while returning to Kathmandu on the final day of a pilgrimage trek. Luke Costanzo, 30, was travelling with a group that last made contact at the Gyirong Port border crossing between China and Nepal, according to a statement released by his family on Tuesday afternoon. WA man Luke Costanzo is missing in Nepal. The Gyirong Port area was the first to be hit by the flood, caused by a glacial collapse that sent water and debris across the border region on August 26. Costanzo had been in Tibet visiting Mount Kailash with the Isha Foundation, the family statement said.



“It is with heavy hearts that we share our dear son and brother, Luke Costanzo, is one of the Australians still unaccounted for in Nepal following the flooding disaster last week,” it said. Related Article Floods Second Australian found after Nepal disaster, ‘grave concerns’ for 42 still missing as death toll passes 1000 “Luke is an extremely strong, compassionate, disciplined and spiritual person. “Once he makes a decision he commits to it fully and he was so excited to be visiting Mount Kailash on a pilgrimage trek with the Isha Foundation. “We truly appreciate all the love and support from friends and family that we’ve received and ask everyone to keep Luke, and all those affected, in your thoughts and prayers.



“We can do nothing but continue hoping for a miracle that Luke, and the others who remain missing, are found alive and well. “For those wishing to help in some way – and are in the position to do so – we suggest donating to aid the wonderful people on the ground who continue with rescue efforts.” Earlier on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong revealed a second Australian missing in the disaster had been found safe on the Tibet side of the border, but there were “grave concerns” for the 42 citizens still unaccounted for. The person, who was not identified by the government, was contacted by Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials. “It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days,” Wong said in a statement on Tuesday.





However, NSW hiker Michael Keats was confirmed to have died in the tragedy. Like Costanzo, Keats was returning from a journey to Mount Kailash and had reached the border crossing into Nepal when the disaster struck. In an online fundraiser, his partner Emily Boyd said his loss “had changed everything for my son and me”. “We are trying to navigate the shock and grief of losing someone we love deeply while also suddenly having to face life without the person who was such an important part of our family and our household,” she said. with Nick Newling and Brittany Busch

World.title: Ex-AFL star Dale Thomas hit with $600,000 lawsuit for unpaid taxes
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Ex-AFL star Dale Thomas hit with $600,000 lawsuit for unpaid taxes Lachlan Abbott September 1, 2026 — 7:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former AFL footballer and media personality Dale ‘Daisy’ Thomas has been sued by the tax office for $600,000 over allegedly unpaid income taxes. The Australian Tax Office launched action in the County Court against the high profile former player in July, claiming Thomas owed money for as far back as the 2019-20 financial year, which includes his final season playing for Carlton. Dale Thomas at the Logie Awards last month. Getty Images for TV Week The Collingwood premiership player’s alleged debts ramped up in the years that followed. The ATO claims Thomas still owes income tax of $52,538 for the 2021-22 financial year, $129,142 for the 2022-23 financial year, $134,259 for the 2023-24 financial year, and $189,613 for the 2024-25 financial year.



Interest charges worth $93,176 and a $1565 penalty for failing to lodge a return bring the ATO’s total claimed bill to $599,293 as of July 16. The tax office claims further interest and legal costs should the dispute drag on. Thomas, a commentator for Seven and Triple M, said he was unaware of the lawsuit when The Age called on Tuesday morning. He later added: “I haven’t received this correspondence that you have got from the ATO.”



After The Age sent him the writ, Thomas then said: “Now I’ve given it to my accountant to work through with the ATO, and we’ll sort it.” The Deputy Commissioner of Taxation’s statement of claim says Thomas was issued nine notices about his outstanding taxes, penalties and interest charges from May 2022. Five of those alerts were sent on October 3, 2024, when the ATO amended its assessment of the tax Thomas owed in the 2021-22 financial year to add $85,839.65 to the bill. Dale Thomas with a one-eyed Collingwood supporter after winning the 2010 premiership. Vince Caligiuri Thomas played 258 games for Collingwood and Carlton across a 14-year career that peaked with the Magpies’ premiership in 2010 and his All-Australian selection the following year as a dashing wingman.



He joined rivals Carlton on a four-year deal from the 2014 season with an annual salary close to $700,000, reuniting with coach Mick Malthouse, whom he played under at Collingwood. Dale Thomas in action for Carlton in 2019. Morgan Hancock But his time at the Blues was less successful: The team struggled and Malthouse was sacked in 2015. Thomas was hit by injuries and struggled to recapture his best form. He enjoyed a renaissance in a defensive leadership role late in his career, but Carlton did not offer him a contract at the end of 2019. After retirement from football, Thomas appeared on I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out Of Here! and released a children’s book. He sold his home in Glen Iris in early 2021 for $2.51 million and began a full-time media career, becoming part of Seven’s Friday night commentary team and other AFL shows.



His Instagram profile shows he has partnerships with Nissan, TaylorMade, Adidas, and PointsBet. He is also listed as a “creative partner” at golf fashion brand Found. Property records show Thomas still owns houses in Blairgowrie and Carnegie. Dale Thomas goes down the slide as Mick Malthouse for FightMND Big Freeze earlier this year. Getty Images An ATO spokesperson said they were unable to comment on the tax affairs of specific taxpayers due to confidentiality laws. “The ATO generally takes a gradually escalating approach to debt collection,” they added.



“Depending on the circumstances, taxpayers may receive SMS reminders, letters, phone contact and opportunities to engage with us before firmer or legal recovery actions are considered. “The specific steps taken will depend on the taxpayer’s individual circumstances and the nature of the debt.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: A Melbourne school classified 90% of students as having ‘extensive’ needs. Now it could face a $23m bill
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaSchool funding A Melbourne school classified 90% of students as having ‘extensive’ needs. Now it could face a $23m bill Alex Crowe September 1, 2026 — 7:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Melbourne independent school is facing a federal government demand to repay taxpayer-funded disability payments worth nearly $23 million. Hester Hornbrook Academy, a special assistance school, announced deep cuts to programs and staff numbers on Tuesday after the school was told by the Education Department that it had claimed $22.9 million in disability funding to which it was not entitled. Hester Hornbrook Academy has been ordered to pay back tens of millions of dollars in Commonwealth disability funding. It is the largest instance of alleged over-claiming that has been made public since the federal government began cracking down on what it called “inaccurate claiming” of its $5 billion Commonwealth schools’ disability funding. The sum being reclaimed from Hester Hornbrook dwarfs the combined $12 million the department had recouped from 300 schools in the four years to March 2026.



Hester Hornbrook principal Sally Lasslett told staff on Tuesday that the school did not accept the department’s assessment and would fight against the demand to pay back the large sum. But in a “change impact statement” sent to workers on Tuesday, Lasslett conceded that “increased scrutiny on evidence and consistency” by the government, meant that the school would have “significantly” less money in the coming years. Teachers, youth workers, education support employees and other staff at the school have been summoned to meetings on Wednesday morning to learn if their jobs are to be cut as the school slashes costs. Auditors were sent in by the Commonwealth Department of Education this year, as part of a broader national crackdown on schools’ over-claiming disability funding. The auditors found that Hester Hornbrook had classified more than 90 per cent of its students in the highest “extensive” bracket of disability support needs, against a national average of 2.8 per cent.



Related Article Education Schools of last resort grow fast as classroom disengagement booms The school, founded in 2017 by Melbourne City Mission, caters for young people who are disengaged from mainstream education, charges parents no fees and is largely funded by grants from the state and federal governments. The academy has grown rapidly, from fewer than 40 students at one site in South Melbourne, to more than 700 enrolments across five campuses last year. The school’s Commonwealth grant revenue – 82 per cent of its total income – has soared from under $21 million in 2023 to more than $36 million last year, according to financial reports lodged with the charities regulator. Hester Hornbrook students were funded at about $64,000 each in 2024, three times the average rate of children at Victoria’s government schools and well in excess of students at Victoria’s most expensive independent school, Geelong Grammar, who were funded at $48,000 each in 2024.



Students are nominated for disability payments at their school’s discretion and without medical diagnoses, but schools must, under the rules, be able to demonstrate that the money is used to provide disability “adjustments” for the children. Education Minister Jason Clare and his department hoped to save about $463 million over four years by cracking down on what they call “inappropriate allocation” of government funding, with $40 million allocated in the May budget to greater scrutiny and accountability for the payments. Clare’s office declined to comment on the Hester Hornbrook audit and the Education Department said it would not publicly discuss “compliance” matters. Editor's pick Exclusive

Victorian Parliament Victoria secretly slices $2.4b from public schools, delays funding promise A spokesperson for Melbourne City Mission, which still owns the academy, said the school had tried to comply with the funding guidelines, which are set out by the Nationally Consistent Collection of Data (NCCD) framework.



“Hester Hornbrook Academy has always acted in good faith to comply with the NCCD guidelines and has participated openly in all audit and review processes,” the spokesperson said. “We don’t accept the department’s draft determination and are carefully considering a range of options available under the Education and Training Reform Act to ensure we can continue to deliver the most effective outcomes for our students. “We are committed to continuing to offer this support to students and their families and are keen to work collaboratively with the Department of Education. “At this stage, our priority remains supporting our students and working constructively towards a positive resolution while planning responsibly for a range of possible outcomes.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Former ADF combat medic killed while volunteering in Ukraine
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Former ADF combat medic killed while volunteering in Ukraine David Crowe September 1, 2026 — 8:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A former Australian Defence Force soldier hailed as a legendary combat medic has been killed in Ukraine while under fire from Russian forces, drawing praise for his “selfless” commitment to others. The soldier, known by his call sign “Mozzie” in Ukraine where he was fighting as a volunteer, was killed in action last Wednesday, according to his former Australian Army colleague, federal Liberal MP Phillip Thompson. Thompson said Mozzie served with the Townsville-based 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, and was deployed to Butterworth in Malaysia and Papua New Guinea. The news of “Mozzie’s” death drew emotional reactions from supporters of the volunteer soldiers who have fought for Ukraine. Instagram “He was a valued member of the battalion’s heavy weapons platoon, affectionately known as the ‘Fatboys’, and earned the respect of all who served alongside him,” he said in a statement.



“After leaving the Australian Army, Mozzie travelled to Ukraine where he saw significant combat and later joined Med Team Alpha, serving as a combat medic and support specialist with the 1st Foreign Legion Squadron. “Through his courage, skill and selfless commitment to others, Mozzie saved countless lives on the battlefield. He was the kind of bloke who never hesitated to put others before himself. Loading “He was a good man, a great soldier, and someone his mates could always rely on when it mattered most.” The news drew emotional reactions from supporters of the volunteer soldiers who have fought for Ukraine, including the Protect a Volunteer (PAV) group.



“Mozzie was a legend,” one group member posted on social media site Reddit. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Government has abandoned Oscar Jenkins in Russian prison: Australian interviewer “The stories about him are crazy but true. He once transfused his own blood, several times over several days, to stabilise a guy and make him able to get evacuated. “Another time he [exfiltrated] himself due to injury then went BACK and saved Fifty. “I never actually met him myself. I only met his teammates because Mozzie was always out in the field. But he holds the all-time record for people contacting PAV just to say good things about him.”



The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has not made any public comment on his death. Mozzie’s full name was not released due to a request from his family for privacy. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Your typical Aussie cricket boy’: Why Oscar Jenkins went to fight in Ukraine Another former Australian Army soldier, Samuel Pedrazzini, died in June in the Donetsk region of Ukraine. Pedrazzini, 26, had trained Ukrainian soldiers in the United Kingdom, as part of a longstanding NATO project, before resigning from the ADF and travelling to Ukraine to volunteer as a soldier last year. A funeral service for Pedrazzini was held in the western Ukrainian town of Chukalivka, near Ivano-Frankivsk, early in July.



His commander, whose call-sign is Alex, praised the Australian for his military skill, according to a report in The New Voice of Ukraine. “Sam was an excellent machine gunner, a great marksman and a skilled medic. He was a person who could do absolutely everything,” Alex said. Loading “Prior to enlisting, he volunteered at stabilisation points to save wounded soldiers. Samuel deeply loved Ukraine and wanted to stay here. “At some point, he realised that he wanted to fight for Ukraine, defend its freedom and independence, and become a part of this society.”



The news follows the emergence of a video interview with another Australian volunteer fighter, Oscar Jenkins, who was captured by Russian forces in December 2024 and is now in prison. Jenkins was sentenced by a Russian court to 13 years in a penal colony, in a decision that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described as an outrage. In the interview, Jenkins told Australian interviewer Mark Lowe, a teacher and amateur journalist based in Vladivostok, that he had offered to fight for Russia but had been turned down. World.title: One Nation is not conservative, it’s reckless
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters One Nation is not conservative, it’s reckless September 1, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. NET ZERO As we watch the ongoing horror and human tragedy of Nepal, face our own record El Niño and see Europe on fire we are treated to a total reversal of what it means to be conservative on climate action.

Barnaby Joyce claims that One Nation is “the most conservative party in Australia (‴⁣⁣You just can’t’ say we are evil’, Joyce backs Hanson on claim PM inciting violence”, 1/9) as the party symbolically bury the coffin of net zero by 2050. Nothing could be further from the truth.

The parties on the right side of politics have lost sight of what it means to be conservative. Its definition of being careful and cautious, eschewing risk and valuing stability is upended in their rush to gamble ever more recklessly with the future of life on Earth.

Denying the science and evidence of a heating planet, going against the decades of research and work of the vast majority of climate scientists is risky in the extreme. Climate science and the action required to stabilise our planetary future should be a bipartisan policy. It is neither a right or left side issue, but is to be conservative with our future and that of all future generations.

Mary-Jane Walker, Geelong Little time to address climate change effects

Pauline Hanson wants to develop fossil fuels and to get rid of Australia’s goal of reaching net zero carbon emissions. Oh, and she also wants to use nuclear energy. That creates radioactive waste that has to be stored safely for thousands of years, and it would take a long time to develop it.

We don’t have time to wait before climate change becomes irreversible. The devastating Nepalese floods and bushfires in France and Spain demonstrate the tragedy that climate change is bringing the world, unless we work very hard to prevent it.

Although Australia has a small population, we have massive resources of sun and wind, which we can share with other countries. For instance, we are now planning to construct Australia-Asia Powerlink, a subsea cable to export solar energy to Singapore.

Marguerite Marshall, Eltham



Inhumanity appears to be on the rise

I am incredulous. Just three days after the catastrophic landslide and flood in Nepal, which according to scientific experts has been caused by global warming, Pauline Hanson thinks it appropriate to hammer a nail into a coffin marked ‘net zero’. Do her supporters have no compassion?

People who are against renewable energy often cite its cost. Do they ever count the cost of these disasters in economic terms (never mind the trauma and emotional cost to those affected).

When we consider Nepal, the recent wildfires in Canada, USA and Europe, more frequent and severe cyclones/typhoons, the cost of recovering from these disasters needs to be factored in.

I write not because I solely support this economic argument, there are far more existential concerns. I just despair at the inhumanity that surrounds us and appears to be on the rise. Is this what we want for Australia?

Susan Humphreys, Strathdale Joyce distorts Albanese’s words

Barnaby Joyce has put his foot in it again, this time misquoting the prime minster and using words like ″⁣malfeasance″⁣ just to make sure we all understand (1/9).

Albanese didn’t actually use the polarising label ″⁣evil″⁣ in relation to One Nation, he simply highlighted its divisive influence in the Australian community.

Although trying to present himself as the more reasonable, intellectual face of One Nation, Joyce ended up distorting what Albanese said via the lens of his own projections.

The more diplomatic PM had no need to go as far as identifying a ″⁣fundamental character malfeasance″⁣ of One Nation, as it appears they can always manage that very capably themselves.

Bruce Watson, Belgrave THE FORUM First world gripes

It has been suggested that some will be ″⁣punishing″⁣ the major parties by voting for One Nation. That’s a really, really dumb strategy. A bit like chickens voting for KFC. For all their faults, the major parties have us living in one of the world’s most stable and affluent democracies.

Terry Kelly, Coburg Unhappy Vegemites

The cost of living is always trotted out by disgruntled voters wanting change, and especially One Nation voters. They mostly think about the cost of food, insurance etc. which is controlled by huge corporations in it to make a profit.

Voting for One Nation won’t bring down the price of Vegemite or your car insurance.

Polly Mish, Hawthorn



Too little too late

The massive mandate for reform given to Anthony Albanese’s government has been squandered, with the many recommended and needed policies and reforms dismissed as ″⁣populist″⁣, while they continued to govern for big business interests.

Just like the much-needed and supported gas extraction tax, the chance to fix the population issue is now probably a little too late.

John Marks, Werribee Younger MPs needed

Your correspondent urges a reduction in the voting age so that young people can vote in the interests of the planet they will inherit (Letters, 1/9). Indeed, but without a youthful parliament, they will still struggle to bring their issues to the fore. There’s a powerful argument to be made for young people to mobilise and nominate as MPs or to be elevated for preselection by ordinary members of the major parties.

Too often, the preselection process favours factional players who have spent decades cultivating their relationships in order to win the prize and their youth has been left behind. The present parliament, swollen with property investors on both sides, is highly unlikely to favour affordable housing initiatives.

Pat Hockey, Clunes Federalism’s fault

Incompetent and parochial state governments are blocking urgently needed solutions to growing social division and the cost-of-living crisis afflicting many Australians today.

Australia’s federal system of government reached its use-by date long ago.

It’s time for the states to hand over to the Commonwealth a wide range of their jealously guarded powers – especially health, education, aged care and childcare, and infrastructure (particularly roads).

The airport rail link to Tullamarine, for example, is clearly a national issue. Tullamarine is an international gateway serving all of Australia, not just Melbourne or Victoria.

The airport rail link should be the Commonwealth’s responsibility. Over decades, Victoria’s state governments have shown they are incapable of getting it done. There are far too many bureaucratic and political hurdles that have to be negotiated to get things done on time and properly.

Ridiculous duplications and entrenched local interests, aggravated by a lack of financial and technological resources and expertise, are the symptoms of a backward 19th century federal system.

Allan Patience, Newport Future shock

Almost every day, we read or hear commentators on diverse fields of human activity blithely talking about trends and conditions that are likely to play out in the future.

The article, “Melbourne on track for megacity status: How will it cope?” (28/8), examined population growth in Victoria and concluded that after factoring in births, deaths, international and interstate migration, Melbourne “is well on the way to becoming a megacity of more than 10 million people by 2101″. Astonishingly, there is no mention of climate change, and for this reason, it is not too harsh to label its projections as absurd because at the current rate of global heating, some parts of planet Earth will be uninhabitable by the human species by 2101.

Even if this dire situation is avoided, global heating will decimate human populations worldwide in forthcoming decades and render the growth rates assumed in this article as overestimated.

Ian Bayly, Upwey Fast track where?

Melbourne’s growth is not being handled well (″⁣Councils want billion-dollar payout for state growth plan″⁣, 31/8) Developers have had a dream run for the past 20 years with their ″⁣knock down and rebuild″⁣ approach in the inner city, largely without concern for local values or need for green space.

Now, under the guise of meeting housing needs, the Victorian planning minister is fast-tracking development behind closed doors. Arbitrary decisions are made about ″⁣great design with a social housing component″⁣. But we find developers can opt out of any commitments and instead pay a fee towards social housing ″⁣somewhere else″⁣. Where?

I do not know of any social or genuinely affordable housing built in the City of Yarra since the planning minister introduced ″⁣fast tracking″⁣.

This lack of transparency is a recipe for disaster. If a Labor government can break the trust of communities who elected them, how can we hope for density done well as our population escalates?

Susan Mahar, Fitzroy North



Help starts here

The extreme flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet had an underlying cause of global heating due to fossil-fuel burning.

Rather than sending a few million dollars to Nepal, a better federal government response would be to address this by stopping the subsidisation of diesel fuel by $10 billion each year and banning the sale of obsolescent petrol and diesel vehicles in Australia.

Tom Maher, Aspendale Property ups, downs

The fall in property prices may hurt sellers but is a gain for buyers, yet it’s often framed as a crisis (″⁣Property market crunch″⁣, 1/9).

There is a long way to go before reasonable ″⁣affordability″⁣ returns for first home buyers. I purchased my home in 1990 at a multiple of three times my annual salary. To buy an equivalent home in my street now is about seven times the average annual salary.

It remains tough for new entrants, even with fairly small decreases in property prices.

Geoffrey Conaghan, St Kilda Community service

Your correspondents (Letters, 1/9) appear to be unaware that prisoners in Victoria are already put to work on tasks such as manufacturing number plates, furniture, metal goods and agricultural equipment.

While the pay is minimal, the considerable expense of housing prisoners is already fully covered by taxpayers. The government’s proposal is for low-risk prisoners to carry out tasks such as mowing grass, weeding, graffiti removal and rubbish collection to free up road crews for repair work. Nobody is proposing ″⁣chain gangs″⁣.

And this no more amounts to ″⁣slavery″⁣ than the unpaid work routinely required by community service orders.

Mark Summerfield, Northcote Good deeds done cheap

I was very surprised to read that Premier Ben Carroll has proposed low-risk prisoners do road maintenance work around the state. Readers will be surprised that this is not a new idea at all.

Almost 40 years ago, I was the manager of Brunswick Citymission Family Centre. A small group of prisoners worked one day a week weeding the laneway behind our buildings as part of a public works program. The men were certainly not worked hard. They spent time chatting together and with passers-by and enjoying time outdoors.

I wasn’t offended or upset by the program. To me, it looked more productive than being behind bars.

Pamela Bores, Eltham North Restorative justice

“Chain gangs” is surely an exaggeration as is actually fixing potholes, but the idea of low-risk prisoners rehabilitating roadsides, of which we all complain about so vociferously, seems like a reasonable idea, and restorative justice can’t be a bad thing either.

Fiona White, Alfredton



Model masculinity

As a non-binary lesbian, you might think I have non-traditional views on masculinity. But when I read about a hero racing to help a woman (1/9), I feel admiration,

and just want to say “good on you mate”.

And I feel sad if any men feel despair about their masculinity. You’re important, we need you to step up, be a hero in the everyday. Call out misogyny. Stand up for your mates, male or female.

Ange Mackie, Coburg Sky police

Lee Tulloch daringly suggests in her article to speak up ″⁣When passengers behave badly on planes, I speak up″⁣ 1/9). As a frequent traveller, I have also often wondered whether fellow travellers are aware of good travel etiquette.

Yes, instinct does enter into the situation of being crammed into a cylinder for hours on end and a smile can work wonders. We who travel often do not need to act as police in the sky, but to demonstrate good seat-neighbourliness and speak up politely where necessary.

Judith Hudson, Elwood Prince Harry’s move

I don’t understand how this bloke and the wife think (1/9). He resigned his job a few years ago and moved to what he thought were greener pastures. When he did that, he relinquished all rights and perks the old job delivered. Now, he wants what he gave away back.

Many years ago, I retired from a large public company, where I trust my contribution over many years was respected. On the day I retired, I lost my company car, my expense account, and the right to get paid. Why does Prince Harry think his resignation should be treated differently from mine?

Bill Howard, Essendon AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding



One Nation

One Nation is being allowed to make announcements without being questioned. Coal and nuclear power – who will pay for the building of these power stations?

Michael Brinkman, Ventnor Pauline Hanson wants to help Australia and Australians. Well, her policies for use of gas and nuclear energy will destroy it.

Katriona Fahey, Alphington The only political landscape that terrifies me more than an America dominated by Donald Trump is an Australian one presided over by Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce.

Edward Combes, Wheelers Hill Dan Andrews

A Dan Andrews statue is preferable to one of Pauline Hanson’s party in the future. Since $60,000 of $134,000 is completed, we may as well finish the job as a memorial without spite.

Malcolm Cameron, Camberwell Stop blaming Andrews for all the improved rail crossings and stations.

Bruce Dudon, Woodend



Furthermore

Your headline (1/9) on falling house values should have been ″⁣Great news for first home buyers. Property prices are falling″⁣.

Grant Nichol, Ringwood North A simple solution for under 18 voting (Letters, 1/9) would be to give 16 and 17-year-olds the right to vote, but to not make it compulsory.

Neale Woods, Wattle Glen Re AI glasses and privacy (1/9). ″⁣Men seldom make passes, Without wearing glasses″⁣. (With apologies to Dorothy Parker, and the majority of men).

Pamela Lloyd, West Brunswick Finally

First Tony Wright, now Cathy Wilcox. Matt Golding, you had better not be going anywhere! I take my hat off to all the journos and cartoonists that make my day, whether it be for a laugh, or something more insightful. We still have Cathy’s GST cartoon on our fridge. For me, that was the one that started it all.

World.title: The ‘lush oasis’ being built next to Sydney’s busiest motorway
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The ‘lush oasis’ being built next to Sydney’s busiest motorway Cindy Yin September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After spending years as a construction site for one of Sydney’s biggest transport projects, 2.5 hectares on the edge of Warringah Freeway will be transformed into parkland – but residents will have to wait at least another two years before they can access the space. The NSW government has unveiled draft designs for Cammeray Parklands on the lower north shore, with plans to build a synthetic-turf sporting area and courts suitable for basketball or pickleball, as well as open lawns, gardens, shared paths and an outdoor fitness station. An artist’s impression of the new Cammeray Parklands. NSW Government An artist’s impression of the new Cammeray Parklands. NSW Government Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said the parkland would be a “lush oasis” next to one of Australia’s busiest roads, the Warringah Freeway, and open at the same time as the $7.6 billion Western Harbour Tunnel project.



But North Sydney Council’s independent mayor Zoe Baker said the two road projects had created “scarring” impacts on residents and motorists who have endured years-long disruptions. Once construction finishes in late 2028, the three-lane tunnels in the 6.5-kilometre Western Harbour Tunnel motorway will link the Warringah Freeway on the north shore to the WestConnex toll road at Rozelle in the south, providing motorists an alternative to the Harbour Bridge and Harbour Tunnel in the CBD. Aitchison said the new parkland would act as a “connecting piece of landscape” linking existing green space, Cammeray golf course and the nearby Anzac Park. An aerial view of the current Western Harbour Tunnel construction site near the Warringah Freeway. NSW Government The 2.5 hectares of open space will have open lawns, gardens, shared paths, a multi-use half court for pickleball and basketball, a synthetic-turf sports area and an outdoor fitness station. NSW Government



“What this is designed to do is to really give back to the community a green space where they can enjoy their time,” she said. The government was “getting on with delivering the Western Harbour Tunnel but we are also making sure the communities hosting this major construction work see a lasting benefit”, Aitchison added. Related Article Roads ‘Every millimetre counts’: Inside the beast tunnelling under Sydney Harbour Baker welcomed the plans and said every bit of green space that facilitated passive and active recreation was “vital” in North Sydney, but stressed the new parkland did not represent a real increase in open space because it was previously green space and a golf course before it became a construction site. “Overall it’s a net loss but it is better than what we were fearing,” she said. “The Warringah Freeway upgrade meant the loss of 3000 mature trees … When those trees went, there was a loss of biodiversity, and there was a very emotional – rightly so – response from our community. I hope this project will be part of the repair.”



The government is replanting 6000 trees to offset the 3000 lost to road upgrades but workers have discovered there is not enough room to plant them, due to a shortage of land. The Cammeray Parklands are also right next to the golf course that the Minister for Lands Steve Kamper signalled his intent, in March, to hand to Golf NSW, sparking backlash from the council who wanted the land to remain in the club’s hands. Western Harbour Tunnel project operations director Tariq Macan-Markar said Cammeray Park would have a similar feel to a park above the Rozelle Interchange. World.title: Messages of hate strike wrong note at Sydney Marathon
World.content:
NationalNSWAntisemitism Opinion Messages of hate strike wrong note at Sydney Marathon Orly Lavee Doctor September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm

September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I was one of 40,000 people who ran the Sydney Marathon on Sunday. For one morning, a city of more than 5 million people becomes unusually intimate. Nobody cares what you earn, where you were born, which god you believe in or which language your grandmother spoke. It is communal joy in its purest form. Competitors in the 2026 Sydney Marathon. George Chan So perhaps that is why what happened next felt so discordant. Among all of that, I saw accusatory messages of hate directed against Israelis. I cannot know precisely who every person holding those signs intended to address. But in the current social climate, it was difficult not to understand them as being directed at Israelis participating in the Marathon, or at people perceived to be affiliated with Israel.



And for Jewish runners, particularly at a time when the distinction between criticism of Israel and hostility towards Jews is considered by many in the Jewish community as opaque, it was difficult simply to run past that language as though it existed in a vacuum. Related Article Sydney Marathon Sydney Marathon results 2026: Gobena and Jepchirchir crowned champions as thousands participate in Sydney Marathon What struck me most was not simply the politics of the signs. It was their spirit. It was inserted into an event whose entire character was the opposite of conflict: tens of thousands of ordinary people running the same course, drinking from the same cups, being cheered by the same strangers. It was immediately dispiriting not because politics should be confined to parliament, or because protest should always be polite. Some of the most important protest movements in history have been disruptive and uncomfortable. But protest is supposed to communicate something. At its best, it persuades, illuminates, demands, challenges or mobilises. It identifies an injustice and asks other people to see it. These signs seemed to ask nothing. Does telling a stranger they are hated move anyone closer to a solution?



Does importing the language of collective guilt into a community sporting event create empathy for Palestinians – or does it simply create another person who feels frightened, humiliated or despised? Political movements can become so enclosed within their own language and moral certainty that they stop noticing how they sound to everyone outside them. Slogans become articles of faith. The same ideas circulate among people who already agree with one another until expression itself becomes confused with achievement. Related Article Analysis

Antisemitism royal commission Liberals wanted to extend the royal commission. But Jewish groups did not join the call If they were protesting against the Israeli runners – most of whom would be ex-service people given Israel’s policy of conscription – who were raising money for Shalva, a disability NGO that serves Jewish, Muslim, Christian and Druze Israelis, then it highlights the futility in protest that no longer seems interested in persuasion or nuance. If the person passing you is not someone whose mind you hope to change, and not someone with power to implement the change you seek, then what precisely is the purpose of confronting them? Perhaps the answer is simply to make them feel unwelcome. If so, we should call that what it is.



It has been widely explored that criticism of the Israeli government and the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) is not inherently antisemitic but neither is there an impermeable wall separating anti-Zionism from antisemitism. There are circumstances in which the distance between them becomes for some of us very small indeed. Perhaps the most useful test is a simple one: would we apply the same principle to anybody else? Is this a world in which ordinary people may be publicly confronted with the actions of governments, leaders or countries with which they are associated? Russians for Putin. Iranians for the Islamic Republic. Americans for American wars. Chinese Australians for Beijing. Palestinians for Hamas. Israelis for Netanyahu. Australia works, imperfectly but remarkably, because people can arrive carrying different histories, religions, languages, loyalties and inherited griefs and nevertheless meet one another in a public space without demanding that every person answer for everything done by someone who shares their ethnicity, nationality or faith. That social contract is fragile. None of this diminishes the suffering of Palestinians. None of it makes criticism of Israel antisemitic. Those are lazy binaries, and this subject deserves better than lazy binaries.



In our determination to make every public space another battlefield, I wonder whether we understand what we are giving up. Orly Lavee is a doctor who lives in Sydney. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Potholes aren’t just a road hazard – they’re a test of basic governance
World.content:
NationalVictoriaRoads Editorial Potholes aren’t just a road hazard – they’re a test of basic governance The Age's View Editorial September 1, 2026 — 7:15pm

September 1, 2026 — 7:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday, The Age published the chronicle of reporter Benjamin Preiss, with photographs by Jason South, of his road trip north from Melbourne that had one aim in mind: to count the number of potholes encountered. This was not a journey of self-imposed dangers on the highways and byways of Victoria, but to bear witness to the state of our roads. Last month dozens of motorists were stranded on the Princes Highway after their cars’ tyres were damaged from a series of potholes. It is but one of many incidents on our roads and highways. There are hundreds of thousands of potholes in this state. The inbox for The Age’s letters to the editor regularly receives correspondence from readers on road conditions. None of them are complimentary. Road hazard: pothole near Wodonga. Jason South It is to be applauded then that both the Labor government and the opposition are turning their focus on tackling the problem. The Coalition says it will spend $5 billion over four years to eliminate a million potholes. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson announced the spend during a tour of lower house electorates in July, and had been highlighting the issue in social media posts for months. On Monday, Premier Ben Carroll announced a $354 million increase to road funding and will delay some level-crossing removals to finance the removal of 500,000 potholes. The government will also establish a website where Victorians can log pothole sightings. The premier has announced a pilot program to use minimum-security inmates on road maintenance such as mowing grass, controlling weeds, removing graffiti and picking up roadside rubbish. This would free up road crews for pothole repairs.



Related Article Roads The small holes making big news: An unscientific reckoning on Victoria’s roads The numbers proffered by the parties are a sign of the rising stakes at play as the election nears. In the May budget, Labor committed $1 billion for road maintenance; this would repair 200,000 potholes. However, state budget papers show that the government’s target to patch 74,000 square metres of regional roads this financial year is down from 95,000 square metres the year before, and a fraction of the 566,000 square metres completed in 2024-25. This wasn’t a reduction, the government says, but a shift towards resurfacing and rehabilitation works. The Sunday Age reported that data gathered by citizen reporting platform Snap Send Solve shows that reports of potholes and damaged roads rose more than 46 per cent to 37,482 in the year to August 16. The Victorian Farmers Federation also launched a campaign urging regional drivers to document potholes they encounter. Federation president Ryan Milgate said in July such reports would show the scale of the decaying roads, which were “the worst they have ever been. Many are literally falling apart and some are straight-up death traps.” A pothole on the Princes Highway damaged cars earlier last month. Joe Armao Milgate’s comments, when taken with those by Melbourne University pavement geotechnics expert Mahdi Disfani and Deakin University transport engineering professor Ashim Debnath, paint a picture of a pressing need. Disfani said that when several potholes formed, large patches of road needed repair – it was not just about filling in the hole. Debnath saw a pothole in terms of cancerous growths. “If we don’t treat it early, it will just keep increasing in size.”



That Victoria has the worst potholes in the country, as observed by chief executive of the National Transport Research Organisation Michael Caltabiano on the ABC, goes beyond playing catch-up in repatching. The building and design and materials used in road construction need to be reassessed. Related Article Updated

Weather Drivers stranded on Princes Highway as potholes wreak carnage in wild weather across Victoria Debnath’s definition, in its likening to a growth, can be extrapolated into voter sentiment. Motorists are voters. A pothole can be seen of itself and as symbolic of a growing sentiment that Labor has failed to tackle issues that directly affect people. Resolution is a marker of government competence. While it is gratifying to see Carroll moving on the issue, it is also a sign of significant financial pressures that it has had to scrap part of one initiative, the removal of level crossings – a signature policy of Daniel Andrews’ government – to pay for another. It is a lesson that should not need teaching that government, fundamentally, is to serve the people and get the basics right. It is to listen to what the people are saying are priorities for them. One doesn’t need to be a roads scholar to work that out. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Gold Coast filmmaker to face fresh fraud trial after jury dismissed
World.content:
The trial of a Gold Coast filmmaker accused of a multimillion-dollar fraud has been delayed after the jury was dismissed and the judge ruled a mistrial. Luke Sparke, 42, will face a fresh trial at a date to be revealed in coming weeks. He was facing 17 counts of fraud in Brisbane’s District Court over offences allegedly committed between February 2017 and November 2019 when he was a bankrupt. He had pleaded not guilty. Luke Sparke (right) on the set of Occupation: Rainfall. Occupation Two The charges relate to how Sparke secured loans to make his movies, and the fact he gave personal guarantees for those loans while allegedly failing to disclose his status as a bankrupt.



But on just the second day of evidence in a case originally scheduled to take four weeks, the trial was adjourned. Judge Glen Cranny discharged the jury after the prosecution introduced some late evidence. The defence argued this was unfair and sought to have the charges dismissed. Gold Coast filmmaker Luke Sparke, who has been accused of fraud. Chris Pizzello/Invision/AP But Cranny ruled on Tuesday that there had been no improper conduct on the prosecution’s part, and that the trial would begin again with a fresh jury at a date yet to be set. Sparke still faces the possibility of prison, with non-disclosure of bankruptcy when obtaining credit of more than $3000 carrying a potential jail term of up to five years.



On the second day of the trial, in evidence heard before a jury, accountant Terence Rose – who has managed the administration of a number of Sparke-aligned failed companies through insolvency experts SV Partners – told the court that the filmmaker’s debts were well into the eight-figure range. “At one stage … it was around about $11 million, and there were some secured creditors there as well, which were about $6 million,” Rose said. “I recall by the time I did the dividend, they were probably up towards about $17 million.” The company in question was Sparkefilms Pty Ltd, through which Sparke made the science-fiction alien invasion film Occupation, released in May 2018. That company entered administration in early 2018 and was wound up in August 2020. The film was made with a reported $6 million budget, with most of the funds raised through loans from private investors. According to boxofficemojo.com, the film made just under $US22,000 at the cinema.



Four of the people who lent money to Sparkefilms were slated to testify before the court, but they represented just a fraction of those who claim to have lost money through their association with the company, of which Sparke and his wife, Carly Sparke, were directors. Terence van der Velde, who was Sparke’s bankruptcy trustee at SV Partners, told the court: “We identified a number of creditors that weren’t included in the statement of affairs … I think we ended up with about 74 creditors.” Tika Shelton, who led the investigation by the Australian Financial Security Authority that ultimately led to charges being laid by the Commonwealth Department of Public Prosecutions, also testified that Sparke had misled one of his principal backers, Jim Carney. She told the court that Carney advanced money to pay off the debt of almost $700,000 that had resulted in Sparke’s bankruptcy in 2017. “Mr Carney asked Mr Sparke for a statutory declaration declaring all of his debts that he owed at that point in time, which related to personal liabilities and … the debts associated and liabilities with all of his companies as well, so Mr Carney could make an informed decision in how to proceed,” she said.



“There were quite a few creditors and amounts missing from the statutory declaration that was provided to Mr Carney by Mr Sparke. So the true volume, or true dollar value, was not declared to Mr Carney.” The question of what was and was not disclosed by Sparke was at the centre of the case against him. The judge is expected to set a fresh date for the new trial in coming weeks. Sparke, meanwhile, is pressing ahead with plans to make more movies and a TV series called Dinosaurs of the Wild West, primarily using crowdfunding and income ostensibly received from his previous efforts. His most recent outing was the $7 million Vietnam War meets dinosaurs mash-up Primitive War, which has earned about $US1.2 million at the box office since its release in August, 2025.
