World.title: Family of WA man missing in Nepal ‘hoping for a miracle’ as search for survivors continues
World.content:
NationalWAFloods Family of WA man missing in Nepal ‘hoping for a miracle’ as search for survivors continues Cameron Myles September 1, 2026 — 7:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The family of a West Australian man missing in Nepal say they are hoping for a miracle after he was caught up in the glacial flood disaster while returning to Kathmandu on the final day of a pilgrimage trek. Luke Costanzo, 30, was travelling with a group that last made contact at the Gyirong Port border crossing between China and Nepal, according to a statement released by his family on Tuesday afternoon. WA man Luke Costanzo is missing in Nepal. The Gyirong Port area was the first to be hit by the flood, caused by a glacial collapse that sent water and debris across the border region on August 26. Costanzo had been in Tibet visiting Mount Kailash with the Isha Foundation, the family statement said.



“It is with heavy hearts that we share our dear son and brother, Luke Costanzo, is one of the Australians still unaccounted for in Nepal following the flooding disaster last week,” it said. Related Article Floods Second Australian found after Nepal disaster, ‘grave concerns’ for 42 still missing as death toll passes 1000 “Luke is an extremely strong, compassionate, disciplined and spiritual person. “Once he makes a decision he commits to it fully and he was so excited to be visiting Mount Kailash on a pilgrimage trek with the Isha Foundation. “We truly appreciate all the love and support from friends and family that we’ve received and ask everyone to keep Luke, and all those affected, in your thoughts and prayers.



“We can do nothing but continue hoping for a miracle that Luke, and the others who remain missing, are found alive and well. “For those wishing to help in some way – and are in the position to do so – we suggest donating to aid the wonderful people on the ground who continue with rescue efforts.” Earlier on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong revealed a second Australian missing in the disaster had been found safe on the Tibet side of the border, but there were “grave concerns” for the 42 citizens still unaccounted for. The person, who was not identified by the government, was contacted by Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials. “It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days,” Wong said in a statement on Tuesday.





However, NSW hiker Michael Keats was confirmed to have died in the tragedy. Like Costanzo, Keats was returning from a journey to Mount Kailash and had reached the border crossing into Nepal when the disaster struck. In an online fundraiser, his partner Emily Boyd said his loss “had changed everything for my son and me”. “We are trying to navigate the shock and grief of losing someone we love deeply while also suddenly having to face life without the person who was such an important part of our family and our household,” she said. with Nick Newling and Brittany Busch

World.title: Ex-AFL star Dale Thomas hit with $600,000 lawsuit for unpaid taxes
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Ex-AFL star Dale Thomas hit with $600,000 lawsuit for unpaid taxes Lachlan Abbott September 1, 2026 — 7:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former AFL footballer and media personality Dale ‘Daisy’ Thomas has been sued by the tax office for $600,000 over allegedly unpaid income taxes. The Australian Tax Office launched action in the County Court against the high profile former player in July, claiming Thomas owed money for as far back as the 2019-20 financial year, which includes his final season playing for Carlton. Dale Thomas at the Logie Awards last month. Getty Images for TV Week The Collingwood premiership player’s alleged debts ramped up in the years that followed. The ATO claims Thomas still owes income tax of $52,538 for the 2021-22 financial year, $129,142 for the 2022-23 financial year, $134,259 for the 2023-24 financial year, and $189,613 for the 2024-25 financial year.



Interest charges worth $93,176 and a $1565 penalty for failing to lodge a return bring the ATO’s total claimed bill to $599,293 as of July 16. The tax office claims further interest and legal costs should the dispute drag on. Thomas, a commentator for Seven and Triple M, said he was unaware of the lawsuit when The Age called on Tuesday morning. He later added: “I haven’t received this correspondence that you have got from the ATO.”



After The Age sent him the writ, Thomas then said: “Now I’ve given it to my accountant to work through with the ATO, and we’ll sort it.” The Deputy Commissioner of Taxation’s statement of claim says Thomas was issued nine notices about his outstanding taxes, penalties and interest charges from May 2022. Five of those alerts were sent on October 3, 2024, when the ATO amended its assessment of the tax Thomas owed in the 2021-22 financial year to add $85,839.65 to the bill. Dale Thomas with a one-eyed Collingwood supporter after winning the 2010 premiership. Vince Caligiuri Thomas played 258 games for Collingwood and Carlton across a 14-year career that peaked with the Magpies’ premiership in 2010 and his All-Australian selection the following year as a dashing wingman.



He joined rivals Carlton on a four-year deal from the 2014 season with an annual salary close to $700,000, reuniting with coach Mick Malthouse, whom he played under at Collingwood. Dale Thomas in action for Carlton in 2019. Morgan Hancock But his time at the Blues was less successful: The team struggled and Malthouse was sacked in 2015. Thomas was hit by injuries and struggled to recapture his best form. He enjoyed a renaissance in a defensive leadership role late in his career, but Carlton did not offer him a contract at the end of 2019. After retirement from football, Thomas appeared on I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out Of Here! and released a children’s book. He sold his home in Glen Iris in early 2021 for $2.51 million and began a full-time media career, becoming part of Seven’s Friday night commentary team and other AFL shows.



His Instagram profile shows he has partnerships with Nissan, TaylorMade, Adidas, and PointsBet. He is also listed as a “creative partner” at golf fashion brand Found. Property records show Thomas still owns houses in Blairgowrie and Carnegie. Dale Thomas goes down the slide as Mick Malthouse for FightMND Big Freeze earlier this year. Getty Images An ATO spokesperson said they were unable to comment on the tax affairs of specific taxpayers due to confidentiality laws. “The ATO generally takes a gradually escalating approach to debt collection,” they added.



“Depending on the circumstances, taxpayers may receive SMS reminders, letters, phone contact and opportunities to engage with us before firmer or legal recovery actions are considered. “The specific steps taken will depend on the taxpayer’s individual circumstances and the nature of the debt.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: SuperGold card holders missing out on discounts
World.content:
Superannuitants are being encouraged to be more assertive in asking for SuperGold Card discounts they are entitled to, as many are missing out.

A SuperGold Card discount was offered by hundreds of small and big name businesses in New Zealand, but a lack of promotion meant many older people were unaware of the details.

The Warehouse Red Sheds offered a 5 percent SuperGold Card discount on the first Tuesday of the month, but an older couple with a trolly full of goods left the retailer's St. Lukes store this morning without their discount.

"Oh well. Next time," The Red Sheds customer Marcia said, as she loaded up her boot.

Still, she was persuaded to go back to the store and ask for the discount, and returned a few minutes later $18 better off.

"We got $18 out of the SuperGold discount," she said with a broad smile and an armful of canned food items. "So we've just bought . . some extra bully beef, spaghetti, and ... a bit of fruit salad."

She said The Warehouse apologised, which was followed up with a response from the head office.

"We really appreciate this being brought to our attention and we're sorry the couple didn't get the discount they were entitled to the first time around. It's highlighted a gap in how we provide value to our customers - and we're looking at how we can make our offers more visible," a spokesperson from The Warehouse said in a statement to RNZ.

One shopper was unaware that she would get a SuperGold discount at the New World Supermarket at Point Chevalier. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The promotion of the SuperGold Card was something concerning to other shoppers.

A shopper outside the Point Chevalier Woolworths Frances Marychurch also raised concerns about the lack of awareness.

Marychurch said she only used her SuperGold at Woolworths and was unaware she could use it across the street at the New World supermarket.

"So I find it's very difficult to find ways to use your gold card. The ones that are supposed to do it, don't ask you for it," Marychurch said.

New World shopper Ross Horne said: "Personally, I think it is not actually publicised enough. Occasionally you'll see a store with the sticker on the door, with the gold card."

Mike Matthews, general manager of Communicare, which offers community support for seniors, said businesses should do more to promote the SuperGold Card discount, though superannuitants also had a role to play.

World.title: Opponents miss vote as rates cap bill passes first reading
World.content:
The government has progressed legislation for its cap on council rates increases through a first reading in Parliament.

The bill initially sailed through the first reading unopposed, as those disagreeing with it missed their window for voting.

The legislation, which would require councils to increase rates by at least 2 percent and at most 4 percent a year, is not expected to progress further before Parliament rises this month ahead of the election if passed.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said it was aimed at keeping rates stable and affordable.

Labour last week indicated it would give its backing, though spokesperson Tangi Utikere said the party still had concerns including that the government had not pushed ahead with giving councils other options for raising revenue.

He said sending the bill to select committee would provide needed transparency and scrutiny.

The Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and former Te Pāti Māori MPs Tākuta Ferris and Mariameno Kapa-King opposed the legislation, saying it would only mean fees for council services rise; and council rates were going up because their costs were too.

World.title: More safe and affordable housing needed for older people, charity says
World.content:
Older NZers worried about safe and affordable housing Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

A charity says New Zealand could be in "serious trouble" if it doesn't act to address the shortage of social housing for older people - with the population of renters over 65 set to triple by 2050.

Christchurch Methodist Mission executive director Jill Hawkey told Checkpoint some seniors are finding themselves homeless, amidst the shortage of affordable and secure social housing, and others are left with little money for food and medicine after paying rent.

On Tuesday, the group handed a petition to Parliament signed by more than 3000 people, calling for increased targeted investment in housing for seniors.

Data from the Ministry of Social Development shows that over 55s are the largest demographic on the social housing waitlist, and the number of over 65s on the waitlist has climbed 34 percent in four years.

Hawkey told Checkpoint that New Zealand was going to have a problem if it did not invest in suitable housing for older people now.

"Within 20 years, the number of older renters that's over 65 years of age, is going to triple.

"At the moment we've got about 138,000 renters aged over 65, and that's going to be 400,000 renters over the next 25 years, so if we don't start doing something about it now, we're going to find ourselves in serious trouble."

There is also the wider issue of the lack of social housing across the board in New Zealand, with social housing making up just 3.8 percent of all housing stock, compared with the OECD average of about 7 percent, she said.

Hawkey said the human impact was showing up as homelessness among older people.

She said that the first person their homeless outreach team housed last year was a woman in her eighties.

"It's not just Christchurch that we're seeing this, we're hearing similar stories from towns and cities throughout the country" she added, noting that they were finding people over 65 on the streets.

In Christchurch, the waitlist for the Wesley Village just kept growing, and the rent pressure was also growing - with the price of a single bedroom unit costing more than $500 for Papanui, she said.

Hawkey said for seniors who were light on supperannuation, the rents could take up all of their pension and there was little money left for food and medical supplies.

She said there was also concern with the lack of suitable, age-friendly housing, pointing to the fact that a lot of new homes built in Christchurch at the moment had a living room downstairs and bedrooms upstairs, which was unsuitable for older people.

The Christchurch Methodist Mission met with the minister for seniors Casey Costello on Tuesday, and Hawkey said that while there was no commitment yet, there was "lots of interest".

World.content:
Biggest kakapo breeding season on record comes to an end Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The 2026 kākāpō breeding season, the biggest on record, has come to an end with a bumper number of kākāpō chicks produced. The youngest chick has just passed 150 days old, a milestone that marks its independence.

"We had 90 chicks reach that milestone," reports Deidre Vercoe, operations manager for the Department of Conservation's Kākāpō Recovery Programme, who is delighted with the success.

Kākāpō Files II 20 | Kākāpō Numbers Soar Wild Sounds: Kākāpō Files II S7 / E20 Season 7 / Episode 20 Download MP3 30m

Those 90 chicks are officially added to the kākāpō population on Monday, taking the critically endangered night parrot from 235 birds to 325.

Vercoe told RNZ's Kākāpō Files podcast that "to blow through that 300 population mark just knocks my socks off. Even as I say it now I think 'really? 325 - has that actually happened?' But it is true, it is fantastic."

When the Kākāpō Recovery Programme began in 1995 there were just 51 living kākāpō. Kākāpō only breed every two to four years, so it's taken a while to get to the point where the population can increase by a third in just a single breeding season.

Awarua-A3 is now old enough to be added to the population. Mahina Walle DOC

"It took about 16 years to make 90 chicks in the early days of the recovery programme," Vercoe says. "And we've just done that in one season."

2026 Kākāpō breeding season by the numbers:

79 female kākāpō nested

258 eggs laid

106 chicks hatched

48 females produced living chicks

32 dads fathered chicks

90 chicks made it to 150 days

Kākāpō breeding is triggered by the intermittent mass, or mast, fruiting of forest trees such as rimu. In autumn, the ripening fruit is also a great food source for kākāpō mums to feed their hungry chicks, which grow from just 25 grams at hatching to about 1.5-2 kilos in weight at independence.

Intensive management, such as extra food for breeding mums in years when the fruit fails to ripen, has been a feature of kākāpō conservation. This year a very abundant rimu crop ripened on the kākāpō's two breeding islands in Fiordland, meaning mums on those islands did not require any extra food.

However, on Whenua Hou / Codfish Island, near Rakiura / Stewart Island, the rimu failed to ripen and the female kākāpō there still needed supplementary food to raise chicks.

In the past three decades, hand-rearing has also been an important tool, but this season only two chicks that had required medical treatment ended up being hand-reared. The rest were fully raised by kākāpō mums.

DOC Kākāpō Ranger Maddy Whittaker with 2026 chick Matilda-A1 Sarah Manktelow DOC

Stepping back from intensive management, like feeding and hand-rearing, has been a deliberate move. It is an important and necessary change, says Kākāpō Recovery science advisor Andrew Digby.

"It's been a really significant breeding season for us," Digby says. "Obviously it's the biggest one we've ever had, so that's very significant. But I think just as important are the methods that we've employed and some of the things that we've changed this breeding season. And in particular that's that real emphasis on trying to step back and do a little less of the intensive management that we've done in the past, and let kākāpō do things on their own."

Technology has been key to the evolving management regime for kākāpō. Every bird wears a smart transmitter and its activity can be remotely monitored.

Deidre Vercoe says "we were able to put a lot more faith in our remote technology data, and really carefully monitor that data, and make decisions about when we would step in and interfere at a nest, to move an egg or to help a chick, or when we were okay to stay hands off".

2026 kākāpō chick Hananui-A2 is living independently, but still gets regular ranger checks. Sarah Manktelow/DOC

All existing adult kākāpō have names, but Vercoe says this tradition is about to change.

"Not all the chicks will be named this year - some will remain unnamed. That's a bit of a symbol of heading towards a more natural state for kākāpō where they're not all individually managed and individually known."

The last two kākāpō breeding seasons were four years apart, but we won't have such a long wait until next time, Digby says. The key is a pattern of summer temperatures that triggers rimu fruiting.

"We look at temperature differences and that gives us a two-year heads-up. And there's an indication from those differences that 2028 will be another kākāpō breeding season."

While it's exciting news that there'll be more kākāpō chicks in two years time, the rapidly growing kākāpō population faces a challenge - the existing kākāpō islands are already full and we need more safe predator-free places for kākāpō to call home.

Pakiki-A1 is one of 90 chicks that successfully made it to independence in the record 2026 kākāpō breeding season. Sarah Manktelow/DOC

"After this next breeding season we desperately need another breeding site," Digby says. The search is on.

Among the highlights of the 2026 kākāpō breeding season were three four-year-old females that bred for the first time, the youngest females to ever breed.

Ten chicks were conceived through artificial insemination, a technique which is used to boost egg fertility and match-make good genetic matches. Ralph, an original male from Rakiura / Stewart, became a father for the first time as a result of artificial insemination.

The 'dad of the year' was ten-year-old Tūterangi. A first-time breeder, he mated with six females and fathered 10 living chicks.

World.title: Government says cervical screening will be free from March next year
World.content:
The government says screening for cervical cancer will be free from March next year.

Health Minister Simeon Brown and Women's Minister Nicola Grigg made the announcement on Tuesday.

Brown said from 1 March, 2027, all eligible women aged 25 to 69 would have free screenings - implementing a recommendation from successive Parliamentary Reviews since 2018.

He said cervical cancer was one of the most preventable diseases, but cost could be a barrier to screening, with around 55 percent of eligible women now paying anywhere from $35 to more than $100 for appointments.

The policy would make screenings free for an estimated additional 786,000 women, Brown said.

Screening is currently free for Māori and Pacific women aged 25 to 69, Community Services Card holders, and women who have never been screened or are overdue.

Grigg also released the Government's Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan 2026 to 2040.

She said the plan set out the goal to eliminate the cancer, reducing it to fewer than four cases per 100,000 women a year, across every population group, by 2040.

Grigg said the country already had the tools to do it.

"A vaccine that prevents the virus behind almost every case, a test that picks it up early, and treatment that works when it is caught in time.

"Making screening free is part of that."

Grigg said 69 percent of young people had their first HPV vaccine by age 15. She said the plan sought to raise that to 90 percent by 2035.

"Today is a good day for women, but screening only saves lives if it's taken up. So my message to every woman who is overdue is simple. Please don't delay - talk to your healthcare provider today," she said.

World.title: Nature Baby recalls baby onesies over choking hazard
World.content:
Nature Baby is recalling a baby onesie after a dome fastening was found to potentially detach and pose a choking hazard to infants and young children.

The recall affects the Merino Kimono Pointelle Stretch and Grow, product number NB2206, in Lilac, Natural and Thyme.

The affected garments were sold in Newborn, 0-3 months and 3-6 months sizes between 27 February and 27 August, 2026, through Nature Baby stores and online.

Nature Baby said a detached dome fastening may present a choking hazard.

Customers who have the affected garment are advised to stop using it and return it to their nearest Nature Baby store or through the company's online returns process for a full refund.

The garment was previously listed on Nature Baby's website at NZ$44.95.

World.title: 130 jobs on the line as Woolworths considers shifting customer care centre to Australia- union
World.content:
More than 100 Woolworths jobs could be axed under a proposal to shift the company's customer care centre to Australia, according to union Workers First.

The union said staff were told at a 1pm meeting on Tuesday of a proposal to shift the centre across the Tasman, which could result in the loss of around 130 roles.

A Woolworths spokesperson confirmed it had announced a proposal to "explore the integration of its customer care operations" with its operation based in Sydney.

"We acknowledge proposals like this have an impact on our team and we don't take that lightly. Right now our primary focus is on supporting those team members and ensuring customers are not impacted while we consider the proposal."

Woolworths said it was working one-on-one with staff to get their feedback and were looking at redeployment opportunities in the company.

Workers First deputy secretary Rudd Hughes said the proposal prioritised profit over people and would have been "crushing to hear".

"This is yet another example of New Zealanders losing out to Australia because companies like Woolworths see them as expendable," he said.

Hughes said many of the staff in customer care were solo parents who would struggle to find comparable employment if the proposal went ahead.

He said there should be a reasonable expectation that large companies like Woolworths should reinvest in their customer base.

"They're happy to earn big profits in our country and make Kiwis reliant on their supermarkets, but they are planning to throw away more than a hundred of our jobs to save a very small amount of money over the next three years."

Hughes said feedback on the proposal was due on 15 September and warned if it went ahead, New Zealand customers would get worse service.

"Someone calling from Paekākāriki to inquire about a product return, for example, may find it much more difficult to deal with an Australian who lacks local knowledge and local experience."

World.title: Beach sprinting was just the start of Damien Cook's NRL story
World.content:
With a bit of luck, they'll tell the old Damien Cook story one more time.

This weekend, the 35-year-old St George Illawarra skipper will play his final NRL match before heading to Super League side Castleford next year.

His farewell will be at Wollongong Showground, the closest ground in the league to the ocean. When the swell's big, you can almost hear the waves crashing on City Beach from the hill.

Maybe it will be when Cook runs out for the 263rd and last time, or perhaps he'll dart out from dummy half to take on the Parramatta defence with a glimpse of the old quickness.

Maybe it'll be the commentators who say it, maybe it'll just be fans in the stands, but someone, somewhere will almost certainly tell somebody else "you know, he used to be a champion beach sprinter."

It's a story nobody seems to tire of telling — Cook himself still hears about it all the time.

"It's the great Dane Gagai's fault. He mentioned it one day when I was doing media — a few people knew about it, but he said it real loud, the journo I was speaking to did a story on it and it got out from there," Cook said.

"It's never stopped; I still get it every day. Commentators say it, I get it in comments, DMs, Instagram stories; if people see a post about a beach sprinter they tag me in it. You have to laugh."

The yarn got its greatest play during Cook's ascent to becoming one of the best hookers in rugby league, which came almost 10 years ago now, and it's worth breaking it out one more time to celebrate the end of an NRL career with an extraordinarily long tail.

It took a while to get going. Cook spent plenty of time as a second-stringer on second-rate teams.

Cook's NRL career took a while to get going. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

He did not make the run on side for an NRL match until he was almost 23 and wasn't a full-time starter at hooker until the year he turned 27.

But after taking the long way, he made up for lost time immediately, and once the beach sprinting tale got used up, we started to tell others.

Cook can't pick his favourite himself. He is overwhelmed by the memories he's made because there are so many.

This late starter has now played the seventh-most matches of any dummy half in the history of the game, so when you ask him about his favourite match there's so much to choose from.

There's the first grade debut back in 2013, of course, which came for St George Illawarra against Wests Tigers at the Sydney Cricket Ground in Heritage Round. The retro jerseys and brown football made it feel like history even while it was happening.

There was the first game at Wollongong a week later. Cook is proud to finish his NRL journey there, given it's where he grew up watching football and where he played his junior grand finals for Helensburgh.

In a nice full-circle moment, his first match there in the top grade came against the Eels, just like his last will.

"The big one that day was when I got under Fuifui Moi Moi — it wasn't me being brave, he was coming straight at me," Cook said.

"I didn't have much of a choice."

Cook is one of the best dummy halves in New South Wales Origin history. (Getty Images)

There's the late-season cameo for Canterbury in 2015, which first made Cook's name and proved he could ride the lightning, and his debut at South Sydney, where he played more than 200 games and spent his most glorious times.

There's his first State of Origin match in front of 90,000 at the MCG in 2018, when he was one of 11 New South Wales debutants alongside players like Nathan Cleary, Tom Trbojevic, Latrell Mitchell and Cameron Murray.

Cook was the best of them that night in a magnificent beginning, and he always seemed to find something extra for the Blues — among dummy halves, only Ben Elias and Danny Buderus have worn the jersey more.

The 2019 decider, when he scored a scorching try right through the heart of the Queensland defence, was perhaps his single greatest highlight in rep football, but playing for Australia against Tonga in Auckland later that season was another special night.

As the Tongan anthem rang out through the night, Cook thought he'd be crushed by the noise.

"All the Tongans were singing their anthem, just this sea of red. I thought 'bloody hell, nobody is going to sing our anthem; we're up against it here'," Cook said.

"But then all the Tongans sang our anthem as well. The sound of it, I'll never forget it."

The pandemic ravaging international football and the eventual emergence of Harry Grant kept Cook to just four Tests, but he did get the special honour of playing one in Wollongong the following season and duly marked it by scoring a try.

It was no barge-over from close range though — it was an intercept that Cook took 70 metres all the way home.

He could have run along Lawrence Hargrave Drive, across the Sea Cliff Bridge, and up the hill all the way back to Helensburgh and the Kiwis wouldn't have caught him.

Cook ran all the way into an Australian jersey. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Then there's all the club wars as well, because once Cook became one of the best he liked nothing more than testing himself against the top sides.

He says he relished the days where South Sydney had a real shot at being pride of the league again and had it out with the likes of Melbourne, Penrith and the Sydney Roosters with everything to play for and no quarter asked for or given.

All told, when asked to pick a single favourite game, Cook named almost a dozen. He just couldn't leave anything out.

"I know you asked for one, but rugby league has given me so much," Cook said.

"The mates, the moments, the memories, it's why you do it."

Cook himself gave plenty of people similarly glorious memories.

He was fast enough that a dart from dummy half would make the crowd rise, fast enough that he could break into space and round the fullback from anywhere, fast enough that when Wayne Bennett came out favouring the NRL's proposed set restart rules in 2020 some said the wily old coach was doing it just to suit Cook.

But there was more to Cook's game than raw pace. He's a cannier playmaker than some might think — in 2019 he accumulated 18 try assists, more than Grant has ever managed in a single season and equal to Cameron Smith's career high.

Cook was also among the top four players in the league for tackles made in seven of his first eight seasons.

If he gets through 25 tackles on Sunday, which is light work so long as he plays big minutes, he'll pass 10,500 of them for his career, and given the middle of the field is where the giants live, he'll have given up size and weight on just about every one of them.

Cook has never shirked the tough stuff through his long NRL career. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Somehow, he has gotten through those 10,000 blows without ever being seriously broken — this year marks the 10th season in a row Cook will manage at least 23 games.

That's a point of pride for Cook. Once he got a taste of his dream coming true, it became a prize beyond value.

"It took a while to get there, so once I did I never wanted to let it go. I'm very proud of that because I put a lot of time into recovery and working hard and staying fit and being ready for every pre-season so I can get the most out of it," Cook said.

"I've set high standards for myself, which is why I've been able to play consistently. Even in NSW Cup I tried to do that.

"Touch wood, I haven't had a bad injury since I was at the Dogs when I broke my thumb — the other games that ruin my record were getting rested or COVID protocols, and I wish we could take those off.

"Longevity and consistency are something I'm really proud of."

Both Damien Cook and his club have done it tough in 2026. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

In the end, being there all day every day has taken its toll on Cook. It has slowed him down, and the ravages of age have finally overtaken whatever benefits he gained from his late start.

He has just two try assists and one line break for the season and has spent time on the bench and as 18th man. It feels like this change has come at the right time for him.

The wins have not come as Cook or St George Illawarra would have liked in the two seasons since he joined, but that doesn't mean he won't leave a legacy.

The Dragons have a host of young players who hold the future in their hands, perhaps none more than 23-year-old backrower Hamish Stewart.

Despite recent struggles, Cook's efforts have never wavered. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

"It's me, Gutho [Clint Gutherson] and Cooky in the gym. You see him, day in and day out, and he has the most energy of anyone. He never skips a rep," Stewart said.

"He's been massive for all us young blokes, showing us how to run a team and how a club really works.

"I love how he goes about life off the field as well — I feel like I can go to him about anything."

Stewart has played every game this season and earned plenty of plaudits despite the Red V's struggles.

Along with the Couchman brothers, Dylan Egan and Loko Pasifiki Tonga, Stewart is part of the sun that can break through the clouds and of all those players, his tomorrows may be the brightest.

The Dragons have found wins hard to come by during Cook's time with the club. (AAP: Mark Evans)

If Stewart does go on and makes the most of it, Cook will play a role even if they're not packing down together.

The veteran is the kind of guy who can hold a beaten-down town together, and even if the team hasn't been winning, that doesn't mean Cook hasn't been teaching.

In trying to impart the hard-won wisdom of his rise, Cook is leaving behind something that will last once he's gone. His lessons will remain, like footsteps in the sand.

"You have to make sure you're doing the right things all the time, to lead by example. You have to push right along to the end of the season, even if it's a tough one," Cook said.

"It's easy to tick the boxes when you're winning games, but when you're up against it you still have to push hard every day.

"That's a good value to have, and a lot of the players here have that."

If he's right, that could be the longest tail of all for Cook, who leaves the club in a far better place than he found it.

He has shown these boys how to live, but now they must become men without him.

"He's always got a smile on his face every day. You see him when you walk through the doors and you know you're gonna have a good day," Stewart said.

"That's what I'll miss the most."

Cook's ultimate legacy is the players he leaves behind at St George Illawarra. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

For Cook himself, this is an end but not the end.

He's excited about playing for Castleford next year, to have a new challenge in a new place, to have something to prove again, to do the work and love it and to give it everything he's got, which Cook says is all he's ever done.

He's excited for Sunday, to see family and friends in the crowd and, one last time, to live that dream he would not surrender during the hard times.

There's no beach, but it'll be a fine day to get a sprint in.

"If I told my younger self what would happen over the past 14 or 15 years, I don't think he'd believe me," Cook said.

"Definitely after the season it will [sink in], especially when I'm packing up the house and going through some jerseys. That'll bring back the memories.

"But there's still more to do."

World.title: Is Marnus Labuschagne finally out of luck?
World.content:
For a period of 23 Tests, Marnus Labuschagne was statistically the luckiest batter in Test cricket.

He had more genuine chances dropped or missed than any other batter from his debut up until the end of the 2021/22 Ashes series. He was more often than not able to turn those reprieves into significant scores.

In more recent times, it's been slim pickings. In fact, it's been 23 Tests since his last century, dating back to the fourth Ashes Test at Old Trafford in 2023.

He's been left out of the ODI squad travelling to take on Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month. The right-hander has only missed five of Australia's last 56 ODIs, raising questions about his future in the Test side.

"We're still very much working through what that Test squad looks like, but I can say we separate out those formats," chair of selectors George Bailey told reporters when unveiling the ODI squad.

"He has played some really important one-day cricket for us; at his best that looks a certain way, but the way that squad and team is structuring up there just wasn't space for him."

If you break down Labuschagne's career into the period before his last Test ton and the period since, there is somewhat of a trend: his luck has seemingly run out.

The 2023 Ashes series in England was the last time Marnus Labuschagne made a Test century. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

Looking at only genuine chances missed by opposition teams — dropped catches, missed stumpings, opposition teams not reviewing a decision that would have seen him dismissed, or wickets on a no ball — he was given a reprieve 25 times from 75 innings where he faced at least one ball.

That's a chance every three innings from his Test debut in 2018 to his most recent hundred back in 2023.

Across his first 20 Tests he scored six centuries and 12 fifties, earning him a batting average of 62.15. If, in that time, he had been taken at the first opportunity, that average drops to 46.50.

In the 2019-2021 World Test Championship cycle, Labuschagne played 13 Tests and scored the most runs of any other batter in the world. He finished that period with 1,675 runs at an average of 72.82. Across the 23 innings he was required to bat in, he was afforded 12 chances, or one every 1.92 innings.

When you compare that with Steve Smith in the same period, he was given a reprieve four times, which equates to one every 5.5 innings. Smith was still able to score 1,341 runs in that WTC cycle, which highlights Labuschagne's ability to capitalise when given the opportunity.

In fact, his entire Test career has been based on it.

Labuschagne's luck was a key feature of his game in his early Tests, with his ability to capitalise on opportunities given to him by opposition mistakes. (AP: Rick Rycroft)

Labuschagne made his Test debut in 2018 due to the bans handed down to Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft after the sandpaper incident the last time Australia's Test team toured South Africa.

That put him in the frame for the 2019 Ashes squad and, after a red-hot Smith was hit in the neck by a Jofra Archer bouncer at Lord's, Labuschagne got his next chance as the first concussion substitute in the history of international cricket, courtesy of a rule introduced the month before the series started.

In the next Test in Leeds, Labuschagne was dropped on 14, 42 and 60, and England failed to review an edge that would have been given out when he was on 35. He went on to make 80.

That series, including that fortunate knock of 80 at Headingley, cemented his spot in the side, with Usman Khawaja the unfortunate one to make way when Smith returned, a decision that left Khawaja on the outer for three years.

His ability to turn a reprieve into a significant score was a hallmark of his early Test career. Labuschagne's maiden Test century came against Pakistan at the Gabba in 2019 when he scored an impressive 185 off 279 balls. Pakistan fans might still be ruing the fact he was dropped by Asad Shafiq on 33 that same innings.

Labuschagne made a habit of scoring big runs when given a reprieve by the opposition. (AAP: David Mariuz)

In that WTC cycle alone, if he had been taken at the first opportunity, his batting average would drop to 55.68, which would have had him ranked 11th in the world.

It's not just his luck that's seemingly run out; it's his ability to capitalise on it.

From that first Ashes series to his last Test century, Labuschagne was able to turn missed opportunities into scores of 50 or more on nine occasions, including five hundreds.

Since that last century, he has been afforded only four reprieves, and the most he's added to his total is 18 runs.

Loading...

He was briefly dropped from the side after failing to impress as a makeshift opener in last year's World Test Championship final, missing Australia's tour of the West Indies. But, after only three Tests out of the side, he came back in for the 2025/26 Ashes and has remained in the team since.

When you compare that to the likes of Jake Weatherald, who has been in and out of the Test squad with questions around his form, Labuschagne has not just been given chances by opposition fielders; he's also been given them by the Australian selectors.

With an important series against South Africa on the horizon and his omission from the ODI squad, all eyes now look to see if his luck really has run out.

World.title: Dockers 'know what's on the line' ahead of Hawthorn showdown: Longmuir
World.content:
The Fremantle Dockers may be just three wins from claiming the club's first-ever AFL premiership, but coach Justin Longmuir has dismissed suggestions he will be using that as motivation heading into the finals.

The 2026 version of the Dockers is comfortably the best-performed team in the club's history when it comes to the home-and away season.

Fremantle won 19 of its 23 games to race away with the minor premiership, earning the right to host Hawthorn in a qualifying final at Perth Stadium on Thursday night.

Murphy Reid (left) will return for the Dockers against the Hawks after recovering from a groin knock. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos )

It has seen excitement build among the Freo faithful, who are hopeful this could be their year, having made just one grand final since the club entered the AFL in the 1995 season, losing to the Hawks in 2013.

But throughout this year's campaign, Longmuir has urged his players to stay in the moment and focus on more immediate tasks, and he insisted thinking about the ultimate goal is not what would get the job done.

'I'm only human': Fremantle star Jackson dreaming of Dockers' maiden flag Luke Jackson has already been to the top of the AFL mountain and now, with Fremantle just three wins from a maiden premiership, the man known as 'Dogga' is desperate to get there again.

"I just don't feel like we need to [lean into it]. If there's someone at the footy club that doesn't see that carrot, well then you're probably in the wrong game, right?" he said.

"All our players know what's on the line, and we just need to make sure that we use whatever motivation that gives us to give it all to your next moment.

"Everyone feels it in different ways … some players will see it as a stimulus and some players will maybe see it as a distraction, and we'll work through that.

"Everyone sees pressure as different things and we've done some work on that, and it's all about staying in the moment.

Hawks forward Nick Watson will be one man the Dockers are keen to keep a close eye on. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition.

"We've just got to make sure that we give our best to each moment, and the next moment is the most important one."

Fast start wanted

Much of the talk in the build-up to Thursday's game has focused on the Dockers' home-crowd advantage, after they rode the Wharfie Time rallying cry to come from behind to win their last clash against Hawthorn at Perth Stadium.

But Longmuir is hopeful they will not have to rely on the fans to overcome another slow start.

Fremantle got up in Wharfie Time against the Hawks in round nine, but hope they will not need it this week. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

"They're not going to get us over the line if we're not playing good footy, so we've got to give them something to cheer for, and it needs to be from the start," he said.

Key defender Brennan Cox will miss Thursday's match through injury, but Fremantle is set to welcome back the likes of Murphy Reid, Jye Amiss, Heath Chapman and the retiring Sam Switkowski.

Hawthorn is at virtually full strength for the clash, with only two players unavailable on its most recent injury list.

The Hawks enjoyed a comfortable win over West Coast at Perth Stadium in their final game of the home-and-away season.

World.title: Cats coach speaks for first time since club's concussion fine
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott insists he is unsure if Jake Kolodjashnij will play for the Cats again following the club's concussion saga.

Speaking for the first time since Geelong was fined $140,000 for failing to officially let the AFL know about the concussion waiver in Kolodjashnij's contract, Scott kept it brief.

The dual premiership coach referred back to the club's response and was adamant he had stayed out of dealings about Kolodjashnij's future.

Geelong fined over concussion scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

Kolodjashnij, who came forward as the player involved shortly after the story broke and has not played at any level since, returned to the club last week ahead of the finals.

If the defender does play it will almost certainly be at VFL level, with the club premiership favourites to win the second-tier competition.

"I've been really conscious to separate myself from this," Scott said about Kolodjashnij.

"This is one of those situations [where] if I could help, I would.

"But I'm told, and I believe independently, that I just wouldn't be any assistance, so I just don't get in the way."

The penalty was $100,000, plus a suspended sanction of $40,000, which stems from the league fining Geelong last October after an investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

"Hand on heart, I don't really even know the facts, so I'm certainly not going to be swayed by people who understand the facts less than I do," Scott said.

"So my go-to is that I just support the club's position … whether some people accept that wholeheartedly, that's something you can ask them privately.

"But the club's position is, it's best for us to say, 'OK we acknowledge certain aspects, and we're keen to move forward.'"

After having the pre-finals bye, Geelong will face red-hot Carlton in an elimination final at the MCG on Friday night.

Speaking on Monday, experienced midfielder Tom Atkins denied the saga was a distraction for the Cats as they aimed to win their fifth premiership this century.

AAP

World.title: Sharks want to play their home NRL finals match at their home ground
World.content:
Cameron McInnes would not be surprised to see the NRL deny Cronulla a home final at Shark Park, warning players were now used to head office making rule changes "at the drop of a hat".

Out of form on the eve of finals, the fifth-placed Sharks are nevertheless guaranteed to host a week-one elimination match against one of South Sydney, North Queensland or Newcastle.

But the finals suitability of dilapidated Shark Park, the NRL's lowest-capacity regular venue at 15,000 seats, has been a discussion point in recent years.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

The NRL pockets ticket sales from finals games so would take a financial hit from hosting in the shire rather than the Sydney Football Stadium or Stadium Australia, which each have more than twice the capacity.

Shark Park has been deemed unfit for use in week two or three of the finals, but hosted week-one finals matches in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

The NRL is unlikely to publicly confirm venues until after round 27 finishes this Sunday, and told clubs in the pre-season it had the discretion to determine where finals games were played.

The possibility of playing elsewhere did not sit well with England-bound McInnes, who could be playing his last game at Shark Park against Melbourne this Saturday.

"I was under the impression the rule was if you earn a home semi, whether you're first or second, or fifth or sixth, you get to play it at your home. Our home is Shark Park," he said.

"I don't know if that was a rule change that they can just put in, but then again, the NRL changes rules all the time.

"Rule changes just happen at the drop of a hat now, don't they? So as a player, you just have to adapt."

The league most recently trialled a change to the kick-off rule in Melbourne's defeat of Brisbane last week, having introduced six-agains, 20/40 kicks, two-point field goals and captain's challenges since the start of the decade.

The NRL has also made less prominent changes to its trainer and interchange policies in that time, as well as reverting to one on-field referee per game.

"How much do you need to change? I understand at the end of the day, it's entertainment, I get it," McInnes said.

"But it's like someone's constantly sitting there going, 'The game's going really well, but now let's change something else'."

Inconsistency around ruck infringements was most dismaying to veteran McInnes, who sympathised with the league's match officials.

"When you bring that [six-again rule] in, I get it, to speed the game up and have the speeds to score long-range tries with fatigue, but it also creates an inconsistency in the game," he said.

"[It's] hard for the refs, isn't it? Because it's so subjective.

"If someone gets hit in the face and is offside, that's clear as day, but with the six-agains, it's just sort of a lottery."

AAP

World.title: Former rival says Nick Kyrgios's drug ban 'pretty much expected'
World.content:
Stefanos Tsitsipas says he was not surprised when Nick Kyrgios was suspended from tennis for drug use.

Kyrgios was banned earlier this month after he revealed he tested positive for cocaine in June when he was in Spain to play at an event.

The Australian could be suspended for four years, though a lighter punishment is expected.

Tsitsipas was asked about Kyrgios on Monday after upsetting 10th-seeded Arthur Fils in the first round of the US Open.

The former world number three, who had a famously contentious relationship with Kyrgios, said he was surprised the suspension did not come sooner.

"I mean, to be entirely honest with you, I knew about this before the announcement. Myself, I knew about it," Tsitsipas said.

"So, what can I tell you? I will just tell you the truth. I knew about all of this before any announcement was made, and when I saw it on social media, I was, like, 'Here we go'. I kind of expected it, to be honest."

Tsitsipas and Kyrgios played a fiery match at Wimbledon in 2022 , when Kyrgios reached his only Grand Slam final. Tsitsipas blasted a couple of shots directly at Kyrgios, intentionally hit a ball into the crowd, and afterward called Kyrgios a "bully".

Kyrgios has largely battled injuries since and said when he was suspended that he had felt "helpless and alone", though added that "none of that excuses what I did".

Nor did it come as a shock to Tsitsipas.

"I knew that those were things that were happening away from the tennis courts. I will tell you that," he said.

"I'm not going to try and cover up someone that I know the truth for. I'll consider myself a nice person with everyone, but these were behaviours that I personally heard on the tour and heard other people in that same environment saying those sort of things to me.

"So, when I saw it, I was like, 'Well, pretty much expected, to be honest'. I am surprised it came so late, though."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Messi's legendary run for Argentina almost never happened after heartbreak
World.content:
Lionel Messi's retirement from the Argentina national side brings down the curtain on one of world football's most storied international careers.

The records and achievements of Messi are stuff of legend, and his status in international sport is reserved for only the very greatest of their craft.

Messi was denied the perfect finish to his Argentina career in July, defeated in a thrilling FIFA World Cup final by Spain that went to extra time.

But the loss in New Jersey only denied the fairytale finish, and did not diminish the legend that Messi created for himself, or the legacy that he has left among his people.

But the love and admiration of his people, the two Copa America wins, and the 2022 FIFA World Cup triumph, which brought Argentina back to the pinnacle of world football and raised Messi to the legendary status of fellow countryman Diego Maradona, almost never happened.

Legend at Barca, struggles with Argentina

Messi has been on top of world football for two decades, winning the coveted Ballon d'Or as the world's best player a staggering eight times.

From 2004 to 2021, he won 10 La Liga titles, seven Spanish Cups, seven Spanish Super Cups, four Champions Leagues, three UEFA Super Cups and three FIFA Club World Cups with Barcelona.

Football great Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina team The announcement comes just weeks after the death of his father Jorge.

In a legendary 2012, he scored 91 goals in all competitions, a record haul for a calendar year, and slotted 50 goals in the 2011-12 La Liga season.

Trophies, accolades, love and admiration grew and grew for the Barcelona great, but success for Argentina was not forthcoming.

Coming through the ranks, Messi led Argentina to a Youth World Championship in 2005 and the Olympic medal at the Beijing Games in 2008.

But in the very big tournaments, trophies were harder to come by.

When Messi made his senior debut for Argentina in 2005 against Hungary, the South American giants had not won a trophy since the 1993 Copa America.

Messi's final tears As the champion wept on the pitch after the World Cup final defeat, Argentina may well have wondered with trepidation what life will look like in the post-Messi era.

Messi's Argentina senior debut was nothing to write home about either, sent off after less than a minute on the pitch for elbowing an opponent.

But Messi overcame that infamous beginning to establish himself as a star, and the hope of a nation that Argentina could return to the top of South America, and the world.

What followed was a string of bitter disappointments.

Argentina made the final of the Copa America in 2007, but was soundly beaten 3-0 by arch rival Brazil.

At the 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa, Messi failed to score at the tournament as Argentina exited at the quarterfinal stage.

Argentina was then knocked out again at the quarterfinal stage, this time at the 2011 Copa America, by eventual winner Uruguay.

These were bitter disappointments for Argentina and Messi, but the pain was about to increase, and it led to the great man announcing he did not want to be part of it anymore.

Three years, three finals, three painful defeats

Heading into the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, it had been 21 years since Argentina's last major trophy.

But the blue and whites marched into enemy territory intending to claim international football's greatest prize, and doing it in the backyard of their greatest rival.

Loading...

Argentina won all three group games — over Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iran, and Nigeria — to top the group, beat Switzerland 1-0 in extra time, and finally won a quarterfinal by defeating Belgium 1-0.

A scoreless semifinal against the Netherlands, finalists in 2010, went to penalties, where Argentina won 4-2, including a successful spot kick from Messi.

But the joy ended there.

In a major final for the first time in seven years, Argentina faced a German side that had just humiliated Brazil 7-1 in the semifinal.

Like all of Argentina's games to that point, the game was tight and tense. It went to extra time, but the strike of German Mario Götze sealed Germany's triumph.

A photograph of Messi looking at the World Cup trophy after the defeat, captured by Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily in China, became the defining image of Messi for years.

Lionel Messi walking past the FIFA World Cup trophy after defeat in the 2014 final. (Supplied: Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily via X)

The heartbreak only continued for Messi and Argentina.

The Copa America was held in 2015 and 2016, with Argentina reaching the final both times and losing to Chile each time.

Both finals ended scoreless and went to penalties. Messi converted his penalty, the only Argentinian player to do so, in the 2015 defeat, but the great man missed his spot kick in 2016.

The pain of the 2016 final defeat was too much for Messi, who announced he was retiring from Argentina.

"For me, the national team is over," he said after the loss to Chile in 2016. "I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion."

"It's been four finals, I tried.

"It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over.

"I think this is best for everyone. First of all for me, then for everyone.

"I think there's a lot of people who want this, who obviously are not satisfied, as we are not satisfied reaching a final and not winning it."

World football was that close to never seeing Messi reach the heights he would achieve.

Six-week retirement, 10 years of legacy building

When Messi announced on Sunday, June 26, 2016, that he would no longer play for Argentina, he ended what was by any other measure a magnificent international career.

He had made 113 appearances, scored 55 goals and led his country to four major finals.

But the absence of a trophy was not good enough — not for someone as great as Messi.

On July 10, the world watched Cristiano Ronaldo lift an international major trophy as Portugal won the 2016 Euros.

On August 12, Messi announced that he was back.

What followed after his six-week retirement is, on its own, one of the greatest international careers ever forged.

Messi would add another 94 caps to his name, score another 70 goals, and more importantly, end Argentina's trophy drought.

And Messi didn't just win one major trophy for Argentina; he won four.

The 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia was another familiar quarterfinal exit for Argentina, but it was the precursor to an era of success.

Argentina finally broke through to win the Copa America in 2021, and they did it against Brazil, in Brazil.

Lionel Messi was thrown into the air in celebatrion after Argentina ended a 28-year trophy drought. (Getty Images: MB Media)

With the COVID-19 pandemic keeping many fans away from the famed Maracanã Stadium in Rio, Argentina ground out a 1-0 win to claim the nation's first major trophy in 28 years.

Messi was hoisted in the air by teammates in images that went around the world.

The drought was over, and the rain was here to stay. Argentina won a second trophy in 2022 when they defeated European champions Italy in the relaunched Finalissima, but greater prizes were to come.

By this stage, Messi had surpassed everything achieved by Maradona, except one.

Maradona almost single-handedly won the World Cup for Argentina in 1986, and gave him a legendary status that was near God-like.

Now, it was Messi's time to do the same.

He did it in Qatar at the 2022 World Cup, leading the blue and whites back to the top of world football.

The final against France, the defending world champions, was anything but ordinary. Those who were accustomed to Argentina grinding out 1-0 wins got the shock of their lives when they traded blows with France in one of the greatest finals ever played.

Messi scored two goals, including in extra time, while Ángel Di María also scored for Argentina. But the South Americans met their match in France, or more specifically, Kylian Mbappé, who scored a hat-trick, including a 118th-minute penalty to send the final to spot kicks.

In the penalty shootout, Messi converted, Mbappé converted.

Argentina was perfect. France was not.

When Gonzalo Montiel's shot hit the back of the net, Argentina was world champion and Messi had reached the God-like status that had only been reserved for Maradona.

The image of Messi kissing the World Cup became the defining image of his illustrious career.

Lionel Messi finally got his hands on the FIFA World Cup trophy, which had eluded him for so long. (Getty Images: China News Service/VCG/Cui Nan)

One more trophy would follow for Argentina, another Copa America in 2024 to make it three major trophies in four years.

That trophy was icing on the cake for Messi's legacy, which by now was in uncharted territory.

Messi's international career by numbers

1

Lionel Messi led Argentina to the FIFA World Cup title in 2022. He also led his country to two more finals, 2014 and 2026, which both resulted in 1-0 defeats in extra time.

2

Lionel Messi led Argentina to two Copa America titles in 2021 and 2024. Before then, the last time Argentina was champion in the Copa America was in 1993.

6

Lionel Messi has played in a record six FIFA World Cups — 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022 and 2026. Only Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo has also managed that feat.

21

Lionel Messi scored 21 goals at the FIFA World Cup finals. He is second on the all-time list behind French star Kylian Mbappé, who has scored 22 from just three tournaments.

34

Lionel Messi holds the record for the most FIFA World Cup finals matches played. He was on the field 34 times for Argentina in a FIFA World Cup tournament. Ronaldo is second on the list with 27 appearances for Portugal.

125

Lionel Messi holds the Argentina goal-scoring record, netting 125 times for his country. That is more than double the previous record holder, Gabriel Batistuta, who scored 54 times for his country.

207

Lionel Messi made 207 appearances for Argentina, a national record. He made his debut in 2005 against Hungary, and played his final match against Spain in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final. Ronaldo holds the world record for international appearances, playing 233 times for Portugal.

World.title: Labuschagne dropped as Australia names ODI squad for African series
World.content:
Australia has named its ODI squad for its back-to-back series in Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month, with World Cup winner Marnus Labuschagne among five players dropped.

Australia are reigning ODI world champions, after a stunning final win over India in Ahmedabad in 2023.

Labuschagne scored a half-century in that final, but his struggles since then have led to him being dropped from the ODI squad that will play in Africa, almost a year out from the next World Cup, which will be held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

Labuschagne has missed five of Australia's previous 56 ODIs, but the 32-year-old has been dropped, along with Matt Short, Ben Dwarshuis, Todd Murphy and Liam Scott, from the squad picked to play in Pakistan and Bangladesh in May and June.

Pat Cummins and Mitch Starc will play in the ODIs against South Africa, while Mitch Marsh and Travis Head return after not playing in Pakistan or Bangladesh.

Emerging stars Cooper Connolly, Oliver Peake and Joel Davies have been added to the Australian ODI squad.

Australia ODI squad: Mitchell Marsh, Pat Cummins (SA only), Xavier Bartlett, Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Joel Davies, Nathan Ellis, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Spencer Johnson, Oliver Peake, Matthew Renshaw, Billy Stanlake, Mitchell Starc (SA only), Adam Zampa

Tech.title: TP-Link’s first Wi-Fi 8 router is almost here
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Wi-Fi 8 standard is far from finalized, but TP-Link is almost ready to release its first hardware targeting the next-gen spec. It unveiled the Archer 8 Ultra tri-band router and Deco 8 Ultra mesh system at IFA 2026, which utilize the upcoming IEEE 802.11bn standard to “address the connectivity problems people actually notice” instead of focusing on speed upgrades, according to TP-Link’s announcement.

The Archer 8 Ultra features 18 internal antennas, and can deliver wireless speeds of up to 19Gbps and 10Gbps over wired connection. The Deco 8 Ultra mesh system provides up to 22Gbps over wireless and 10Gbps wired connectivity, according to TP-Link, with a three-pack covering up to 9,800 square feet and supporting more than 200 connected devices.

TP-Link hasn’t revealed any prices, but says the Archer 8 Ultra will be available for preorder in “select regions” starting on September 30th. Availability for the Deco 8 is planned for sometime in Q1 2027, with other Wi-Fi 8 products — including range extenders, adapters, and the Roam 8 travel router — to follow in Q2 2027.

The Wi-Fi 7 standard was only finalized in January 2024, so these new products are set to arrive before many people have had the chance to upgrade to the previous specification. Wi-Fi 8 also isn’t expected to receive a finalized certification until May 2028. TP-Link clearly wants to get ahead of the competition, however, and soothe any concerns regarding how its next-gen products will be impacted by the US ban on foreign-made routers — while TP-Link’s Wi-Fi 8 products use Broadcom, Qualcomm, and MediaTek chipsets, it says it’s using “US-led hardware and software engineering to deliver the most reliable Wi-Fi ever built.”

Tech.title: John Ternus is now the CEO of Apple
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For the first time since 2011, one of the world’s most valuable companies has a new leader, as today marks John Ternus’ first day as Apple’s CEO. He’s replacing Tim Cook, who will continue on as the executive chairman on Apple’s board and departed with a letter to employees that remarked, “This place is proof that culture triumphs over everything. We share a belief that what we build matters, and that we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to leave the world better than we found it.”

Ternus is taking over a company dealing with the rise of AI, shortages of RAM and other components due to that growth in AI, and a political and economic situation that is only getting more complicated as time passes. He will also do it without many of the executives who worked with Cook and Steve Jobs, like Phil Schiller, who Bloomberg reported will step down from his role leading the App Store.

Here’s a look at Apple’s senior leadership team as it stands today:

Apple’s senior leadership at the start of the Ternus era.

The first Apple hardware event of the Ternus era is just around the corner on September 9th, where we expect to see new iPhones including a foldable “Ultra.” It will give us an early glimpse of what to expect, and the new public faces of the company going forward.

Tech.title: Dyson made a camera-equipped toothbrush that flosses for you
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Dyson is once again expanding its line of personal care products with a device that focuses on your teeth instead of your hair. As the name implies, the $499 CameraJet is the first electric toothbrush to incorporate a camera into the brush head. Available starting today in ceramic blue or ceramic pink color options, it can let you inspect the inside of your mouth by livestreaming video over Wi-Fi to your phone. But the camera also works alongside an AI algorithm to detect and blast the gaps between your teeth with mouthwash. So while you’re brushing, the CameraJet simultaneously takes care of flossing.

That price isn’t cheap, but it’s also only slightly more expensive than other premium smart toothbrushes that don’t have its camera-plus-spray setup. It could be worth the splurge for those of us who are bad at regularly flossing and don’t like dealing with a disappointed dentist.

The CameraJet uses Wi-Fi to stream a live view of the inside of your mouth to a smart device so you can see what a dentist does. Image: Dyson

Just below the brush head is a tiny camera with a 100,000-pixel resolution and a strobing light. The toothbrush’s AI analyzes 28 live images from the camera every second as part of a feature Dyson calls Gap Optical Targeting, without storing them on the device or sending them to the cloud. Within 100 milliseconds of a gap between your teeth being detected, the CameraJet emits a cone-shaped blast of mouthwash to clean out the space. Dyson uses a wider blast than what water flossers typically employ so it can effectively remove plaque with less pressure, making the CameraJet’s flossing mechanism gentler on enamel and gums

A strobing LED light next to the toothbrush’s camera helps produce stabilized images used to detect gaps between teeth. Image: Dyson

The replaceable brush heads use a combination of softer outer bristles that safely clean along the gumline and stiffer inner bristles that are better at scrubbing away tooth stains. The brush head oscillates nearly 1,000 times each second while the angle of oscillation is constantly changing to improve the effectiveness of your brushing. Pricing on replacement brush heads isn’t known, but each one features an RFID tag so the CameraJet can track usage and alert you when a replacement is needed every three months.

The CameraJet is available in ceramic pink (left) and ceramic blue (right) color options and comes with a charging dock that automatically refills its mouthwash tank. Image: Dyson

To ensure its mouthwash reservoir can effectively pump no matter how the CameraJet is held — even upside down — instead of sticking a tube into the reservoir, there’s an air bladder inside the tank that slowly inflates to fill empty space, minimize air pockets, and maintain a constant pressure. An elaborate docking station recharges the toothbrush and can automatically fill its built-in 12.5ml mouthwash reservoir in just three seconds.

While the CameraJet will work with your regular toothpaste and mouthwash, Dyson also plans to sell its own non-foaming toothpaste and a low-foaming mouthwash so the toothbrush’s camera can more effectively see inside your mouth.

Tech.title: The Google TV Streamer now costs $50 more
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google raised the price of its 4K streaming box to $149, up $50 from its original $99 price. The new price is currently live at the Google Store and Best Buy, but Amazon appears to still be offering the original price.

The price hike comes just a couple of weeks after Google launched its new lineup of Pixel 11 phones with a $100 price hike over their Pixel 10 counterparts.

The Google TV Streamer originally launched in 2024 and doubles as a smart home hub. It isn’t the only streaming device getting more expensive — component shortages have been driving up prices on everything from laptops to game consoles. Earlier this month, Amazon increased the price of its Fire TV Stick 4K Max by over 40 percent to $84.99. The Apple TV 4K also similarly costs more after Apple’s sweeping price hikes in June, bringing it up to $199 for the 64GB version and $249 for the 128GB version.

Tech.title: JMGO’s very bright all-in-one projector looks ideal for gamers and sports
Tech.content:
is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

JMGO’s 4K 120Hz Iris Ultra Max all-in-one Google TV projector is now available outside China. It gets its name from a new dual-iris system that lets it produce an impressive 10,000:1 native contrast, according to JMGO. It boosts the contrast — always an issue with projectors — by placing two separate physical apertures (irises) along different points of the internal optical path to control light scatter and brightness far more aggressively than a single iris can. It also promises to produce a very bright 6,500 ISO lumen image from its triple-laser light engine.

Last year at IFA, 6,000 lumens from an all-in-one projector was breaking new ground. At IFA 2026, it’s shaping up to be table stakes, alongside 4k imagery purring along at a smooth 120Hz for fast-moving sports and gaming. Just note that I found JMGO’s N3 Ultimate to be unwatchable at peak brightness due to color distortion — so best wait for the reviews on this one.

Like that previous flagship, the new Iris Ultra Max is mounted on a motorized pan-and-tilt gimbal for useful Wiimote-like control. That, combined with an 0.88–1.7:1 optical zoom and V±130% / H±53% lens shift, gives you unparalleled image placement options that also preserve optical image quality.

A look around back. Image: JMGO

JGMO’s also tossing in VRR and ALLM to keep latency low and reduce tearing when gaming on the IRIS Ultra Max, with support for Dolby Vision HDR at 4K 120Hz. It will eventually list for $3,499, but that drops to $2,999 for preorders that begin today, ahead of an October 19th ship date.

Tech.title: FTC lawsuit alleges Amazon has been ‘secretly and systematically’ overcharging for ads
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The FTC and 22 state attorneys general are suing Amazon for allegedly using a “secret ad surcharge” to drive up prices for ads on its website and app. FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson claims in a blog post on the lawsuit that the higher advertising prices “were largely passed on to American consumers.” According to the complaint, Amazon violated the FTC Act and over a dozen state laws. This lawsuit comes almost a year after Amazon agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle an earlier FTC lawsuit over Prime subscription practices.

In Amazon’s “second price” auctions for ads on its platform, the winning bidder is supposed to only pay one cent more than the second-highest bidder. However, the FTC’s complaint alleges that Amazon has been “manipulating” the auctions since 2019:

Amazon’s advertising organization (“Amazon Ads”) decided to set and charge customers higher prices for advertising placements itself. After Amazon runs its ad auctions and determines the winning and second-place bidders, it then replaces the price determined by the auction with a higher price designed to maximize Amazon’s profits and decrease the cost efficiency of its advertisers’ campaigns. As explained internally by Amazon’s Senior Vice President in charge of Amazon Ads, in Amazon’s auctions “the second price isn’t set by an actual bidder, but rather by” Amazon in the form of a “proxy 2nd price that we calculate.”

The complaint claims this practice “has likely illegally extracted over 20 billion dollars from [Amazon’s] unwitting advertising customers.” Amazon responded in a blog post saying the FTC’s lawsuit is “misguided” and claiming that “from 2019 to 2024, the average winning bid for Sponsored Products search ads fell 50%.” It also disputed the FTC’s claim that higher advertising prices were passed on to consumers.

Tech.title: I went to the loneliest baseball game on Apple Vision Pro
Tech.content:
This weekend, I strapped on an Apple Vision Pro to watch a baseball game in immersive virtual reality for the first time. It was technically impressive, visually pretty remarkable, and also didn’t make that much sense.

Apple and Major League Baseball chose a classic match-up of the Boston Red Sox and the New York Yankees for the first of its series of four games streamed on the device. I do not review tech for The Verge, but I do watch a lot of baseball — if there’s a game on and I’m at home, it’s likely on my television. If this is the future of sports, live events, and wearable technology in general, I’d like to see what all the fuss is about.

The first thing to know about baseball is that it is long: in season, in game time, and in the arc of history. Right off the bat, this reality makes having a screen strapped to your face a hard sell. It’s not just the physical burden — like many others, I find the Vision Pro heavy and cumbersome — but also because it’s a time-honored tradition to get up and go do something else for a moment while the game is on. It’s America’s pastime for a reason: the slowness, the buildup, the culmination of a long, sticky season where teams slump and get hot. Some nights are duds and others are classics; you are playing (and watching) the long game. Even at the ballpark, you might get up to grab food or another beer, and the seventh inning stretch is built right into live play to give fans a break. With an immersive environment, I struggled with whiplash; coming in and out of the headset’s reality, going from zero to one hundred and back again anytime I wanted to grab a drink, walk around, or eat dinner.

That said, the first time I put on the Vision Pro to watch the pregame show, I screamed — it’s surreal to see the players so close, from a new, intimate angle and proximity. It was arresting, surprising, and a little scary. As Yankees starting pitcher Cam Schlittler was warming up in the bullpen, all I could think was, “He really is so tall.” A pregame interview with Jazz Chisholm Jr. made me feel like I was standing uncomfortably close to him. The broadcast on Apple Vision Pro was clearly tailored to an audience who might not be as familiar with MLB or baseball in general: There was a lot of explaining how to watch the game, and many shoutouts to the Vision Pro viewers, of course.

The feeling of being terrifyingly close didn’t last very long, though. On Vision Pro, you watch the game primarily from two angles, next to each team’s dugout when that team is batting (you’re stuck there, you don’t get to move around as you please). I liked this angle for certain batters, because you can see the vertical movement of pitches come in without anything blocking them. But for say, a righty batter whose team is watching from the third base dugout (or a lefty whose team is watching from the first base side), their body partially obstructs the view. The immersive view also doesn’t track the action in the outfield — your perspective is frozen next to the dugout. As a result, I felt both in the thick of it and at a strange remove; even ground balls and infield plays feel a bit far away, especially if you’re watching from the third base side and there’s traffic on first and second base.

The immersive broadcast includes a floating jumbotron-style screen that shows a more traditional TV broadcast, along with player stats. I often found my attention drifting up to the standard broadcast, because once the ball leaves the vicinity of the batter, it’s quite hard to track what’s actually going on. The immersive replays from new vantage points like the outfield or closer to first base helped to bridge the feeling of being at a distance. But the Vision Pro’s view isn’t very reactive to what’s happening in real time. When Red Sox second baseman Nick Sogard hit a fly ball early in the game, it almost was a home run — but the immersive view was not very compelling.
